title: Fast Iterative Design Optimization for Reliability Vibration Tests in Automotive
authors: Marco Bonato, PhD, Valeo Thermal Systems; Key Words: Design Optimization, Accelerated tests, Vibration, Fatigue Damage
summary:
The development of an engine-cooling module (ECM) for an European carmaker faced a major blocking point. The stalemate concerned the design of the suspension rubbers separating the engine-cooling radiator (the ECM carrier) from the chassis.
From the one hand, the damping rubbers had to be soft, in order to be compliant with noise, vibration & harshness (NVH) criteria - acoustic noise and vibration transmitted to the cabin.  On the other hand, their softness would provoke such high amplitude response during shaker tests that the module carrier (the radiator) would fail at the early stage of vibration testing – a leakage was observed after 10 hours of the targeted 90 hours duration.
New rubbers, designed for durability purposes, would fail to meet the NVH criteria.
The project development team went through a double-faced dilemma: how to design rubbers with an acceptable trade-off between NVH and durability of the engine-cooling radiator, and how to find a quick and efficient way to validate the design in order to be compliant with vibration validation tests.  Together with the customer, our company (automotive tier-1 supplier) established an iterative design optimization of the damping rubbers, based on the simultaneous feedback from the acoustic response and the durability predictions.  The goal was to develop a strategy permitting a quick an effective criteria for damage estimation for each design proposed.
conclusions:
A new robust methodology for the analysis and quantification of vibration fatigue damage has been applied to the design optimization of a set of suspension rubbers of an automotive engine-cooling module.
The damage quantification is based on the analysis of the output vibration measured on the module carrier (the engine-cooling radiator) during short vibration measurements performed on shaker table.
This approach here described was implemented to achieve a quick and effective optimization of the design of suspension rubbers.  This has showed to be the best time and money effective solution, when compared to standard approaches used for durability assessment (structural simulation calculations and shaker validation tests).
The procedure presented is simple and practical, and can be easily tailored to a numbers of situations involving the comparative analysis of vibration fatigue damage, and to other automotive components.

title: Challenge and Response for Corner-Case Robustness Improvement
authors: Joe Schwendler, Hypertherm Inc.; Chris Kang, Phd., Hypertherm Inc.; Dan Worts, Hypertherm Inc.; Key Words: Corner-Case, Challenge and Response Protocol, Verification
summary:
System robustness in corner-case use can be difficult to model and improve for complex industrial system applications.  We, the authors, hypothesized that an industrial metal cutting system could be methodically exposed to challenging test case input factors while closely monitoring system outputs and the normalized occurrence rate of events that may be disruptive to the end user.  This empirical study of system inputs and outputs with data reduction capabilities that enabled sifting through large datasets for disruptive occurrences enabled both better targeting of improvement and subsequent verification of design improvement effectiveness, especially as relates to more stressful corner-case use conditions for complex systems.  Exposing our XPR system to challenging use profiles outside of normal operating parameters exposed improvement opportunities and demonstrated the effectiveness of a challenge and response protocol approach for system improvement.  Three levels of organizational communication and reporting were shown effective to promote effective mitigations, monitor progress, and maintain initiative support.  The authors submit that the challenge and response test method of methodically imposing concurrent stressful inputs within a data capture infrastructure to capture detailed system response data has value for complex system corner-case behavior improvement.
We submit that challenge and response work in design organizations may be aided/facilitated by securing the following checklist of items:
1. Clear understanding of corner-case disruptive event descriptors/symptoms.  2. Study of field service calls.  3. Study of field returns.  4. Customer complaint tallies for corner-case end users. 5. Management support to disposition reliability engineering and business design team resource for multiple challenge and response experimental block efforts and mitigation efforts.  6. Subject matter expert judgement and field evidences that support a set of definable key factors to vary at 2+ levels. 7. Subject matter expert judgement and field evidences supporting factor setting levels: normal use and corner-case use.  8. Test environment capable to achieve bold test factor challenge settings.  9. Data system able to collect environmental context variables, test lab inputs and system commanding inputs, internode bus communication monitoring and diagnostic code monitoring and outputs, and relevant human touch events to the systems under test. 10. Data reduction/analysis/reporting resources capable to provide meaningful/effective information at multiple detail levels for key audiences of the challenge and response work.

title: Strategic Uses of Different Shapes and Shifts in Weibull Plots
authors: Sarath Jayatilleka, Daikin Applied Americas; Key Words: : Weibull Plots, shape parameters, design life
summary: This valve is a classic example of an under-design component. Most components going into repairable systems are not reparable components, therefore under-design components need new part replacements at the failure. The duty of a proper reliability program is to verify the parts against reliability requirements across and beyond the design life. This is accomplished only through well-planned accelerated life tests to verify demonstrated reliability against the requirement before a product is introduced to market.
conclusions:
During the product development processes, components and subsystems go through test-fix-test cycles until the final configurations surpass the design life to exceed the reliability goals. When failure modes are uncovered before reaching the design life, design configurations are improved to eliminate failures. Early failures can be mixed with several failure modes commonly lead to lower shape parameters. Systems that are mature that survive close to design life may have higher and steeper slope parameters. During the component-subsystem development process and design maturity, shape parameter changes associated with reliability growth are illustrated with examples. As designs reach or surpass design life with design maturity, failure modes can be single out to unique shape parameters. Separating different shapes and patterns of Weibull curves help identifying different failure modes thereby leading to failure mode-wise reliability analysis. Such analysis help prioritizing the fixing process of each failure mode based on returns on investment.
On the other hand, if a product was launched before it  reaches the design life and meets reliability goals, field failures become inevitable. Such field failures can also be modeled with Weibull Analysis. Parts that fail short of the design life are commonly called under-developed designs. Such designs can be mixed with multiple failure modes. Different shapes and shift of curves can be strategically isolated for separating design weaknesses and investigations before catastrophic failures erase evidence of root causes. For example, shape parameters and patterns of underdeveloped parts can be helpful in isolating manufacturing issues from design issues. This paper addresses how to perform data analysis in order to strategically enhance the further use of Weibull plots, its shapes and pattern recognition for speedier product development and customer satisfaction.

title: Overview of the New SAE J3168 Standard on Reliability Physics Analysis of EEE Equipment, Modules and Components
authors: James McLeish, DfR Solutions; Keith Hodgson, Ford Motor Company; David Locker, US Army AMRDEC; Lloyd Condra, DfR Solutions; Key Words: Reliability Physics Analysis, Computer Aided Engineering, Durability Simulation, Virtual Reliability Growth
summary:
Reliability Physics Analysis (RPA) is becoming the preferred science-based method to assess failure risk and mitigate the consequences, of failures in EEE systems and equipment.  Its acceptance becomes more widespread as faster and easier-to-use CAE software analysis tools become more readily available to users in the AADHP industries.
SAE J3168 is being developed jointly by the SAE Automotive and Aerospace division, to provide a much-needed standard RPA process for AADHP industries.  Experienced CAE modelers and Physics of Failure/Reliability Physics practitioners who want to become involved in reviewing and further developing the J3168 slash sheet subdocument can request to participate by contacting the staff representative of the SAE Aerospace or Automotive committees who are sponsoring the standard.
SAE Avionics Process Management Committee  https://www.sae.org/works/committeeHome.do?comtID=TEAAPMC
SAE Automotive EE System Reliability Standard Comm.,
https://www.sae.org/works/committeeHome.do?comtID=TEVEES15 .
conclusions:
SAE J3168 is a new, joint SAE Aerospace and SAE Automotive Standard.  It defines a common Reliability Physics Analysis Process (RPA) for Electrical, Electronic and Electromechanical (EEE) equipment, modules and components, used in high reliability and safety critical application in the Automotive, Aerospace, Defense and other High-Performance (AADHP) industries.
RPA is a modern, science-based engineering approach, derived from Physics of Failure (PoF) research based on the material science principle of stress driven damage accumulation in materials.  RPA uses Computer Aided Engineering (CAE) durability simulations and models that apply knowledge of EEE failure mechanisms and the conditions that initiate and drive them to fail, to perform design and application specific failure risk assessments and design optimizations.  CAE simulations can accurately calculate failure mechanism susceptibilities and durability of EEE equipment, due to stresses such as mechanical shock, vibration, temperature cycling, etc.
RPA enables the identification of potential failure risks, early in the design phase via a “Virtual Reliability Growth” process, so that failure risks can be designed out in order to efficiently design high reliable and robustness into electronic products.  This process that is more time and cost efficient than the traditional approach of multiple rounds of physical Design-Build-Test-Fix Reliability Growth Testing, is applicable to any type of electronic products.
The reliability and safety critically needs of emerging autonomous systems were motivator for developing J3168.  Since EEE technology evolves very rapidly and with the intense competition to develop autonomous vehicles/drones and their extreme processing speed needs, advanced EEE technologies will be used as soon they are produced.  Without years of field failure history, the classical MTTF/MTBF reliability prediction, part counting tabulations of historic, failure rates will be ineffective and inaccurate, since with every new EEE technology the failure mechanisms and reliability-durability performance change.

title: A Branch and Bound Algorithm for Single Machine Scheduling with Two Stages of Failure Process
authors: Samareh Azimpoor, Ryerson University; Sharareh Taghipour, PhD, Ryerson University; Key Words: branch and bound, production scheduling, inspection; replacement, minimal repair, optimization; Introduction; Modern production systems rely on optimal production and maintenance planning for their elements. The motivation to study the integrated problem, in addition to cost saving, is to better utilize the production systems.
conclusions:
In this paper, we investigate a model for joint optimization of job orders and inspection policy for a single machine with stochastic failures. We derive recursive formula for the expected makespan. Unlike the previous works, the model includes time varying  defect and failure arrival rates, which is more realistic. It eliminates redundant solutions which is the case for fixed rates; however, it adds to the complexity of the problem. The proposed model will help companies to implement an appropriate maintenance strategy by incorporating an optimized inspection plan. The model incorporates the possibility of performing either minimal repair or replacement at inspection time which avoids the waste of resources within companies due to necessary replacements even for minor defects and keeps a balance between inspection implementation downtime and maintenance downtime.  We assume replacement or minimal repair is conducted, if a defect is detected through an inspection before a job. However, if the system fails while it is processing a job, it is correctively replaced and the interrupted job is restarted. We develop a branch and bound algorithm to optimize the model. The objective of the proposed article is to investigate the properties of the stochastic feature of the failure process under inspection policy and to see how a branch-and bound algorithm can be applied to construct a baseline schedule which minimizes the total expected makespan. Our  computational experiments conﬁrm the B&B efficiency in terms of easy implementation, rapid computation, and considerable accuracy. We found that, the optimal solution depends on the input parameters of the model, most importantly, the downtime parameters and the distributions of the defect arrival and delay time. As future research, new lower bounds can be introduced in order to improve the B&B performance. Moreover, new exact methods can be proposed and compared to the branch and bound algorithm. It is also recommended to solve this problem in more complicated environments, such as flow shop and job shop.

title: Joint Optimizing the Production Sequence and Maintenance Plan for a Single-Machine Multi-Failure System
authors: Mani Sharifi, PhD, Ryerson University; Sharareh Taghipour PhD, Ryerson University
summary: In this paper, we consider a single-machine manufacturing system in which data about the status of its critical components are instantly available. We aim to optimize simultaneously the jobs sequence and maintenance actions to minimize the total cost of the considered production system. Since the machine parts are subject to several failures during the production, the maintenance actions are either to imperfect repair or replacement, taking into considerations that parts’ imperfect repair do not make these parts as good as new. The manufacturing system’s cost includes the machine’s parts repair or replacement cost, and the penalty if the jobs completion time exceeds a predefined threshold. We assume that the lifetime of the machine’s parts has a Weibull distribution. We study a machine cutting tool and engine among others. We consider that the failure of the cutting tool decreases the product’s (job) quality, and this product (job) needs to be restarted processing after the imperfect repair or replacement of the tool. For this part, we consider an age-based threshold; if the tool has failed before the threshold, the maintenance action is imperfect repair; otherwise, the tool is replaced by the new one. One of the model objectives is to find the optimal value of this threshold. If the engine fails during the processing of the job, the maintenance action is imperfect repair. The failures of the engine have no effect on the product quality; thus, the product process resumes after engine imperfect repair.  The tool and engine imperfect repairs affect the life distribution parameter (scale parameter of Weibull distribution, ), but tool replacement makes the tool as good as new and presents a mathematical model with the aim of minimizing the total production cost when the system is subject to these two-failure modes. Since the lifetime of the machine’s parts follows a Weibull distribution, we use a Monte Carlo simulation for calculating the jobs’ completion time and the system’s total cost. Job scheduling and maintenance planning problems are NP-hard problems, so we use a Genetic algorithm (GA) to solve the presented model.

title: When Life Is Too Long To Test: Combining Multiple Methods To Minimize Risk
authors: Russell Watts, Thermo Fisher Scientific; Key Words: apportionment, DRBTR, lifetime, test
summary:
Longer life expectations and greater amounts of usage during that lifetime pose significant challenges to traditional methods of reliability.  Simply using reliability apportionment and testing components to some system level goal like 90% reliability with 90% confidence at 10 years with near 100% usage profile is not feasible.  This paper presents a strategy that focuses on achieving high fielded reliability by using a combination of quantitative and qualitative tools in such a situation during the product design.  The focus is on anticipating likely modes of failure, then creating tests that are targeted to answer the specific question of whether the anticipated modes of failure may or may not exist based on observed evidence.
Specifically, a standard “one size fits all” approach of assuming a single stress such as temperature or simple cycles, is replaced with a more focused approach where causes of failure and their related stresses are anticipated prior to testing through good DfR practice.  The goal is to properly assess the question “Does degradation occur that supports the existence of a predicted mode of failure.”  This is in contrast to the more traditional approach of simply applying a statistical test to a high number of cycles or time and asking the question, “Does it fail during the test?”  A lack of failure during an improperly designed test does not mean something is reliable.  Alternately, a test that does not yield statistically significant results may still provide very valuable information as to the true reliability risk of a component or system.
The end output of such an approach yields a well-supported and well-understood reliability risk assessment of components and sub-systems.  Which stresses can and cannot lead to a reliability-related failure become known.  What poses a true risk and the corresponding mitigations can be more effectively determined and more cost-effectively dealt with.  This is in contrast to a simple pass / fail assessment as determined by a composite statistical score.  In many situations, obtaining such a score may not even be feasible within the time and cost constraints of a program.
It should be noted that Design for Reliability (DfR) is an essential aspect of any successful reliability program, but details are not addressed in this paper.  No development testing should be undertaken until aspects of DfR are first addressed.
conclusions:
Reliability is the customer’s experience, not just a number.  This is something that must be kept in mind at all times.  The method described herein is a shift from a purely numerical target-based assessment of reliability toward a risk-based approach, which is actually more in-line with many modern process standards.  It is through focused insight into the functionality and usage of a component that a holistic evaluation plan can be constructed.   Such an approach allows for realistic and feasible program planning, but more importantly it seeks to actually improve reliability and not just measure it.
Systems with high reliability and long life expectations can benefit most from such an approach.  Products that are very simple, have limited expectations of reliability, or very short life spans may be better suited to a more pass/fail type approach since the customer expectations or test resources required are not as high.  Savings of both development costs and warranty costs can be expected with such an approach.  Since the testing is focused and targeted with confirmed or anticipated failure modes, and since a high statistical target isn’t required, then fewer samples are needed, the content and value of the results obtained is higher, and development cycles are shorter.   It is true that more resources will be required for upfront assessment and post-test analysis.  However, the effectiveness of such a methodology drastically can drastically reduce the number of late term project delays and field failure costs.
While the method described in this paper can be very effective, it must be treated as one portion of an overall reliability process.  A component focus is important, but similar understanding of the overall system must drive an appropriate evaluation plan at that level.  The system level assessment is not directly addressed in this paper.  However, through effective evaluation of the components in a timely fashion, the higher level evaluation is allowed to focus more on those system level interaction risks thus making the system level assessment more effective.  It should be noted that the traditional component apportionment mathematical techniques ignore these system level interaction risks entirely.  A simply derived multiplicative value is assumed to be the system reliability when in fact such a number is unlikely to correlate with field experience in complex systems.
One critique sometimes heard regarding this method is that there is a lack of a numerical quantification of risk.  Standards such as “ISO 31010: Risk Management - Risk Assessment Techniques” offer many possibilities.  It is left to the each program to select techniques most applicable to a situation.
In summary, as project schedules shorten and resources to test shrink, every bit of information both quantitative and qualitative must be brought to bear to make informed decisions regarding reliability.  A thorough understanding of a system results in an effective evaluation scheme which will reveal the vast majority of reliability concerns within a time frame in which positive results can be achieved.

title: Neural Networks Based Feature Selection Approaches for Prognostics of Aircraft Engines
authors: Phattara Khumprom, North Dakota State University; Nita Yodo, PhD, North Dakota State University; David Grewell, PhD, North Dakota State University
summary: The majority of the Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) models proposed during the past few years have shown a significant increase in the amount of data-driven deployments. While more complex data-driven models are often associated with higher accuracy, there is a corresponding need to reduce model complexity. One possible way to reduce the complexity of the model is to use the feature (attribute or variable) selection and dimensionality reduction methods prior to the model training process. In this work, the effectiveness of multiple filter and wrapper feature selection methods (correlation analysis, relief forward/backward selection and etc.), along with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) as a dimensionality reduction method, was investigated. A basis algorithm of deep learning, Feedforward Artificial Neural Network (FFNN), was used as a benchmark modeling algorithm. As a case study, the prognostics of aircraft engine data from NASA Ames prognostics data repository was used to test the effectiveness of the filter and wrapper feature selection methods. The findings show that applying feature selection methods helps to improve model accuracy and significantly reduced the complexity of the models. This study hopes to be a baseline assumption for future complexity reduction solutions that can help in improving the deep learning approaches employed in the PHM domain.
conclusions:
The feature selection approaches for ANN model proposed in this paper is considered to be a preliminary study. The final models that have been included in this paper are only vanilla ANN–one hidden layer models.  The results of this paper indicate that the best algorithm for feature selection of an ANN model is the forward selection method. In the future, other deep learning algorithms must also be included in order to test the results from multiple feature selection methods. In addition to the better modeling algorithms, more feature selection methods must also be included for a complete comparison, especially brute force and evolutionary selection algorithms. The ultimate goal is to find the most suitable feature selection methods and the best set of features for training neural networks based or deep learning data-driven model for prognostics of aircraft engine data and the training framework for prognostics dataset in general.

title: Visualizing a Compass to Excellence
authors: Nikolaos Salmatanis, Chevron Energy Technology Company; Larry Bowden, Chevron Energy Technology Company; Key Words: Repairable Systems, Risk Analysis and Management, Asset Integrity Management, Reliability Analysis
summary: In the field of reliability engineering, the energy industry is challenged with analyzing localized and distributed assets associated with pipelines and distribution systems.  To advance reliability engineering capabilities, we have evaluated and implemented technology for our assets called predictive analytical reliability tool-sets (PARTs). This technology enables reliability engineering advancements, which began from predicting a fleet failure component (i.e. equipment or corrosion and time of +/- 7 days) to now predicting a specific system failure component (i.e. valves or pipes and time +/- 2 days) and predicting specific failure mechanisms on a specific component throughout a large asset base (i.e. packing/seals/O-rings on valves and external corrosion and time +/- 12 hours).  This paper discusses the philosophy and process using modular components to address varying degrees of confidence based on the quality and type of available data.  Design, environmental, operational, and maintenance data are all used to not only predict when a failure could occur, but to analyze the impact of the maintenance philosophy for the specific failure (repair versus replace) and to provide guidance on possible cost-effective preventative and mitigative actions using a barrier model (Physical/Engineered (design, guarding, protective equipment), Administrative (training, communication), Individual (operation, human factors)).

title: Soft Sensor Application to Predict Remaining Useful Life of Components of the Exhaust System of Diesel Engines
authors: Martin Diesch, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, University of Stuttgart; Kevin Lucan, University of Stuttgart; Thomas Bubolz, MTU Friedrichshafen GmbH; Bernd Bertsche, University of Stuttgart
summary: In this paper, the application of soft sensors for the estimation of the load on a component as well as the further use of the resulting load-time-signal are described.  In the first step the exhaust system of diesel enignes as well as all unput and output variables are characterized.  In the following step, the soft sensor is modelled to estimate the load on a component.  Furthermore, the derivation of load spectra from the soft sensor and the future usage for the prediction of the remaining useful life are discussed.

title: An Entropy-based Approach for Modeling Lithium-Ion Battery Capacity Fade
authors: Alireza Namdari, Western New England University; Zhaojun Steven Li, PhD, Western New England University; Key Words: Entropy, Lithium-Ion battery, Capacity fade, Predictive modeling
conclusions: Entropy can quantify the regularity of a time series and assess the predictability of a data sequence. Thus, it can be applied to battery discharge voltage data as an indicator for battery health. This paper proposes a method based on entropy for predicting battery capacities. In this study, entropy quantities are used as a quantifier for indicating the degradation of the batteries. We use Shannon, Permutation, Renyi, Tsallis, Approximate, and Sample entropy quantities of the battery voltage sequences as the input variables, and the battery capacities as the response variable. In order to model the relationship between the entropy quantities of the battery voltage sequences and the battery capacities, we use Support Vector Machines (SVMs). Our numerical results reveal that the entropy quantities are capable of detecting the degradation of the batteries mainly caused by the degradation of the cathode material. It is shown that the proposed method performs well due to its ability to predict the next-cycle battery capacities. Detecting the degradation of batteries due to the aforementioned reasons is of great importance in practice. Among the various entropy measures examined, Shannon entropy (ShanEn) has the greatest predictive power since it yields the minimum Mean Squared Errors (MSEs).

title: Reliability Analysis of Crude Unit Overhead Piping Based on Wall Thickness Degradation Process
authors: Eric Bediako, Delek US Holding.; Yisha Xiang, Ph.D, Texas Tech University.; Susan Alaswad, Ph.D, Zayed University.; Liao Ying, Texas Tech University.; Liudong Xing, Ph.D, University of Massachusetts.
summary:
Assuring the reliability of crude unit pipelines in the downstream oil and gas industry is highly essential since unexpected failures of these pipelines can result in a number of negative impacts to the business, including safety, environmental, and economic impacts. The objective of this work is to understand the degradation behavior of the piping system so we can know in advance when the degraded pipeline will reach the minimum thickness threshold.
The damage mechanisms in atmospheric crude tower overhead piping has been well researched. Hydrochloric Acid (HCL) corrosion is one major type of damage mechanisms seen in the atmospheric crude tower overhead piping. This type of corrosion is time-dependent and also influenced by different operational conditions such as temperature, adequacy of the neutralization of the formed HCL and pipeline interior protection using corrosion inhibitors. To better monitor the degradation of these pipelines and to reduce cost associated with scheduled inspections, a number of refineries are resorting to real time thickness monitoring using Ultrasonic instruments mounted at vantage locations on the pipeline, to provide continuous, non-destructive corrosion and erosion monitoring.
The focus of this paper is to use a stochastic degradation model, which is suitable for characterizing wall thickness degradation data, to estimate the failure probability of the pipeline in the midst of inadequate data. We model the degradation of the crude overhead pipeline using a stationary Gamma process. To capture the substantial heterogeneity among different thickness monitoring locations on the pipe line, random effects are incorporated in our stochastic degradation model. We illustrate the proposed random effect method using the gamma process to model pipe wall thickness degradation data observed over a period.

title: Reliability Inference for Failure Mode of Sequential Hard and Soft Failure with Application on Crack data
authors: Zan Li, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Chengjie Chinese Academy of Sciences; Qingpei Hu, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Dan Yu, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Key Words: Lifetime distribution, Degradation process, Delayed degradation, Crack initiation, Crack growth
summary: Degradation process has been successfully applied in modeling the deterioration failure modes like wearout and corrosion for reliability assessment. However, deterioration failure modes are different from each other due to different physical mechanisms with different products operated under different environments, and specific attentions should be paid for non-standard circumstances. As it is well known, the failure with fatigue crack is composed of two sequential stages: the crack initiation and the crack propagation. The lifetime distribution models have been applied for the crack initiation, and the degradation process is well modeled by degradation process. Intuitively, a lifetime delayed degradation process (LDDP) would provide a general framework for such typical mixture failure mode composed of hard and soft ones sequentially. In this study, a general reliability inference approach has been proposed for the LDDP based on the maximum likelihood method, with numerical simulations and practical application with real testing data. Furthermore, the inspection planning issue is also studied for LDDP, with the first inspection time addressed which can increase the efficiency of inspection.
conclusions:
In this paper, we introduce a LDDP model to estimate the lifetime of products with sequential failure mode.  Based on the previous works, we divide the total life model into the summation of a life distribution model for crack initiation and a degradation model for crack propagation and aim to write the joint likelihood function that contains as much information as possible in order to obtain a more accurate failure time. Exponential distribution, Weibull distribution and logarithmic normal distribution are usually taken into consideration to fit the initiation time. In this paper, we simulated these three models separately and obtain statistical inference. For the crack propagation process, we assume that it denotes Wiener process.
Using the measurable degradation data to infer the initial degradation time of the product, we can make information fully used to the analysis of the entire degradation process of the product, resulting in better inference results including parameters estimation and the estimation of MTTF and reliability. We also compare the empirical bias between different parameters settings and different models, trying to find some principle between them. Moreover, we compare the two-step strategy method with the MLE from joint likelihood function, proving we provide a better estimate method for fatigue lifetime distribution.
Considering the inefficiency of traditional inspection planning, we provide another test planning under the fixed sample number, inspection number and certain test duration, which is significantly better for LDDP model.

title: Probabilistic Risk Assessment for Acceptance Testing
authors: Kevin Singer, US Army ARDEC; Manoj Menon, US Army; Key Words: Design of Experiments, Monte Carlo, Statistical Quality Control, Risk Analysis, Risk Management
summary:
This case study discusses a situation where both the government and contractor are working towards an acceptance protocol that would increase production throughput while properly balancing risk between the two parties. There are multiple competing risk factors in this instance: the risk to the Warfighter risk of accepting underperforming weapons (consumer’s risk), the risk of turning away quality weapons (producer’s risk), and the risk associated with reduced throughput and not meeting weapon fleet requirements.
This case describes, in particular, the dispersion requirements of the weapon. The weapon should have a 90 percent chance of ten out of ten rounds in a shot-grouping landing in a four-inch circle out to 50 meters consistently throughout the weapon's lifetime. [1] The only way to determine this in a binary sense would be to shoot ten targets, and that only for a point estimate. More targets would be required for any level of statistical confidence in the results. In order to convert this to a continuous response, weapon dispersion was taken to be a bivariate normal distribution where the standard deviation describes the spread of the individual shots. Data from Production Verification Testing (PVT) was used to calculate shot group standard deviations and link them to a probability of being covered by a four inch disk via Generalized Linear Models (GLM).
Initially, the contractor utilized an in-line quality inspection approach in order to determine production quality for the dispersion performance. This 100% inspection method was particularly time consuming in that each weapon had to be removed from the production line, brought to a firing range, and a ten round shot grouping had to be fired to test the weapon’s dispersion. The use of this inefficient quality inspection method meant that throughput could not be increased to meet the fleet requirements of the Joint Services. A traditional approach would require a variables sampling plan in the form of MIL STD 414 (ANSI/ASQC Z1.9). [2] In this case study, a probabilistic approach was taken in order to model future acceptance outcomes and make sampling trade-offs. In order to accomplish this, a resampling technique that was able to develop probability distributions for acceptance based on existing historical data was utilized. Shot group data from previous 100% testing Lot Acceptance Tests (LAT) was used to generate a database of by weapon standard deviations from which to simulate various sampling procedures and make risk based decisions on implementing sampling procedures to increase throughput while still managing risk.
conclusions: There exist theoretical methods for estimating risk levels when planning for acceptance testing. In this case study these theoretical assessments were used for initial guidance. Then historical of the system was leveraged to develop an acceptance testing model. This model created a data set of potential results from proposed acceptance procedure. These results provided a probability of lot acceptance that is based strictly on historical data of the system and makes fewer assumptions about the distributions of data than traditional methods. Using simulations based on actual data, we are able to assess the risks of switching from 100 % inspection of a lot to a sampling plan.  This will allow increased throughput to meet fleet requirements.

title: Using System Availability to Drive Logistics Decisions
authors: Alastair Moubray, Raytheon Integrated Defense Systems; Jorge Hiraldo, Raytheon Integrated Defense Systems; Michael Flanagan, Raytheon Integrated Defense Systems; Thaddeus Mateja, Raytheon Integrated Defense Systems; Key Words: MTBF, Availability, MTBCF, Data Collection, Logistics
summary:
Keeping a large system fully functional for decades of 24/7 operation is a complicated logistics challenge. This task becomes substantially easier when accurate and comprehensive information on system reliability and availability is available, and kept continuously updated.
This paper documents the process used on one major defense site to address this need for system reliability information. The process has been very successful in collecting accurate information, and ten years’ worth of information is now available for some portions of the system. Program management has repeatedly used this information in identifying, quantifying, and prioritizing issues to address.
Finally, the paper addresses some issues in extending this process to other systems that are less amenable to providing such continuous and accurate reliability information without additional design effort.

title: Reliability-Equivalent Field Reference Usage and Stress Level When Both are Random for Product with Weibull Life Distribution
authors: Fengbin Sun, Ph.D., Tesla Inc.; Key Words:  Distributed usage and stress, Reference value, Reliability equivalence, Life test design, Weibull life
summary: This paper derives, based on reliability equivalence principle, the analytic expression of the equivalent single-valued usage and stress level when the underlying life distribution is Weibull with a known shape parameter (slope). Numerical example is provided to illustrate the advantage of the method for reliability life test design over the traditional practice, especially for a high-reliability product.
conclusions: This paper derives, based on reliability equivalence principle, the analytic expression of the equivalent single-valued usage and stress level when the underlying life distribution is Weibull with a known shape parameter (slope). Numerical example is provided to illustrate the advantage of the method for reliability life test design over the traditional practice, especially for a high-reliability product.

title: Estimation Of Operational And Maintenance Tasks Influence On Equipment Availability Through Petri Net Modeling
authors: Carlos Alberto Murad, University of São Paulo; Arthur Henrique de Andrade Melani, University of São Paulo; Miguel Angelo de Carvalho Michalski, University of São Paulo; Adherbal Caminada Netto, University of São Paulo; Gilberto Francisco Martha de Souza, Ph. D., University of São Paulo
summary:
The availability of a power plant is dependent not only on the equipment reliability but also on plant operational aspects and on maintenance planning. The availability prediction during an operational campaign is important information for plant managers. This prediction can be obtained by numerical modeling of the plant.
Among several modeling methods, stochastic Petri nets stand out when compared to traditional reliability tools like reliability block diagrams or fault tree analysis due to their ability to model aspects such as the dynamic behavior of the system during operation.
This paper presents a modeling proposal based on the use of Petri nets to not only predict system availability, but also to evaluate the influence of human errors during maintenance activities on the availability of power generating units and their components.
Due to the importance that hydroelectric generation still has globally, and particularly in countries with great hydraulic potential already exploited such as Brazil, hydrogenerators were considered the focus of the work. For an initial approach, though, it was decided to evaluate the influence of errors related to maintenance activities on auxiliary equipment such as pumps, motors, fans, and compressors. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model, hypothetical Weibull and exponential distributions were considered for stochastic transitions associated with time to failure and time to repair, respectively, and the results are very promising.
It is noted that, in fact, the availability of the evaluated equipment is sensitive to maintenance errors and, therefore, efforts should be made to improve maintenance actions in order to prevent errors from occurring. In future work, the intent is to explore the applicability of the proposed method to evaluate the impact that not only errors in maintenance, but also errors in operation have on system availability.

title: Reliability: Enablers for Sustainment through Supportability Focused Design Influence
authors: Kenneth A. Crooks, Northrop Grumman Corporation; Mark H. Nanney, Northrop Grumman Corporation; Key Words:  Design Influence, Integrated Logistics, Reliability, Maintainability, Supportability, Virtual Reality
summary: Supportability requirements and processes traditionally suffer from functional stovepipes that can inadvertently result in a negative impact to system readiness, availability, and life cycle cost. The challenge as program acquisition schedules become more aggressive, new technologies and processes are required to maintain the ability to complete trade studies to ensure a producible and supportable design. Reliability can provide a medium between design and sustainment with emphasis on supportability impacts by design decisions through analyses and metrics performed by the discipline. This case study highlights the multi-disciplinary collaboration approach by our Reliability team to identify and correct challenging or erroneous designs decisions early in the design process. The approach is demonstrated by focusing operational effectiveness through enhancement to methods in regards to people, processes and tools during EMD. The improvements resulted in the team’s ability to reduce turnaround time on trade studies, increase awareness on risk reduction opportunities and cost avoidance on potential design changes and their impacts on the overall sustainment phase.

title: An Empirical Study of Comparison of Code Metric Aggregation Methods and Software Reliability Evaluation
authors: Zekun Song, Beihang University; Yichen Wang, Ph. D., Beihang University; Pengyang Zong, Ph. D., Beihang University; Lin Wang, Ph. D., The Fourth Complex System Laboratory; Guiya Feng, The Fourth Complex System Laboratory
summary:
How to evaluate software reliability based on historical data of embedded software projects is one of the problems we have to face in practical engineering. Therefore, we establish a software reliability evaluation model based on code metrics. The model uses code metrics to score software reliability. This evaluation technique requires the aggregation of software code metrics into project metrics. What are the differences among different aggregation methods in the software reliability evaluation process, and which methods can improve the accuracy of the reliability evaluation model we have established are our concerns. In view of the above problems, we conduct an empirical study on the application of software code metric aggregation methods based on actual projects.
Firstly, we construct a software reliability evaluation model based on code metrics for a total of 82 embedded software projects of a software organization. Secondly, we collect 42 code-level metrics of these projects, and separately studied the distribution of these metrics, then find the statistical distribution of some metrics by means of data fitting. Thirdly, we adopt a combination of statistical value method, metric distribution method and econometric method to aggregate code-level metrics into project-level metrics.  Then the accuracies of the evaluation model under different data aggregation methods are compared, and a combined data aggregation scheme is proposed to improve the accuracy of the model effectively.  Additionally, based on the results of the metric aggregation solutions, we extend the research on the modeling method of software reliability evaluation model. The effects of two data dimensionality reduction algorithms----correlation analysis and principal component analysis, and three sorting algorithms---- logistic regression, K-nearest neighbor algorithm and BP neural network on the performance of software reliability evaluation model are compared.
Our paper introduces a method for constructing a software reliability evaluation framework based on historical data. Since we have encountered problems with metric data aggregation, a search on software metric distribution and aggregation has been carried out. It turns out that our reliability evaluation model has an accuracy of more than 50% and an appropriate data aggregation solution can improve the accuracy of our model.
conclusions:

Our research proves that code metrics can be used to evaluate or predict software reliability. title: CLAIM:  An Enhanced Machine Learning Technique for Discrepancy Report Analysis
authors: Myron Hecht, The Aerospace Corporation; Jaron Chen, The Aerospace Corporation; Phanitta Chomsinsap, The Aerospace Corporation; Key Words: Discrepancy Reports, Machine Learning, Classification, Failure Modes
summary: CLAIM is a tool for analyzing and classifying discrepancy reports that allows for the incorporation of domain expert knowledge into a semi-supervised machine learning (ML) process (a semi-supervised learning uses a small number of manually labeled data and a much larger amount of unlabeled for training a machine learning algorithm).  By using this domain knowledge, classification accuracy is higher than conventional ML approaches.  The advantages are particularly apparent with small, imbalanced data sets that are quite common in discrepancy report data sets (an imbalanced data set has an unequal distribution of documents categories within each category).    The CLAIM method is robust against human bias and can tolerate misclassifications of up to 20% of the training set.  The increased accuracy of the CLAIM methodology makes ML a viable tool for safety, reliability, and software development process decision making.  The modest human labor requirement enables use of the method under circumstances that previously made free text discrepancy report analysis infeasible due to resource, scheduling, and cost constraints.

title: Effects Assessment for Requirements Faults of Safety Critical Software in Nuclear Industry
authors: Boyuan Li, The Ohio State University; Carol Smidts, Ph. D., The Ohio State University; Key Words: software safety, hazard rate distribution, remaining faults
summary: In a context where software has been pervasive in safety critical applications, trust in software safety is challenged by software complexity and lack of systematic methods to assess the effects of remaining faults. To expand the use of digital technology in the nuclear industry, systematic methods are required to assess the effects of remaining faults for software-based Instrumentation & Control (I&C) systems in safety critical applications. In this paper, the effects of the remaining requirements faults are assessed using a probability density function (PDF) of their hazard rates. A hazard-based effect analysis (HEA) method is developed to obtain the probability distribution of the hazard rates of a remaining requirements fault. The HEA method is applied to a Reactor Protection System (RPS) in the case study. The probability density functions for the introduced faults, detected faults and remaining faults in the requirements phase of the RPS system on the domain of hazard degree are obtained.
conclusions: In this paper, a hazard-based effect analysis method is proposed to assess the distribution of the hazard degree of a remaining requirements fault. The PDF of hazard degree are obtained for the faults introduced, detected and remaining on the domain of hazard degree. The HEA method is applied on an RPS system in the nuclear power plant. The distribution of the hazard degree of the faults remaining in the RPS are obtained.

title: Real-Time Management of RAM Data Using OT and IT Infrastructure in Oil & Gas Operations
authors: M Rashdan Mahmood, PETRONAS; Brandon T. S. Tan, PETRONAS; Key Words:  reliability management, operation technology, digitalization, analytics, brownfield
summary:
Managing safety-critical systems in real-time, across geographically diverse multiple oil & gas installations, both offshore and onshore, is in itself a huge challenge for any corporation. PETRONAS, through its Exploration, Development & Production subsidiary PETRONAS Carigali Sdn Bhd, has successfully deployed a digital solution to remotely manage multiple safety-critical systems under different operational technology (OT) sites from a centralized location in real-time over its existing corporate information technology (IT) infrastructure. Thus, creating the first approach to reliability domain-based information data lake to assist real time operation of safety-critical systems and improve production efficiencies.
In this paper, readers be given an insight into the journey of PRiME-IO, the digital solution currently overlooking real-time operation of multiple OT safety-critical systems such as DCS and safety PLCs across hundreds of offshore and onshore sites. Challenges in OT/IT convergence, including but not limited to cybersecurity and data transmission reliability, and the solutions adopted to overcome these, will be discussed at length.
Apart from the hardware and infrastructure aside, key human factor considerations such as competency upskilling of engineers and technicians, enabling fast feedbacks on decisions, as well as changes in work processes and improved productivity, will also be highlighted.
Tangible operational benefits such as lower risk & exposure to frontline operations, faster response time and lower day-to-day logistic costs will also be demonstrated

title: From Manufacturing Process Control to In-Field Reliability: Case Study of Automotive Heat Exchangers
authors: Marco Bonato, PhD, Valeo Thermal Systems; Key Words: Accelerated tests; Automotive; Durability; Heat exchangers; Stress-Strength interference, Manufacturing.
summary:
One of the strategies aimed at improving the reliability of new or existing components is the reduction of the variability of the product strength.  From a manufacturing point of view, a well-controlled process diminishes the variability of the product resistance facing in-service stress, therefore reducing the area of the stress-strength interference region (probability of failure).
This paper proposes a new methodology that relates the accuracy of the manufacturing process to the durability of the component in the field.  The manufacturing-induced variability is obtained from life data analysis of destructive accelerated validation tests, and quantified by the coefficient of variation (CV) of the component strength.  Indeed, a lower variability of the component endurance on the bench (e.g. number of cycles to failure) indicates a higher level of process control.
A case study of a brazed aluminum alloy heat exchanger (a car engine cooling radiator) undergoing thermo-mechanical fatigue loadings will be presented.  The comparison of the CV calculated for a range of radiator technologies and from different production units permits to estimate the variation and control level of the manufacturing process.  The example shows that the CV is a robust indicator that should be used to assess the variation of the manufacturing procedure, and to better predict the in-service durability of the heat exchangers. Further practical applications of the indicator CV will also be described.

title: Real-Time Optimization of Maintenance and Production Scheduling for an Industry 4.0-Based Manufacturing System
authors: Mageed Ghaleb, Ryerson University; Sharareh Taghipour, PhD, Ryerson University; Hossein Zolfagharinia, PhD, Ryerson University; Key Words: industry 4.0, real-time optimization, production scheduling, preventive maintenance, random breakdowns
summary:
The adaption of state-of-the-art inventions in information technology and industrial informatics in manufacturing has led to the advent of Industry 4.0, commonly known as the fourth industrial revolution. Industry 4.0 will take manufacturing productivity and quality to new levels and create enormous opportunities for business and revenue growth. Unlike classical manufacturing systems, Industry 4.0-based manufacturing systems are supported by several advanced technologies (known as Industry 4.0 concepts), which include cyber-physical systems (CPS) and internet of things (IoT), among other Industry 4.0 concepts. The adoption of such technology (i.e., Industry 4.0) allows for the delivery of real-time actionable data for smart decision-making. In order to fully realize the potential of such technologies, real-time decision making should be present in all aspects of the manufacturing process. This includes two core components of manufacturing: maintenance and production scheduling.
In this paper, we consider the production line of a manufacturing company that has installed smart monitoring technology (Industry 4.0-related technology) in order to have real-time connectivity and control over their shop-floor activities. The production line under consideration has three stages, the first and second stages both use identical hydraulic press machines, while the third stage is a manual assembly process. The company follows a time-based preventive maintenance policy. Maintenance activities take time and during this time the machines undergoing maintenance are out of production. This time could ideally be utilized for additional production but delaying maintenance activities to increase production could result in more machine failures. Therefore, we believe that scheduling maintenance activities and scheduling production should be integrated instead of considered independently. In addition, with the smart-monitoring system, real-time information about the current state of the machines and the work in progress (WIP) is available, which allows for more convenient maintenance and production planning.
The company has a problem with utilizing the information that is available through the smart-monitoring system to generate and update their production schedules on the fly. Therefore, we are proposing a three-stage optimization model in order to solve this problem. In the first stage, we find the optimal preventive maintenance (PM) age for each machine based on historical data. Then, in the second stage, we integrate the optimal PM policy into an offline scheduling model to generate the initial production schedule. Finally, in the third stage, the real-time information is incorporated into an online scheduling model to generate new production schedules according to the current state of the production line.
conclusions:
In this paper, we developed a three-stage real-time integrated optimization model. In the first stage, the model begins by finding the optimal preventive maintenance (PM) age for each machine in the production line. In the second stage, which is an off-line optimization model, the model uses the optimal PM policy and generates the initial integrated production schedule. Finally, in the third stage, the model reacts to machine failures by incorporating real-time information that is available through the smart-monitoring system. This stage is the on-line optimization stage in which real-time integrated production schedules are generated on the fly.
A case study is provided in which a numerical example is solved to demonstrate the proposed real-time optimization model. In addition, we compare the results obtained from using the real-time optimization model with the results of the current procedure (which is the schedule repair by right-shifting). The results show that the schedules generated with the proposed model were much better than the schedules generated by simply repairing the current schedules by right-shifting.

title: Dual-Ring Network Reliability Analytical Solution with Application to Large Video Systems
authors: Les Warrington, Les Warrington Consulting
summary:
Reliability of complex network systems is frequently assessed using Monte Carlo simulation because an analytical solution is not available or is overly complex.[1]
A variant of dual-ring redundancy has been implemented to support high reliability requirements of large video display systems such as advertising billboards, stadium displays and traffic management systems.  This network scheme, with data feed segments being daisy-chained to network nodes in 2 directions (forward and reverse), can offer significant reliability benefits beyond simple parallel redundancy without increase in complexity.
This paper describes an analytical solution for reliability calculation that is simple and can easily be applied to dual-ring networks with any number of nodes.  This solution avoids problems common to expansion of terms when using the addition law of probability. [3]
This paper further explores the common failure independence assumption and notes that the dual-ring network reduces to an N+1 network in cases of dependent failures such as common-cause and common-mode.  Analytical solution is also provided for system reliability with both independent and dependent failures present.
Dual-ring networks for application in large video systems are found to be superior to other redundancy types with equivalent segment reliabilities.  Such networks are no more complex than active parallel or N+1 networks.
With these analytical solutions, reliability design trade-off studies can be undertaken using simple spreadsheet rather than the more complex Monte Carlo simulation.
conclusions:
Examination of large video display system architectures suggested that Monte Carlo simulation methods would be necessary to estimate field reliability and to facilitate trade-off studies of these complex networks.  However, this paper has developed an analytical solution that allows simple spreadsheet comparison between alternate architectures and component reliability choices. (11)
This paper has also noted a similarity between N+1 and dual-ring system reliability calculations.  Test lab and field analysis of video systems with these architectures, also confirms that physical implementation using multi-core cables introduces competing failure modes applicable to both system architectures.  For example, failure of individual cores is applicable to the dual-ring architecture, whereas a connector failure disrupting bi-directional data-feeds simultaneously, would be applicable to the N+1 system architecture.
Using total probability decomposition, overall system reliability can be calculated notwithstanding a duality of architecture within a single system. (14)
A spreadsheet using (1), (2), (4) and (11) was used for Table 3.  In addition to illustrating the use of the derived analytical solution for dual-ring system reliability, Table 3 also highlights that under equality of segment reliabilities, the dual-ring network offers the highest system resiliency / reliability.
Thus, the analytical solution for dual-ring system reliability provided by this paper is a benefit to large video system design trade-off studies.

title: A Multivariate Correlation Degradation Model for Reliability Analysis Based on Copula
authors: Wen Chen, Beihang University; Guangyan Zhao, Beihang University; Key Words: mixed copula, multivariate correlation degradation, cosine similarity, reliability analysis
summary: Degradation process modeling is an important part of reliability analysis. At present, most researches about it focus on univariate degradation models. The independence assumption is adopted to analyze multivariate degradation indicators. In order to describe the correlation between two or more degradation indicators more accurately, a multivariate correlation degradation model based on copula was proposed to analyze system reliability in this paper. First, the univariate degradation model was established for different degradation process. Then, the cosine similarity measure was used to calculate the overall and local correlations for every two degradation indicators. Combining the cosine similarity values with each copula characteristics, the appropriate copula function was selected to compose Mixed Copula (M-Copula), which could describe the correlation between two degradation indicators well. Based on that, the optimization model with the residual minimization as the objective was constructed and solved to obtain the degradation correlation reliability model. Copula functions with different characteristics are screened by cosine similarity in this method, which could improve the accuracy and efficiency of reliability modeling and life prediction. It could also save cost. Finally, a case was calculated to verify the feasibility and effectiveness.
conclusions: This paper introduced a multivariate correlation degradation model for reliability analysis in practical engineering. Cosine similarity was used to measure the overall and local correlations of degradation indicators. Copula was adopted to describe the correlation of degradation indicators and it could avoid the degradation principle in mechanism. The values of cosine similarity determine the Mixed Copula. The method mentioned in this paper filters the unsuitable Copula and reduces the number of Copulas in practical applications. Solving the optimization model with the residual minimization as the objective obtain the degradation correlation reliability model.

title: A Fractal-Cluster-Based Analytical Model for Spatial Pattern of Congestion
authors: Xiang-Yu Zheng, Beihang University; Ning Huang, PhD, Beihang University; Ya-Nan Bai, PhD, Beihang University; Shuo Zhang, China Ship Development and Design Center; Key Words: spatial pattern, fractal-cluster, fractal dimension, congestion
summary:
Research has shown that spatial patterns of congestion is neither compact as expected by typical model of cascade dynamics nor purely random as in percolation theory. Analyzing spatial patterns of congestion is critical for mining spatial-temporal characteristics of congestion evolution. Spatial patterns of congestion are the result of congestion interaction, which appears as the dependency relationship of the adjacent edges and the dependency relationship of the non-adjacent edges with a certain range in the network. Previous models which analyze spatial patterns of congestion mainly considers the dependency relationship of the directly connected edges, but lack the consideration of the dependency relationship of the indirectly connected edges. Therefore, this paper presents a fractal-cluster-based analytical model considering the dependency relationship of the indirectly connected edges to describe the dominant mechanism governing the formation and evolution of spatial pattern of congestion. First, we introduce the edge dependency coefficient to quantitatively describe the dependency strength of the adjacent edges. Next, we regard the basic fractal element of the network as a cluster and introduce the cluster dependency coefficient to quantitatively describe the dependency relationship of the non-adjacent edges with a certain range in the network. Finally, we construct a weighted network in which the weight of edges represents the congestion level of edges and introduce a novel load transfer mechanism to describe the results of congestion interaction. Based on this, a fractal-cluster-based congestion evolution model is established to analyze spatial patterns of congestion. To quantify spatial pattern, we use the fractal dimension of the weighted network  (a measurement of objects’ irregularity). The simulation comparison results have verified the feasibility of this indicator. Furthermore, simulation results have shown that our proposed model is more in line with the observed congestion propagation process, which verifies the effectiveness of our proposed model. This work can give precious hints on which step of the process is responsible for the congestion duo to the its mechanistic analysis of spatial patterns.

the resilience coefficient

the initial load coefficient
the usual traffic coefficient

conclusions: This paper establishes an analytical model for the dominant mechanism of spatial pattern of congestion which consider the dependency relationship of non-adjacent edges with a certain range. Based on the fractal characteristics of traffic networks, the step-structure fractal element is the largest range of the collective effect on congestion of the dependency relationship of non-adjacent edges. By construct a fractal network model, a congestion evolution model based on the load transfer mechanism which considering the effect of two forms of congestion interaction, namely the dependency relationship of adjacent edges and the dependency relationship of non-adjacent edges with a certain range. A novel indicator, that is, the fractal dimension of the weighted network is introduced to quantify spatial pattern of congestion. Simulation results verify the feasibility of the indicator and the effectiveness of our proposed model. This paper presents a model for analyze the dominant mechanism of spatial pattern of congestion and describes the interaction of non-adjacent edges through the structural characteristics of traffic networks. Moreover, a parameter that can be parsed through network structure and traffic flow is introduced to quantify spatial pattern of congestion. Future work will focus on the effect of the edge dependency coefficient and the cluster dependency coefficient on spatial patterns. This work provides a new perspective to understand congestion evolution mechanism. Duo to the mechanistic analysis of spatial patterns, we can give precious hints on which step of the process is responsible for the congestion and furthermore guide congestion control.

title: Simulation of Anode Corrosion In The Electrowinning Process Of Non-Ferrous Metals
authors: Christoph Rosebrock, University of Wuppertal; Stefan Bracke, University of Wuppertal; Key Words: Empirical corrosion study, lifetime estimation, reliability modelling, testing.
summary:
In the electrowinning process of non-ferrous metals, electroplating with insoluble anodes is used.  The electrolysis process causes electrochemical wear of the anodes such that they have to be replaced after a certain time.  Due to very diverse conditions at different electrolysis plants, the lifetime of those anodes varies from 1 to 7 years.  The superordinate target of the research work is to analyze the reliability of the anodes.  The lifetime of the anodes can be determined experimentally by analyzing their corrosion rate under certain process conditions.  The experimental effort can be reduced by developing a model to simulate the corrosion of the anodes considering different process conditions.
In this study, a model for the simulation of the corrosion of lead anodes, which are used in the electrowinning process of non-ferrous metals, is presented.  The model is based on Faraday’s law of electrolysis which is extended by an enhancement factor.  This enhancement factor has to be determined empirically.  In a first step, an experimental study on a model scale was carried out while several simplifications were made for the size of the electrolysis bath, the alloy of the anodes and the neglection of a volume flow.  The evaluation of 63 single experiments provided a functional relationship between the enhancement factor and the temperature of the electrolyte.  Up to now, an empirical corrosion rate as a function of the temperature was determined under simplified conditions as mentioned before.  The obtained corrosion model was implemented in the open source CFD code OpenFOAM® to simulate the corrosion in arbitrary bath geometries under various process conditions.  The simulation model was validated within a grid study as well as by comparing simulation results with experimental results.  The simulation results were in good accordance to the experimental results such that the simulation model can be used as a basis for further analysis.
conclusions: In this study, a simulation model for the corrosion of lead anodes in the electrowinning process of non-ferrous metals is presented.  The model is based on Faraday’s law of electrolysis which is extended by an enhancement factor.  In a first step, an experimental study on a model scale was carried out to determine this enhancement factor empirically as a function of the temperature of the electrolyte.  63 single experiments were evaluated to describe the relation using the Arrhenius model.  The obtained corrosion model was implemented in the open source CFD code OpenFOAM®.  The simulation model was validated within a grid study as well as by comparing simulation results with experimental results.  The simulation results were in good accordance to the experimental results such that the simulation model can be used as a basis for further analysis.  The simulation model can be extended easily when influences of further process parameters will be determined under more realistic conditions using the test rig on a larger scale.

title: Software Assurance of Autonomous Spacecraft Control
authors: Ben Smith, PhD, Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Martin S. Feather, PhD, Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Terry Huntsberger, PhD, Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Robert Bocchino, PhD, Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Key Words: assurance cases, autonomous control, software hazard analysis
summary:
The work described addresses assurance of a planning and execution software system being added to an in-orbit CubeSat to demonstrate autonomous control of that spacecraft.  Our focus was on how to develop assurance of the correct operation of the added software in its operational context, our approach to which was to use an assurance case to guide and organize the information involved.  The relatively manageable magnitude of the CubeSat and its autonomy demonstration experiment made it plausible to try out our assurance approach in a relatively short timeframe.  Additionally, the time was ripe to inject useful assurance results into the ongoing development and testing of the autonomy demonstration.  In conducting this, we sought to answer several questions about our assurance approach.  The questions, and the conclusions we reached, are as follows:
Question: Would our approach to assurance apply to the introduction of a planning and execution software into an existing system?  Conclusion: Yes.  The use of an assurance case helped focus our attention on the more challenging aspects, notably the interactions between the added software and the existing software system into which it was being introduced.  This guided us to choose a hazard analysis method specifically for software interactions.  In addition, we were able to automate generation of assurance case elements from the hazard analysis’ tabular representation.
Question: Would our methods prove understandable to the software engineers tasked with integrating the software into the CubeSat’s existing system?  Conclusion: Somewhat.  In interim discussions with the software engineers we found the assurance case style, of decomposing an argument into smaller pieces, to be useful and understandable to organize discussion.  Ultimately however we did not persuade them to adopt assurance cases as the means to present review information.  We attribute this to reluctance to deviate from JPL’s tried and true style of holding reviews.  For the CubeSat project as a whole, hosting an autonomy demonstration was already a novelty.  Combining this with presentation of review information via an assurance case, with which our reviewers would be unaccustomed, would have exacerbated the unfamiliarity.
Question: Would conducting our methods prove to be compatible with the (limited) time available of the software engineers?  Conclusion: Yes.  We used a series of six brief meetings (approximately one hour each) with the development team to first identify the interactions as the area on which to focus, and to then perform the hazard analysis on those interactions.  We used the meetings to confirm, or correct as necessary, our understanding of the software system and the spacecraft context.  Between meetings we studied the existing software documentation, did preliminary analyses by ourselves, and documented the results in a concise form suitable for discussion with the team.
Question: Would our methods yield useful results to the software engineers?  Conclusion: Yes.  The hazard analysis systematically confirmed existing hazards’ mitigations, and drew attention to a mitigation whose implementation needed particular care.  In some cases, the analysis identified potential hazards – and what to do about them – should some of the more sophisticated capabilities of the planning and execution software be used.  These capabilities, not exercised in the initial experiments on the CubeSat, may be used in future experiments.  We remain involved with the developers as they prepare for these future experiments, so our analysis results will be of benefit as these proceed.

title: A Systems Approach to Rapid Logistics
authors: Rodney Benson, Acquisition Logistics Engineering; Stephen Brunner, Acquisition Logistics Engineering; Darryl Kellner, Acquisition Logistics Engineering; Steve Rogers, Acquisition Logistics Engineering; Key Words: Design Optimization using R&M Techniques, R&M Applications in Supportability
summary:
In today's rapidly changing world, great challenges exist in outfitting the warfighter with the most advanced and effective equipment necessary to complete the mission.  One method developed to facilitate introduction of cutting edge technology to the battlefield was the Rapid Fielding Initiative (RFI) which speeds up the normal design and fielding processes to outfit the warfighter during pre-deployment or in the field of operations.
The RFI process encounters challenges ranging from outfitting the warfighter with clothing to deploying a new weapon system into the field.  In the latter, logistic support issues exist that are imperative to identify and plan for prior to the fielding of the equipment in order to ensure a cost effective logistic support structure solution.  There are three alternatives for defining logistic support: no logistic analysis, traditional logistic analysis, and Rapid Logistics.
The biggest obstacles to traditional logistic analysis are cost and timeliness of the results.  Performing no logistic analysis leaves the probability of successfully supporting RFI programs completely to chance resulting in a potentially costly and unsupportable system.  Analyzing the logistic support structure is a necessary part of fielding all new systems. The analyst must consider the real world obstacles to supporting the equipment and recommend an implementation strategy for the support system. If the logistic support system is not properly analyzed, equipment is fielded with insufficient or no analysis in the area of logistics, life cycle cost (LCC), and/or supportability, resulting in inefficient or excessive consumption of resources, often resulting in equipment being deemed unsupportable.  Unsupportable equipment neither satisfies the objectives of the RFI, nor does it fulfill the needs of the warfighter.
To preclude an unnecessarily costly support structure or unsupportable equipment, a method is required to identify and assess support system drivers and provide near real-time insights that can be employed to optimize the support system.  Rapid Logistics represents an analysis environment that can be expanded or contracted to compliment a spectrum of RFI programs.  This paper provides an overview of the process and a discussion of its implementation, including the challenges faced and benefits realized.
conclusions:
Rapid Logistics is a low cost, streamlined version of supportability analysis to be performed on a spectrum of systems requiring a fast turnaround solution to their initial support structure.  Rapid Logistics has the ability to use limited program resources for evaluating support alternatives for initial implementation and monitor that implementation for a fast response when change is needed in the field.  These ideals are tailored to support the crucial demand for a support structure on rapid fielded programs where the traditional alternative is not possible.
