title: Metalized Film Capacitors: The Need for a Reliability Test Standard
authors: Garron K. Morris, Rockwell Automation; Behnam Gohari, Rockwell Automation; Key Words: metalized film capacitors, capacitors, humidity, reliability testing
summary:
Printed Circuit Boards Assemblies (PCBAs) play a critical role in the operation of Variable Frequency Drives (VFD).  Failure of any circuit boards can cause a failure of the drive leading to unplanned downtime and substantial revenue loss for customers.  Demands for increasing power in smaller VFD packages, coupled with the desire to run VFDs with minimal environmental conditioning has presented significant reliability challenges through increasing exposure to applications with high temperatures and relative humidity.
Metalized film capacitors are among the most widely-used types of capacitors in electronic and electrical devices. These capacitors are extensively utilized to reduce electromagnetic interference (EMI) in power engineering due to the self-healing ability, high voltage capability, and open-circuit failure modes. Metalized film capacitors are used in a wide range of applications including EMI/RFI filtering, DC link and power semiconductor snubber applications, and switching power supplies, which are all found in VFDs.
In this paper, a temperature humidity biased test (THB) was performed on three types of commercially available metallized film capacitors. The inconsistency in the failure rate of the capacitors, even for the capacitors from same manufacturer, emphasizes the need for an industrial standard to evaluate the reliability of these capacitors. Then, detailed discussion covers currently available standards and verification methods such as IEC 60384-14, IEC 60068-13, and MIL-HDBK-198A that are incapable of simulating and accelerating all the relevant failure mechanisms of these capacitors, because they do not apply temperature, humidity, and voltage stresses simultaneously, as the film capacitors experience in the actual industrial application. Finally, an internal test procedure is developed to evaluate the reliability of the metalized thin film capacitors.
conclusions:
Metallized film capacitors have been extensively used in EMI suppression applications due to their self-healing characteristic. The applications of metallized film capacitors has expanded and they are often placed in environments where temperature and humidity are uncontrolled. Humidity is one of the environmental factors that has a great influence on the life time and performance of the metallized film capacitors and use of such caps in humid environment should be investigated.
This paper emphasizes the degradation of metallized thin film capacitors in humid environments and discusses the failure mechanisms associated with these caps that can lead to product failures in the field. Moreover, the available industry standards are also reviewed and it was showed that there is no standard to evaluate the life time of the film capacitors with concurrently applying humidity, temperature, and electrical stresses. Such a standard is required in industry to ensure the safety and reliability of the products. It is the authors’ belief that professional societies and individuals on standards committees should work to issue such standards.

title: U.S. Army Software System Safety Process, Case-Study, and Success Stories
authors: David G. Fernald, Jr., U.S. Army Evaluation Center; Key Words:  software safety, safety process, U.S. Army system
summary:
Software is an important part of the capability drivers for many modern United States Army systems.  The importance of improved software system safety processes are highlighted in the last revision to Military Standard (MIL-STD)-882.  MIL-STD-882E added software system safety techniques and practices.  However, many Army systems pre-date the current revision.  This paper provides an overview of how the Army Air Defense community is applying the software system safety guidance and techniques to an Air and Missile Defense system.  The Patriot Air and Missile Defense (AMD) system is used for the case study.  The case study illustrates the process and demonstrate safety analysis effectiveness.  As part of the case study there is a discussion of the various Army safety organizations and the synergies between them.
The case study involves part of the Patriot AMD system, discussed in section 1, limited to the software fielded in 2018, Post-Deployment Build-8 (PDB-8) and development of the next software iteration, PDB-8.1.  The improved Software Safety process resulted in minimizing risks to Soldiers during an Urgent Materiel Release (UMR) (providing a capability early to the field to meet an operational need) of PDB-8 and identified firmware as the next target for improvement.  Additionally, as part of development of PDB-8.1 a software and hardware component was changed resulting in a significant reduction in Safety Critical Requirements (SCR) as shown by a reduction in Software Hardware Risk Indexes (SHRI) 1 through 4.

title: An Automotive EHPS Software Reliability and Testing
authors: Yanshuo Wang, Dare Auto, Inc.; Jim (Jinming) Yang, Ph.D, Dare Auto, Inc.; Mbiye N. M., Dare Auto, Inc.; Key Words:   Software Reliability, Design for Reliability, Testing, DFMEA
summary:
The electronic control plays an important role in the modern automotive world. As more software is embedded in the vehicle electronics, software quality and reliability becomes essential to the vehicle reliability. This paper summarizes the embedded software reliability and testing performed at Dare Auto, Inc. for an automotive EHPS (Electro-Hydraulic Power Steering) pump. The ASPICE (Automotive Software Process Improvement and Capability Determination) process has been used during the design and development. The component, sub-system and vehicle level testing have been conducted before releasing for production. The lessons learned and the issues have been identified.
Traditional E/E (electrical/electronic) environmental and durability testing on the bench cannot fully simulate the vehicle conditions for the control software because the testing was designed only for hardware validation. New validation specifications and test strategies are needed to include the embedded software components:  the vehicle level software control strategy, CAN (Controller Area Network) communication, and DCR (Design Change Request) to the software.  All must be validated thoroughly before going to production to avoid unexpected failures after mass production begins.
conclusions:
Automotive OEMs requires the supplier to validate the component before production. The DV and PV validations must be completed successfully without any failure, then the PPAP can be granted. Usually, the E/E environmental and durability test specifications, and the component’s function, performance and durability specifications are applied for the DV and PV.
However, the traditional E/E specifications and component specifications do not cover the embedded software explicitly. Also the system and vehicle level control and CAN communication, DTC need be tested in order to pass the PPAP. Traditionally, the software reliability was not validated potentially causing zero-mileage and warranty issues. That is the reason there are many re-flashing or recall of mass production parts in the automotive industry.  Our methods include the software in the reliability plan from the beginning.
DFMEA is a very useful tool for analyzing the potential embedded software failure modes before the software coding. It guides the software review and tests during development and it is a powerful tool for DFR.
We have extended the DFMEA to incorporate the lowest software modules and added diagnostics.  The analysis provides the justification for modifying requirements if needed. DFMEA required organizing the software into independent modules with specific functions like any other mechanical or electrical components.   The addition of diagnostics to DFMEA allows the detection and correction of non-conformances at the earliest time in the project and improves the quality of the product.

title: Monte Carlo Simulation for Reliability
authors: Rodney Benson, Acquisition Logistics Engineering; Darryl Kellner, Acquisition Logistics Engineering; Key Words: Monte Carlo Simulation, Reliability, Degradation Analysis
summary: This paper provides an introduction to Monte Carlo simulation and its applicability to reliability engineering.  It provides an example of how Monte Carlo simulation can be used to help answer questions regarding the length of time complex systems can operate in a degraded state before falling below performance thresholds, and how it can be used to assist in program development by comparing alternative designs.  By developing a custom Monte Carlo model, various outputs can be provided to provide insights into how changes to the design affect the reliability of the system.
conclusions:
The example shows the ability of Monte Carlo simulation to provide quick estimates of mean time to failure for complex systems that are difficult to model using traditional reliability analysis methods.  By developing a custom program, the structure of the program can be changed to provide various output files that are further analyzed using a spreadsheet tool.

title: Reliability Test Profile Design Of Hydraulic Automatic Transmission For Forklift Trucks
authors: Hou Weiguo, Ph. D., China Electronics Reliability and Environmental Testing Institute; Zheng Kun, China Electronics Reliability and Environmental Testing Institute; Yan Tingting, China Electronics Reliability and Environmental Testing Institute; Key Words: hydraulic automatic transmission, task profile, vibration stress, reliability test profile
summary:
The hydraulic automatic transmission is the core component of the forklift truck. Its reliability and service life are directly related to vehicle's durability and safety performance. According to daily use of a forklift truck automatic hydraulic transmission and runway test, task profile is established. Combined with value of test stress, reliability test profile of transmission is designed. Transmission task profile is mainly based on important events such as stable operation and turning according to operation phase of the product. The data of each working condition, its duration and speed are determined according to daily usage and runway test. Task profiles include tasks such as stable operation, turning, obstacles, climbing, lifting and lowering loads. Environmental stress and working stress are sensitive stresses of transmission. At each task stage, temperature and vibration data were collected under both no-load and full-load conditions. The oil temperature and transmission casing temperature are obtained by a temperature collector. The vibration acceleration signal is collected by selecting connection position of damper and transmission, output (input) shaft bearing, upper part of torque converter housing, middle position of the upper part of the transmission, etc. According to measured data, task phase, duration, vehicle speed, load, output speed, oil temperature, power spectral density are listed separately. Since the bench test output is the output torque, the torque stress is combined with other stresses to form a reliability test profile.
This paper combines typical task profile and daily use of forklift truck and runway test to determine task profile of automatic hydraulic transmission. By analyzing the environmental stress and working stress, the sensitive stress of the automatic hydraulic transmission is determined as the temperature, vibration, speed and load stress. After specific measurement and analysis, temperature stress is 110℃, vibration stress spectrum is drawn, and relationship between the speed and torque of automatic hydraulic transmission and vehicle speed is obtained. According to the specific measured data, task phase, duration, vehicle speed, load, output speed, oil temperature, power spectral density, and torque are listed respectively, and a reliability test profile of a hydraulic automatic transmission is formed. Based on above research, simulation test will be carried out on test bench to provide reference for manufacture and use of the automatic hydraulic transmission.

title: Building a Winning RE Culture
authors: Stewart Harwell, Chevron; Fil Colon, Chevron; Key Words: Oil and Gas, Organizational Strategy, Reliability Analytics, Reliability Engineering
summary:
The Reliability Engineering (RE) department at Chevron’s refinery in El Segundo, California, was inconsistently conducting technical reliability engineering work and more commonly facilitating reactive reliability processes (investigations, bad actors, studies…etc.). The group struggled to differentiate itself as a valuable technical function and often missed opportunities to address critical questions or problems. This ultimately led to fewer requests for support from internal business leaders, which made the group unappealing to top engineering recruits. The challenge was to re-focus the department on showcasing its reliability engineering expertise and providing valuable technical solutions for the business. This would, in turn, fulfill experience for engineers and improve the department’s reputation and brand appeal. Complicating the challenge is the structure of the role: a two-year rotational assignment for early career design engineers.
Over the last two years the team has shifted its focus to address these critical challenges and elevated its status in the organization by developing an accelerated learning framework, building marketing and communication capabilities, and taking advantage of opportunities to strengthen the RE brand.
For this paper, I plan to show how we rebranded the RE department from Low Value administrative tasks to champion of complex analytical tool applications that address high value reliability problems.

summary: This paper extends the established tables of conversion factors used for converting failure rates or mean time between failures (MTBF) between environments found in MIL-HDBK-217 to the Missile, Flight (MF), Missile, Launch (ML), and Cannon, Launch (CL) environments when used for comparative reliability predictions. title: Transient AMR Project for Semiconductor Products
authors: Ashok Alagappan, ANSYS – DfR Solutions; Stevan Hunter, ON Semiconductor; Key Words: electrical overstress, absolute maximum ratings, transient pulse
summary:
Absolute maximum ratings (AMR) warn against electrical overstress (EOS), the cause of electrically induced physical damage (EIPD) and the ensuing semiconductor part failure.  EOS can cause subtle latent damage, rendering the part reliability unpredictable, or the EIPD is catastrophic, resulting in immediate failure of the semiconductor part.  EOS usually occurs from unknown aggressor pulse or pulses after parts have left control of the manufacturer.  Customer returns of failed parts have continued for decades with few root causes discovered.  Customer who has any concerns about AMR should still not violate, but always discuss with the manufacturer.  The manufacturer may have further information or may agree to experimentally determine transient limits for a particular aggressor pulse on a particular pin.
Methods for simulating or experimentally measuring susceptibility to particular transient pulses exist, though the time and resource investment to accomplish this may not be warranted, unless there is a specific customer need.

Methods for simulating or experimentally measuring susceptibility to particular transient pulses exist, though the time and resource investment to accomplish this may not be warranted, unless there is a specific customer need.

title: Grouping of Activities for Improving Maintenance Planning
authors: Emelia K. S. Nielsen, Technical University of Denmark; Anne-Marie R. B. Thuesen, Technical University of Denmark; Kristoffer V. Sigsgaard, Ph. D., Technical University of Denmark; Niels H. Mortensen, Professor, Technical University of Denmark; Key Words: complex facilities, grouping of maintenance activities, opportunistic maintenance planning, visualizations
summary:
This paper presents a framework for improving maintenance planning in industrial facilities based on an opportunistic approach of grouping maintenance activities. The framework proposes a visual decomposition of the facility into subsystems combined with its maintenance activities to incorporate the functional dependencies of equipment in the planning of maintenance. The proposed framework is based on principles from Theory of Technical Systems and Product Architectures combined with opportunistic maintenance.
The main motivation for developing the framework is the current limitations in opportunistic maintenance on complex facilities. The literature stresses the importance of improving synergies between maintenance activities to reduce production loss and set-up costs. However, when dealing with complex facilities, it becomes more complicated to apply methods within opportunistic maintenance and capture these synergies.
To support this, a framework for connecting the physical aspects with its maintenance activities is developed based on a deductive approach. The framework creates a baseline for opportunistic maintenance planning and proposes two opportunistic procedures: (1) grouping of maintenance activities requiring the same shutdowns and (2) grouping of both preventive maintenance (PM) and corrective maintenance (CM) activities. The framework contributes to the overall understanding of opportunities in the grouping maintenance activities on complex facilities, by providing a visual overview of the functional dependencies within the facility.
The framework is applied to a case study within a global oil and gas exploration and production company, where the two procedures of grouping maintenance activities are validated. The first procedure identifies a great potential of reducing the total days of shutdowns and the second procedure identifies a great potential of savings in set-up costs and man-hours.

title: Data-Driven Systematic Evaluation of Preventive Maintenance Performance
authors: Kristoffer V. Sigsgaard, Technical University of Denmark; Julie K. Agergaard, Technical University of Denmark; Niels-Henrik Mortensen, Technical University of Denmark; Iman Soleymani, Technical University of Denmark
summary:
This paper introduces a method for visualizing existing preventive maintenance actions and their performance. The current literature focuses on the mathematical evaluation of preventive maintenance actions but lacks a connection to available historical data. By utilizing historical data and policy knowledge already available in the company, the proposed methodology enables maintenance managers to make data-driven decisions.
The method is applied in an offshore oil and gas company. Currently, the company tracks their preventive maintenance policies in separate document for each system. By implementing the method, it was possible to create an overview of the preventive maintenance policies described in the separate documents. This was combined with historical data to give an overview of preventive maintenance performance that was not available before.

title: Healthcare’s Resilience During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Case Study of Nursing Operations Adaptation
authors: Catherine S. Fernald, DNP, RN, ChristianaCare; Austin F. Mount-Campbell, PhD, ChristianaCare; Monica F. Rochman, PhD, RN, ChristianaCare; Key Words: resilience, crisis, response
summary:
The spread of COVID-19 has transformed our world over, propelling individuals and organizations to adapt quickly.  Often, changing directions mid-step as new information becomes available.  This has subsequently evolved the concept of new knowledge learning to quantum levels.
The nursing workforce is the largest profession within healthcare systems and is central to the response and prevention efforts of COVID-19.  Registered Nurses (RN) are the front-line caregivers for the sickest of COVID-19 patients in the intensive care arena.  Therefore, it is imperative nursing operations monitor, adapt, and function in times of constraint while exhibiting essential principles of resilience to survive under surge conditions. These principles are: Top-level Commitment, Just Culture, Learning Culture, Awareness, Preparedness, Flexibility, and Opacity.  The focus of this paper is to present a case study with lessons learned on COVID-19 nursing operational initiatives within the context of the principles of resilience.
The principals of resilience were demonstrated during the initial response to the pandemic through multiple operational initiatives.  The Incident Command structure directed decisions and action items through an even sharper lens for driving outcomes.  This was impacted by a sense of urgency in responding to social media influences, overt staff fear of the disease and potential impact to self and their families, and the evolution of incoming scientific information on disease management.
Staff quickly adapted to the education while sustaining an ability to provide direct care to patients.  There were 932 hospital admissions with 895 successful COVID-19 hospital discharges from March - May 2020.  The remaining 114 admissions were resulting in-hospital COVID-19 related deaths.  During the escalation of the COVID-19 crisis, 2845 ChristianaCare employees were tested for COVID.  Five hundred and one tests came back positive for the disease. One hundred and fifty three positive tests were nursing staff that worked on the dedicated COVID-19 patient care units.  Interestingly, the hypothesis in the beginning of the crisis was that the COVID patient care staff were at more risk for exposure and acquired infections.  These statistics infer that the directed attention of RNs from COVID-19 units on education resulted in purposeful application too proper Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and hand hygiene practices, along with a preparedness for working in the stressful environment.  This coupled with purposeful leadership presence and responsiveness to staff feedback, resulted in better system resilience among COVID-19-unit staff versus non-COVID-19 unit staff.  Opportunities have emerged to inform recovery plans in the future to include opportunities for providing acute care in the population health setting with supportive technology.

title: Impact of Repair Logistics on Product Reliability
authors: Paul Franklin, McKissack and McKissack; Key Words: Repair logistics, reliability metrics
summary:
This paper describes an approach to extracting reliability data from transaction data and performing analysis on it. Of interest to management was developing rules that would identify problematic equipment.  A large population was analyzed for mean time between repairs (a measure of failures) and mean time between returns (a measure of how well a device remained in service).  These measures were computed as a function of the number of installations, number of repairs, and number of times a device was in service for 30 days or less.
As a result of this work, it was suggested that an individual device be repaired no more than 2 times and that the combination of a trouble call coupled with a short service time leads to increased costs.
conclusions:
This experience report only scratches the surface.  There are a few rules that can be noted.
Repeated installation tends to result in an increased fraction of population repaired
Mean time between returns is a more useful metric than mean time between repairs since it measures service life, and the ability of a device to generated income through rental fees.
At most, repair a device 2 times.  A single repair is indicated if a device is retuned for repair within 6 months of the first repair.  Such devices should be culled from the population.
The combination of short in house coupled with one or more trouble calls is an indicator that a device will be expensive to operate and maintain.  These devices should be culled from the population.
This set of rules can be deployed easily.  They are simple, and they are self-updating if the analysis is repeated quarterly or semi-annually.  They identify specific devices rather than groups of devices, although if there is a systemic defect, these rules might be useful in detecting it.
It is important to understand how to develop rules like these to manage the logistics of the repair cycle.  In this application, the notion of having equipment in service is directly related to the ability to generate revenue.  This is only one part of the total cost of ownership.
Previous work has explored two other key ideas.  Cost models could be developed for these rules to understand how they might be used most effectively. [4] In addition, management of the inventory of spares so that the minimum number of devices are held in the optimum locations [5].
This current work indicates that it is possible to identify a subset of a population that is responsible for a significant fraction of logistics related costs by identifying suspect devices.  These devices, if they are identified early, are key sources of data that can lead to the field failure modes that are important cost drivers.

title: No Problem Found Framework Based on Analytics and Machine Learning
authors: Patrick C. Herbert, Rockwell Automation; Biman Ghosh, Ph.D., Rockwell Automation; Stephen Tiber, Rockwell Automation; William Clay, C. W. Consultants; Francis Wolff, Ph.D., Case Western Reserve University
summary:
Disruptive events from field returns are difficult to analyze at best and can result in a “no problem found” (NPF) classification.  The percentage of NPF is very high, ranging from 40% to 70% of customer returned products [1−3].  The difficulty is further compounded when the customers’ environment cannot be reproduced at the manufacturer diagnostics testing facility, whereby uncharacterized NPF results in incomplete information and risks in future product designs.
The analytics framework assists in looking for areas that would lead the reliability engineer to the issue of component vulnerability, which should minimize the complex process of elimination.  A methodology of correlations and query lookups will be much faster compared to iterative supplier interactions, which could take weeks.  The framework is not going to solve the problem.  The knowledge base and big data can collate information, with the intent of cutting time, by pinpointing areas that would prioritize the diagnosis path, rather than solve every possible scenario.
Applying analytics for customer returns works best when problems can be found but leaves “no problem found" as unidentified with no ability to diagnose, predict and prescribe as shown in Fig. 1.  In order to address the unidentified analytics, we must correlate components with other known products, customer usage, and supplier provided information.  This methodology requires the big data approach in order to capture as much data as possible from the manufacturer, supplier, and customer environments.  Correlation, pattern discovery, and trends are built on using machine learning techniques.  The value in big data and machine learning is the speed in which the reliability engineer can correlate this data.
This framework integrates several modeling approaches which addresses the unidentified areas due to NPF.  These approaches combines business analytics process, big data, bio-inspired behavioral modelling and machine learning artificial intelligence (ML/AI) techniques to discover new relationships.  Big data typically means more data is better.  Traditionally, the manufacturer only tracked component data on the board in order to analyze NPFs from customer returns.
A knowledge base allows for integration of existing big data information from various environments relating to the board.  These sources of information cover the scope from supplier, manufacturer and customer.  NPF returns are tracked using bio-inspired behavioral models.  The business analytics allows manufacturers to be proactive and predictive for NPF.  Self-organized maps are used as an ML/AI technique to discover new relationships.
In conclusion, the business analytics framework and architecture is improved by a bio-inspired model which allows business analytics to become proactive and predictive.  The big data methodology allows us to expand the parameters for the supplier, manufacturer and customer in order to make better decisions.  It also helps focus attention on analysis and consider what is significant and not significant.  Furthermore, it helps reduce sustainment cost across multiple product lines.  The machine learning discovers new failure mode relationships between the three mission profile environments.  This enables pinpointing of diagnostic paths for the No Problem Found (NPF).

title: Deep Learning-based Anomaly Detection for Compressors Using Audio Data
authors: Pooyan Mobtahej, Lamar University; Xulong Zhang, Lamar University; Maryam Hamidi, Lamar University; Jing Zhang, Lamar University; Key Words: Anomaly Detection, Midstream Infrastructure, Deep Learning
summary:
By pressurizing natural gas in pipelines, the compression system interlocks upstream gas production and downstream consumer use. Considering the installation cost of $1 to $2 million US dollars for a compressor, the failure of the component can be costly. Therefore, the anomaly detection for the compression system is essential. In this paper, a deep learning-based anomaly detection method is proposed to identify the failure of midstream compressors using audio sensor data. Firstly, short-term Fourier transform (STFT), Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC), and spectral centroid (SC) features are computed using the input audio signals. Secondly, deep learning-based feature extraction is applied to create high-level features. Finally, a principal component analysis step and a support vector machine are applied to classify normal and anomaly audio signals.
The proposed method was evaluated using two datasets with a total of 10196 audio signals collected from a compressor. The experimental results demonstrate that MFCC features are better than STFT features for anomaly detection and the combined deep MFCC features and SC features can achieve the best normal and anomaly signal classification performance, 100% for both datasets, using the proposed method.
conclusions:
Anomaly detection is critical in reducing the cost of midstream components maintenance. A deep learning-based anomaly detection method is presented in this paper to identify failures of the audio data collected from a compressor. MFCC, STFT, and SC features were computed using the input audio data, and then the high-level features extracted from MFCC/STFT by a deep learning network were fed to the PCA and SVM for classifying normal and anomalies classification. Two datasets with a total of 10196 audio signals were used to evaluate the proposed method. The experiments demonstrated that MFCC performed better than STFT for this research and the combined deep MFCC features and SC features achieved the best performance for normal and anomalies classification with 100% for four evaluation metrics used in the experiments.
The future work includes using other bigger audio signal datasets to test the performance of the proposed method, classifying the anomaly samples into sub-classes that correspond to different types of component failures, applying other deep learning networks (e.g., LSTM network) to analyze one-dimensional raw audio signals, and combining one-dimensional and two-dimensional audio signal features for anomaly detection.

The authors also acknowledge the National Science Foundation for the high performance computing cluster at Lamar University supported under award No. 1726500. This research is supported by the Center for Midstream Management and Science at Lamar University.

title: Structured Data for Product Performance Improvement
authors: Priya Peter, Collins Aerospace; Carol Parendo, Collins Aerospace; Key Words: Product performance, Reliability metrics, MTBUR / MTBF, FRACAS, Voice of Customer, Big data, Data integrity Speed of data, Portability of data, Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
summary:
Aftermarket reliability data is a cornerstone to understand the performance of one’s products against requirements.  A successful aftermarket data system goes beyond the basics of supplying reliability figures. Its attributes also include additional metrics for an effective alerting and reporting system to enable proactive response to aftermarket issues. While these system features are key, the implementation and maintenance methodology of the system is crucial to its success.  This is because these systems involve big data. In the case presented, it is data which spans several years, for a variety of model numbers on a variety of aircraft platforms or applications.  Each set of circumstances yields different reliability figures and associated metrics.  With this big data, it is equally crucial to its success to have a methodology to address data integrity, the speed of data, and the portability of data.  Our solution with this successful methodology of these features is called Structured Data.
A good aftermarket data system is a backbone for any successful organization.  A good system in the aerospace industry goes beyond ATA Spec 2000 [1] formatted data and standard reliability figures such as MTBUR (Mean Time Between Unscheduled Removal) and MTBF (Mean Time Between Failure).  It is also beyond implementing a Failure Reporting and Corrective Action System (FRACAS).  A comprehensive system in the aerospace industry includes several additional measures (i.e. frequency, severity, risk) to represent the Voice of the Customer.  And with a built-in mechanism for proactive response to the data, the system can then be considered World-Class.
While designing a system with these features is important, its success also hinges upon the methodology of implementation and maintenance.  As stated earlier, aftermarket data is considered big data due to the volume of highly specific data.  With this big data, it is critical to success to address data integrity, the speed of data, and the portability of data all within a user-friendly experience.  For data integrity, do we trust the data?  This takes on many forms from cross referencing input and output data to determining an accurate mixed fleet factor.   For speed of data, do we have a system in place to handle the cadence of data efficiently?  For portability, do we structure our data in such a way where we can be agile to serve potential changes to our system or new systems as our company evolves? For a user-friendly experience, can we structure the data for intuitive analysis for all stakeholders?  Thus in the proposed system, all of these aspects of data integrity, the speed of data, the portability of data, and formatting the data per   stakeholders are addressed.  Our solution with this successful methodology of these features is called Structured Data.
The benefits of this newly developed Structured Data extend beyond ATA Spec 2000 in which it is based.  The data is structured in a dynamic and interactive environment.  This environment includes intuitive analysis and a system of prioritization for corrective action.  The key benefit of this Structured Data system is proactive response to aftermarket data analysis.
conclusions:
The structured data implementation evolved from the legacy aftermarket dashboards.  Aim of this implementation was to have a single database that can be easily accessible by multiple stakeholders as well as to implement a robust system.   A reliability tracking system cannot be focusing only on the MTBF and MTBUR numbers. A successful system should drive a proactive reliability improvement and early identification of product reliability issues.  At the same time the data needs to be accurate and trustworthy.  We could achieve this by integrating the actual field population, production configurations, and by monitoring each component by the current state.
The database has a good repository of MRO data, shop findings, and customer identified failure modes.  This data is well managed and are available to the user.  This data could be a good resource to optimize the failure mode libraries for custom made parts.
The data visualization for this dashboard is realized using Tableau data visualization software.  This platform controls the access privileges to internal and external users.

title: Reliability Modelling in HVAC & Other Industry Equipment Using Big Data
authors: Sarath Jayatilleka, DaikinApplied Americas; Judith Peters, PE DaikinApplied Americas; Key Words: Reliability Data, Energy Modeling, Design Life, Warranty Data, Design for Reliability
summary:
Design life is an integral component of the scientific  definition of reliability. Lack of design life as a design input parameter to the design systems hinders the accelerated ‘life’ test planning and overall designing for reliability. This paper primarily provides the methods of deriving the engineering requirement of design life using big data at system and components levels. In addition, energy modeling was used in HVAC systems with big data in modeling and model validation in order to derive component life. Finally, big data can be helpful in system and component level real time performance monitoring and reducing impact on customers.
The next frontier in big data is the combination of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Research on self-learning to serve individual customer loads and usage effectively and energy efficiently, has great potentials in the near future.
conclusions:
In the traditional world, field reliability data for the Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) industry, and many other industries’ equipment, provide lagging indicators due to the inherent delays in data acquisition. Warranty databases were the commonly used resources for analyzing field failure percentages and predictions of warranty costs. Warranties takes care of the customer after the damage has happened. Therefore, the warranty provides a lagging unreliability indicator and the failure has a negative impact on the brand name associated with the equipment. In addition, root cause analysis is harder on failed systems due to the catastrophic effect on the system, as well as on the interfaced systems, followed by possible destruction of evidence.
Today’s real-time data acquisition systems provide not only real-time failure data but also system degradation and early warning before real failures occur, thus serving as leading indicators. These data can be used to improve  systems before failures occur. In addition, improvements can be incorporated into future systems before releasing to the customers. These concepts are discussed in this paper with examples.
The survival probability of a system and/or its components is defined as the expected design lifetime. It is a crucial component within the reliability definition. While the system-level design life is commonly in terms of years, the components’ lifetimes are derived in terms of functional usage duty cycles (FUDC) of such subsystems and components. A classic example is the ball bearing lifetime defined in its number of revolutions across  20 years for the 90th percentile customer usage. With the FUDC information, accelerated life testing can be accurately planned. Many industries struggle to define the subsystem and component design life in terms of FUDCs. This leads to ambiguous reliability requirements provided to design teams and critical part suppliers. Big data is of great help to fulfill this need. This paper discusses the concepts of defining the design life in FUDC using big data.
Most consumer equipment goes through seasonal patterns due to annual climatic conditions. HVAC equipment provides classic examples of such seasonal usages.  Dynamic energy modeling can be effectively used to model seasonal demands and behaviors of HVAC equipment. The big data acquired from cloud-based intelligent HVAC systems and dynamic energy modeling can be developed to have symbiotic relationships. For example, ideal application conditions are not practically available from big data. However, acquired big data from an actual building data system can be used to validate and fine-tune the dynamic energy modeling for that application. Thereafter, energy models can be used to create data for the ideal application conditions. These data can be used to define the design life of subsystems and components in FUDCs. These concepts are discussed using examples in HVAC applications.
In summary, this paper presents how big data can be useful to improve and influence leading indicators and improve design for reliability with accurately defined design lifetimes in terms of FUDCs for accelerated life testing. In addition, this paper discusses how dynamic energy modeling can be beneficial in designing for reliability.

title: Predicting Corrosion Growth and Reliability of the Oil Pipeline
authors: Abdulsalam Ahmed Alqarni, North Dakota State University; Om Prakash Yadav, North Dakota State University; Bimal Nepal, Texas A & M University; Key Words: corrosion rate, linear model, Monte Carlo method, pipeline, reliability analysis
summary: This paper proposes a general model to predict the corrosion growth process over time in the pipeline and combined with the Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) to assess the pipeline's reliability. Although several models have been proposed to capture corrosion behavior in the pipeline, the linear corrosion growth rate model is widely used due to its simplicity and capability to predict the corrosion process over time despite the scarcity of more detailed pipeline information. Therefore, we propose a linear model, but it differs from the existing linear corrosion growth models where it is applicable to include multiple in-line inspection datasets. The proposed model is called multiple in-line inspections (M-ILIs) based-linear corrosion rate model. Also, this paper is conducting a comparative study of the M-ILIs model with the other three common existing linear models, such as single-value (SV) corrosion rate model, single in-line inspection (S-ILI) based-linear corrosion rate model, and two in-line inspections (T-ILIs) based-linear corrosion rate model. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over other models, especially for long-term prediction, where it gives more accurate prediction outcomes, which makes the M-ILIs model encouraging and could be useful for reliability analysts and managers to utilize it in corrosion prediction regarding buried oil and gas pipelines.
conclusions:
This paper proposes a general model to predict the corrosion growth process over time in the pipeline by assuming multiple ILIs data are available. A comparative study is also conducted with three other common linear corrosion growth rate models. In the study, we assume three different scenarios to evaluate each model's effectiveness using the RMSE metric to measure each model's prediction accuracy. The RMSE values of the model we propose are significantly less than other models’ RMSE values. Also, the prediction accuracy of MTTF reveals that the M-ILIs model provides more accurate prediction outcomes.
The MCS technique is also used to evaluate the pipeline’s reliability of each model. The reliability estimation results show that the M-ILIs model gives more realistic outcomes than others. In contrast, the other models, SV, S-ILI, and T-ILs models, provide inaccurate and unstable reliability prediction results in each scenario. Therefore, these linear models are not desirable to use in reliability analysis applications unless multiple ILIs data are used because they provide conservative reliability prediction outcomes.
This paper finds that the M-ILIs model is sufficient for long-term prediction and can be an appropriate alternative to the non-linear model as the non-linear model needs the operator’s knowledge to get the soil and pipe properties parameters, making the non-linear model is a challenge.

title: A Framework for Performing Quantitative Fault Tree Analyses for Subsystems with Periodic Repairs
authors: Sakurai Atsushi, FS-Micro Corporation; Key Words: fault-tolerant subsystem, ISO 26262, Markov chain, minimal cut set, PMHF
summary:
The second edition of ISO 26262 came into effect in 2018, seven years after the publication of the first edition in 2011.  Various improvements have been made, one of which is the revision of the equations for the probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF).  The PMHF is so important, as it is one of the design specifications for the hardware of electronic control units (ECUs) in automobiles.  However, the mathematical definitions and assumptions underlying the PMHF in the standard are still ambiguous.  As the standard provides only the resulting formula for the PMHF, engineers have difficulty calculating the PMHF using quantitative fault tree analysis (FTA).
Many papers have addressed safety analysis according to ISO 26262; however, very few papers have examined the PMHF calculation.  Although a few papers have presented methods of calculating the PMHF using quantitative FTA, none of these papers is based on the PMHF equation, which has periodic inspections and repairs.  Thus, inadequate methods have been widely adopted in the industry for calculating the PMHF from the perspective of ISO 26262.
Our research aims to provide a framework for quantitative FTAs, while considering periodic inspections and repairs that are the key assumption of the standard.  Our framework is based on models of the Markov stochastic process and the PMHF equations derived from those models.  The use of unreliability in the PMHF calculation is a conservative evaluation, and thus compliant with the standard; however, it has proven to be a severe design constraint on the design of fault-tolerant systems.  Therefore, it is reasonable to use the unavailability in the PMHF calculation.
We applied a framework to correctly calculate the PMHF for a particular vehicle subsystem, using an existing paper as an example.  Specifically, we found that the existing methodology underestimates the PMHF 2.7-fold in an autonomous emergency braking (AEB) subsystem.  As an underestimation of the failure probability is a dangerous systematic failure, such underestimation should be avoided.  Therefore, our framework can greatly benefit the automotive industry, as it allows quantitative FTA to be efficiently performed to accurately evaluate the PMHF.
conclusions:

The PMHF is so important, as it is one of the design specifications for the hardware of electronic control units (ECUs) in automobiles.  However, the mathematical definitions and assumptions underlying the PMHF in the standard are still ambiguous.  As the standard provides only the resulting formula for the PMHF, engineers have difficulty calculating the PMHF using quantitative fault tree analysis (FTA).
Many papers have addressed safety analysis according to ISO 26262; however, very few papers have examined the PMHF calculation.  Although a few papers have presented methods of calculating the PMHF using quantitative FTA, none of these papers is based on the PMHF equation, which has periodic inspections and repairs.  Thus, inadequate methods have been widely adopted in the industry for calculating the PMHF from the perspective of ISO 26262.
Our research aims to provide a framework for quantitative FTAs, while considering periodic inspections and repairs that are the key assumption of the standard.  Our framework is based on models of the Markov stochastic process and the PMHF equations derived from those models.  The use of unreliability in the PMHF calculation is a conservative evaluation, and thus compliant with the standard; however, it has proven to be a severe design constraint on the design of fault-tolerant systems.  Therefore, it is reasonable to use the unavailability in the PMHF calculation.
We applied a framework to correctly calculate the PMHF for a particular vehicle subsystem, using an existing paper as an example.  Specifically, we found that the existing methodology underestimates the PMHF 2.7-fold in an autonomous emergency braking (AEB) subsystem.  As an underestimation of the failure probability is a dangerous systematic failure, such underestimation should be avoided.  Therefore, our framework can greatly benefit the automotive industry, as it allows quantitative FTA to be efficiently performed to accurately evaluate the PMHF.

title: Novel Approach to CBM+ Implementation on Aviation Systems
authors: Kenney Crooks, Northrop Grumman Corporation; Nathan Plawecki, Northrop Grumman Corporation; Key Words: CBM+, Condition Based Maintenance Plus, Predictive Maintenance, Reliability
summary:
As next generation aircraft design evolves, so do the capabilities for predictive and prognostic advancements.  These developments have been key to the transition from the traditional reactive maintenance concepts to more proactive strategies.  This paradigm shift has fostered an increased readiness of aviation platforms through Condition Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) constructs as a continuous improvement program.  The goal of CBM+ is to leverage efficient processes and procedures coupled with sensing and monitoring technology to predict when failures will occur whilst taking action before a failure can occur to mitigate operational downtime.
Introducing CBM+ programs on platforms can be challenging.  There can be a degree of difficulty in identifying appropriate CBM+ enablers early in a program lifecycle when establishing maintenance concepts is the most beneficial.  This is due to immaturity of the design coupled with the unknowns or unobserved failure modes and system behaviors that drive the evidence of need for this benefit.  These challenges are even more evident on aviation programs as there are a multitude of constraints – such as weight, cost, and schedule – that make significant CBM+ constructs more difficult to realize.
This case study highlights a new approach for planning a CBM+ program to help alleviate constraints and challenges evident on aviation programs and demonstrate the benefits from such an initiative. The strategy includes a Functional System Modeling approach and tailored gap analysis in concert with unique testing. The gap analysis simplifies the CBM+ selection process whilst ensuring cost, schedule, safety, and reliability are considered.  Item specific testing is recommended for early implementation to precipitate failure behaviors and postulate predictors when limited fielded experience is evident.  Furthermore, introducing a digital thread is principal to ensure successful implementation of a modern CBM+ development program to facilitate robust information from the platform and visibility into the product life cycle.

title: Capacity Degradation Modeling for Li-Ion Batteries using a Multiscale Gamma Process Approach
authors: Sara Kohtz, University of Illinois; Pingfeng Wang PhD, University of Illinois; Key Words: Gamma Process, Kalman Filter, Degradation Modeling
summary:
A gamma process was implemented within a dual extended Kalman filter framework for simultaneous estimation of SOC and SOH of Li-ion batteries. The results show that utilizing gamma random variables as capacity degradation increments has satisfactory performance. However, the gamma process alone is not enough for precise estimation. There needs to be some parameter updates within the filtering framework for optimal inference. This can be done by updating parameters directly within the filter; or it can be implemented with a shape or scale function within the gamma process. The advantage of the shape function is that the model has less parameters to update.
Table 4 – Results Summary MSE
Figure 4 SOH Estimation Results Using the DEKF with GP/NN and the Power law Shape Parameters
There still should exist some middle ground between having 52 parameters to estimate (which provides a near exact estimation) and 9 for the gamma process (which has good estimations but not quite as precise).
There are some aspects of this study that would benefit from future work, including the exploration of various parameter functions for the shape variable, different extensions of the gamma process, and another measurement function. A power-shape parameter was utilized for this method, but there are other options that may fit better to capacity degradation, for example an exponential shape parameter. In addition, the scale parameter can also be defined as a time-dependent function, although it seems unlikely that it will make a difference since capacity degradation values remain in a small range. Also, the gamma process is a time-dependent random variable, there are formulations in [2] for a transformed gamma process, which is both state and time dependent; this may be valuable to implement with this framework. Finally, the measurement function within the state space model can take many forms, and there are numerous functions to implement in the literature, including some that consider temperature. In addition, it would be useful to know how well this model deals with pulsing current data, as the NASA dataset has only constant current measurements.  Overall, this study provides the implementation of a random process within an extended Kalman filter framework and shows promising results.

title: A New Approach for the Assessment of Maintenance Policies on Stochastically Deteriorating Systems
authors: Xinyang Liu, University of Illinois; Pingfeng Wang, University of Illinois; Key Words: Policy Evaluation, Condition-based Maintenance, Stochastically Deteriorating Systems
summary: This paper presents a new methodology for the long-run performance assessment of condition-based maintenance policies on stochastically deteriorating systems, by analyzing the steady-state performance of the systems. Both a simulation-based heuristic approach and a Markov Chain (MC)-based approach are adopted for the steady-state performance analysis and compared for the evaluation of different condition-based maintenance policies. To illustrate the developed framework and methods, threshold-based maintenance policies applied to battery energy storage systems are evaluated using both reliability and economic assessment metrics. With the developed approaches, the analysis has discovered that a higher battery replacement threshold will lead to higher fulfillment of the capacity requirement while resulting in more operating cost as well. The presented case study demonstrated the efficacy of the developed performance assessment framework for condition-based maintenance policies on stochastically deteriorating systems.

The presented case study demonstrated the efficacy of the developed performance assessment framework for condition-based maintenance policies on stochastically deteriorating systems.

title: Cascade Effect Analysis in Torrential Context for Prioritizing Check Dams Maintenance Strategies
authors: Nour Chahrour, Univ. Grenoble Alpes; Jean-Marc Tacnet., Univ. Grenoble Alpes; Christophe Bérenguer, Univ. Grenoble Alpes; Key Words: cascading events, check dams' series, degradation modeling, maintenance strategies, natural hazards
summary: Natural hazards in mountains pose threat to people, properties, and infrastructures.  Several mitigation strategies aim to reduce the induced risk and to protect vulnerable issues exposed to such dangerous phenomena.  Check dams are one type of structural protection measures constructed in series along mountain streams. They constitute a critical interdependent multi-component system that deteriorates over time and requires regular inspection and maintenance.  The propagation of damage is influenced by failure dependencies existing within a single dam and/or between multiple dams.  Such cascading events reduce the efficacy of the overall system in providing protection.  Due to limited budgetary resources, it is essential to identify the most critical structures involved within the system and to capture the state of degradation at which preventive maintenance should be carried out.  Consequently, performing a dependability analysis of such systems is highly important.  This requires analyzing the dynamic deterioration of each dam and the local or distant effects of its partial or total unavailability on other consecutive dams.  The present study integrates physical numerical models analyzing the dynamic state evolution of check dams while being subjected to a series of torrential flood events over a specified period of time with stochastic Petri nets modeling the maintenance processes.   The developed models are applied on a simple protection system composed of two check dams.  The results achieved permit analyzing the behavior of one dam in the presence or the absence of the other dam and prioritizing several proposed maintenance strategies taking into consideration economic constraints.
conclusions: In this article, physical and reliability analyses of a system of check dams are presented.  In particular, the proposed approach aims in modeling quantitatively the bi-directional dependencies between check dams located in series.  Of course, at this stage, the achieved results are not generic and correspond to the proposed case study.  Several features (e.g. longitudinal slope, distance separating the dams, etc.) could have resulted in different types of dependencies.  All the used data were assumed and assessed by experts.  Consequently, imperfection resulting from uncertain, inconsistence, imprecise, or incomplete data propagates within the model and of course may have an influence on the results of the analysis.  Hence, the model could be developed further by taking into account information imperfection and performing sensitivity analysis.

title: Visualize Maintenance Data to Identify Safety Issues and Opportunistic Maintenance Possibilities
authors: Kasper Barslund Hansen, Technical University of Denmark; Kristoffer Vandrup Sigsgaard, Technical University of Denmark; Julie Krogh Agergaard, Technical University of Denmark; Niels Henrik Mortensen, Technical University of Denmark; Key Words: hazard identification, maintenance data, opportunistic maintenance, visualization
summary: In this paper, a proposed visualization method for identifying safety issues and opportunistic maintenance possibilities is presented. The focus is on the practicability of opportunistic maintenance and hazard identification, which is lacking in both literature and industry (i.e. case company). The proposed method uses visualization and system drawings for communicating the potential issues and opportunities to maintenance planners. The visualization is data-driven and uses common maintenance data for highlighting potential safety issues and opportunistic maintenance possibilities on system drawings. The applicability of the method was tested at a case company and the results confirm that benefits can be achieved by using the proposed method. Through the use of the method, issues and opportunities were identified which would not have been discovered or would have taken a considerable amount of time to derive using the existing maintenance planning procedure.

title: Maintenance Management Optimization to Improve System Availability Based on Stochastic Block Diagram
authors: Carlos Alberto Murad, Ph. D., University of São Paulo; Arthur Henrique de Andrade Melani, Ph. D., University of São Paulo; Miguel Angelo de Carvalho Michalski, University of São Paulo; Gilberto Francisco Martha de Souza, Ph. D., University of São Paulo
summary:
One of the most adopted strategies by the industrial sector for asset management is the monitoring of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), which contribute to determine whether an organization is achieving its predetermined objectives. Amongst the most widespread, availability is an important KPI in the management of an asset, since it expresses its percentage of actual uptime relative to the total service hours. There are several factors that can affect the availability of an asset, such as its design characteristics, the mode of operation, the medium in which it is used, and the quality and agility of the maintenance actions practiced in it.
Several techniques have been developed over the years to estimate asset availability. Among them, the Reliability Block Diagram (RBD) has become one of the most used, as it manages to determine, through a simple graphical representation, the reliability, availability and maintainability of repairable systems. However, this tool has a number of limitations regarding the dynamic behavior of the system under study, as it does not allow factors such as the size and workload of the maintenance team to be taken into account, nor the presence (or absence) of spare parts in stock.
With this in mind, this work aims to use Stochastic Block Diagram (SBD), which combines the graphic representation of RBD with Monte-Carlo simulation, to estimate and evaluate the availability of a dynamic system.  In the proposed method, factors such as the supply and stock of spare parts, as well as the size and workload of the maintenance team, are taken into account for a more precise estimate of the availability of the system under study.
As a case study, the method is implemented in a hydroelectric plant. The results obtained from the plant model allow the optimization of the size of the maintenance team and the number of spare parts in order to improve system availability. The proposed method proved to be capable of assisting maintenance management regarding decision making to increase maintenance performance.
conclusions: The SBD was able to determine the availability of the system under study and also managed to show the impact that the size of the maintenance team and the number of spare parts has on the system's performance. Through the results obtained, it is possible to optimize the management of systems maintenance, determining the ideal conditions for obtaining greater availability. In future work, it is intended to use SBD in other systems to test its adaptability. It is also intended to structure the interpretation of its results in order to contribute to the maintenance management decision process. In addition, it is intended to take advantage of the results from the Monte Carlo simulation to analyze the influence of the uncertainties of the input parameters. Finally, it is also intended to develop an algorithm that seeks the optimal operational scenario automatically.
keywords: reliability, maintainability, availability, RBD, Monte Carlo, spare parts

title: Pitfalls of Accelerated Validation Test on Automotive Components
authors: Marco Bonato, Ph. D., Valeo Thermal Systems France; Ewelina Czerlunczakiewicz, Valeo Thermal Systems Poland; Key Words:  Accelerated validation tests; fatigue damage; automotive; heat exchangers
summary: Starting the production of automotive components on schedule is a big challenge faced by tier 1 suppliers. Both design validation (DV, on prototypes) and product validation (PV, on serial parts) heavily rely on sign-off testing activities.  Indeed, the execution of an inappropriate validation test often results in the over testing of the component, thus increasing the probability of incurring into unrepresentative failure modes.  The consequent corrective actions would significantly increase manufacturers’ R&D and operational costs, resulting in over-designed products.  On the other hand, the outcome of unsuitable validation tests might as well be the under testing of the component, with potentially severe consequences on the durability once the product is in-service.  This paper gathers some of the most common pitfalls encountered during the development and implementation of accelerated validation tests. The avoidance of such pitfalls will give a better chance of successfully launching new products without incurring in unexpected costs and difficulties.  The proposed practical examples deal in particular with components that are responsible for the thermal management of the vehicle.
conclusions:
This paper describes some common pitfalls encountered during the generation, the execution and the analysis of accelerated validation tests. Troubles related to pitfalls in validation tests can produce either an over test of the part (with consequential over-design) or an under test (with concrete risk of incurring in early field failures and warranty risk).
By focusing on automotive heat exchangers undergoing mechanical fatigue failure, the study highlights the importance of generated and running representative tests, in order to avoid delays during product validation phase.

title: Fall-Back Analysis using Model-Based Engineering
authors: Evan Apostolou, PHM Technology; Jacek Stecki, Ph. D., PHM Technology; Daniel Chan, PHM Technology; Andrew Thorn, PHM Technology
summary:
Mission Assurance is a discipline which aims to identify and mitigate technical risk that can impact mission success. Fall-Back Analysis (FBA), a technique proposed by PHM Technology, supports Mission Assurance objectives by identifying alternate pathways (Workarounds) for a function to be successfully executed by a system if a critical component experiences a Functional Failure.
Model-based simulation and analysis of Reliability, Safety and Diagnostics allows FBA to be performed concurrently during the design process - increasing the likelihood of mission success. The concepts behind FBA are not new (e.g. loss of oxygen tank on the Apollo 13 and the resultant ‘workaround’, and large-scale industry projects on offshore oil and gas rigs/platforms), but what is novel is formalizing this approach into a methodology that can be readily applied by leveraging outputs from model-based Mission Assurance.
This paper uses the MADe modelling environment to identify potential component Functional Failure Modes and conduct Fall-Back Analysis to ensure mission functions can still be satisfied.
conclusions:
This paper has outlined the formal process of performing a Fall-Back Analysis (FBA) for an engineering system, while utilizing a model-based engineering tool, MADe.
The FBA is an engineering analysis performed by design and/or operation engineers which is crucial for identifying and mitigating system and localized risk. The FBA was shown to be useful in improving Mission Assurance by planning executable actions which otherwise would have been ad-hoc tasks for a given functional failure of a component in a system, significantly reducing its criticality.
The process of performing an FBA has been clearly defined with and without the use of a model-based engineering software.

title: Model-Based RAMS: Optimizing Model Development in a Distributed Working Environment
authors: Paddy Conroy, PHM Technology; Ho-Bin Kim, PHM Technology; Khoi Tran, PHM Technology; Daniel Chan, PHM Technology; Key Words: data discipline, project definition, process, model-based systems engineering
summary:
The challenges of conducting Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, Safety (RAMS) analysis in a distributed work environment have become exacerbated in the post-COVID world. The reality is that distributed operations may become the new “norm” for industry, and it is essential that RAMS (the cornerstone of system safety, reliability and cost of ownership attributes) can adapt to this paradigm, particularly in the context of increasingly complex systems that leverage Industry 4.0, the IoT and model-based engineering.
To ensure that the analyses supporting RAMS are sufficiently comprehensive, consistent, and repeatable requires that a defined methodology to ensure optimized processes  are in place. Model-based RAMS is the obvious answer.
Model-based engineering platforms are primarily analytical in purpose and function, often overlooked is the use of them as a communication method between stakeholders (within and between teams, departments, organizations, and projects). A model functions as a technical baseline with the capability to act as a singular knowledge management solution for the decision making, assumptions, and soft institutional knowledge that goes into a product development process, improving traceability and accountability. Naturally, then, there is a need to explore the constraints of developing a RAMS model in a distributed work environment.
This paper provides an approach and methodology for ensuring that organizations developing RAMS models in a distributed environment can address the issues of: segmented technical responsibilities (internal – between departments and groups; and external – with the supply chain); configuration management (of models, and their parameters at different stages in the product lifecycle), analysis consistency (the advantages of analysis process automation), data consistency (structure and nomenclature of functions and failures), and future-proofing by digitizing the process for extensibility.
conclusions:
Typically attributes such as process consistency (Standard Work), automation and traceability are key attributes that inform technology decisions at the enterprise level - particularly for larger organizations with distributed workplaces. It is our expectation that these same criteria will be considered in selecting the tools an organization will use to perform / support their RAMS function.
The advantages of adopting a model-based engineering framework is not limited to the increased effectiveness of technical analyses or value-added analysis outcomes. It is a powerful communication medium to enhance the product’s development and operational life cycle by establishing a cohesive baseline for knowledge capture and management.
As we expeditiously move into this increasingly distributed working climate the requirement for a model-based engineering approach is firmly justified, but the optimization of such a shift leaves somewhat of a vacuum. Luckily, this is easily manageable through the structuring of initial and ongoing model development efforts. Once an organization makes the choice to jump the initial hurdles (such as organizing/ coordinating existing data and integrating standardized taxonomical systems), they may establish the key requirement of an optimized model development effort. These were discussed to be key elements such as: establishing modelling “roles” within and external to the organization, defining modelling boundaries driven by project objectives, “goal-oriented” modelling and model outputs, and proactively modelling for collaboration. With a targeted effort to optimize the model development process, the encumbrances around segmented responsibilities and distributed work environments take a back-seat while data discipline and analytical consistency become inherent, to ensure unhindered productivity growth.

title: Effect of Uncertainty in Prior Knowledge on Test Planning for a Brake Caliper using the Probability of Test Success
authors: Alexander Grundler, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, University of Stuttgart; Bernd Bertsche, University of Stuttgart; Key words: prior knowledge, probability of test success, reliability demonstration, test planning, uncertainty
summary:
In order to demonstrate a product’s reliability requirement, it is necessary to plan efficient tests that are firstly capable of demonstrating this requirement and, secondly, have a minimum sample size and conserve as many resources as possible. The concept of the Probability of Test Success [1], [2] is a highly suitable assessment method in this regard. In addition to the α error (type-I error) of the test, it also allows the β error (type-II error) to be considered, therefore enabling test assessment using the statistical power. Since statistical power can only be calculated for a certain effect size, prior knowledge is required for planning tests. In existing concepts, prior knowledge has been assumed to comprise scalar values of the parameters of a failure distribution. In reality, however, this prior knowledge is always associated with uncertainty. The aim of this paper is to outline an approach for incorporating this uncertainty into test planning and to demonstrate how it affects planning. For this purpose, tests are planned for a brake caliper from a commercial vehicle’s brake system. The prior knowledge stems from prior end-of-life (EoL) tests.
The studies show that the uncertainty of prior knowledge (implemented in the form of a bootstrap Monte Carlo simulation) can be effectively taken into account when calculating the Probability of Test Success. For the brake caliper, tests with failures are compared to tests without failures (or with only a few failures) to demonstrate reliability. There is a clear disadvantage when using tests without failures, although considering uncertainty makes this even more pronounced and generally leads to a reduced Probability of Test Success. This serves to emphasize how the uncertainty of prior knowledge should be taken into account in reliability-test planning. Otherwise, a test might be selected that does not have the desired properties and—in the worst-case scenario—will not demonstrate the reliability requirement, which would incur significant additional effort in testing.
In general, there are two very common reasons for reliability testing, the first of which is estimating failure distribution. The second is demonstrating the reliability requirement. The former is usually planned as a test with failures; an end-of-life test [3]. The latter is usually planned as a test without failures; a “success run” (SR) test [3], [4]. The approach presented here is novel in the sense that all possible test types can be considered for the reliability demonstration and are compared objectively. In addition, it can be seen that the EoL test often has a clear advantage over the SR test, even for the sole purpose of demonstrating reliability, while still allowing for an estimate of the failure distribution. The concept of using the Probability of Test Success and assessing all available test types and configurations enables the reliability engineer to gain a holistic view of planning for reliability-demonstration tests and makes for a very efficient test with minimal risk.
