title: A Taxonomy to Classify Discrepancy Reports for Space Systems
authors: Naoko Okubo, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency; Yasushi Ueda, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency; Noboru Tonoya, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency; Masafumi Katahira, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency; Key Words: discrepancy report, on-orbit failure, taxonomy, failure category
summary:
Discrepancy reports contain a rich source of information on failure modes and corrective actions. However, to fully use the discrepancy reports, it is essential to analyze the discrepancy reports and prepare for the subsequent use.
In this paper, we propose a novel taxonomy to classify the discrepancy reports for space systems. The categories in the taxonomy are expected to be use as a label for the classification task by the semi-supervised method and enhance the analysis of the discrepancy reports. Furthermore, since the discrepancy reports are expected to prevent similar failures, the proposed taxonomy has categories organized with the failure feature.
Two decades of on-orbit satellite anomalies from discrepancy reports has been utilized to confirm the validity of the proposed taxonomy. Also, we clarified the necessity of the novel taxonomy with the comparison of the conventional taxonomy. The comparison suggests that the proposed taxonomy well represents the characteristics of the population of discrepancy reports and highlights the necessity of the novel taxonomy.
conclusions:
In this paper, we proposed the novel taxonomy to classify the discrepancy reports for space systems. The proposed taxonomy has categories organized with the feature of the failure rather than according to the process, sub-system, or technical detail. Since space systems are non-mass-produced, it is important to learn from experienced failures presented in discrepancy reports. The taxonomy categories are expected to be used as labels for classification by a semi-supervised method and to enhance the analysis of the discrepancy reports. In the proposed taxonomy, we defined seven categories: (1) random hardware failures, (2) hardware design and manufacturing failures, (3) systematic failures, (4) human error, (5) transient failures, (6) degradation without failure, and (7) unknown. These categories represent the high-level causes of failure in discrepancy reports and support analyzing the experienced failures from a product perspective. Also, the categories can be treated as label data for semi-supervised classifications. The success of the classification with machine learning may determine the appropriate effort balance for the analysis and improving the visibility of analysis workload on free text in discrepancy reports.
The proposed taxonomy has been used to show the two decades of on-orbit anomalies recorded by the organization. As a result, the categories in the proposed taxonomy can enable us to understand the circumstances of on-orbit satellites well. Also, we clarified the need for our taxonomy by comparing its results with those of the conventional taxonomy. The comparison suggests that the conventional taxonomy is inadequate to represent the shifting of current space systems development. In future work, confirming the accuracy of the classification result with the labels from the proposed taxonomy will be essential.

title: DC 6 Through 737 MAX – Identifying Unreliability with In-service Precursors to Avoid the First Crash
authors: Jan B. Smith, PE, PMF Series; Precursors, Event Intervals, LaPlace Trend Test, Design Flaws, Probability, Monte Carlo, Event Interval Probability Analysis
summary:
Before the first design flaw related crash or emergency landing in an aircraft fleet, there are less severe events that signal a reliability problem.  The significance of these precursor events is easily recognized in hindsight during crash investigation; however, they are often unnoticed or dismissed prior to a crash or emergency landing.  Intentional use of precursors provides an early opportunity to recognize a reliability issue and to eliminate even the first design related crash or emergency landing.  This paper reviews the DC 6, DC 8, DC 10, Boeing 787, and Boeing 737 MAX.  These planes had design flaws that existed on the day they were placed into service, and they caused major events – crashes and emergency landings.  These major events were preceded by precursor events that occurred after the fleet was placed into service, but before the first major event.  Of the 937 fatalities caused by the design flaws in this review, 96% are shown to have been avoidable with attention to in-service precursors and data analysis of the precursor and major event intervals.
The precursor analysis uses a newly developed data analysis method - event interval probability analysis (EIPA).  EIPA was very recently used on major aircraft events, using data existing at the time of the events.  Hundreds of fatalities were shown to be avoidable with incorporation of p-values in fleet grounding decisions [Ref 1, 2, 3].  EIPA applies statistics, probability and reliability theory, and Monte Carlo simulation to event intervals.  This paper is focused on application of the method to precursors.
The design flaw, major events and precursors are described for each airplane type.  Fleet unreliability is determined with EIPA probability values (p-values).  P-values test a null hypothesis that event intervals are consistent with the then existing world-wide jet carrier fleet fatal accident rate.  With the null hypothesis that the fleets are as reliable as their contemporaries rejected, computer simulation generates departures to event probability distributions.  From these probability distributions, the risk of operation over any future number of departures is determined.  This quantifies the unreliability of the fleets and informs as to how fast the design flaw must be corrected and whether the fleet should be grounded.
In the fleet reviews, the early unreliability of the new fleets was unrecognized.  Precursors were not sought out by the industry.  When precursors were uncovered, they often were dismissed out of hand.  In this review there was no case in which corrective action upon precursors was sufficient to avoid the major event.  Meaningful action was taken only after at least one crash or emergency landing.  This paper makes the case that precursors should be vigorously sought out and used.  The DC 10 and 737 MAX case studies are reviewed in some detail to show why this will require both a paradigm shift in how precursors are viewed and routine data collection with a defined taxonomy and automated contemporaneous event interval probability analysis applied to the in-service precursors.  Because statistically significant precursors are rare, there will be a massive number of negative results; therefore, practical application will require management by exception.  Routine and automated data analysis should screen and report for review only the very small number of precursor interval p-values that flag need for investigation.
This paper has nothing to do with design and development of the aircraft.  It considers events that occur after the plane is placed into service.  This allows automated EIPA to monitor and alarm on in-service aircraft fleet reliability/safety performance problems independently of the design and certification process.  While assurance of the safety of new designs is being continuously improved, growing design complexity will continue to assure lack of perfection.  Both history and common sense suggest that independent in-service performance monitoring is required.

title: An Effective Prediction Approach for Satellite Probability of Success
authors: Wei Huang, PhD, Maxar Technologies; Roy Andrada, Maxar Technologies; Dale Borja, Maxar Technologies; Sabrina Way, Maxar Technologies; Key Words: Satellite platform, MIL-HDBK-217, on-orbit demonstration, prior distribution, Bayesian posterior estimator
summary: Reliability prediction (probability of success) using the MIL-HDBK-217 models is deemed conservative compared to actual observed reliability.  This paper proposes an approach to adjust satellite probability of success prediction from the MIL-HDBK-217 models supplemented with on-orbit flight data.  Using a proposed adjustment factor, this paper narrows the gap between the predicted and on-orbit demonstrated probability of success.  The contribution of unit types to the adjustment factor is also developed.  A Bayesian posterior estimate is used in order to avoid dramatic changes in the adjustment factor due to on-orbit data fluctuation.  An example is provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in predicting the probability of success.  And, finally, a proposed path-forward is outlined.
conclusions: This paper proposes an approach for adjusting the system level reliability prediction from MIL-HDBK-217 models based on on-orbit flight data.  An adjustment factor is introduced to narrow the gap between the prediction and on-orbit demonstrated probability of success.  The influence of unit types to the adjustment factor is considered.  A Bayesian posterior estimate is also proposed to avoid dramatic changes in on-orbit demonstrated probability of success caused by temporal data fluctuation.  The example demonstrates the effectiveness in estimating the on-orbit probability of success.  Although this paper focuses on satellite platforms, the proposed approach can be applied to any type of system or subsystem.  Also, the established adjustment factor values are per the size of unit type B only.  To make the adjustment factor more consistent with any design configuration, a more comprehensive study needs to be performed to incorporate other types of design features and/or units in order to establish a complete set (or matrix) of adjustment factor values so that each design configuration has a value that most reflects the design.  This work warrants a possible future study.

title: Analytical Modelling and Simulation Of DRX Mechanism for Energy Harvesting
authors: S. Dharmaraja, IIT Delhi; Anisha Aggarwal, PhD, IIT Delhi; Kamlesh Naresa, IIT Delhi; Key Words: Active State, DRX, Non- Active State, User Equipment
summary: We investigate energy harvested by the UE using continuous time Markov model. We focus on the energy harvesting results obtained using four states Markov model. These results are obtained using two different scenarios based on the timings for which harvester is on, depending on the Radio Resource Control (RRC). The energy consumption results under these scenarios are also analyzed in both situations when UE is harvesting energy and when it is not harvesting energy. The results are obtained by performing simulation in the Network Simulator 3, NS3, which includes detailed models of all the layers and functions of long-term evolution, LTE.

title:
Analysis of Safety-Critical Cloud Architectures 
with Multi-Trajectory Simulation
authors: Armin Zimmermann, Technische Universität Ilmenau; Thomas Hotz, Technische Universität Ilmenau; Volker Hädicke, Thales Transportation Systems Deutschland; Martin Friebe, Thales Transportation Systems Deutschland; Key Words: Discrete Event Modeling & Simulation, Fault Tolerance and Safety Critical Systems, Reliability Modeling
summary: Dynamic safety-critical systems require model-based techniques and tools for their systems design. The paper presents a stochastic Petri net model of an industrial safety-critical cloud server architecture for train control. Its reliability has to be evaluated to assess tradeoffs in architecture and level of fault tolerance. Simulation methods are too slow for such rare-event problems, while numerical analysis techniques suffer from the state-space explosion problem. The paper extends a recently developed multi-trajectory simulation algorithm combining elements of simulation and numerical analysis such that it increases the accuracy of rare-event simulations within a given computation time budget. Simulation experiments have been carried out with a prototype tool.

title: Machine Learning Models for SSD and HDD Reliability Prediction
authors: Riccardo Pinciroli, Ph. D., Gran Sasso Science Institute; Lishan Yang, William & Mary; Jacob Alter, Ipsos North America; Evgenia Smirni, Ph. D., William & Mary; Key Words: Supervised learning, Classification, Data centers, Storage devices, SSD, HDD
summary: This paper compares hard disk drives (HDDs) and solid-state drives (SSDs), the two most used storage devices in data centers, which frequently fail and are among the main causes of data center downtime. Using a six-year field data of 100,000 HDDs from the Backblaze dataset and a six-year field data of 30,000 SSDs from a Google data center, we characterize workload conditions that prompt drive failures. %and show that they differ from common expectation. We develop machine learning models that accurately predict the drive failure state several days in advance and provide highly interpretable results that are useful to identify the causes and symptoms of drive failures.
conclusions: In this paper, we investigate SSD and HDD failures using two traces from production environments. Daily logs for 30,000 SSDs are collected at a Google data center, while 100,000 HDDs are observed at a Backblaze data center. We train and test different classifiers to predict faulty SSDs and HDDs, and note that Random Forest models provide accurate predictions with a short training time. Their high interpretability makes them the best predictor for the analyzed problem. We observe that splitting each dataset based on attribute values of its observations allows increasing the performance of random forests. The drive age is a critical attribute for predicting SSD failures; drives failing before being three months old can be detected easier than other drives. When predicting faulty HDDs, a higer detection rate is observed for drives with head flying hours (SMART 240) longer than 40,000 hours.

title: Data Mining and Machine Learning Methods for Robust Reliability Predictions on Automotive Components
authors: Marco Bonato, PhD, Valeo Thermal Systems, France; Murali Krishnamoorthy, Valeo India; Philippe Goge, Valeo Thermal Systems, France; Key Words: Data mining, machine learning, natural language processing, reliability predictions, big data.
summary:
The ability to deliver fast and accurate reliability predictions is a key factor in order to accelerate the design validation phase during product development.
Like any other worldwide organization, the authors company (a major tier-1 automotive components supplier) relies on several IT solutions to store diversified types of data: from production/manufacturing parameters to warranty claims, from customers’ specifications (accelerated durability tests) to results of bench validation tests.
Data mining (DM) is the process of generating insights from large datasets.  The approach involves multidisciplinary tools across disciplines like data science (mainly artificial intelligence), statistics, and database management.  A data mining approach has proven to be of great help in obtaining needed information by digging into the company's existing databases and collecting sets of desired data. title: Reliability-Aware Requirements Development for Autonomy Software
authors: Leila Meshkat, Ph. D., Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Gudjon Magnusson, Fraunhofer CMA; Madeline Diep, Ph. D., Fraunhofer CMA; Mikael Lindvall, Ph. D., Fraunhofer CMA; Key Words: goal-based, requirements, reliability, decisions
summary:
Autonomy is the ability of a system to make decisions and take actions in the presence of uncertainty.  Validating autonomy, therefore, is a matter of validating that the system makes intelligent decisions even when there might be discrepancies between the observed and the expected state of the world as well as when the possible outcome of the possible courses of action is uncertain. During the requirements engineering phase, the functions and their expected behavior are specified. However, in the case of autonomous system, it is challenging to specify all possible scenarios that they may encounter. Since autonomous behaviors cannot always be predetermined, it is difficult to reason about their completeness and correctness. While these challenges are also faced with non-autonomous system, they are more prevalent for autonomous system due to their complexity and emergent behavior.
Our efforts have been threefold.  We developed a goal-based method for requirements decomposition.  We embedded the method into a system engineering framework and developed methods for decision and reliability analysis during operations.  We used simulation analysis to validate the theoretical methods and provide feedback.
The decision analysis approach (DA) helps in identifying and mitigating the run-time risks by bringing to the forefront the uncertainties, decisions, interactions, and other factors that may cause autonomous software to make erroneous decisions. The DA is used to quantify, for each decision that the software can make, failure risk due to uncertainties. The information about key decisions and circumstances that can cause autonomous systems to make incorrect decisions are used to generate test scenarios to be run in a simulator to ensure that the system can handle error-prone circumstances. The simulated decision outcomes are leveraged to further gain insight of the assured system.
We combine a goal-based approach with simulation analysis to facilitate requirements development for autonomous systems and provide a method for run-time systems level reliability considerations during the autonomous software development process.  The DA and the reliability analysis methods provide a formalism for the consideration of uncertainty in the run time decision-making process for autonomous software.  This formalism considers the uncertainty involved in the outcome of different courses of action, in terms of performance and cost, as well as a method to consider the system level reliability implications.  System level reliability considerations for autonomous software decision making contribute to the satisfaction of the system level goals over the lifecycle of a given mission.  We demonstrate our approach using a hypothetical rover path planning requirements example based on literature about Mars rovers and lessons learned from real world observations at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) [2]. The specifics of the Mars rovers, which have not been cleared for external release, are not used for our demonstrations.

title: Leveraging Traditional Design for Reliability Techniques for Artificial Intelligence
authors: Benjamin Werner, Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center; Benjamin Schumeg, Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center; Key Words: design for reliability, artificial intelligence, machine learning, trust and assurance
summary:
Across academia, industry, and government there has been a resurgence of interest and development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as it emerges from a second winter.  With advances in microchips, networks, sensors, and data storage, AI and Machine Learning (ML) are becoming more accessible and feasible for utilization in fielded products to assist end Users with faster decision making and lightened cognitive load.  However, with these advances in technology there is also concern of deploying products that may behave in unpredictable, erratic – or, in general, unreliable ways.  These concerns, among others, have been voiced by boards, organizations, and government appointed commissions such as the Defense Innovation Board (DIB) and National Security Commission on AI (NSCAI).  Even at the highest levels of leadership, the Secretary of Defense has stated that “Our development, deployment, and use of AI must always be responsible, equitable, traceable, reliable, and governable” [1].  All the voices and reports have a common theme and request: a push for means and methods to ensure assurance of AI enabled systems, and ultimately trust from evaluators and users.
The concepts of assurance and trust depend on the system exhibiting expected or desired behaviors.  This can be closely correlated to the definition of reliability in an engineering sense: the probability of a system performing its intended function under expected conditions for a given period of time.  While there have been pushes across government and academia through working groups and commissions to develop means to assure AI, it is imperative to derive lessons learned from how reliable and assured systems have been developed in the past.  There is a vast compendium of knowledge of reliability that can and should be leveraged in the design and development of AI enabled systems.  While the introduction of AI may bring with it new challenges, the basic tenets and principles ultimately are steadfast.
The use of Design for Reliability (DfR) tools and techniques should be applied to design and development, just like for any other traditional system.  It is understood that there may be some required augmentation or adaptation, but the intent of tools originally designed for traditional systems can be leveraged for AI enabled applications.  The DfR tools reviewed in this paper will include the Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Reliability Block Diagram (RBD), Highly Accelerated Life Testing (HALT) and Physics of Failure Analysis (PoF).  Successful and effective execution of these tools requires the integration of reliability engineers into design and development teams to truly influence the design and build in reliability.  These tools have been demonstrated and recommended for use in the development of traditional systems and will be presented here as means to develop and design for reliability and assurance in AI enabled systems.  The application of such tools and processes will begin to establish a framework to develop, qualify, and release reliable and assured AI.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Health State Diagnosis and Prognostics
authors: Gabriel San Martín Silva, UCLA; Enrique López Droguett, PhD., UCLA; Key words: Risk, reliability, quantum computing, machine learning, qubits, prognosis and health management, fault diagnosis
summary: Quantum computing is a new field that has recently attracted researchers from a broad range of fields due to its representation power, flexibility and promising results in both speed and scalability. Since 2020, laboratories around the globe have started to experiment with models that lie in the juxtaposition between machine learning and quantum computing. The availability of quantum processing units (QPUs) to the general scientific community through open API’s (e.g., IBM’s Qiskit) have kindled the interest in developing and testing new approaches to old problems. In this paper, we present a hybrid quantum machine learning framework for health state diagnostics and prognostics. The framework is exemplified using a problem involving ball bearings dataset. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to harvest and leverage quantum computing to develop and apply a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning approach to a prognostics and health management (PHM) problem. We hope that this paper initiates the exploration and application of quantum machine learning algorithms in areas of risk and reliability.
keywords: reliability, availability, PHM, prognostics, machine learning

title: Reliability Analysis with Partially Observed Information
authors: Yanwen Xu, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Pingfeng Wang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Key Words: Adaptive sampling, GP-based model, Missing data, Partially observed information, Reliability analysis.
summary: This paper presents a new method for reliability analysis with partially observed information, which integrates the Bayesian Gaussian process latent variable model (BGP-LVM) with adaptive sampling to iteratively select new partially observable training sample points to improve the reliability modeling efficiency. BGP-LVM is used to exploit all available information, instead of using the fully observed part only. Then, a new adaptive sampling criterion is designed for partially observed information considering the missing frame and information cost and used to iteratively select new training sample points to further improve the efficiency of the surrogate model development process. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first work designing adaptive sampling and adaptive surrogate modeling approaches for the dataset containing missing values. The numerical experiments demonstrated that the proposed adaptive surrogate modeling method can effectively utilize all available information including fully observed data and partially observed data. More importantly, it provides a more accurate and cost-efficient result by taking advantage of extra partially observed information.
conclusions:
An efficient adaptive surrogate modeling technique is proposed to iteratively select new partially observable training sample points to improve the reliability modeling efficiency. The main goal of the current study is to utilize information from different sources even different dimensionalities comprehensively for system performance estimation and reliability analysis, instead of only using fully observed information that might be expensive to obtain or difficult to derive. A novel adaptive sampling strategy is designed for the partially observed information, and the proposed PV sampling criterion takes the missing frame and cost of different information into consideration. The first example shows that the proposed strategy can be easily extended to incorporate traditional sampling criteria. The second experiment shows that the proposed adaptive surrogate strategy employing the PV sampling criterion provides a more accurate result by incorporating partially observed information and reduces the sampling cost.
Although the proposed adaptive surrogate strategy for partially observed information performs well, we see an opportunity to get further improved in few areas. First, the instability of the surrogate modeling strategy can be further reduced by initialization strategies. Second, the optimization can also be added into the updating process to minimize the total cost for both data collecting and design process, such as the reliability-based design optimization problems.

title: Improving Reliability by Reducing Complexity with Axiomatic Design
authors: Harry W. Jones, Ph.D., NASA Ames Research Center; Key Words: Axiomatic design, System Complexity Metric, SCM
summary:
Axiomatic design theory was developed by Suh at MIT in 1990 and has been widely applied.  Axiomatic design develops a hierarchy of subsystem requirements and designs together in a top-down, back-and-forth process.  A coupling matrix is used to control the relationships between the subsystem functions and design concepts.  Axiomatic design can improve system design by formalizing and rationalizing the design process.
A complex system has many different parts and many interconnections between them.  More complex systems often have higher costs and lower reliability. Axiomatic design produces a hierarchy of decoupled subsystems with deliberately reduced complexity.
The System Complexity Metric (SCM) is a measure of complexity that can be used to track the reduction of complexity in design and to roughly predict the relative cost and reliability of alternate designs.  The SCM is equal to the number of different subsystems or nodes, N, in the system plus the total number of one-way interconnections, I, between them. SCM = N + I.  The SCM can be found by direct inspection of the system block diagram.  It is intended to provide an early indication of relative system cost and failure rate.  Typically, the estimated system cost increases linearly with SCM and estimated and measured failure rate increases exponentially with the SCM.
Higher complexity makes failure diagnosis difficult.  When components or interconnections fail, the system schematic is simplified and the fault usually can be found quickly.  Some faults such as unexpected interactions or connections make the system diagram more complicated and are much more difficult to diagnose.  The need to reduce system complexity and the increased difficulty of diagnosis for more complex systems seem to reflect human limits on cognitive span and short-term memory.
The System Complexity Metric (SCM) is innovative.  It quantifies the intuitive human appreciation of complexity.  It can be used as the of measure of complexity for axiom 2 of axiomatic design.  It quantifies how hierarchical systems design reduces complexity.  It predicts relative system cost and failure rate.  It explains that failures that reduce complexity are easier to diagnose than those that increase complexity.

title: A System and Method for Assessing Reliability Improvements of Design Upgrades
authors: Bob Gissler, Halliburton; Pankaj Shrivastava, Halliburton; Key Words: Reliability Modeling, Reliability Management, Life Data Analysis, Design Optimization
summary:
Intelligent completion tools are permanently installed downhole in severe operating conditions and are designed to achieve high operational reliability in high temperature and pressure applications. The primary function of any intelligent completion is to allow the operator to remotely control the production or injection as well as to obtain real-time sensor data for each zone. This data feedback and accurate flow-control capability allows the operator to optimize reservoir performance and enhance reservoir management capabilities.
Flow control and permanent monitoring devices require hydraulic and/or electric power to perform their intended functions. Therefore, a hydraulic and/or electric umbilical are typically required. The downhole umbilicals presented in this paper are permanently installed in severe downhole environments and are rarely retrieved for any failure analysis or maintenance. The components of the baseline hydraulic umbilical design were used to design the electric umbilical. The electric umbilical includes the same primary pressure barrier as the hydraulic umbilical. The umbilical can be terminated at various locations along the completion string. These locations can include control, sensing, monitoring and/or communications modules.  Thereafter, a secondary pressure barrier was included to improve the reliability of the electrical umbilical. It was important to assess the reliability improvements of these design upgrades using a structured approach to determine if the system reliability targets have been met.
The reliability block diagram (RBD) was identified as the design-for-reliability (DfR) tool to model the system reliability of hydraulic and electric umbilicals and help assess the reliability improvements. An RBD for hydraulic/electric umbilical was developed by identifying the key subsystem and components comprising the umbilical. Each subsystem and component were then represented by a block. This block contains the reliability characteristics of the subsystem or component. The hydraulic umbilical currently operating in the field was considered as the baseline umbilical design. The RBD of the hydraulic umbilical was developed. And reliability characteristic of each block was evaluated by analyzing the field operational data using life data analysis techniques. The hydraulic umbilical reliability was allocated at the subsystem and component levels using a weighted approach based on the applied stresses on the components. Finally, these blocks were connected in a fashion that accurately represents the interaction required to sustain successful system operation.
An electric umbilical includes pressure components that are the same or like the pressure components of a hydraulic umbilical. The reliability of the pressure components was leveraged from hydraulic umbilical system reliability analysis. The reliability of some of the electrical umbilical components was estimated using reliability qualification test results of an intelligent completion tool. An increase of 3.5% was estimated for the reliability of electric umbilical with the use of a secondary pressure barrier. This results in significant increase in reliability of multizone completions where multiple terminations are used across different completion tools.
The standard based reliability prediction approach was used for estimating the reliability of both electric and pressure components, where reliability information wasn’t available from field history or test performance data. Reliability of the upgraded electrical umbilical was estimated by developing an RBD which represents the arrangement of components in the upgraded design. This paper highlights a successful application of RBD to develop a system and method for the reliability assessment of downhole electrical umbilical design upgrades.

title: Implementing Risk Management in a Public Transportation Agency
authors: Paul Franklin, McKissack and McKissack,; Darius Broughton,; H. J. Russell,; Key Words: Risk management, project controls, project management
summary: This paper is an experience paper that discusses implementing a risk management approach in a public transportation system.  MARTA, the public transit agency in Atlanta, is beginning a multi-decade capital expansion program. Experience with a prior project, the Atlanta Streetcar, indicated the need to become systematic and consistent with risk management.  The Authority has begun the process of implementing a standardized risk management process.  This process has been in place less than a year and is yielding results.

title: The Importance of Creating a Reliability Network
authors: Stephen May, PhD, Wood; Key Words: Reliability, Strategy, Networking, Tools, Techniques
summary:
Two networks are important for reliability.  There is a need to build a knowledge base covering reliability techniques and product awareness.  There is also a need to grow and maintain a network of internal and external contacts.
Many reliability tools and techniques are linked to one another.  If the connections are not created and refreshed, opportunities will be lost for maximizing reliability.  For example, technical risk, qualification, Failure Modes, Effects and Criticality Analysis (FMECA), Reliability, Availability and Maintainability (RAM) analysis and life data analysis are all interlinked.
Identifying technical risks at the start of product development or early in the project lifecycle is key to maximize the ability to address the risks.  Knowing what is being changed or is novel will ensure actions can be completed so the changes will not negatively impact reliability.  Applying appropriate effort to identify and mitigate risks through suitable qualification activities is possible if causes can be identified, by FMECA for example.
RAM analysis is a useful tool to predict system performance.  Developing RAM models in conjunction with FMECA allows the impact of failure to be documented and modelled correctly.  Output from any RAM model is highly dependent on the quality of the inputs used.  Capturing and analyzing actual product data for use in a RAM model is important.  Revisiting a model over the operational life of a project as actual data becomes available allows validation of the model and the potential to address differences through refining the model inputs.
Robust data capture, reporting and analysis of operational data is required to validate product and system performance.  Reliability data from actual usage should be determined and used to reassess and verify earlier analysis and conclusions remain correct.
As important as developing a network of tools, and arguably more critical, is the investment of effort into growing a network of people.  Even with the advent of Big Data and the Internet of Things, knowing who can provide access to information is key.  Also knowing and building trust with your sources and customers, internal and external to your organization, is essential.  Building a robust relationship with the leadership team to ensure adequate resources are provided for reliability is essential.
Continually pushing the boundaries of your network will help deliver robust products and systems by ensuring focus is given to reliability and the right information can be sourced.

title: Air Defense System-of-Systems: Reliability Concerns, Practices and Challenges
authors: Hava Avshalom, Israel Aerospace Industries; Grauer Emanuel, Israel Aerospace Industries; Tahar Effi, Israel Aerospace Industries; Key Words: Air Defense, Mission Critical Failures, MTBCF, System of Systems
summary: Military defense products are mission critical means to eliminate threats to citizens and strategic assets.  They are expected to operate for decades, under harsh environmental conditions, in different mission profiles.  Inevitably, the above characteristics are imperative for these products to be significantly reliable.  An Air Defense System (ADS) is a highly sophisticated System-of-Systems (SoS) built of fundamental elements, where each element may be considered an SoS in itself.  Achieving high reliability in ADS is a challenging task.  It starts in the early design stages, continues through production screening, testing and demonstration and ends with field monitoring.  This paper presents the major concerns regarding ADS reliability late activities, considers the limitations of qualification as against reliability demonstration, focusing on the interface between the seller and the customer. The use of MTBF calculations is compared to that of MTBCF calculations, and the effect of the repair policy on the MTBCF is discussed.  Besides specifying contractual reliability goals, both sides must establish a mutual effort to properly capture effective field data, demonstrate the reliability of the ADS, analyze field failures and initiate reliability growth processes if required.  These efforts are long term and require continuous cooperation, understanding the customer needs and the seller limitations.  Following each of these concerns, the paper presents best practice based on lessons learned, such as minimization of expected conflicts, by defining in advance, preferably in a Reliability Demonstration Plan (RDP), clear guidelines for failures classifications. Also, the best practice for data collection via FRACAS and field data analysis is indicated. Alternative methods to cope with these issues are also suggested.
conclusions: Military defense products are mission critical means to eliminate threats to citizens and strategic assets.  They are expected to operate for decades, under harsh environmental conditions, in different mission profiles.  Inevitably, the above characteristics are imperative for these products to be significantly reliable.  An Air Defense System (ADS) is a highly sophisticated System-of-Systems (SoS) built of fundamental elements, where each element may be considered an SoS in itself.  Achieving high reliability in ADS is a challenging task.  It starts in the early design stages, continues through production screening, testing and demonstration and ends with field monitoring.  This paper presents the major concerns regarding ADS reliability late activities, considers the limitations of qualification as against reliability demonstration, focusing on the interface between the seller and the customer. The use of MTBF calculations is compared to that of MTBCF calculations, and the effect of the repair policy on the MTBCF is discussed.  Besides specifying contractual reliability goals, both sides must establish a mutual effort to properly capture effective field data, demonstrate the reliability of the ADS, analyze field failures and initiate reliability growth processes if required.  These efforts are long term and require continuous cooperation, understanding the customer needs and the seller limitations.  Following each of these concerns, the paper presents best practice based on lessons learned, such as minimization of expected conflicts, by defining in advance, preferably in a Reliability Demonstration Plan (RDP), clear guidelines for failures classifications. Also, the best practice for data collection via FRACAS and field data analysis is indicated. Alternative methods to cope with these issues are also suggested.

title: Sustainable Quality
authors: Joseph Diele, Dell Technologies; Key Words: sustainable quality, continuous improvement, quality culture, quality strategy
summary:
What if, with relative minimal investment, your company was able to save between 20 and 30 cents of every dollar it earns or increase revenues or market share by like proportions? This isn’t a rhetorical question; rather this is what is attainable if one improves the quality of the product or service they deliver.  By eliminating poor quality activities and increasing good quality activities - companies save money and improve their bottom line.
Consider how much could you save if you did everything “right the first time”?  If you knew that everything was done right, you would not need to spend time (and money) on:  inspecting, re-inspecting, design changes, bug fixes, testing, re-testing, reworking, scrap, trouble-shooting problems.  You also would not need dedicated staff that deal with irate customers, complaints about poor service, product issues, or incur all the costs associated with returned products or service calls.
It is not unusual for companies that do not measure their Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ), to be spending as much as 30% of sales on poor quality activities.  That means that one & one-half days per week, you are re-doing work that was not done right the first time.  How much could you save if you cut that down to 1 day per week?  How about 4 hours per week?
The best way to understand the costs associated with poor quality is using a methodology called the Cost of Quality (COQ).  COQ splits quality costs into four categories:  prevention, appraisal, internal failures and external failures.  It is the internal and external failure costs that are associated with the Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ).
Let’s say a business made $30,000,000 in revenues last year.  If their COPQ was really at 30%, they would be spending $9,000,000 per year or $750,000 per month to do things over.  If the COPQ was reduced from 30% down to 20%, you would be saving $3,000,000 per year or $250,000 per month.  Ideally, you would like to have COPQ down below 10%.  This is not to say this it is easy, but it is possible.  This paper is intended to present some thoughts and ideas on how that might be achieved.
I have been working in quality for over 30 years, in both large corporations and small startups.  Reflecting back over my career, I kept coming back to a perplexing question.  Why is continuous improvement not continuous?
Before I try to answer “why”, think about all of our well-known quality models and when they were created.
Statistical Process Control (SPC) started in 1924.
Total Quality Management (TQM) started in 1985.
Six Sigma started in 1986.
ISO 9000 started in 1987.
Lean started in 1988.
These models are all over three decades old.  Clearly, they are still used today and continue to provide value.  However, business and the workforce have changed significantly over the last three decades.  Over the last thirty years, consider some of these changes.
Technology has evolved at an exponential rate.
Social media has connected us and created absolute transparency.
Global logistics have transformed supply chains.
Social movements have increased awareness to equal rights.
Pandemics have changed the workplace dynamics and structure.
Don’t you think we are about ready to take a more contemporary approach to how we view Quality?  I believe there is a new holistic way to look at quality.  One that takes into consideration all that has changed and will continue to change in our world.  One that embraces diversity, values, recognizes the individual.  This new model needs to provide just enough structure to make implementation and ongoing improvement truly continuous.  I call this new approach the Sustainable Quality Model, shown in Figure 1 [1].
Sustainable Quality starts by building a solid foundation, based on a culture of quality.  You need a strong positive culture that engages the workforce and brings out their best. Building on this type of foundation, you can develop a clear quality vision of where you want to be.  A vision that rallies the workforce and gives them purpose.  Your strategy should provide a roadmap for where you are going, with clear goals and objectives to get you there.  Once you have set the direction, you need to provide the right tools and the training to accomplish those goals and objectives.

Building on this type of foundation, you can develop a clear quality vision of where you want to be.  A vision that rallies the workforce and gives them purpose.  Your strategy should provide a roadmap for where you are going, with clear goals and objectives to get you there.  Once you have set the direction, you need to provide the right tools and the training to accomplish those goals and objectives.
I have had the opportunity to see firsthand what the impact can be when these concepts and practices are successfully implemented.  Being successful with quality, and more importantly sustaining that level of quality, is easier said than done.  It is my belief, that culture is the critical factor in whether a quality effort fizzles out or truly attains continuous improvement.  In fact, culture is a critical factor for any business success.
Much has been written about culture and how it can make or break a company.  Yet so many companies today are either unaware or unwilling to invest in the type of culture that elevates their business.  When your business is dealing with dysfunctional teams or worse, high turnover it should be no surprise that you are also dealing with a high cost of poor quality.  You might not recognize it as a quality cost, but you are likely struggling with excessive waste, low productivity, and repeated mistakes.
It is difficult to start a process improvement effort when the workforce is not yet ready for change.  In these situations, it is not unusual for people to just go through the motions.  At best, efforts slowly fade.  Worst case is trying to introduce change into a disengaged or even toxic environment.  In this type of culture, it is highly unlikely that people will go “above and beyond”.  In a toxic culture, people are doing the bare minimum until they can find a way out of that situation.  They most certainly are not focused on process improvement.  You must fix the culture before you can fix the process.
This new quality model is about management for the future, with the hope of raising businesses to a whole new level.  It is my strong belief that a better understanding and appreciation of quality and its direct correlation to culture will help you achieve that.
The sustainable quality model consists of three tiers.  Tier One is about building the right culture.  Tier Two is creating a quality vision and strategy.  Tier Three is using the right tools and training to make your implementation successful.

title: Predictive Maintenance Application in Healthcare
authors: Shafiya Sabah, American University of Sharjah; Mostafa Moussa, American University of Sharjah; Abdulrahim Shamayleh, Ph.D., American University of Sharjah; Key Words: Predictive maintenance; Healthcare; IoT; Remaining useful life; Deep learning; Big data; Data mining
summary:
Effective maintenance management of medical technology influences healthcare service quality delivery and the profitability of healthcare facilities. The objective of this study is to review recent research focused on medical equipment predictive maintenance. Predictive maintenance is a term that describes the use of sensors and forecasting techniques to anticipate when a device or machine would fail, so that preemptive measures can be undertaken to lessen the effects of an impending failure and subsequently improve service quality. In healthcare, this mostly pertains to medical devices and can be an invaluable tool that would save medical institutions money and time, and more importantly, mitigate adverse effects to patients that require these devices. Predictive maintenance is a means of providing some control in an otherwise chaotic and arbitrary industry; doctors, nurses, and administrators often do not see the value in repairing or replacing a device before it fails, especially if it were not crucial in their day-to-day or emergency operation. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of work that pertains to predictive maintenance in healthcare published between 2014 and 2019. The works reviewed were published in scientific journals and conferences, and for each one, we were interested in (1) what predictive maintenance techniques were used, such as Internet of Things (IoT) or deep learning (DL), (2) what devices/equipment were used to obtain results and (3) whether or not they were medical devices/healthcare-related, if not, how could this application apply to healthcare and (4) whether or not predictive maintenance is proven to be more effective than simply waiting for the lifespan of the device to come to its end. The reviewed papers all showed great potential in the techniques used for predictive maintenance and showed promising results for a variety of medical devices. The significance of this work lies in helping healthcare professionals realize the potential benefit that predictive maintenance can bring to the table, and how it fits with the cost-sensitive nature of the industry.
This review paper focused on the currently published researches that were specific to the concept of predictive maintenance in the healthcare industry. To the best of our knowledge and research, there is no review paper as of yet published on this topic.
We described in brief two of the most widely employed methods for predictive maintenance of medical devices namely- IoT and machine learning/deep learning. We described in detail the network architectures and some notable research works for each method.
Apart from IoT and machine learning/ deep learning we also discussed some other methods such as thermography, vibration analysis, and event log analysis for performance prediction of medical devices.
The review included predictive maintenance of simple medical devices such as infusion pumps and clinical analyzers to some of the high-tech critical medical assets such as the MRI. Also, highlights were provided of some of the design challenges that might be faced by healthcare organizations while implementation of IoT and big data technologies for predictive maintenance.
Overall, predictive maintenance though faced with certain challenges has the potential to improve the quality of patient care, reduce equipment repair costs, improve device reliability and prevent unexpected device breakdown. It is expected that more research will be done in the coming years to further validate the effectiveness of predictive maintenance strategy in the healthcare sector.

title: Solving the Problem of Medical Device Poor Quality
authors: Richard A. Harpster, PE, Harpco Systems Inc.; Key Words: FMEA, ISO 14971, ISO 13485, Risk Based Medical Device Life Cycle Management
summary:
Inadequate risk management by medical device providers is significantly impacting the safety of the customers they serve, the quality of their products and their profitability.  Billions of dollars are being spent yearly in the medical device industry on the direct costs of poor quality.  One would not expect this to be happening given that the medical device Industry is one of the most regulated industries in the world.  The required steps and volume of paperwork required to obtain medical device approval is second to no other industry.  The question that must be asked is if all this work is being done why are the direct costs of poor quality so high?
This paper will show that the current methods used by medical device providers being driven by standards such as ISO 13485:2016 “Medical devices — Quality management systems — Requirements for regulatory purposes” [2] and ISO 14971:2019 “Medical devices — Application of risk management to medical devices” [1] are ineffective at managing risk because they are ineffective at defining the root causes of risk exposure. The reader will learn how a medical device provider can consistently comply with these standards while creating medical devices that will fail to meet the users’ needs.
The paper will introduce the reader to Risk Based Medical Device Lifecycle Management™ (Risk Based MDLM™).  Risk Based MDLM™ is very effective in reducing/removing the root causes of medical device poor quality through the systematic management of risk over the medical device’s entire life cycle from definition of user needs through to decommissioning and disposal of the medical device if applicable.
Risk Based MDLM™ uses tools many readers may have heard of such as Design FMEAs, Process FMEAs and Application FMEAs.  Because of this some may come to the incorrect conclusion that there is nothing new in Risk Based MDLM™.  Although they have the same names, the FMEAs used in Risk Based MDLM™ are fundamentally different than the FMEAs being used by 99% of the companies in the medical device industry.  The paper will explain why the vast majority of FMEAs currently being performed by medical device companies are ineffective in managing risk and why the FMEAs used in Risk Based MDLM™ are the most effective risk management tools in existence.  Existing medical device industry paradigms about the purpose of FMEAs and the steps required for their proper performance are the greatest barrier to the effective implementation of Risk Based MDLM™ and the significant benefits it can provide.

title: Causal Inference in Longitudinal Studies Using Causal Bayesian Network with Latent Variables
authors: Phat Huynh, North Dakota State University; Leah Irish, PhD, North Dakota State University; Om Prakash Yadav, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Arveity Setty, MD, University of North Dakota; Trung (Tim) Q. Le, PhD, North Dakota State University
summary: Longitudinal studies have been broadly used in clinical research to investigate the associations between exposures or treatments and the outcome of the diseases, such as disease onset, subsequent morbidity, and mortality. However, few studies emphasize the causal relationships between observed variables and latent, time-varying confounders. The causal Bayesian network (CBN) shows promise in handling multiple causes and effects. This paper presents an extension of the Bayesian Network for Latent Variable (BN-LV) framework that quantify the causal effects of the latent variables in CBNs by imposing various constraints for the identification of latent structures and the structure learning algorithms. The proposed model employs unit-level causal inference methods that can learn instance-specific causal mechanisms. The proposed model also provides “near” causality inference from the observational data, eliminating causal edges from the traditional BN-LVs framework. The method was validated using a case study: Temporal Associations Between Daytime Napping and Sleep Outcomes. The results showed the quantification for the average causal effects of napping on nocturnal sleep measures and the construction of a learned causal graph involving latent variables.
conclusions:
In this paper, we proposed a new method to address two shortcomings of CBNs, which are instance-specific causal structure learning and the identification of LVs. In addition, we extended the framework to apply in longitudinal studies by imposing multiple constraints in both the LVI algorithm and the structure learning algorithms. We applied unit-level causal inference techniques after the CBN structure was learned to learn about the instance-specific causal mechanisms. This helps validate the “near” causality inferred in structural models from the observational data and eliminate incorrectly learned causal edges from the BN-LV methods. The proposed model was validated in a case study to investigate the temporal associations between daytime napping and sleep outcomes. The results have quantified the causal effects of napping on nocturnal sleep measures and constructed a complete causal graph with LVs.

title: An Unsupervised Machine Learning Framework for Availability Improvement of CT Systems
authors: Ikenna Anthony Okaro, Ph.D., Royal Philips; Olaf van der Burgt, Royal Philips; Key Words: Prognostics and Health Management, Big Data, and IoT Applications in R&M.
summary:
A data-driven framework and a methodology were presented in this work for improving the availability of fielded CT systems. It started with identification of unlabeled data which were relevant to a failure mode - overheating, as established from physics of failure and FMEA. Next, dimensionality reduction was performed on the dataset to extract useful features. Unsupervised ML based on the K-means algorithm was applied to the features to identify good and bad systems, with current, voltage, scan time and heat considered.
The elbow and silhouette methods were used to validate the ML prediction and its uncertainty was evaluated with Monte Carlo analysis. Thereafter, right-censoring was applied to the scan times and 2-parameter Weibull analysis was performed to generate the system reliability profile. Finally, the instantaneous availability was estimated by deriving MTTR and uptime from data.
The advantage of the concept lies on its ability to combine ML and classical reliability analysis in a way that promotes efficient system optimizations, in the face of scarce labeled life data. In future work, PCA may be compared against other feature selection methods. K-means performance may also be compared against hierarchical clustering. A model that involves the use of few labelled data and lots of unlabeled data would be interesting to study.

title: Fault Associated Propagation Hazard Analysis for Shared Resource Based on Model Checking
authors: Hongli Wang, Ph. D., China University of Labor Relations; Deming Zhong, Ph. D., Beihang University; Key Words: shared resource, hazard analysis, fault associated, fault propagation, model checking
summary:
Resource sharing is the most important feature of complex integrated system, so as to reduce the allocation of redundant resources in the system, and improve the utilization rate of resources and the overall efficiency of the system. However, such an integrated system has a low tolerance for fault of a single shared resource. Once the fault of shared resources occurs, the internal association can cause the collapse of the whole system, which increases the inherent hazard of the system.
The existing hazard analysis methods of shared resource fault correlation propagation, such as common cause analysis, network-based method and graph theory based hazard analysis method, can solve the problem of fault association propagation hazard analysis in a certain aspect. However, many existing methods have difficulty describing the potential causal relationship of fault propagation in the face of complex systems with high degree of integration. To solve the above problem, this paper proposes a hazard analysis method of association propagation based on improved model checking. The extended system modeling language is used to avoid the problem of isomorphism among different languages. A method of transformation from extended system modeling language to formal model is proposed. The hazard analysis method of associated transmission is mainly based on formal technology, and the analysis and verification are carried out from different aspects to find out the potential associated propagation path and impact.
Finally, a cockpit display system case is presented to illustrate how to analyze the hazard of fault associated propagation for complex integrated systems. The results of the case study show that the proposed method can help analyze potential associated propagation, and increase the efficiency of safety analysis work.
conclusions:
This paper has analyzed the influence of hazard associated propagation mode of shared resources in complex integrated systems. In view of the difference between system design model and safety analysis model, a hazard analysis method of associated propagation for complex integrated systems based on model checking in this paper.
System modeling language is adopted to improve the associated propagation model and describe the definition of transformation rules. The associated propagation model is transformed into a formal model. On this basis, the hazard analysis of associated propagation is carried out, and the path and influence of associated propagation is revealed.  This method can make clear the hazards of associated propagation of shared resources and their potential propagation path.
The findings of this paper open a new paradigm in complex integrated system hazard analysis, improving the efficiency of hazard analysis work.  It can replace NuSMV with other model checking tools such as SPIN or UPPAL, though further research is needed.

title: Using Big Data and Machine Learning to Improve Aircraft Reliability and Safety
authors: Marcos Salvador, Airbus Canada; Soumaya Yacout, Ph. D., Polytechnique Montréal; Ayman AboElHassan, Polytechnique Montréal; Key Words: artificial intelligence, machine learning, aviation, aerospace, risk analysis, safety assessment, risk assessment
summary:
The evolution of aircraft systems monitoring technology has made it possible to acquire increasing amounts of data.  The big volume of available information has helped aerospace companies to increase the reliability and availability of their products and to improve the safety of aircraft, flight crew and passengers.  In the event of system failures, the high complexity of the new aircraft systems, combined with the large amount of data provided by them, make the management of risk assessments a more complex activity and make the decision-making process more accurate but challenging. This process may lead to excessive conservatism when evaluating risk levels, which may in turn impact operation costs and production costs; increase the flight crew’s workload due to possibility to add more work to their normal tasks to deal with systems failures; or, conversely, lead to an underestimation of the criticality of the risk, thus exposing aircraft occupants to an unacceptable level of risk.
Logical Analysis of Data (LAD) makes it possible for input signals variables or condition indicators of different physical components to be combined and compared in multiple scenarios, in a process known as pattern recognition and interpretation of physical condition.  This paper addresses the potential for machine learning and pattern generation and interpretation to support reliability and safety in the aerospace industry.  It examines a set of three scenarios from industry practice: in the first two, Machine Learning (ML) is used as a supporting tool for reducing costs, and improving reliability and safety, respectively.  In the final scenario, ML is embedded in the system architecture to highlight the challenges of the use of ML in association with the current design assurance levels for software and real-time risk assessment.  The paper ultimately aims to lay the groundwork for a better decision-making process, supporting quantitative and qualitative assessment of the level of risk in an aircraft system.
conclusions:
Machine learning and pattern generation has potential applications in the aerospace industry, in support of improvements to reliability and safety. During the aircraft program’s in-service phase, the use of ML in risk assessment and re-design of components leads to the improvement of reliability, cost reduction and in a deeper evaluation of the interoperability between multiple systems. More specifically, ML facilitates the identification and consideration of unknown-unknown failure combinations, thus overcoming the limitations in human beings’ analytical capabilities.
In the development phase, machine learning and pattern generation is implemented in two ways: (a) in real-time systems, which is not covered in this paper, and (b) as a component embedded in the system, in interaction with other components of the same system that are not machine learning driven.  In this second case, the “classical” software approach does not seem to be an adequate method to support software based on ML. More research is thus necessary.
The increasing complexity of aircraft systems, evidenced in the rise of autonomous aircraft, for example the unmanned aerial systems (UAS), and electric vertical takeoff and landing [eVTOL] vehicles, among others) has brought new challenges in terms of ensuring the reliability and safety of aircraft.  The application of artificial intelligence is a promising area, with the potential for real benefit to the industry.  However, more research is still required to explore the full capacity of AI in the aerospace industry, which may require the adaptation of current regulation, and the creation of analysis support tools for risk assessment.
keywords: reliability, availability, safety, risk assessment, machine learning, AI

title: Functional Hazard Analysis of an Adaptive Cruise Control System - A Software Safety Requirements Engineering Case Study
authors: Vu N. Tran, Naval Air Warfare Center; Viet N. Tran, University of Southern California; Long V. Tran, University of Southern California; Dao N. Vu, University of California, Los Angeles; Key Words: Software safety, functional hazard analysis, software safety requirements.
summary:
As software rapidly replacing specialized hardware in safety-critical control systems, the need for software safety increases.  Software faults can trigger system hazards, which, if untreated, may result in system mishaps that can harm people, systems, and the environment.  Software safety, a subdiscipline of system safety, focuses on eliminating or reducing the software contribution to system hazards in safety-critical systems.  Functional Hazard Analysis (FHA) is an analysis method for removing or controlling hazards and hazard risks in systems [1].  When applied to safety-critical software subsystems, FHA can be used for identifying, analyzing, and mitigating software hazard risks.
Investigations of many high-profile system failures involving embedded software control consistently points to defective requirements as a primary cause [2].  Defective requirements are requirements that are incomplete, incorrect, conflicting, untestable, or unsafe.  Adding FHA into a software requirement engineering process can help improve the safety quality of the software requirements.  However, recent studies reveal that FHA has not been widely adopted in practice [3]. This problem is due to several reasons, including 1) software safety is presently not a topic covered in software engineering education and 2) practicing safety engineers often do not have sufficient software training to perform effective software hazard analysis [4], 3) engineers often mistook software safety as software reliability.  Heeding the call for more publications on software safety practice, we have published a series of papers on the use of hazard analysis methods in software development to fill this knowledge gap within the software community [5][6][13].
In this paper, we illustrate the use of FHA for software safety requirements engineering. We utilize the MIL-STD-882E FHA for this illustration.  Our goal is to introduce software engineers to the prescribed steps of an FHA process. We will use this method to develop the safety requirements for an automobile Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) system. Safety requirements include technical and process requirements to assure the system built is functionally safe.

title: Formulas of the Probabilistic Metric for Random Hardware Failures to Resolve a Dilemma in ISO 26262
authors: Sakurai Atsushi, FS Micro Corporation; Key Words: EOTTI, Markov Chain, Multiple-Point Failures, PMHF, Stochastic Process
summary:
The second edition of ISO 26262, which is the functional safety standard for automobiles, came into effect in 2018.  One of the improvements over the first edition is the revision of the probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF) formula.  The PMHF is the time-averaged probability of the violation of a safety goal (VSG) leading to inoperability during the life of a vehicle; it is a crucial metric since it is one of the target values for the hardware design of an automobile's electronic control unit (ECU).
However, the mathematical definition is not provided in the standard, and only the formula for the calculation is presented in Part 10-8.3.2.4.  Moreover, the standard does not describe the methodology for deriving the PMHF formula.  Therefore, in our previous paper, we verified the correctness of our model and the methodology by matching the PMHF equation of the first edition of the standard.  The second edition introduces the reparability of the intended functionality (IF).  However, the PMHF equation based on our methodology and the standard formula do not agree because the case analysis of the second edition may be insufficient.
The standard specifies a fault classification that includes detected multiple point faults (MPFs) and latent MPFs.  However, the standard does not describe whether to repair a fault after it has been classified as a detected MPF.  If a detected MPF is not repaired, it is considered a latent fault (LF), but an LF is a dangerous fault, which contradicts the definition of the latent fault metric in the standard that a detected MPF is a safe fault.  Therefore, there seems to be a dilemma in the standard.
The objective of this study is to resolve this dilemma by making a clear model based on a plausible real-world scenario and to derive a new PMHF equation using a validated methodology.  Specifically, we classify detected MPFs as being in the operational state of the IF and exclude them from the calculation of the state probability leading to a VSG.  Furthermore, for the first time, we derive a generic PMHF equation that is compliant with the standard.
The PMHF equation in the standard might overestimate the PMHF value, and this overestimation may lead to an excessive design constraint in terms of an emergency operation tolerance time interval (EOTTI).  The PMHF formula derived in this study can reduce the EOTTI by a factor of 40 compared to the value given in Part 10-Table 6 in the second edition.  Hence, our approach has the potential to mitigate the overdesign of automotive ECUs.

title: Decision Fusion for Fault Classification in Industrial Processes
authors: Ahmed Ragab, Ph.D., CanmetENERGY; Mouloud Amazouz, Ph.D., CanmetENERGY; Key Words: Decision Fusion, Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning, Energy Efficiency, Fault Detection & Diagnosis, Process Industries.
summary: This paper proposes an ensemble-based method that combines decisions produced by diverse machine learning classifiers, each with distinct pattern representations. The proposed method exploits the advantages of each classifier as a complementary information source to efficiently classify faults in industrial processes and provide plant operators with unified decisions. It uses the behavior knowledge space (BKS) method and updates its corresponding lookup table based on the F1-scores calculated for every single classifier. In this paper, the method is validated on a pulp mill process benchmark using simulated data. The obtained results demonstrate that the accuracy of the proposed ensemble is higher than the accuracy of every single classifier on this challenging application.

title: Physics-based Machine Learning with Filtering for Failure Prognostics Partially Observable Dynamic Systems
authors: Sara Kohtz, University of Illinois-Urbana-Champaign; Pingfeng Wang PhD, University of Illinois-Urbana-Champaign; Key Words: Kalman Filter, Physics-informed Machine learning, Neural Network
summary: This paper demonstrates a useful hybrid methodology for online capacity estimation of lithium-ion batteries. Essentially, a Kalman filter was embedded with a physics-informed neural network to optimize the connection between observable measurements and the hidden state. In this case, for the lithium-ion battery application, the hidden state is capacity, and the observable measurements are voltage. Fundamentally, the physics-informed neural network is a residual model, where the data-driven neural network models the error between the physics model and the noisy measurements. Overall, this structure performs well and has significant improvements over traditional Kalman filter frameworks. The paper is organized as follows: section 1 provides an introduction, section 2 explains the methodology, section 3 shows the results, and section 4 concludes with a discussion.
