title: On-Line Roughness Fault Detection Using Current Profile Measurement
authors: Mahmoud Awad, Ph. D., American University of Sharjah; Ali Y. Ebraheem, American University of Sharjah; Key Words: Fault detection, Roughness measurement, Multivariate process control
summary: With the advent of new technologies, customers are becoming more demanding of inexpensive and higher quality products. As a result, manufacturers are becoming keener to early fault detection during and post manufacturing processes. Fault detection has many benefits such as failure cost reduction, unplanned machine downtime reduction, and safety enhancement.  In this paper, a hybrid fault detection method is proposed to differentiate between high and low roughness surfaces during turning using motor current measurement. The proposed method is based on modeling spindle motor current profile and using profile parameters to detect any major deviations from the average healthy state.  Since several parameters are monitored simultaneously, multivariate statistical process control is utilized to flag deviations. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated, using two data sets of two different materials, Al 6061 and Al-SiC metal matrix composite. The proposed method successfully detected all faulty profiles in the two cases, when using sum of sine functions. However, one healthy profile was identified by proposed method as faulty in the case of Al-SiC. The proposed method is scalable and can be further refined and to actual manufacturing settings
conclusions:
FD is a critical step due to its significant in industry and impact on customer safety and satisfaction. It can save a lot of impact on customer safety and satisfaction. It can save a lot of cost and time through the detection of faulty semi-finished or finished products and avoid expensive internal and external poor-quality costs. In this research, FD is used to differentiate between rough and smooth surfaces machined using turning process. The proposed approach is a hybrid data-model driven FD method. It requires some understanding of the physics of turning in terms of roughness and power consumption and it utilizes modeling and charting of current profile. The current measurement is easy to obtain compared to vision, vibration, or acoustics sensor-based methods discussed in the literature review section.
Figure 1-Fitted line plot using the sine function
Figure 2 -T2 control chart
The proposed method is based on current profile monitoring using MVSPC-.  Profiles were modeled using sum of sine functions which found to be the best fit for the data collected.  Two different materials were used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The proposed method was successful in detecting all rough surfaces defined by specification for both Al-SiC MMC and Al 6061 materials.
The work pieces were machined by changing the turning parameters to generate surfaces with different roughness values. In real settings, machine parameters are fixed for the same product, so the profiles will be very similar to each other. In the presence of a special cause such as worn nose, cracked tool, improper setting, or formation of a chip, the profile will be significantly different. As a result, the detection of rough surfaces will be easier.  For future work, several ideas can be investigated. First, this study can be repeated with fixed turning parameters to investigate the impact of cutting-tool wear diagnosis. In this case, the decision is not limited to healthy versus faulty, but to the cause of increased roughness.  The economics of implementing this approach as a surrogate to other traditional ones is also warranted. Finally, more extensive studies to estimate false alarm occurrence rate and possible refinement to reduce it is worth pursuing.

title: Tools, Techniques and Methods for Complex, Phased Mission and Scheduled-Maintenance Systems Analyses
authors: Arun K. Somani, Iowa State University; Key Words: Reliability Analysis, Phased Mission Systems, Scheduled Maintenance Systems, Phase Algebra
summary:
All certification processes require designers to analyze the reliability of a system to predict its expected lifetime to guarantee performance and build user’s trust in the design. This is specifically true when the system needs to be deployed in critical applications. Most often than not, such systems are not designed, operated, and maintained differently. In today’s automated world, it is expected that specific monitoring and on-line and off-line repair mechanisms and aids are included where the system is maintained, repaired, or reconfigured during the system operation. Moreover, redundancy in components is used to achieve high reliability and fault tolerance in ultra-reliable systems. Accurate analysis of the reliability of a system requires that all major variations in the system’s design and operations are accounted for.
Most reliability analysis techniques and tools assume that a system is used for a mission consisting of a single phase. However, multiple phases are natural in many missions. The failure rates of components, system configuration, and success (failure) criteria may vary from phase to phase. In addition, the duration of a phase may be deterministic or random. Moreover, individual components may be repaired (if failed) such that repairs do not conflict with operations of the system. In other words, such repairs are independent of the system state. In many situations, the system may go through regularly scheduled maintenance, called maintenance check times, where specific components are repaired fully. Such systems are called Scheduled Maintenance (SM) systems. Therefore, the starting or dispatch state for an individual mission may be any of the possible operational states.
We describe various scenarios for an application to operate, and present techniques for reliability analysis of such complex systems. Our technique yields exact results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by analyzing several examples.
conclusions: Component redundancy is used to achieve high reliability and fault tolerance in ultra-reliable systems. Accurate modeling of such systems is an important and complex problem in the reliability analysis field. We presented various techniques to analyze systems that depict complex behavior and variable operation environment, including phased mission, scheduled maintenance, and monitored systems. We presented Phase Algebra that allows us to model phased mission system efficiently Our techniques are beneficial for a large class of systems where the system behavior can be described using fault trees, and components are either not maintained or maintained independently when not in use. Our techniques are computationally accurate and efficient, reduce solution time, and have been incorporated in reliability analysis tools.

title: Numerical Problems in the Solution of Markov Models for RAID Systems
authors: Andrew M. Shooman, PhD, Dell EMC; Martin L. Shooman, PhD, New York University; Key Words: Markov modeling, analytic methods, numerical methods, disk arrays, RAID
summary:
Markov models are used in a wide variety of reliability problems because it is easy to model complex devices and systems using nodes to represent combinations of failed elements and arcs between the nodes to represent failures and repairs.  For example, Figure 1 represents a system in which there are two groups of elements.  Node (State) 00 represents no failures in either group of elements, State 10 represents one failure in Group 1, State 01 represents one failure in Group 2 and State 11 represents one failure in each group.  All of these four states are successful.  If there are two failures in either group, the system enters the failed state X.  Since there are N disks in each group, each with a failure rate λ, the failure rate of the transition between states is Nλ.  The repair rates for each group of disks is μ1 or μ2.  Thus, a Markov model for a complex system is fairly easy to construct.  Each Markov state leads to a first-order differential equation.  Solution of this set of equations can be difficult. This paper examines some of the solution difficulties for Markov models in general, and specifically for several fairly complex RAID disk storage system models.
In this paper, we consider two different methods of solving Markov models: analytic and numerical.  The analytic method involves the Laplace Transform and the solution of the roots of the associated polynomial. Closed-form solution of this polynomial is limited to three or four states.  Higher-order polynomials require numerical methods to solve for the roots.  Since we have encountered problems in certain root-solving programs, we employ Newton's Method to improve the accuracy in solving for roots of cubic and higher-order polynomials.  As an alternate solution technique, we discuss the design and implementation of a deterministic Markov simulator.  Thirdly, in order to reduce the complexity of Markov models, we explore approximations via deleting low-probability states and merging equivalent states to simplify and facilitate solution.

Of course, the results apply to Markov reliability and availability models in general.  The simplest RAID system employs a backup disk for each data disk.  However, this is expensive.  Modern RAID systems employ one or more disks to back up a group of data disks.

Node (State) 00 represents no failures in either group of elements, State 10 represents one failure in Group 1, State 01 represents one failure in Group 2 and State 11 represents one failure in each group. Thus, a Markov model for a complex system is fairly easy to construct.  Each Markov state leads to a first-order differential equation.  Solution of this set of equations can be difficult. Of course, the results apply to Markov reliability and availability models in general.  The simplest RAID system employs a backup disk for each data disk.  However, this is expensive.  Modern RAID systems employ one or more disks to back up a group of data disks.

title: Cybersecurity Modelling for SCADA Systems: A Case Study
authors: Benny N. Cheng, PhD, Naval Surface Warfare Center, Corona Division; Key Words: cybersecurity, MTTSF, SCADA systems, attack and countermeasure trees
summary:
This paper describes a cybersecurity model for Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition system (SCADA) using techniques similar to those used in reliability systems modelling. Previously, cybersecurity events were considered a part of the reliability events of a cyber physical system . Our approach identifies and treats such events separately as unique class of events by itself. Our analyses shows that the hierarchical model described below has the potential for quantifying the cybersecurity posture of a SCADA system, which goes beyond the usual pass/fail metrics that are currently in use . A range of Mean Time to Security Failure (MTTSF) values as shown in the sensitivity studies below can capture both peacetime and wartime cyber risk assessment of the system. While the Attack and Countermeasure Tree (ACT) constructed below could be taken as somewhat simplistic, more detailed security events can be readily introduced to the ACT tree to reflect a better depiction of a cyberattack. For example, the Common Processing Systems (CPS) systems themselves can be further resolved into constituent components that are vulnerable to cyberattacks. Separate models can also be developed for each of the individual failure events, i.e. confidentiality, integrity, and availability, instead of combining them into one failure event as done below. The methodology for computing the MTTSF metric can be extended to other similar cybersecurity metrics, such as those formulated by the Center for Internet Security (CIS) , e.g. mean time to restore to operational status, etc. Additional improvements to the model can be obtained with the incorporation of the repair and restore portion of the semi-Markov chain in Figure 3, which will likely require the use of more advance modeling packages.

title: Software Reliability: Development of Software Defect Prediction Models Using Advanced Techniques
authors: Mayur Jagtap, John Deere India; Praveen Katragadda, John Deere India; Pooja Satelkar, John Deere India; Key Words: Defect prediction, Fuzzy logic, Growth model, Neural network , Software reliability, Software metrics
summary:
Development of next generation of smarter machines and services requires building an easy-to-use technology stack.  These technologies include hardware, embedded software, data, and applications.  Smarter machines support carrying out the precise job, better decision making, and create new ways of doing things to reduce cost and increase speed, accuracy, and automation.  As technology meets iron through smart machines, there is increased embedded software within products.  To provide distinctive customer experience for a solution system, along with reliability of hardware, development of reliable software also plays a critical role.
This paper proposes models in which software reliability is a function of the number of residual faults and is measured with the help of software metrics based on development data.  The intent is to establish a statistical relationship between product metrics (that deal with the measurement of the software product) or process metrics (the process by which it is developed) with measures of quality.  Using both a pattern recognition algorithm approach for classifying fault proneness and applying fuzzy logic to software metrics for defect prediction is found to be beneficial for improving software reliability prediction in early development phases. This paper proposes non-parametric models like Artificial Neural Network from deep learning to predict expected number of failures utilizing past failure data for software reliability estimation and release readiness during launch.
conclusions:
Reliable software is of great importance in product performance, safety, and customer satisfaction.  Software reliability can be approached in two ways
Software reliability estimation
Software reliability prediction
In this paper, we have studied applications of advanced techniques like deep learning and fuzzy logic, using them for software reliability estimation and prediction of embedded software for the off-highway equipment industry.  We have leveraged representative software metrics data from the early development phase and software defects data during testing for software reliability prediction.  We have applied the following three approaches:
Neural network-based cumulative number of software failures prediction during the testing phase
Pattern recognition algorithm for classifying fault prone software revisions
Fuzzy logic application to software metrics for number of software failures prediction
Performance of the neural network-based approach for cumulative number of software failures prediction is found to be superior to use of traditional software reliability growth models in testing phase.  Using both a pattern recognition algorithm approach for classifying fault proneness and applying fuzzy logic to software metrics for defect prediction is found to be beneficial for improving software reliability prediction in early development phases.

title: A Systems Approach for Cybersecurity Risk Assessment
authors: Leila Meshkat, Ph. D., Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Robert L. Miller, Ph. D., Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Key Words: cybersecurity, reliability, zero-day vulnerability
summary:
This paper presents a methodology for assessing the cybersecurity risk of an information system to support trade studies between competing architectures, risk mitigation, and risk-informed decision making.  It draws on key concepts from the fields of risk analysis, reliability engineering and cybersecurity. Standard system reliability studies do not readily translate to cybersecurity since (1) the cyber-failures are not random but caused by an attacker, and (2) the behavior of the attacker is not predictable.  In this paper, a new approach is presented to extend key concepts from risk and reliability engineering to include cyber failures.  The methods developed in this paper can be readily applied to quantitatively assess system cyber risk and provide reliability metrics.  These methods are therefore very practical for real world applications.
Cyber vulnerabilities are divided into three classes: known vulnerabilities with known threats; known vulnerabilities with unknown threats; and unknown vulnerabilities, which can occur due to zero-day vulnerabilities, or from a failure to follow procedures or successfully scan for identifiable vulnerabilities.  The classic definition of risk is extended to encompass cyber exploits.  The failure behavior of systems due to cyber exploits is defined and modeled using a combination of Markov Chains, Weibull analysis and Fault Trees.  Knowledge about a system’s network topology is used to assess exploitation paths.  Data used for quantifying the likelihood of an exploit is based on system performance metrics, such as cyber-hygiene; history of vulnerabilities, threats and exploits; and finally, industry statistics.
conclusions: This paper provides a systems analysis of cyber-risk and a methodology for finding the time-dependent likelihood of an exploit for a given networked system.  Novel classification and problem formulation methods transform a cyber security problem into one that can be addressed with reliability engineering techniques.   Key concepts from the disciplines of risk analysis and reliability engineering are then extended for the purpose of cybersecurity risk analysis.   A classification scheme is proposed to take into consideration the different factors that can cause an exploit for a given host, and the likelihood of occurrence for each of them.  These likelihoods are then integrated within a reliability analysis framework to yield the likelihood of occurrence for a given scenario of interest.  The methods developed in this paper have been demonstrated on several case studies with promising results.  The next step is the inclusion of these methods in security analysis tool-suites, so that quantified cyber reliability is used as a metric for analysis and decision making.

title: Modeling a DO-178C Plan and Analyzing in a Semantic Model
authors: Daniel Russell, GE Aviation; Abha Moitra, Ph. D., GE Research; Kit Siu, GE Research; Craig McMillan, GE Aviation; Key Words: certification, software development plan, system modeling, semantic model, MBSE
summary:
For years, the certification of software has been achieved by following the approach laid out in various DO-178 revisions. The general approach starts with defining a plan that describes the process to follow and the artifacts to produce in the course of developing and verifying the software. This plan must document how each of the objectives described in DO-178 will be addressed. This plan is then reviewed and agreed to with the Certifying Authority. Certification is then granted based on judgement on compliance: how well did the resulting artifacts demonstrate that the software development and verification plan was followed.
Traditionally this plan is made up of a series of textual documents. In a document-based approach, it is difficult to see how changes in various process steps impact other steps. Review of adherence to this plan is primarily a manual task—while certain checks can be automated, a human is still required to interpret the plan to identify those checks. Documents are not easy for an average user to reference on a daily basis—you often have to read the whole document(s) to get the appropriate context. And finally, because certification is the target, documents are often organized to aid the auditor and not optimized for use by an average engineer.
In this paper, we show how system modeling can be used in a novel way—to model a development process in addition to the product that is being developed. We demonstrate a SysML model focused on the Software Development Process, part of a software certification plan, and show its traceability to DO-178C objectives. We further demonstrate how the process modeled in SysML can be translated into a semantic model to analyze adherence to a plan, for example, making sure that source code is generated after the requirements review. The modeling approach described in this paper is different from that addressed by DO-331, which provides guidance on usage of model-based development tools in airborne software. Rather, the model introduced in this paper is that of the certification plan itself.
conclusions: A model of a development plan provides a clear, consistent, and unambiguous definition of the processes, with precise definitions of activities and artifacts produced. This is of great benefit to an average engineer because it eliminates inconsistent, individualize interpretations. It is equally beneficial to an auditor because the same model provides up-to-date views reflective of any changes to the process. Finally, analyzing the plan using a semantic model and reasoning engine  provides safety by ensuring adherence to the development plan.

title: Evaluation of the Robustness of MLE Method for Selecting the Best Fitting Lifetime Distribution
authors: Rose M. Ray, PhD, Exponent, Inc.; Ke Zhao, Exponent, Inc.; Key Words: warranty, Weibull, robust methodology, accuracy
summary: Warranty data and other time-to-failure data is frequently analyzed through the estimation of the parameters of one or more lifetime distributions including: two-parameter Weibull, three-parameter Weibull, Lognormal, Logistic, Gumbel, Gamma.  The form of some lifetime distributions is derived from the nature of the failure process, e.g., the Gumbel is used to model the maximum of a number of samples from the same distribution.   Other lifetime distributions, e.g., Weibull can be used to fit a wide variety of failure mechanisms.  When the form of the lifetime distribution is not specified by the failure mechanism, and there is no historical precedent demonstrating that a particular family of distributions is a good fit for the data in question, goodness of fit methods can be used to choose the form of the lifetime distribution that best fits the available data. The lifetime distribution chosen may have a large impact on the inferences drawn from the data, particularly when the subject of interest is future reliability or reliability projected beyond the range of the currently available data. Maximum Likelihood is one of the most popular distribution selection methods.  The robustness of Maximum Likelihood for choosing the ‘best’ lifetime distribution, and the impact of choosing the wrong distribution was evaluated by using Monte Carlo simulation to generate samples from four specified lifetime distributions. The Reliasoft® Weibull++ software and SAS were used to estimate the best fitting distribution and to estimate the B50, age at 50% failure, B90, the age at 90% failure.  Results of the research include the proportion of Monte Carlo runs that the specified lifetime distribution was correctly chosen as the best fitting distribution, and  comparison of the accuracy of estimates of B50 and B90 when calculated from the best fit distribution as compared to the B50 and B90 when calculated with estimated parameters for the Actual distribution. In this study, the Lognormal distribution was usually correctly selected while the Weibull and the Logistic distribution were frequently misidentified as another lifetime distribution.  Suggestions for addressing the practical implications of  misidentified lifetime distributions are discussed.

title: Reliability Demonstration Test Planning for Field Load Spectra – an Approach for Identifying the Optimal Test Parameters Considering Individual Cost and Time Constraints
authors: Achim Benz, University of Stuttgart; Alexander Grundler, University of Stuttgart; Thomas Herzig, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, University of Stuttgart; Bernd Bertsche, Ph. D., University of Stuttgart
summary: Over the past decades, product development cycles have become shorter and shorter, with reliability requirements increasing while budgets for testing have decreased.  To select a test that makes the best use of resources (cost and time) for reliability requirement with a sufficient level of confidence, a simulation is performed.  In previous work by Herzig et al. [3] and Grundler et al. [4] the concept of Probability of Test Success () introduced by Dazer et al. [1] was applied.  To improve the applicability of the test planning procedure, a load spectrum rather than a single field load level is now to be evaluated.  This is necessary because many products are not subjected to a single field load, but to fluctuating conditions that have natural causes such as the seasons, time of day or individual users.  Finally, a case study is evaluated for individual parameters of a test scenario to minimize test time and cost while maximizing .
conclusions: The approach presented in this paper allows the integration of load spectra and therefore damage accumulation into the planning of accelerated EoL tests.  Furthermore, the Probability of test success (), as well as costs and time can be used to determine the optimal test strategy for the presented example.  For this purpose, the optimal load levels and the respective number of specimens can be determined.  In summary, this means that reliability demonstration tests for accelerated and non-accelerated EoL tests can now be planned with real field spectra and potential savings in time and costs can be capitalized on.

title: Analyzing ALT Data with Time-varying Stress Profile
authors: Rong Pan, Ph. D., Arizona State University; Key Words: accelerated life test, stress profile, proportional hazard, Poisson regression, reliability prediction
summary: We are interested in analyzing the accelerated life testing data obtained under time-varying stresses. This is a generalization of step-stress accelerated life test, where the stress levels are kept constant at each step. Our study shows that the time-dependent proportional hazard model, commonly appeared in the survival data analysis literature, is not applicable for ALTs, because this approach does not take accounts of the cumulative damage that the stress profile exerts on test units. Instead, we assume that products possess constant failure rates over small time intervals, and the change of failure rate by the stress variable still have the proportional hazard property. With these assumptions, it is possible to formulate the data according to a generalized linear model and statistical inferences on model parameters can be carried out. We demonstrate our models and inference procedures by using both synthetic and real datasets.
conclusions:
In this study, we investigate the PH regression model for the profiled-stress ALT analysis. It is found that due to the cumulative damage concept the PH property cannot be maintained in the overall product failure time likelihood function; however, under the stricter assumption of stepwise exponential distribution, the PH property can be preserved for the failure rates of constant stress levels over a short time interval. This in turn facilitates the data analysis, as we can estimate the stress effect via a Poisson regression approach. As aforementioned, the optimal stress profile segmentation scheme needs to be further researched. Furthermore, extending this approach to Weibull distribution seems to be possible, worth of further investigation.

title: Accelerating Fatigue Qualification Tests
authors: Andrew Halfpenny, PhD, Hottinger Bruel & Kjaer UK Ltd; Balaje T. Thumati, PhD, Hottinger Bruel & Kjaer Inc.; Key Words: Accelerated Testing, Fatigue, Vibration, Qualification Testing, Reliability Testing
summary:
Fatigue failure occurs through long term exposure to time varying loads. Although modest in amplitude, these loads give rise to microscopic cracks that steadily propagate and eventually result in catastrophic failure.
Components are often qualified using accelerated reliability tests. Traditionally these are based on historical experience or national test standards. In many cases engineers have little information on which to determine the inherent safety margin of the tests. Consequently, these tests have led to unnecessary over-design and, in the worst cases, operational failures.
Test standards such as MIL-STD-810G have addressed this problem by introducing a process called ‘Test Tailoring’. However, these standards typically consider only vibration tests and not closed load path tests on structural components. This paper focuses particularly on these components. It considers the four most common types of structural test. A ‘decision tree’ is presented to illustrate where one test is preferable over another.
conclusions:
This paper has presented an overview of fatigue qualification tests with a focus on event data compression techniques for structurally loaded components.
It follows a highly structured process known as ‘Mission Profiling and Test Synthesis’. This process was introduced by several international design standards; however, these have tended to concentrate only on ‘Test Synthesis’ for vibration-induced loads. This paper has extended this to include tests used for structurally loaded components using both inertially reacted, and closed load-path tests.
The following structural tests were considered:
Constant amplitude tests.
Block load tests.
Peak-valley extraction.
Time-correlated fatigue damage editing.
A decision tree was developed to help the reliability engineer to select the most appropriate test method for the component/subsystem under test. The synthesized test will replicate the same fatigue damage as described in the ‘Mission Profile’ over an accelerated period.

title: Challenges of and Lessons Learned from Implementing an MBE FMECA in the DoD
authors: R. Christopher DeLuca, Office of the Under Secretary of Defense Research and Engineering; Timothy Schwartz-Watjen, Science Applications International Corporation; Walter Tomczykowski, Tomczykowski Group LLC; Key Words: Failure modes, effects, and criticality analysis, model-based engineering, digital engineering, risk identification
summary:
Over the past three years, DoD and industry Reliability and Maintainability (R&M) Engineering practitioners collaborated to develop methods to transition the Failure Modes, Effects, and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) process to a Model-Based Engineering (MBE) process.  The intent is to take advantage of MBE methods to support the move from delivery of a static document to delivery of a model that allows the program office and other users to query FMECA data, resulting in faster engagement, decreased design cycle times, and increased design influence. The collaboration identified challenges and lessons learned for DoD and industry R&M Engineering practitioners to transition to MBE methods to improve the FMECA process.
The transition of the FMECA to MBE methods is consistent with the DoD Digital Engineering Strategy. Digital engineering (DE) is an integrated digital approach using an authoritative source of truth (ASOT) consisting of system data and models as a continuum throughout the development and life of a system. DE updates traditional systems engineering practices to take advantage of computational technology, modeling, analytics, and data sciences. DE includes the use MBE methods in a consumable and computational environment that enables the integration of the R&M discipline with other engineering models.  Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) is a sub-discipline of MBE. For this effort, we are focusing on MBE.
DoD and industry tested the implementation of an MBE FMECA Systems Modeling Language (SysML) profile Data Item Description (DID) on a fictitious program called “Iron Horse,” an autonomous ground vehicle to carry troop supplies.  The team modeled the Iron Horse systems, subsystems, and Line Replaceable Units in SysML to test the use of the machine-readable SysML profile.  The team entered failure modes and effects information into the profile with the objective to automatically generate standardized views based on the query.  The team identified key challenges and lessons learned throughout the effort of identifying As-Is to To-Be methods and implementing the MBE FMECA SysML profile on the fictitious Iron Horse program.

element names and definitions across various disciplines and across FMECA methods and standards.

The intent is to take advantage of MBE methods to support the move from delivery of a static document to delivery of a model that allows the program office and other users to query FMECA data, resulting in faster engagement, decreased design cycle times, and increased design influence. element names and definitions across various disciplines and across FMECA methods and standards.

title: ADMP-03: A New NATO Standard for Classification and Analysis of RAM Events
authors: Hervé du Baret, Direction Générale de l’Armement, France; Nicholas Barnett, Ministry of Defence, United Kingdom; Nicolas Boutet, Directorate General Material Ressources, La Défense, Belgium; Jenny Lee, Army Futures Command; Jason Gargrave, Army Futures Command
summary:
ADMP-03 (Allied Dependability Management Publications #3) [1] is a recently published (2021) NATO standard that provides guidance for classification and analysis of dependability (or RAM) events.   ADMP-03 provides a means to compare the reliability as well as other dependability aspects of NATO defense systems.  Some significant contributions of ADMP-03 are:
the structured approach it proposes for classifying RAM events (cause, impact),
definitions and examples of RAM metrics that can be assessed using the classified event data.
STANREC 4174, which is a NATO recommended standard for dependability aspects [2], and all current ADMPs are available at https://nso.nato.int/nso /nsdd/listpromulg.html, free of charge. This paper presents the most important aspects of ADMP-03 and provide illustrative examples of application.

title: Machine Learning Assessment in Reliability & Maintainability
authors: Kenney Crooks, Northrop Grumman; Abhishek Paul, Northrop Grumman; Nathan Plawecki, Northrop Grumman; Key Words: machine learning, reliability & maintainability, predictive maintenance
summary:
As acquisition programs become more complex, Reliability and Maintainability (R&M) has an increasingly import role in characterizing performance during development and controlling long-term sustainment costs. There is a fine balance between R&M and program constraints that, if not controlled and managed, could drive cost implications as the program matures. To overcome these challenges, there are opportunities to leverage machine learning in the R&M domain to increase efficiencies and influence sustainment cost.
This research highlights R&M opportunities to leverage machine learning in development and sustainment such as reliability predictions and allocation; Failure Modes, Effects and Criticality Analysis (FMECA); maintenance record adjudications; utilization of equipment performance data; and creating predictive analytic capabilities. These opportunities were assessed through a proposed scoring methodology based on problem objective and data assessment. The results suggest four of the five opportunities are very applicable for machine learning utilization whilst one opportunity relative to FMECA is potentially applicable. The FMECA requires further investigation on data available to be introduced as a viable machine learning option.
conclusions: A proposed machine learning assessment defined in this case study has proven successful, as the assessment results are comparable to the project successes in those domains. The case study shows that machine learning can be applied to domains from development to sustainment for Reliability & Maintainability. The primary outcomes of this approach are the awareness of the applicability of machine learning and the importance of the data for applied machine learning. The assessment can be used to identify domains where machine learning may be applicable to reduce manpower and resources needed.

title: COTS Definition Misunderstanding Impacts On Reliability
authors: Greg Cennamo, University of Dayton Research Institute; Key Words: COTS, Commercial Items, Reliability Program Requirements
summary: This paper describes the potential impacts on system reliability and performance when an item is identified as Commercial-Off-The-Shelf (COTS) and does not meet the criteria for that designation.  An item meeting COTS criteria indicates a level of maturity which lowers reliability and performance risks.  Program requirements for reliability are tailored based on the associated risk.  The approach proposed is to validate the COTS designation prior to finalizing requirements and it is suggested this is essential to ensure the program will be successful, reducing the risk of mission failure, excessive downtime, and support costs.

title: Constant-Time Linear Regression Learning and Its Applications on Real-Time R&M Systems
authors: Meng-Lai Yin, PhD, California State Polytechnic University, Pomona; Hovig Aroush, Raytheon Intelligence & Space; Key Words: machine learning, linear regression, efficiency
summary:
Constant-time linear regression algorithms are presented in this paper.  Machine learning techniques rely on a good amount of data to achieve high performance.  However, processing big data is time-consuming and thus limits the potential of applying machine learning techniques to real-time R&M (Reliability and Maintainability) systems.
Linear regression has a long history in R&M applications, which also serves as a basic machine learning method.  Most linear regression applications conduct the learnings off-line, not in real time, which causes the resulting model to be outdated.  Realizing that continuous learning is crucial in real-time operations, this study is devoted to constant-time algorithms findings.  Both lifelong and moving-time-window constant-time linear regression algorithms are presented.  The case study demonstrates the benefits of applying the constant-time algorithms to real-time system monitoring.

title: Utilizing Virtual Reality to Enhance the Digital Twin
authors: Erik Schmidtberg, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Lauren Goff, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Alastair Moubray, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Greg Toy,  Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Key Words: CBM+, Virtual Reality, FMECA, Digital Twin, Immersive Training
summary:
This paper discusses the expanded utilization of modelling methods, processes, and technologies that are created during the design of complex systems, and it addresses how models and applications generated at different portions of the lifecycle can be integrated for enhanced sustainment solutions.  The use of model-based technologies like digital twin for engineering and manufacturing purposes is well-defined and industry has already begun extending these technologies into the deployment of systems for predictive maintenance.  Similarly, technology in virtual reality, augmented reality, and gaming engines for training, maintenance, and product improvement has paved a path for the digital thread to extend to the sustainment phase of the product lifecycle. The integration of digital twin and virtual reality throughout the lifecycle of a product would not only provide valuable insight into the design and function of a product, but could enhance current training applications to drastically reduce operator training costs long-term.
When paired with an integrated digital twin and a networked Condition Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) solution, 3D models of a system become living, emergent work products.  This creates a virtual environment where local and remote operators can validate system configurations, perform system simulations, practice maintenance tasks, and collaborate on design enhancements to the system.  This creates the potential for a 3D-enhanced digital twin that models a system from design to sustainment via the CBM+ strategy for Aerospace and Defense products.
conclusions:
In addition to the decrease in sustainment costs and continuous product improvement brought about by digital twin technology, virtual representations of systems would allow vendors tangible insight into the design and use of systems even before hardware prototyping. This technology would also enable real-time inspection and design collaboration between vendors and end users throughout the product lifecycle, which would reduce costs incurred by frequent in-person collaboration events and increase feedback loops into system design.
The integration of high-fidelity digital twins into immersive training applications offers end users the ability to perform training with realistic, emergent systems models even before systems are fielded, and could significantly reduce the money spent every year on New Equipment Training (NET) and live fire events by familiarizing end users with the system in virtual environments prior to hands-on equipment training.
The value of real-time interaction with physical systems can never be fully replaced with virtual reality, but immersive interactions with high-fidelity, digital systems models could significantly decrease redesign costs through frequent, collaborative feedback into system design, increase system reliability and minimize downtime through system modelling and emergent training capability, and decrease training time and cost by increasing operator proficiency in system use prior to fielded use.

title: Accelerating Optimal Test Planning With Artificial Neural Networks
authors: Philipp Mell, University of Stuttgart; Fabian Karle, University of Stuttgart; Thomas Herzig, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, Ph. D., University of Stuttgart; Bernd Bertsche, Ph. D., University of Stuttgart
summary:
In this paper, artificial neural networks for use in an algorithm for determining an optimal test plan are investigated.   The neural networks serve to estimate the Probability of Test Success and the expected duration of a reliability test for a product with prior knowledge about the failure distribution.   This estimation in negligible time enables the efficient pre-selection of promising test plans.   Without such a pre-selection, a comparison of all possible test plans would lead to an unfeasibly large amount of simulation due to the high number of parameters.
It is shown that this method is applicable for the most common reliability test types, including different kinds of censoring.   Building on previous studies, several layouts of shallow neural networks are trained, tested and compared.   It is shown that for all test types, a mean error on the Probability of Test Success of below 2.5 % can be reached.   There is no systematic error to be found and the yielded neural networks are reproducible with high stability.   As a result, fully connected two and three layer designs can be recommended for most test types.   Their application allows a fast and therefore practical comparison of test plans made up from several common test types to find the one fitting best to the given product and reliability requirements.

title: Developing an Assurance Case for an Optical Communication Mission in a Model Based Setting
authors: Martin S. Feather, PhD, California Institute of Technology; Steven L. Cornford, PhD, California Institute of Technology; John W. Evans, PhD, NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance; Anthony J. DiVenti, NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance; David Kotsifakis, NASA/Goddard Flight Center
summary:
NASA's Office of Safety and Mission Assurance has  adopted an objectives-based approach to standards to ensure that the Safety and Mission Assurance disciplines and programs are addressing the challenges of NASA’s changing missions, acquisition and engineering practices, and technology.  Starting with the Reliability and Maintainability discipline, an objectives hierarchy was developed to systematically decompose technical considerations that form the basis for that discipline.
This paper shows how the objectives-based approach can be applied to SETH+, a mission concept with a novel aspect - demonstration of optical communication from a smallsat spacecraft to Earth across a distance of 0.1 AU (Astronomical Unit) - approximately 15,000,000 km.  The objectives hierarchy supports development of an assurance case, done in a manner that draws upon Model Based Systems Engineering's representations of model information.

title: Data and Predictive Modeling for Aerospace Mission Critical Parameter Assessment
authors: Vincent Andersen, Jensen Hughes; Erin Collins, Jensen Hughes; Tom Daniels, Jensen Hughes; Josh Kaffel, Jensen Hughes; Key Words: common cause failure, data analysis, master logic diagram
summary: This paper provides an overview of data and analytic approaches for evaluating the reliability and risk of space missions. Various methodologies and tools are utilized, starting with the Master Logic Diagram (MLD) that identifies the initiating events that cause system failure by evaluating different systems, sub-systems, and components.  The MLD is then translated to a Functional Event Sequence Diagrams (FESDs) that evaluate the different success and failure paths, which ultimately help create the Event Tree (ET) to model event progression.  The ET provides a road map to creating a Fault Tree (FT) which models potential failures, given the conditions in the ET.  The FT provides the basis for performing all of the quantitative assessment.  The collection of data is crucial in quantifying the ET and FT to assess a predictive model of the overall risk or reliability.  Most of the time, aerospace vehicles have multiple redundancies in their systems architectures, so the concept of Common Cause Failures (CCF) is critical, because it evaluates the likelihood of concurrent failures in similar or identical systems.  These tools and techniques have been applied to a variety of missions and to non-aerospace projects as well to develop predictive models that provide insights beyond those available from the data alone. This approach helps pinpoint weaknesses in systems and missions before their launch, providing an improvement in mission success by focusing investments where greater reliability is needed.

title: Evaluation of Copper and Gold Wire Bonds in PEM Devices
authors: Brian Myer, Raytheon Technologies; Eric Gallardo, Raytheon Technologies; Steve Melosky, Raytheon Technologies; Dustin Aldridge, Raytheon Technologies
summary: The shift from gold (Au) to copper (Cu) wire bonds used in PEMs (Plastic Encapsulated Microcircuits) has been gradual for the last few years. Many agencies and critics question the long-term robustness and reliability of Cu wire bonds; however, PEM manufacturers have been thoroughly evaluating and optimizing the Cu wire bond process over the last few years to produce highly reliable products. When the manufacturing process is optimized and closely controlled and monitored, Cu wire bonds can be a reliable and stronger alternate to Au wire bonds. This paper details a Cu wire bond study that specifically compares Cu wires against Au wire bonds following combined environmental stress/life test conditions. In this study, bond pull testing indicated good performance of both copper and gold wire bonds. The methods used in this analysis (Destructive Physical Analysis (DPA), wire pull testing and environmental testing) were effective techniques for evaluation of bond wire integrity, detection of manufacturing defects, and overall assessment of the copper and gold wire bond processes. Based on wire bond testing in this analysis, the reliability/integrity of optimally developed copper wire bonds appears to be superior or even stronger than gold wires in the same package type.

title: Automated Support for the Project-Specific Instantiation of Standards
authors: Martin S. Feather, PhD, California Institute of Technology; Steven L. Cornford, PhD, California Institute of Technology; Anthony J. DiVenti, NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance; John W. Evans, PhD, NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance; Key Words: assurance, objective hierarchies, plans, reliability, standards
summary:
We have developed a prototype to demonstrate how automated support for applicable standards can assist and benefit space mission projects as they develop their plans.  The desirable characteristics it exhibits are:
Assistance to develop a plan – a set of activities – compliant with NASA standards
Freedom to plan the activities best suited to the project and its need to show fulfillment of overall objectives of safety, reliability, and mission success.
Flexibility to introduce activities not already present in the lists of recommended choices
Ability for the project to record justifications for their choices
Automated generation of outputs that blend the NASA standards’ guidance with the mission-specific characteristics
A production quality implementation is now underway, inspired by the capabilities demonstrated in our prototype.

title: Application of Isotonic Regression in Predicting Corrosion Depth of the Oil Refinery Pipelines
authors: Abdulsalam Ahmed Alqarni, North Dakota State University; Om Prakash Yadav, Ph.D., North Carolina A&T State University; Ajay Pal Singh Rathore, Ph.D., Malaviya National Institute of Technology; Key Words: corrosion growth, isotonic regression model, machine learning, pipeline corrosion
summary:
This paper presents a powerful machine learning (ML) model called isotonic regression to predict the corrosion growth process in the oil and gas pipelines. The paper mainly aims to show the powerfulness of this model in predicting corrosion depth in the pipeline. The isotonic regression model is selected in this study because it is a non-parametric model that can be freely shaped without assuming any shape of target function to overcome the highly stochastic nature of the corrosion growth mechanism. The other reason, the isotonic regression model is also designed to predict the monotonic increasing degradation mechanisms such as corrosion. The paper also evaluates three machine learning models used in regression analysis: linear regression, isotonic regression, and power regression based on the actual corrosion depth data collected from five sensors attached to the studied pipeline. Jupyter notebook is used in the evaluation process of each ML model performance. Four types of prediction accuracy metrics are used to calculate the prediction performance of each ML model, such as mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), root mean square error (RMSE), and R-squared .
This paper finds that the isotonic regression model is promising to overcome the complexity issue associated with the corrosion depth prediction application as the corrosion growth nature is associated with high uncertainties, stochastic, and randomness. Finally, this paper recommends utilizing this model by the pipeline operators in the oil refineries in order to have an effective predictive maintenance plan that avoids the need for more complex maintenance activities and maximizes the pipeline's usage.
conclusions:
This paper evaluates three machine learning models used in regression analysis: linear regression, isotonic regression, and power regression based on the actual corrosion depth data collected from five sensors attached to the studied pipeline. The comparative study aims to find the most appropriate model for predicting the pipeline's corrosion depth over time. The study finds that the isotonic regression model is the most powerful and stable in predicting corrosion depth in all five scenarios. It outperforms the other models and provides the best fit to the corrosion depth data. Not only this, the  squared values are equal to 1 in all five scenarios, indicating that the isotonic regression model is the most suitable model for describing the corrosion growth process. The other prediction accuracy metrics are too small, close to zero, which gives the same indication of the powerfulness of this model in predicting corrosion depth over time in the pipeline. On the other hand, linear regression and power regression are not recommended to predict corrosion depth because they provide less prediction in each scenario because they are both parametric models, which means they both have a restricted shape. Their prediction accuracy in each scenario is also not stable because they can not deal with the stochastic and randomness inherited in the nature of the corrosion growth process.
This paper concludes that the isotonic regression model is promising to overcome the complexity associated with the corrosion depth prediction application as the corrosion growth nature is associated with high uncertainties, stochastic, and randomness. Finally, this paper recommends utilizing this model by the maintenance managers and decision-makers in the oil refineries in order to have an effective predictive maintenance plan that avoids the need for more complex maintenance activities and maximizes the pipeline's usage.

title: A Genetic Algorithm-Based Approach to Identify Near-Optimal Non-Equidistant Checkpointing Strategies
authors: Priscila Silva, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Brendan Thibault, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Vidhyashree Nagaraju, PhD, University of Tulsa; Lasitha Dharmasena, PhD, Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology; Lance Fiondella, PhD, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth
summary: Software intensive systems rely on checkpointing to prevent loss of computation, by performing periodic backups. Non-equidistant checkpointing strategies have been proposed for specialized hardware and software applications as well as specific failure distributions. However, a general method to identify a non-equidistant checkpointing strategy for an arbitrary combination of application and failure distribution would be beneficial. This paper proposes an approach to identify a near optimal non-equidistant checkpointing strategy with a genetic algorithm, which only requires knowledge of the failure distribution. Experiments suggest that the approach consistently outperformed the traditional strategy of equidistant checkpoints under (i) a range of total processing times and (ii) different values of distributions exhibiting increasing, constant, and decreasing failure rates.
conclusions:
This paper presented a near optimal approach based on the genetic algorithm to identify a non-equidistant checkpointing strategy. Simulation was employed to evaluate the fitness of candidate solutions in terms of the average total time required for the computation to complete. The approach was validated through a series of examples, which illustrated that the near optimal non-equidistant approach consistently outperformed the traditional strategy of equidistant checkpoints. The conditions under which the proposed approach outperformed the traditional strategy included: (i) a range of total processing times and (ii) different values of the Weibull distribution, including increasing, constant, and decreasing failure rate. While the simulation-based genetic algorithm was efficient for the range of values considered, running the algorithm for a range of bits in each chromosome required more time. However, this time may be justified especially for high performance computing platforms, where the time saved compensates for the time to identifying a non-equidistant checkpointing strategy prior to execution.
Future research will explore alternative evolutionary algorithms and examine enhancements to the genetic algorithm that improve its computational efficiency.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Survival Analysis For Industrial Equipment Performance Management
authors: Ahmed Ragab, Ph. D., CanmetENERGY, Natural Resources Canada; Mohamed Elhefnawy, CanmetENERGY, NRCan; Mohamed-Salah Ouali, D. Sc., Polytechnique Montréal; Key Words: Machine Learning; Reliability Modeling; Energy Efficiency; Abnormal Event Prognosis; Remaining Useful Life.
summary: This paper proposes an artificial intelligence-based survival analysis method to predict the time to occurrence of an abnormal event in industrial equipment as the main prescriptive maintenance decision criterion. The method exploits maintenance historical data comprising event data and continuous observations to build an updated set of survival models that reflect the ages and operating conditions of equipment. The event data is used to build the survival models while the continuous observations are labeled according to the equipment operating conditions to train an ensemble of different machine learning (ML) classifiers. Given a new observation collected from the monitored equipment, the trained ML ensemble predicts the probabilities of different health states and their corresponding survival curves, and then the overall equipment’s survival curve is updated accordingly. The updated curve is then used to predict the time left for an abnormal event to occur in the monitored equipment. The proposed method is validated on NASA turbofan engine data, a common dataset in the realm of prognostics, to predict the remaining useful life (RUL) of a group of equipment working under varying operating conditions. The obtained results show the effectiveness of the proposed method and the ML ensemble used decreases the RUL prediction error by an average of 35.6% compared to the best-performing classifier in the ensemble.

title: Reliability Growth Modeling Across New Product Introduction Using Weibull Parameters
authors: Sarath Jayatilleka, DaikinApplied Americas; James McLinn, retired; Key Words: Weibull Parameters, Reliability Growth, New Product Development, Design for Reliability.
summary:

With the trends change Weibull parameters too changed to a certain trend. These trends can be used to model as parameter growth and predict the future parameter sets. As the popularity of Weibull analysis grew during the last few decades and more companies used phase gate NPI methods, this method can be very useful in tracking reliability growth helping the strategic business decision making processes.
In the section 4, the use of this model as a reliability degradation measurement system when field replacement parts seem to have degraded reliability is discussed. These reliability degradation Weibull plots somewhat resembles to Weibull plots when there is reliability growth. Despite the similar looks, inappropriateness of such reliability degradation application is discussed, and more appropriate method was referred [6.]
This model can be applicable to NPD reliability programs in several ways. One method is explained herein as a summary point. The model provides log(β)=a log(η) +b type linear equation where ‘a’ being the coefficient and ‘b’ being the constant. Also available is the reliability equation (1.3.) For a given reliability requirement such as R(T)>0.999, where T= design life, above two equations can be used to derive β and η. These two Weibull parameters give the point on the Reliability Growth Plot, a future state when the reliability requirement is met. These indications can be used in a NPD reliability program to re-strategize resources accordingly.
conclusions:
Analysis of the change in reliability over time, usually applied during new product development processes (NPD) is referred to as reliability growth analysis. It provides the means by which the reliability is tracked over time, allowing the product development team to predict future reliability values based on the current rate of growth of the reliability measurement of interest. This paper focus on design-iteration wise reliability growth within NPD period to support proactive reliability strategies before product launch to the market.
During a new product development process, reliability analysis begins with virtually conceptualized designs. When design realization process translates from virtual state to physical configurations, it undergoes a series of design iteration testing. As test- fix/improve-test cycles progress, the design system’s overall reliability improves, congruently. While the improvement of a designed-in reliability is the primary objective of the reliability growth monitoring process, it also helps improving the program’s reliability growth models. A two design iterations of prototype testing can be a simple example of a reliability growth model that helps predicting the reliability status of the third improvement. As the current reliability program continues, reliability growth model needs to provide future status if and when reliability objectives can be achieved. This prediction helps to re-strategize the current reliability programs such as addition of new resources in order to match the new product introduction (NPI) timeline to market needs.
During a new product introduction process in an appliance industry, each design iteration’s reliability test data analysis with Weibull Analysis revealed that Weibull parameters were changing in certain predictable trends based on particular deign and reliability program. The single assumption in this model is the existence of this predictable trends when linearized unreliability curves of design iterations on Weibull plots were apparently getting steeper while moving to the right on time axis, reflecting the reliability growth. This simple growth model of two Weibull parameters was found to be useful in reliability growth measurements across NPI design iteration cycles. The predictions of the next level Weibull parameters are helpful in early strategizing of design for reliability resource allocation and forecasting (for tests, people, tools, and time) in order to bring product to the market on time. Several examples from appliances industry NPI projects are used to illustrate the trends for Weibull parameter growth and modelling the future parameters. Since, two Weibull parameters fully define the future reliability status, this paper discusses how companies could be beneficial from this model for strategizing reliability programs and meet program goals during NPI.

title: The abcd Reliability Growth Model
authors: Harry W. Jones, Ph.D., NASA Ames Research Center; Key Words: Reliability growth, abcd model
summary:
The abcd parameters of the model are determined by the failure test data, which is the time of each successive failure.  If the failure rate reaches a constant value, that value is c.  If Reliability growth testing is terminated at td, the remaining uncorrected failures have a failure rate of d.  The values of a and b are determined by fitting a t-b to n(t)/t -c.  Typically, b = 1.0, reflecting the fastest possible reliability growth, where each failure mode contributes only once to the failure count and its effect on the average failure rate declines linearly with time.
The abcd model was developed by combining an initial phase of exponential Duane Crow reliability growth model with a constant long term failure rate with two potential components.  The failure rate n(t)/t = a t-b + c + d, where a t-b describes exponential reliability growth, c is the constant accepted failure rate, and d represents the potential failure rate reduction obtainable by further reliability growth testing.

title: Applying the Logistic Model to Predict the Number of Problem/Failure Reports During Integration and Testing
authors: John Evans, PhD. NASA Headquarters; Natesan Jambulingam, PhD. NASA Headquarters; Mark Kaminskiy, PhD. NASA Goddard Spaceflight Center; Robert Moreland, NASA Headquarters; Bhanu Sood, PhD. NASA Goddard Spaceflight Center
summary:
Analysis of monthly number of problem/failure reports (PR/FR) data collected during spacecraft integration and testing (I&T) phase shows that the cumulative number PR/FR as a function of time can be well described by the logistic model, widely used as a reliability growth model.
Reliability growth is process applied in development whereby the outcome of a test program in terms of system relaibility may be estimated based on the performance of an organization. Specifically, outcomes are based upon analyzing failures and applying resources to implement corrective actions. As such, reliability growth models will exhibit diminishing returns and are monotonically increasing with time. The Duane model is widely used and is often applied as an aid to estimate test times. However, other models may be better suited for more specific situations. In this paper we have demonstrated that for spacecraft I and T, the logistical model is an excellent fit to estimate outcomes for robotic spacecraft development.
Using the fitted logistic model (based on current data) and constructing the statistical confidence limits for the model, a methodology for predicting the cumulative number of PR/FR at the end of the I&T phase is suggested, and its estimated accuracy is shown to be practically applicable.  The suggested methodology and its accuracy in terms of confidence and point estimates is illustrated by two case studies.
Unlike other growth type models, the methodology demonstrated here is not primarily intended to predict a failure intensity of a design or the number of cumulative failures at a point in the future (although it does do that).  The intent of this analysis is to use it as a tool to help monitor overall I&T progress with respect to its planned phase completion.  This information could allow managers to take appropriate action (i.e., additional focused resources) early enough in the process to either maintain the schedule, or use it as input to appropriately project a more accurate completion date.

title: Power Transmission Grid Operation & Maintenance Prioritization Based on Cox Models
authors: Mathieu Payette, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières; Olivier Blancke, Hydro-Québec; Miguel Diago, Hydro-Québec; Georges Abdul-Nour, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières; Denis Valiquette, Hydro-Québec
summary: Statistical modeling of failures on power transmission assets is essential to support asset management strategies that ensure long term operation of the grid. Transmission grids are composed of a large number of diverse assets geographically distributed across the territory. Widespread equipment aging requires increasingly accurate inspection and replacement schedules to guarantee reliability of critical assets. This allows the optimal use of limited resources, to maintain continuity of service and therefore to maximize the value of the assets. In most cases, prioritization tools consist of aggregation algorithms developed from knowledge of domain experts and maintenance workers. This paper proposes an approach that leverages advanced statistical reliability analysis to improve a risk matrix used to prioritize and optimize asset management decisions. An approach to model reliability considering the effect of specific equipment covariates is presented. The approach is based on the well-known Cox model. A Proportional Hazard Model (PHM) is applied to reliability data and geographical information system (GIS) data to estimate their effects on the reliability of the grid assets. For each asset, the resulting tool reports the failure probability rating according to its related characteristics. An application of these models to the Hydro-Québec electric power transmission network is proposed. The results of the study show that several characteristics are more influential than its age in its aging process. The combination of statistical analysis and expert knowledge provides additional information to decision makers.
conclusions: The objective of this research was to apply statistical methods to simplify the calculation of failure probability ratings. The case study provided by Hydro-Quebec allowed us to model the reliability of transmission equipment from real data, with biases and uncertainties. The application of Cox models will allow a more accurate estimation of the effect of covariates, and thus improve asset management. The models showed that certain equipment characteristics had a significant effect on the failure rate. These results demonstrate the applicability of these methods and will allow for more targeted AM policies to be implemented. However, the application of these methods will require several iterations to obtain good long-term results. This project presented the first tests and highlighted the next steps to be implemented. Indeed, the organization should put efforts to improve the quality of the data, to be able to include other relevant variables in the model.

title: Plant Prioritization for Updating Maintenance Policies: A Power Sector Case Study
authors: Arthur H. A. Melani, Ph. D., University of São Paulo; Fabio N. Kashiwagi, University of São Paulo; Tiago G. Rosa, University of São Paulo; Gilberto F. M. Souza, Ph. D., University of São Paulo; Emerson Rigoni, Ph. D., Federal University of Technology – Parana
summary:
In order to reduce unnecessary maintenance services and return valuable time to industrial plants, several companies have been engaging in updating their maintenance schedules and strategies. Several techniques to achieve such a goal have been developed, for example, Reliability Centered Maintenance (RCM), Risk-based Maintenance (RBM) and Condition-based Maintenance (CBM). The complex process of implementing such techniques can, however, offer several challenges to companies, such as how to properly train maintenance teams; what are the best tools or software to use on a daily basis; which performance indicators to use for decision making; etc.
After the implementation process, one of the first difficulties faced especially by large companies, composed of several plants, is where to start the RCM effectiveness evaluation aiming at identifying the possible needs for improvement to optimize maintenance strategies.
In general, one of the plants in the company's asset portfolio should be chosen to be the first to receive the methodology improvement. In this way, the implementation process can be put to the test so that its successes and failures are properly recorded, allowing the lessons learned to be used to improve the implementation in the other plants of the company.
The choice of the pilot plant must be made carefully, in order to highlight the advantages of the new maintenance strategy while allowing the implementation process to be optimized. In this context, this work proposes a method for choosing the pilot plant through the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), which is a multi-criteria decision method widely used for ranking the alternatives of a decision problem. The proposed method will be implemented in a company in the Brazilian energy sector whose portfolio of assets is composed of several hydroelectric plants.
The company already uses the RCM for the elaboration of the maintenance plans but intends to improve the methodology based on quantitative reliability analysis aiming at optimizing maintenance intervention intervals. The method will be used to evaluate RCM implementation maturity in each asset in order to define the most suitable plant to be used in the improvement process.
conclusions: The proposed method has been implemented in a company in the Brazilian energy sector whose portfolio of assets is composed of several hydroelectric plants. The method proved capable of ranking assets in terms of the performance of the current maintenance policy and managed to define not only which could be the pilot plant, but also the order in which the maintenance strategy update can be implemented in order to optimize the potential benefits to be obtained. It is also worth noting that the performance indicators monitored by the national regulatory agency proved to be effective in representing the overall performance of each plant and, therefore, can help their managers in decision-making regarding asset management strategies.

title: Design for Manufacturability Best Practices for PCBs and PCBAs
authors: David M. Spitz, Ansys; Key Words: DFM, PCB design, PCBA design
summary:
The quality and reliability of printed circuit board assemblies (PCBAs) is highly dependent upon the PCB fabricator and the PCB assembler.  However, PCB design also plays a critical role and can have a significant impact on the success or failure of the manufacturing suppliers.  Today, designing and manufacturing PCBAs is increasingly difficult due to higher lead-free processing temperatures, the increasing density of electronic assemblies, and the use of smaller and smaller components.  Not only does this create challenges for PCB designers, but it also increases the complexity of the PCBA manufacturing processes and puts additional demand on those manufacturing suppliers.
This paper will give a brief introduction into the design for manufacturability (DFM) process and then explore some DFM best practices in the areas of PCB fabrication, component selection, and PCB assembly.  It will also examine the dependencies between the design and manufacturing processes.
DFM is a proven, cost effective, and strategic methodology.  It reduces overall product development time, results in smoother production launch, and improves time to market.  It helps to reduce overall costs by helping to ensure the product is designed and built right the first time, resulting in less rework, scrap, and warranty issues.  It also helps to improve the quality and reliability of the product, leading to higher customer satisfaction.
conclusions: The deployment of a DFM process by electronics product designers is an excellent way to improve both the manufacturability and reliability of their products. Careful consideration of DFM best practices should have a positive impact on overall product cost and reliability which will ultimately lead to improved customer satisfaction.

title: Machine Learning & Uncertainty Quantification: Application in Building Energy Consumption
authors: Fahimeh Fakour, University of California Los Angeles; Tarannom Parhizkar, PhD, University of California Los Angeles; Ramin Ramezani, PhD University of California Los Angeles; Ali Mosleh, PhD, University of California Los Angeles; Key Words: machine learning prediction, regression, uncertainty quantification, conformal prediction, risk assessment
summary:
One of the main tasks in reliability and risk assessment of complex systems is to predict system behavior under uncertainty. Different machine learning (ML) methods can be used to predict system behavior; these methods are able to predict system performance/status in different operating and environmental conditions.  In addition to predicting the system’s performance, the uncertainty level of the output is important for reliability and risk assessment methods. In this paper, a method for uncertainty quantification of machine learning-based prediction methods is applied on real world data.
It is noteworthy that regression ML methods usually output a single point prediction and don’t give an idea of the uncertainty level of the prediction for an unobserved sample. Conformal Prediction (CP) is employed in this study as a means of providing a prediction interval in the regression, thus   quantifying the uncertainty of a prediction sample in the process.
CP is applied to energy consumption prediction models to show the effectiveness of the conformal prediction approach. Results show that conformal prediction is a helpful metric in determining the uncertainty of predictions and provides insight to choosing the optimum ML method for uncertain conditions.
A comparison between the results published in  with the same dataset is performed in this study. The amount of uncertainty for the different models will be investigated, allowing for better conclusions in choosing an appropriate prediction model for data pertaining to varying uncertainty environments.
The results and insights of using CP leads us to believe that uncertainty quantification, in addition to error measurement metrics such as test set Mean Squared Error (MSE), can provide a better means of predicting and avoiding potential high-risk scenarios.

title: Automatic Database Alignment Method to Improve Failure Data Quality
authors: YuPing Liang, Universty of Montreal; Olivier Blancke, Institut de recherche d’Hydro-Québec; Mohamed Gaha, Institut de recherche d’Hydro-Québec; Alain Côté, Institut de recherche d’Hydro-Québec; Guillaume St-Jean, Hydro-Québec
summary: Life-cycle data analysis mainly relies on coherent failure data. Generally, in the industry, failure data are recorded in various Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) databases and can lead to inconsistent failure data analysis. The aim of this paper is to propose a new method to automatically merge existing failure datasets into one main database to reduce inconsistency and allow valuable analysis and stochastic/predictive models. The methodology is as follows. First, the data is cleaned using rules from domain knowledge. Second, similar features between the two databases were evaluated by applying correlation technique. Finally, we developed a rule-based engine to merge existing failure datasets into one main database. Our rule-based engine was calibrated according to the distribution of the observed distance between similar features. At first, we were able to match the failure data by 65%, then we enhanced our algorithm using Natural Language Processing (NLP) technique and we were able to reach an outstanding score of 85%. Traditionally this data alignment is done yearly by human experts. This is an extremely time-consuming task, and our automatic matching algorithm reduces workload by 70% and biases in life-cycle data analysis. With a confidence level our algorithm interactively suggests matches according to their distances.
