title: Estimating the Reliability of Consumer Electronics from User Survey Data and Test Data
authors: Neda Shafiei, University of Maryland; Jeffrey W. Herrmann, University of Maryland; Aaron Krive, Amazon Lab 126; Mohammad Modarres, University of Maryland; Key Words: drop test, hierarchical Bayesian, Kullback-Leibler divergence, user survey, users’ bias, reliability test.
summary: When a manufacturer develops a new product, assessing its reliability is challenging because it has insufficient historical data.  However, reliability assessment is needed to avoid releasing a product with low reliability, resulting in financial loss due to returns, replacements, or repairs, and may be dangerous to users in safety-critical products.  Collecting reliability data from returned products, as a common approach, is time-consuming.  Reliability data from user surveys can be collected faster than data about returned devices.  Reliability assessment based on user surveys has several difficulties, however.  First, using the calendar time for reliability assessment ignores the effect of different stress profiles, which describe the frequency and intensity of use over time.  Therefore, there is a need to define an equivalent usage time (or cycle) for products that undergo different stress profiles.  Second, survey responses may be biased, and using this data may result in an inaccurate reliability estimate. This paper proposes a mathematical framework for analyzing new product’s reliability using the user survey data and reliability test results.  A stress index (SI) model is introduced to combine different stress adjustors (i.e., the conditions or activities that increase or decrease the impact and damage from the applied stress or enhance stress absorption).  A stress-life model is then used to convert the SI values into the usage time or cycles and estimate the time-to-failure distribution.  The bias of the survey data is estimated by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence value between the time-to-failure distribution estimated from the unbiased reliability results such as reliability test data and the distribution estimated from the user survey data.  The remaining parameters of the stress-life model are approximated by integrating the bias-removed survey data and reliability test data through the hierarchical Bayesian method.  This paper presents a case study that applies the proposed approach to an electronic device using simulated user surveys and reliability test datasets.  To validate the approach, it is assumed that the simulated test data follows a known reliability model, which is called the “true model”.  The analysis shows that the true model and the estimated reliability models from the test and survey results are close.
conclusions: This paper presented an approach for improving reliability estimation of products by integrating user survey data and reliability test data. The stress and stress adjustors of the surveyed and tested devices were separately combined through a stress-index model and were converted to the equivalent cycles under a reference stress profile using a stress-life model. The user biases of the surveyed devices’ equivalent cycles were corrected using the Kullback-Leibler divergence method.  The bias-corrected survey data was then integrated with reliability test data through the hierarchical Bayesian method to improve the reliability estimate.   Simulated datasets for a hypothetical electronic device with the failure mode of cracking were also generated assuming a known reliability model (known as the true model).  The parameters of the reliability model were then estimated through the proposed approach. The analysis was repeated using the additive SI model, multiplicative SI model, and different reference stress profiles.  In all cases, the true model was within the uncertainty region of the estimated reliability model. The proposed framework is generic and flexible and can be used for estimating the reliability of a wide range of products, including consumer electronics with various failure modes.

title: Asymmetric ϵ-Support Vectors Regression for Remaining Useful Life Distribution Estimation
authors: Yanan Wang, Tsinghua University; Muxia Sun, PhD, Tsinghua University; Yan-Fu Li, PhD, Tsinghua University; Key Words: remaining useful life estimation, asymmetric ϵ-support vectors regression, restricted regression quantiles
summary:
Estimating the remaining useful life (RUL) of industrial components is essential in predictive maintenance practice. In real-world applications, both aleatoric uncertainties (e.g., randomness due to uncontrollable factors) and epistemic uncertainties (e.g., ignorance about the model correctness) exist. Therefore, uncertainty quantification is expected to be associated with the point estimation, i.e., an estimation of the RUL probability density function (PDF) is necessary. However, existing data-driven methods which can give a probabilistic estimation of RUL have limitations when applying to real-world industrial systems: statistical methods often rely on certain assumptions on the degradation process; probabilistic machine learning methods usually have large complexity and need some prior knowledge on the parameter distribution and/or likelihood model.
In this paper, we seek to design an effective model-free approach to estimate RUL distribution with few assumptions, when prior knowledge on the system is not available. The basic idea is to incorporate asymmetric ϵ-support vector regression (ϵ-SVR) into the framework of restricted regression quantiles (RRQ), to approximate mutually uncrossed quantile curves of RUL. Then, for a given input vector, among all distributions that fit the estimated monotone quantiles, a robust RUL probability density could be selected as the final estimation. We apply SVR as the basic learning machine due to its solid theoretical foundation and ability to process small training sets and multi-dimensional data. The effectiveness of our proposed method is validated by numerical experiments on a dataset of turbofan engines. It has the potential to be applied in RUL distribution estimations for increasingly complex industrial systems whose mechanism is hard to be understood completely.
conclusions:
In conclusion, our proposed model can realize estimation of RUL distribution by incorporating asymmetric ϵ-SVR into RRQ. This is a new way to obtain probabilistic estimation apart from the mainstream Bayesian approaches. Compared to widely studied deep learning methods, it has solider theoretical foundation and can be more easily implemented.
Our model has the potential to be widely applied in practice. Since the proposed framework is based on SVR, it is suitable for small training set. Besides, so far in numerical experiments, we have only taken the current state as input. The results reflect that it also works well when history data is unavailable. The performance evaluations show that our model not only provides better point prediction than similarity-based model, but also gives uncertainty estimation that conforms to the real frequency distribution.
The main drawback in this model is the assumption of similar error distribution pattern along the input domain. But in real world, due to certain behind physical principles, the RUL distribution pattern usually does not change significantly as the system ages. There are some improvements which could be done in the future. For example, more features could be included as the inputs of the model, such as those extracted from historical data. This framework could be extended to general distribution estimations other than the RUL. Furthermore, we can take advantage of global optimality of SVR and combine it with maintenance optimization problems.

title: Two-stage Stochastic Programming for Maintenance Optimization of Multi-component Systems
authors: Zhicheng Zhu, Texas Tech University; Yisha Xiang, Ph.D., Texas Tech University; Ying Liao, Texas Tech University; Key Words: Maintenance optimization, Multi-component systems, Stochastic programming
summary:
As the complexity of modern industrial systems increases faster than ever, it is imperative to a develop cost-effective maintenance plan to secure system safety while lowering maintenance cost for complex systems. However, most maintenance studies focus on single-component systems, which are not applicable to complex multi-component systems due to the various interactions among components, such as stochastic dependence, structure dependence and economic dependence. Economic dependence is the most commonly seen one among these interactions. Economic dependence means that any maintenance action incurs a system-dependence cost, regardless of the number of components maintained. Significant cost savings can be achieved by maintaining multiple components jointly instead of separately.
In this paper, we study the maintenance optimization problem of multi-component systems with economic dependence among components. The objective is to determine the maintenance actions at each decision stage over a finite planning horizon so that the total maintenance cost is minimized. Such a maintenance optimization problem is challenging due to the combinatorial maintenance grouping problem with the stochastic component failure process. We present a two-stage stochastic programming model for this problem, which analytically expresses the total cost as a function of maintenance decisions. Progressive hedging algorithm is applied to solve this problem. We conduct a case study by using real-world pavement deterioration data. Experiment results provide insights on how economic dependence affects single-component maintenance decision.

conclusions: In this paper, we propose a two-stage stochastic program to analytically model the maintenance optimization problem for multi-component systems over the finite planning horizon subject to the uncertainty of component lifetime. The impacts of economic dependence and setup cost are investigated through a road maintenance case. The results show that the optimal PM interval increases when considering economic dependence. In the future research, we will further explore the model structure and analyze the optimal grouping pattern in a more rigorous and comprehensive way.

title: General Transitions Probabilities and Maintenance Inspection Interval Optimization of a Weighted k-out-of-n System
authors: Mani Sharifi, Ph.D., Ryerson University; Sharareh Taghipour, Ph.D., Ryerson University; Abdolreza Abhari, Ph.D., Ryerson University
summary:
One of the most critical issues in manufacturing systems is maintaining the production equipment [1]. The planned maintenance activities may cause the stoppage of the production line. On the other hand, lack of proper maintenance may cause several unplanned stoppages of the production line due to machines/equipment failures. In both cases, the production cost increases. So, it is critical to optimize  inspection intervals for proper maintenance [2].
This paper considers a system consisting of  identical components in a multi-state system, where the failure rate between two consecutive system states is constant. The system structure is weighted k-out-of-n, which means that the system continues working until the sum of the performance rate of working components is more than or equal to . Although the failure is detected online, the failed components can be repaired only at inspections due to some restrictive conditions. The inspection intervals' duration is optimized to minimize system inspection cost per time unit (SICPTU). The SICPTU consists of the system inspection cost, components' repair cost, system repair cost, and system downtime cost [3].
To optimize the SICPTU, firstly, the system's states are defined. Then, transition probabilities between the states of the system and the transition matrix are calculated using the Universal Generating Function (UGF). This procedure is general and can be applied to a system with any desirable components. Next, SICPTU is calculated for a known value of inspection interval using a new matrix-based method which is presented by Sharifi et al. [1]. Finally, using a full enumeration technique, the optimal value of the SICPTU is determined.
To illustrate the provided method to calculate the SICPTU, an example consists of five water pumps is solved, in which each water pump has three different working states and one failed state. This example is inspired by a real-case problem from a water transition station. The results show the applicability of the proposed model in this real-case problem.
conclusions:

On the other hand, lack of proper maintenance may cause several unplanned stoppages of the production line due to machines/equipment failures. In both cases, the production cost increases. So, it is critical to optimize  inspection intervals for proper maintenance [2].
This paper considers a system consisting of  identical components in a multi-state system, where the failure rate between two consecutive system states is constant. The system structure is weighted k-out-of-n, which means that the system continues working until the sum of the performance rate of working components is more than or equal to . Although the failure is detected online, the failed components can be repaired only at inspections due to some restrictive conditions. The inspection intervals' duration is optimized to minimize system inspection cost per time unit (SICPTU). The SICPTU consists of the system inspection cost, components' repair cost, system repair cost, and system downtime cost [3].
To optimize the SICPTU, firstly, the system's states are defined. Then, transition probabilities between the states of the system and the transition matrix are calculated using the Universal Generating Function (UGF). This procedure is general and can be applied to a system with any desirable components. Next, SICPTU is calculated for a known value of inspection interval using a new matrix-based method which is presented by Sharifi et al. [1]. Finally, using a full enumeration technique, the optimal value of the SICPTU is determined.
To illustrate the provided method to calculate the SICPTU, an example consists of five water pumps is solved, in which each water pump has three different working states and one failed state. This example is inspired by a real-case problem from a water transition station. The results show the applicability of the proposed model in this real-case problem.

title: Reliability Engineering with Excel and Pivot Tables The Tools You Have / The Techniques You Should Know
authors: Eric E. Alden, Xerox Corporation; Key Words: Pivot Tables, New Product Development, Reliability Breakdown Structure. Reliability Growth, Pareto Charts, Data Structure
summary:
Numerous “Clean Sheet” production products were developed and launched with reliability engineering support utilizing MS Excel and PivotTables.  Dedicated reliability software was available but found insufficiently flexible to support all aspects of the required analysis and reporting. This was due to multiple packages required, and data input and output format requirements and limitations.
The first step is to create a Hierarchical Reliability Breakdown Structure of the subsystems and functions that make up the product.  This breakdown structure is used throughout the program as it defines the subsystems.
The next steps involve aligning the Bill of Materials with Reliability Breakdown Structure.  FMEA’s (failure mode and effect analysis) and MTTF (mean time between failures) estimates are made for each part and function and converted into overall failure rates for each subsystem and the overall product.
Each of the subsystems can then be allocated reliability targets where sum the failure rates equal 100% of the total product reliability target.  This can be graphically represented using a Pie Chart.
Reliability Growth Duane Curves can be constructed to define the target trajectory to mature performance and be aligned to business run cost and timing goals.
Graphic communication is critical while tracking the product performance through testing and launch.   Pareto Charts with cumulative curves are one of the most effective tools for communicating points.  More complex Frequency Dot Plots can additionally be created to show occurrences of failures by subsystems over time.  Patterns of chronic, intermittent, and resolved issues become evident.
A good working knowledge of MS Excel’s database features and required table structure along with strategic structuring can enable the analytics and graphics to support product development throughout the cycles from concept to launch.  Excel and Pivot Tables provide a powerful analytical tool without the need for costly specialized software.

title: Robot Fault Detection: At the Analog-Digital Boundary
authors: Ian D. Walker, Ph. D., Clemson University; Key Words: robotics, fault detection, quantum computing, fault trees
summary: Robots are complex electromechanical systems which often exhibit rapid, unpredictable, and potentially dangerous behavior in the presence of faults. In this paper, we present a novel quantum-inspired approach to fault detection within robot systems. The approach is based on a new fault detection model termed Quantum Analytical Redundancy (QAR) within a Fault Tree framework. The QAR method evolves quantum states with the ability to represent the internal dependencies of data within a provably complete set of fault detection tests. Our research centers on simulation of the approach, with testing and evaluation planned on rigid-link robot manipulator hardware.

title: Connecting Sustainment Deliverables to Troubleshooting with Condition Based Maintenance Plus
authors: Erik Schmidtberg, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Christopher Conrad, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Stephen Fecteau, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Alastair Moubray, Raytheon Missiles & Defense; Key Words: CBM+, Troubleshooting, FMECA, IETM, Data Collection
summary:
The Department of Defense (DoD) and other Aerospace & Defense (A&D) customers are continuously seeking to maximize system Operational Availability (Ao) and reduce total lifecycle ownership cost.  A key driver to both metrics is the effectiveness and efficiency of the maintainers who sustain systems.
This paper discusses a methodology to improve maintainer performance through the integration of information technology solutions and sustainment technical data deliverables (e.g., Failure Modes, Effects and Criticality Analysis – FMECA, Reliability Block Diagrams, Interactive Electronic Technical Manuals – IETMs, etc.).  We describe how digitally integrated solutions can be utilized to improve fault management and troubleshooting efficacy via the deployment of an Automated Guided Troubleshooting Toolset and a Condition Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) user interface.
The proposed integrated architecture combines industry-leading commercial troubleshooting software with OEM-generated system design data and a live condition data stream generated by the system-under-observation to create a powerful and dynamic troubleshooting solution.  The architecture dynamically generates and iterates fault isolation results and maintenance recommendations based on evolving inputs, automatically drawn from the system or manually injected by the maintainer.  Once the maintainer has validated system-generated results, they are then able to directly access relevant IETM work packages describing required service procedures, review part/tool availability, create work-orders to track completion of required repairs and automate the creation of reports.
An Automated Guided Troubleshooting approach creates a cohesive, end-to-end user experience where the maintainer’s workflow is guided via software from initial fault notification, through troubleshooting and onto service planning and execution.  Maintainer workload and mental burden is reduced through automated synthesis and aggregation of data.  The risk of human error is minimized via human-machine and machine-machine collaboration.  The speed and accuracy of troubleshooting is increased.  All of these factors combine to improve system availability and reduce costs associated with unnecessary service resulting from erroneous fault isolation and the speed of maintenance.
conclusions: Aerospace and Defense systems are increasing in complexity as technology evolves.  This is placing ever increasing challenges on the maintainer of those systems, which creates the need for more effective maintenance and troubleshooting solutions.  By leveraging commercial troubleshooting software and a CBM+ architecture, the authors have developed an innovative solution for using sustainment deliverables and system condition data to drive situation relevant Automated Guided Troubleshooting directly to the maintainer.  This results in a more empowered Maintainer and maximizes system Operational Availability.

title: NLP for Data Cleansing in DoD Maintenance Data: Case Study of Work Unit Code Correction for LAU-127
authors: Jack Francis, Ph.D., KBR, Inc.; Kim Cates, KBR, Inc.; Douglas Dvorak, KBR, Inc.; Marc Banghart, Ph.D., KBR, Inc.; Key Words: reliability-centered maintenance, natural language processing, work unit code, data cleansing, DoD
summary:
The objective of this paper is to develop a data-cleansing approach that leverages text data in Maintenance Action Forms (MAF) to improve the data quality of coded fields, such as Work Unit Code (WUC) for the Department of Defense (DoD) maintenance data. The poor data quality of DoD maintenance data is a critical issue, experienced by a wide range of organizations, that leads to poor predictive modeling, lack of transparency in performed maintenance, and adverse downstream effects due to incorrect reporting.
The most common example of poor data quality in DoD data is in coded fields, such as WUC. Maintainers have a variety of codes that can be entered in these fields, with the expectation that the code entered corresponds to the maintenance action performed. When poor data quality is noticed by stakeholders, large teams of SMEs are brought in to read the text description provided by maintainers to update the coded fields. It is generally assumed in DoD maintenance applications that the text provided in the MAF is a highly accurate representation of the maintenance event. Thus, there is an opportunity to use Natural Language Processing (NLP) to automate the process of updating coded fields using the text fields directly.
We address the current data quality issues by proposing a three-pronged approach based on NLP to automate the discovery of mislabeled codes in DoD MAFs using the MAF text fields directly. Our approach leverages domain expertise from subject matter experts (SME), semi-supervised learning (SSL) to use small amounts of labeled data from SMEs, and an ensemble approach; each of which identifies potentially mislabeled MAFs. This approach allows for the integration of domain expertise and machine learning to update incorrectly coded fields.
We demonstrate our automated data cleansing approach through a case study of the LAU-127 Launcher, which has 67k MAFs from July 2010 – July 2020. For our case study, we specifically examine the WUC field, but our method can be applied to other coded fields in MAFs.  By applying our method to a collection of MAFs to update the WUC, we identify 10k mislabeled MAFs using our rule-based approach, 14k mislabeled MAFs using SSL, and 5k MAFs using our ensemble method.  Altogether, our approach identified 29k MAFs with mislabeled WUC. This result is within the range of expected mislabeled incorrect MAFs, 28k-35k MAFs, provided by the dataset maintainer and SME (D.M.S.). Further, a subset of our WUC corrections were validated by a maintainer and identified to be 87% accurate. These findings present an automated cleansing solution to poor data quality through NLP approaches, data science, and SME validation.
conclusions:
MAFs underly the DoD’s push towards RCM, by recording key information about maintenance events, however, these MAFs often contain coding errors and general poor data quality. Currently, large teams of SMEs read MAFs one-by-one to update the coding issues. Our three-pronged approach provides an automated method for data correction that incorporates domain knowledge directly from SMEs. Our approach applies a rule-based method, SSL approach, and an ensemble model to identify mislabeled MAF. We apply our method to a dataset of MAFs from the LAU-127 and find that our approach identifies MAFs to update in line with the quantity expected by the D.M.S. From this, we can conclude that our approach is an effective tool for automatic data cleansing of MAF datasets.
While our approach was demonstrated using WUC, it can be applied to other codes within MAFs, which are known to be heavily correlated with the text descriptions provided in MAFs. Thus, our approach can more generally, provide DoD analysts with a method for correcting the data quality in MAFs.

title: Reliability Improvement by Detecting Failure Mechanisms Through Advanced Analytics Tools
authors: Ranjeet Patil; Key Words: DFR, Failure Mechanism, Diagnostic Analytics, X Analytics, Predictive Analytics and Alert System
summary:
In line with emerging technology trends, our efforts should be to integrate DFR (Design for Reliability) to enable minimum or zero downtime of product. Five step integrated intelligent approach of DFR (Design for Reliability) and advanced Data Analytics tools is step towards zero downtime with reliability improvement by detecting failure mechanism through advanced analytics tools. We have observed below benefits:
Prevent primary and associated secondary failures
Proactive reliability management approach
Enables quick decision with data centric approach
Customer centric cost avoidance approach
Integrated intelligent system
Background and Introduction
In today’s dynamic environment, seasonal product’s application operating window in the field is getting limited, machine uptime is very important for commercial products availability to customers, and it is critical to enhance uptime by optimizing vital performance parameters and early detection of failures using different tools/methodologies to improve the life cycle reliability performance of systems/components. By evaluating specific machine downtime failure mechanism due to mechanical, thermal, electrical, and chemical processes which is prior state of failure mode, it is essential to have integrated intelligent system for sensing and preventing failures to deliver robust reliable products. We have demonstrated one case study for effective use of integrated Design for Reliability (DFR) and key advanced analytics tools/methodologies for driving sustainable results through detection of downtime failure mechanisms using key tools and commercially available software’s such as Minitab, Weibull++, Python and Cloud Platform.
3. Downtime Failure Mechanisms and Modes
Failure mechanism is prior state of failure mode. Failure mechanisms are either due to mechanical, thermal, electrical, and chemical processes. If product is nonoperational in field or non available to customer for application due to failure mode causing from mechanism refers to downtime mechanism. Machine uptime is very important for seasonal commercial products availability to customers to avoid cost impact.
Methodology
Integrated Design for Reliability (DFR) and Advanced Analytics techniques for detection of downtime failure mechanisms to prevent failure modes enables improvement in proactive reliability management. As shown in Figure 1 below, the proposed methodology having five key phases or steps which includes A. Downtime Failure Mechanism - Deep dive analysis through PoF (Physics of Failure) and Diagnostic analytics techniques. B. Detection - Early detection of failure mechanisms by leveraging X analytics techniques depends on parameter from failure mechanism such as mechanical, thermal, chemical, and electrical. C. Alert system – In this step considering Predictive analytics model for identified parameter need to monitor threshold values for proactive communication. D. Preventive action and E. Reliable Product to customers
Figure 1. Proposed Methodology
Case Study
We have identified agriculture product cab windshield wiper system for demonstrating proposed methodology. Wiper system is necessary system during heavy rain or snow for agriculture product operation to perform seasonal applications during limited window. Weather such as heavy rain or snow affects product operating window, nonavailability of wiper system in adverse weather results downtime of product. We have considered only one failure mechanism and associated analysis in this case study to demonstrate five steps methodology as below for identified system.
A - PoF and Diagnostics Analytics
Physics of Failure (PoF) is structured technique in design for reliability for understanding the processes and mechanisms which induces failure to predict reliability and improve product performance. PoF includes and not limited to modeling of root causes, understanding usage requirements, attributes of product, manufacturing processes, stresses, variations, and key relationship. Diagnostic Analytics is one of the stages of analytics focuses on why failure occurred, finding hidden patterns, discover relationship by using various techniques of root cause analysis (RCA). By integrating PoF and Diagnostics Analytics we need to identify vital few downtime failure mechanisms in entire product, their causes and associated failure modes. This can be accomplished by deep dive analysis of baseline data from test and field failures. Finding hidden pattern, relationship discovery, correlation and causation from data is key for mapping downtime failure modes with specific mechanism by leveraging key tools or commercially available software’s such as Minitab, Weibull++ and Python
For case study windshield wiper system, identified failure mechanism is electrical overstress, failure symptom is wiper blade moving slowly and projected failure mode is wiper motor failure.
B - X Analytics
X Analytics is the ability to run any type of analytics where X is the data variable for a range of different structured and unstructured content such as text, audio, and video. In line with previous step, depends on failure mechanisms and associated variables or parameters we need to perform analytics through data captured by different sources and available connected devices in product by leveraging key tools or commercially available software’s such as Python and Cloud Platform
For case study windshield wiper system, we have early detection of electrical overstress even before wiper blade start moving slowly. Lower Specification Level (LSL) range of speed and upper limit established using baseline data as shown in picture, when speed reaches to upper limit of LSL there is trigger point for alert prediction model through connected devices like automatic rain sensing wiper system available in automobiles.
Figure 2. Lower Specification Limit
C - Predictive Analytics
Predictive analytics is one of the stages of analytics focuses on what will happen next by using algorithms based on type of variable data, identified relationship and correlation in step A. Predictive analytics is complimenting previous X analytics step B, we need to perform step B and C simultaneously. Considering specific variable identified for each vital downtime mechanisms and using baseline and connected device data need to develop and deploy predictive models.
For case study windshield wiper system, predictor variable or parameter is X which is first instance of speed reaches to pre-established LSL range. Rule based algorithm applied for illustrated case study, we need to utilize specific algorithm in line with parameter and available data for other applications or parameters. Alert on cell phone through integrated system for proactive communication is deployed aligned with speed predictive model. Key tools or commercially available software’s such as Weibull++, Python and Cloud Platform leveraged for establishing parameter range using baseline data, predictive algorithm by leveraging real time sensor data.
D - Preventive Action
Preventive action is proactive step initiated to avoid potential failure of product. Time for action when potential risk identified per prediction model. Based on previous steps for specific alert set with vital failure mechanisms mapping with failure cause (s), need to perform resolution either repair, or replace by evaluating specific failure mechanism and cause.
For case study windshield wiper system, removing dirt or other debris from wiper blade is one of the causes. Resolution of this cause helps to maintain wiper motor RPM in normal condition and reducing electrical overstress.
E - Reliable Product with Higher Uptime
Reliability is all about component/system/product will perform it’s intended function for specified period under stated conditions. In extension with inherent reliability of component/system/product considering dynamic usage and environment, required intelligent system to detect potential failures and early prevention. With structured integrated previous steps, we can prevent failure mode (s) or downtime resulting higher product uptime and improvement in Reliability. This is ultimately helping product availability for utilizing seasonal application operating window and robust approach for dynamic environment by minimizing effect of weather.
For case study windshield wiper system, wiper system availability whenever needed is contributing to higher uptime. Using intelligent integrated approach, we have ensured product to perform intended function by continuously enhancing time by optimizing cost impact due to downtime vs additional connected devices in product.
conclusions:

title: Assurance of Model-Based Autonomy for Robotic Space Missions
authors: Martin S. Feather, PhD, California Institute of Technology; Steven L. Cornford, PhD, California Institute of Technology; Klaus Havelund, PhD, California Institute of Technology; Key Words: assurance, autonomy, models, space missions
summary:
NASA's robotic space missions must make use of on-board automation and autonomy to control themselves when communication with Earth is slow (due to light-time delays across the solar system) or unavailable.  As mission concepts become more ambitious, increasingly capable forms of autonomy are required - ones that go well beyond executing a single preformulated script.  Assurance of autonomy - the means by which would-be mission proposers, reviewers and managers will be provided the confidence to trust their expensive assets to autonomous control - is a challenging necessity.
In this paper we look at assurance of some more capable forms of autonomy that use models - models of the environment in which system is to operate, and models of the asset (spacecraft, rover, helicopter, etc.) itself.  The latter models must cover the different factors crucial to the asset’s health and operation.  For example, managing electrical power - its source, storage and consumption -  is needed, and models are used to predict the power balance over time.  Likewise important is managing the thermal conditions - temperature of the asset, its sensitive instruments, its mechanisms, etc.  These models are used by the on-board controller to plan and schedule the asset's activities and to monitor the health of the hardware to take remedial action if need be when things go wrong (due to temporary faults, or permanent degradations and failures).
However, the computational resources on-board are typically but a fraction of those available on Earth.  As a result, the on-board models are deliberate simplifications of those created for ground operations, simplified for tractable execution within those limited computational resources.  Several key assurance challenges that stem from this are the following:
What process should we follow to derive simplified models so that the simplifications won’t mislead the asset into performing a dangerous activity?
How will we know the combination of simplified models remains sufficiently accurate (e.g., the power model’s simplifications when coupled with the thermal model’s simplifications don’t compound one another)?
What can we have the asset do to detect if things are straying too far from model predictions in time to do something about it?
This paper describes approaches to answering these questions, through a combination and adaptation of techniques for analysis, testing and monitoring drawn from other (non-space) domains.

title: Using Open-Sourced Programming Tools to Develop Economical Statistical Software
authors: Robert A. Belinski, PhD, P.E., Wabtec Corporation; Lydia Belinski, Ohio University; Key Words: Big Data and Internet of Things Application in R&M, Life Data Analysis
summary:
Over the past several years the major statistical software developers have drastically increased the purchase price and license fees for their products.  This has created a financial hardship for small and medium sized companies, individuals, and students.  In response, some companies have changed policies allowing only a few seats of these products.  Simultaneously, the developers have removed the option of flex licenses so now each individual user would be required to purchase a single seat at costs hovering around 2,000 dollars for some of the major brands.
In this environment, the authors were forced to develop their own software using open source tools such as R, Rstudio, Rstudio-Server.  These tools can be deployed on individual user’s computers or via the web on Rstudio Servers. The latter method allows the masses to connect to a web site and perform the statistical/reliability task that is required.   On a company basis, these individual tools can be tailored to the local user community, their specific needs, and operating procedures.  Considering the idea of a particular user’s requirements, tailored tools can be created allowing for a validated standard method of calculation as dictated by controlled design guides and the company’s quality management system. This contrasts with relying on each individual engineer to develop their own code and individual method to solve a task.  In addition to R based applications, applications utilizing the established office suites were also created.  Also, analysis packages that are part of the standard distributions of office suites, are underutilized.  Often, these “add on” tools are not common knowledge, so their methods are also demonstrated herein.  Included in both sets of tools are standard graphical interpretations of the output. title: Using Machine Learning to Focus on an Object of Interest During Remote Collaboration
authors: Brent Dingle, PhD, Raytheon Technologies; Coleman Eubanks, PhD, Raytheon Technologies; Keith Janasak, Raytheon Technologies; Avery Link, Raytheon Technologies; Alec Moore, Raytheon Technologies
summary:
As the need for world-wide, on-demand, real-time technical support increases, remote collaboration solutions are enabling critical virtual telepresence capabilities for remote Subject Matter Experts (SME). Whether the use case is providing remote technical support during assembly, test, inspection, integration, or troubleshooting and repair, today's commercial remote collaboration solutions face practical utilization challenges. Remote collaboration solutions rely on two-way video streaming. The deployment of these solutions is often restricted, or severely limited, to specific use cases in specific locations because of potential visual data spills. Mitigation of this risk currently means limiting where cameras are allowed and moving objects of interest (OOI) into rooms where cameras are deemed safe to use. Such limitations create a need for automatic filtering of live video streams which is easy for manufacturing and maintenance workers to use.
To address this need it is possible to modify and apply existing video processing solutions. The goal is to automatically limit the field of view to only the OOI and blur or remove the background prior to streaming. To accomplish this, one must identify the OOI and differentiate it from its visual background. This paper presents an investigation and application of machine learning (ML) background removal techniques. Discussion begins with basic approaches. The paper then transitions into more advanced ML methods of object recognition. This includes the possibility of improving ML methods by detecting staging volumes and restricting processing to such. Results will be discussed along with an overview of how implementing such methods can be achieved. Using the techniques discussed in this paper in conjunction with remote collaboration solutions, RAM practitioners will have a more secure method of remotely collaborating without risking visual data spills.

title: A Network Reliability Analysis Method for Complex Systems based on Complex Network Theory
authors: Yu Zang, PhD, China Transport Telecommunications & Information Center; Lance Fiondella, PhD, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Key Words: complex network theory; complex systems; failure scenario; network reliability analysis; reliability analysis
summary: Complex systems are composed of many heterogeneous subsystems and components, which contribute to system failure or degradation. Reliability analysis of complex systems has slowly gained attention, yet most research continues to focus on the degradation of components in complex systems, including multiple failure modes, propagation of failure modes, and uncertainty analysis. Achieving and preserving reliable operation of complex systems requires more complete architectural models, which can utilize the information on the components and interactions between subsystems and their components. To address this limitation, this paper presents a method to conduct network reliability analysis of complex systems. The approach employs complex network theory, including several parameters related to network properties. A network reliability analysis method is subsequently defined and a performance index specified. A case study illustrates the proposed method, interpreting results and identifying opportunities for future elaboration of the model. Our results indicate that the proposed method can evaluate the overall reliability and identify the weak modules and links of a complex system that should be targeted for improvement.

title: All-Terminal Network Reliability Estimation with Graph Neural Networks
authors: Alex Davila-Frias, Ph. D., Escuela Politécnica Nacional; Om Prakash Yadav, Ph. D., North Carolina A&T State University; Saeed Salem, Ph. D., North Dakota State University; Rakesh Jain, Ph. D., Malaviya National Institute of Technology; Key Words: all-terminal network reliability, edge-conditioned convolutions (ECC), graph neural networks (GNN)
summary: All-terminal network reliability is a crucial feature for critical infrastructures such as transportation, computer, and communication networks. Exact all-terminal network reliability (EATNR) calculation is a non-deterministic polynomial (NP hard) and computationally expensive problem, which has led the development of approximate methods based on artificial neural networks (ANNs). Although there have been some research studies on all-terminal reliability estimation using traditional ANNs, they require the upper bound network reliability as input. More recent deep learning (DL) approaches, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), remain limited because networks have varying structures and/or sizes. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been employed as well. However, DNNs require preprocessing procedures that compress the networks information in vectorial representations, e.g., graph embedding methods (GEMs). As an alternative to address these challenges, this study presents a preliminary development of all-terminal network reliability estimation based on graph neural networks (GNNs), a state-of-the-art deep learning technique. GNNs are appropriate for network reliability prediction as they have the capability of making graph-level regression by directly taking the input information from the graph domain in the form of adjacency matrix, and nodes/links features. To use GNNs for all-terminal network reliability estimation, an applicable architecture of GNN is developed. The network adjacency matrix along with topological attributes such as the node degree, clustering coefficient, and network efficiency are considered as node features that shape the inputs for GNNs. In addition, the proposed architecture guarantees the (reliability) output range [0,1]. In summary, All-Terminal Network Reliability Estimation with GNN, has advantages over traditional ANNs,  CNNs, and DNNs. First, traditional ANNs require the upper bound network reliability as input, an additional time-consuming calculation that GNNs do not need. Second, unlike CNNs, GNNs are able to predict the reliability for networks of varying sizes. Third, whereas DNNs require preprocessing methods to convert the adjacency matrix to vectors, GNNs do not, as they can directly capture the input information from the graph domain. Moreover, the experimental results obtained in the present study show enhanced prediction performance. A six-step process is proposed to exploit GNN capabilities by employing the graph domain information of a random set of networks together with the exact all terminal network reliability (EATNR) as target output during training. Different GNN architectures are investigated. The best input-architecture configuration is selected based on the root mean squared error (RMSE) considering cross-validation. A dataset of 6000 Erdős-Rényi random graphs was generated to this end. The best GNN proposed here, based on the RMSE (0.00934), outperforms previous ANN, CNN, and DNN approaches. The GNN achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.9979 and a p-value of 0.28 for a paired t-test between the actual and predicted reliability. There is also a significant computation time reduction achieved by using GNN (40 ms/network).

title: Use of SysML for Quantitative System Reliability and Availability Analysis
authors: Myron Hecht, The Aerospace Corporation; Jaron Chen, The Aerospace Corporation; Key Words: Reliability Models, SysML, Reliability Block Diagrams, System Reliability Prediction
summary: In projects using Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and SysML, it is now possible to easily perform reliability/availability modeling  and prediction starting at the conceptual design phase and continuing throughout the development using the SysML reliability library and SysML profile described here.  The innovation is the way in which the profile extends standard SysML model elements to reliability and availability analysis.  Values for failure rates, restoration rates, recovery probabilities, and other parameters are entered by SysML designers at the time they are creating the system and stored in SysML.  Equations for reliability block configurations (series, parallel, active/standby and k out of n) have been implemented and included in the version of the library presented here.  An example demonstrated the application of the library model elements.  Also discussed were , model verification and how the library can be extended.

title: Early Prediction of Lithium-Ion Battery Cycle Life by Machine Learning Methods
authors: Ankan Mitra, Arizona State University; Rong Pan, Ph. D., Arizona State University; Key Words: feature selection, ensemble machine learning, support vector regression, degradation, reliability prediction
summary: For a lithium-ion battery, its cycle life is defined as the number of full charge cycles that a battery can undergo until its full charge capacity falls below 80% of the design capacity. In a recent study by Severson et al. [1], a large set of lithium-ion battery cycle life experiments were conducted and analyzed, and early cycle data were used to predict battery lives without any prior assumptions on degradation mechanism. In this paper, we reexamine the data and suggest additional features to the model, which also use early cycle data (up to the first 100 cycles), for a better battery cycle life prediction. We suggest an ensemble machine learning method that combines several classifiers such as the k-nearest neighbor classifier, neural networks, support vector machines and decision tree-based classifiers for classifying batteries to low or high lifetime category. It is found that our ensemble approach provides more robust predictions. For predicting cycle life, a support vector regression model is suggested, and we compare it with an elastic net-based regression model. It is found that SVR outperforms elastic net in terms of percentage prediction error.
conclusions: In this study, we analyze the cycle life data of lithium-iron phosphate cells. Early cycle data (up to the first 100 cycles) and their features are carefully examined for building predictive models. It is observed that some of those suggested features (related to temperature and voltage curves), have very high feature importance scores with respect to both classification and regression tasks, which is aligned with the chemical and mechanical changes in the electrodes of lithium-iron battery over its life cycle. We suggest an EML method that combines several classifiers such as k-nearest neighbors, neural networks, support vector machines and decision tree-based classifiers, and this classifier provides more robust prediction over randomly partitioned datasets. For the regression task, a support vector regression model is suggested and compared with the elastic net regression model. It is observed that SVR outperforms elastic net in terms of percentage error over different dataset partitions by fitting nonlinear decision boundaries for the regression task.

title: Large-scale Fault Tree Implementation: A Software Tutorial
authors: Balaje T. Thumati, PhD, Hottinger Bruel & Kjaer Inc.; Jeffery Kemp, Hottinger Bruel & Kjaer Inc.; Key Words: Fault tree analysis, software simulation, binary decision diagrams, minimal cutsets
summary:
Modern systems are becoming increasingly complex and expensive, which requires a systematic method to analyze various failure modes. A common approach is to use Fault Trees (FTs) for quantitative and qualitative reliability analysis. For reliability and safety engineers, one of the key requirements is to determine various combinations of basic events (component faults) that lead to a top-level (system) failure in a fault tree. In this regard, several techniques have been developed to generate Minimal Cut Sets (MCS). A well-known technique is Binary Decision Diagrams (BDD), which help to determine MCS for large fault trees in an efficient manner.
In this work, we present a tutorial to analyze large fault trees using a software implementation of binary decision diagrams. The implemented BDD algorithms allow us to generate minimal cutsets and their failure probabilities efficiently. Therefore, we can quickly find all combinations of basic events that will lead to the occurrence of an undesired failure. A basic event could be a hardware or software component failure, operating conditions, human interference, etc.
We will demonstrate a few different types of fault trees ranging from tens to thousands of gates and events, which could be applicable to various reliability and safety engineering problems. In addition, an overview of the generated minimal cutsets along with probability of failures will be presented. A good software implementation of BDD algorithms should be able to assist engineers with determining availability, reliability, and maintainability of systems through various stages of a product life cycle. Our intent of this tutorial is to present an overview of BDD, discuss about various algorithms for analyzing BDD to generate MCS, and finally present some software simulation results to demonstrate BDD algorithms.

title: Comparison of Modeling Approaches for PRA Models in Different Software Programs
authors: John E. Weglian, Electric Power Research Institute; Jeff Riley, Electric Power Research Institute; Shinsaku Fujita, Tohoku Electric Power Company; Key Words: PRA, probabilistic risk assessment
summary:
Different probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) software tools use different techniques, assumptions, approximations, and modeling practices to create and evaluate the PRA model.  When converting a model from one software tool to another, this will often lead to a difference in the calculated results.  It is important to understand the differences so that the analyst can verify that the model conversion was performed correctly.  In some cases, the differences are expected and can be explained by differences in model construction or quantification.
Some of the differences that can lead to changes in the results include common cause failure modeling, use of initiating events in the fault tree logic, the treatment of house events or flag events, and the calculation of success probabilities.  It is also possible (even likely) that solving the PRA model in a new tool will identify previously unknown errors in the PRA model.
Differences in the final results do not indicate a problem with one piece of software or the other.  PRA models provide risk insights and help to identify risk vulnerabilities.  Risk decisions are often made based on a change in risk calculation or through the use of importance measures.  Slight changes in top event probabilities because of software differences have little impact on these risk metrics that are used to make risk-informed decisions.

title: Insights Available from Cutset Analysis
authors: John E. Weglian, Electric Power Research Institute; Jeff Riley, Electric Power Research Institute; Key Words: cutsets, PRA, probabilistic risk assessment
summary:
Fault trees can be evaluated by generating cutsets—combinations of basic events that, if TRUE, lead to the top event to also be TRUE. These cutsets can provide a number of benefits beyond simply estimating the top event probability.  Most importantly, cutsets help the analyst understand what combinations of failures most often lead to the failure of the fault tree and can tell the “story” of how failures can occur.  Furthermore, cutsets allow the analyst to post-process the results to account for impacts that are too complicated to model in the fault tree directly.  With this information, cutsets provide a quick way to perform sensitivity studies on the results and get importance measures for the items modeled by the fault tree.  With this quick calculation capability, cutsets can be used to perform an uncertainty analysis on the results based on the uncertainty distributions on the underlying failure data.
Cutsets give the analyst the ability to look beyond just the top event probability.  With the insights available from analyzing the cutsets, the analyst can make better risk-informed decisions and provide suggestions to improve the design, operation, or safety of the modeled systems.

title: Reliability Analysis of Carbon Capture and Storage Systems
authors: Bayan Hamdan, University of Illinois; Pingfeng Wang, PhD, University of Illinois; Key Words: Fault Tree Analysis, Bayesian Networks, Multi-fidelity, Carbon Capture
summary: While offshore salt caverns, as part of the carbon capture and storage (CCS) systems, could offer significant advantages in storage carbon dioxide, they are still not widely implemented, partially due the challenges in maintaining the safe operation of such systems with a long-projected storage time. The presented study provided a Fault Tree (FT) analysis for the causal relationships of storage system failures with respect to the root causes, and further the potential integration of the FT with the dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) in order to monitor offshore salt caverns in the long-term operations. The presented study can incorporate both physics-of-failure models and sensory data to update the failure probabilities of the components in the offshore salt cavern storage system. The fault tree considers unintentional flow as the main failure mode and divides the system into three subsystems: the wellhead, the well and the cavern itself. Then, each individual subsystem is studied based on the components in the subsystem and the NORSOK standards for safe well design. The fault tree presented in this study also outlines the relationship between the failure modes and the effect they have on the system failure. Th fault tree analysis tool can then be converted into a DBN to provide a long-term monitoring framework for offshore CCS systems with limited observability, where real-time data can be utilized in order to update the probabilities of failure of components over time.

title: Random Fatigue Modeling using Neural Stochastic Differential Equations
authors: Andreas Joanni, Siemens AG; Ulrich Hipp, Siemens Mobility AG; Key Words: random fatigue, stochastic differential equations, crack growth, neural networks, scientific machine learning
summary:
Due to the inherent randomness observed in fatigue data, stochastic modeling of the corresponding deterioration processes is of crucial importance for estimating and managing the fatigue reliability of components (such as remaining useful life prediction) and has long been the subject of research.  More recently, it was demonstrated how to seamlessly combine classical differential equation models with machine learning and, thereby, to achieve efficiency gains by utilizing all known prior knowledge of the underlying phenomena.  The purpose and novelty of this paper is to apply one of these combined methods, more precisely neural stochastic differential equations, to the problem of random fatigue modeling and to investigate the advantages and drawbacks.
The feasibility and coherence of this particular approach is demonstrated by means of a two-state stochastic differential equation model for crack growth with random fluctuations of the crack growth rate and a nonlinear crack growth law, where the model is trained with experimental fatigue crack growth data reported by Virkler.  The results suggest that the trained neural SDE picks up the experimental values in a reasonable manner, however not as good as a conventional approach comprising extraction of certain features from the experimental data, preprocessing, and fitting a cubic polynomial crack growth law. Nevertheless, there seems to be potential for further improvement for the neural SDE approach, while retaining the advantages of straightforward applicability and flexibility.

title: Lifetime Performance of Conformal Coatings in Harsh Plasma Cutting Applications
authors: Chris Kang, Hypertherm Inc.; Erik Jimenez, Hypertherm Inc; Joe Schwendler, Hypertherm Inc.; Andrew Pillsbury, Hypertherm Inc.; Key Words: Accelerated Testing, Conformal Coating, Electrochemical Migration, Physics of Failure, Reliability, Soft Error
summary:

Conformal coatings protect electronic control boards against moisture, iron dusts, and corrosive chemicals. We introduced a comprehensive verification procedure for qualifying alternative coating materials which are applicable to other industrial systems operating in harsh environments. It aims to cover material suitability and product assurance for performance and reliability at multiple phases. We also observed transient soft errors driven by lower SIR (surface insulation resistance) during testing.  Our weak link analysis, with the most susceptible circuitry, shows that transient behaviors during accelerated test conditions, will be minimal during actual application conditions. Permanent lifetime reduction mechanisms were confirmed with statistical correlation of coating thickness and dielectric strength in the left tail thinner zones.   Statistical modeling is aligned with physics of failure (PoF) offering insights to support ongoing enhancement of conformally coated boards.

We expect the alternative material to provide better performance than the incumbent material in our challenging application conditions as we prepare for more compact board designs.

The primary failure mode involves current leakage caused by electrochemical migration. We observed more intermittent failures in the candidate materials during the accelerated testing at an early stage.
Statistical modeling coupled with failure physics offered technical insight into reliability enhancement of conformally coated boards.  We expect that the risk of transforming transient interruptions into permanent failure will be negligible in our actual use conditions via coating thickness optimization and minimization of moisture or ionic contamination.  Subsequently, its statistical significance will be assured with sufficient sample size of the most sensitive circuitries for soft transient error testing. Eventually, our final candidate material will meet our full acceptance criteria with equivalent, or better, early reliability, soft error, and life test results vs the incumbent.
The rigor of process and contamination control will continue to be reinforced to prohibit moisture diffusion and electrolytic formation, thereby leading to our system reliability assurance. Our technical understanding of degradation behaviors, coupled with transient errors, will pave a quantitative approach for further improvement and optimization in product and process design. This integrated modeling framework will gain sophistication as we collect more data from accelerated life testing and actual use cases from the field.

title: Multi-Scale System Reliability Analysis of Multi-Layer Network Infrastructures
authors: Phat K. Huynh, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Ca Hoang, University of South Florida; Duy Nguyen, Posts and Telecommunications Institute of Technology of Vietnam; Tien Truong, University of South Florida; Trung Q. Le, PhD, University of South Florida

title: Probabilistic AI Reliability Analysis in MBSE and SysML
authors: Sanja Cvijic, PhD, Charles River Analytics; Steve Hookway, Charles River Analytics; Scott Harrison, Charles River Analytics; Andrew Strelzoff, PhD, Charles River Analytics; Key Words: artificial intelligence, Bayesian inference, machine learning, MBSE, reliability analysis
summary:
Systems engineers, using model-based systems engineering (MBSE) environments and languages such as Cameo and Systems Modeling Language (SysML), can effectively model and simulate structural and functional relationships within complex systems.  However, the MBSE tools are insufficient in representing uncertainty in these relationships or uncertainty in the system performance under varying environmental conditions, which is critical in understanding performance and reliability of the created designs.  In particular, reliability engineers using MBSE tools must manually map SysML designs into reliability block diagrams and analyze them in a new suite of tools.  This process is error-prone and leads to a disconnect between the system design and reliability analysis processes.
The solution demonstrated in this paper facilitates ProbSysML, a probabilistic AI plug-in to Cameo that supports evaluation of system performance and reliability under uncertainty using probabilistic inference within Cameo.  The key elements of the plug-in include: 1) expressive representation of uncertainty in system designs and their impact on system performance and reliability, 2) automated conversion of this representation into probabilistic models, and 3) probabilistic inference for evaluating system performance and reliability   based on probabilistic outcomes.  The plug-in is demonstrated on an example of designing a solar panel for a satellite such that the reliability of the design is maximized while considering survivability trade-offs between power requirements, weight, and degradation due to solar storms.

title: Analytical Reliability Prediction for an Industrial Dynamic Furnace
authors: Vinícius Gonçalves, Vale; Bianca Medeiros, Vale; Welbert Alves, Vale; Key Words: Reliability Block Diagram, Complex System, Product Design, Mining, Fault Tree Analysis.
summary:
Reliability block diagram (RBD) is one of the most relevant techniques to predict a product life cycle with complex systems. A RBD is a graphical representation of the components of the system and how they are reliability-wise related. In this work, an analytical study of combined subsystems for the world’s first Dynamic Furnace, using microwave for drying iron ore and curing briquettes, is carried out.
Most problems in building reliable industrial products are a consequence of unstructured reliability plan for modelling probability of failure on demand. Initially, analytical equations are purposed to calculate the probability of success or failure, considering the life distribution of each equipment that assembles the furnace, therefore detailed investigation is deployed for product assurance.
The integration of fault tree analysis (FTA) methods with RBD modelling deals with performance reliability prediction adequately accounting for the fact that complex integrated subsystems have a failure rate varying over time.
The results show that the analytical model combined with empirical data can describe the reliability growth and define optimal strategies for scheduling checkpoints, overhaul time and preventive maintenance for such a heavy and innovative system on industrial shop floor.

title: A Unified Model for Tradeoff of Sample Size, Reliability and Risks During Product Life Cycle
authors: Zhaofeng Carl Huang, Aerospace Corporation; Key Words: Demonstrated Reliability, Confidence Level, Tolerance Intervals, Variable Sampling Plan, Producer and Consumer Risks, Sample Size, Design Requirements, Process Capability, Produce Acceptance
summary: The paper presents a parametric model that ties and unifies key product life cycle attributes with reliability parameters together to support reliability tradeoff and design optimization during product life cycle activities. A unique and significant contribution of this model and its applications is the integration of parametric consideration and evaluation of product development attributes such and design and demonstration requirements, manufacturing capability, life testing, and quality acceptance, and requirement verification and validation with the reliability parameters such as reliability, confidence level, sample size, and produce and consumer risks.  The model is built upon the Normal distribution tolerance interval and tolerance limit theories and methods. The paper discusses several unification features of the model including the unification of the model with literature surveyed sample size determination methods and formulas, the unification with tolerance limits, the unification with variable sampling plans for lot quality level monitoring with hypothesis testing. The paper shows how some challenging product life cycle questions can be addressed by the model with illustrative examples.  The unified model and its vision can be a very valuable tool to support product life cycle reliability evaluation and tradeoff consideration with design and development optimization, and Statistical Engineering implementation [1].

title: Modeling the Impact of Corrosion Orientation and Location on Pipeline Reliability
authors: Nikesh Kumar, University of Arkansas; José Carlos Hernández Azucena, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Haitao Liao, PhD, University of Arkansas; Edward Pohl, PhD, University of Arkansas; Key Words: Reliability modeling, pipeline corrosion, finite element method
summary: The reliability of pipelines, which are critical infrastructures supporting global energy needs and economic activities, is threatened by structural failures induced by corrosion. This research investigates the effects of different corrosion defect shapes and their orientations on pipeline reliability. By integrating Finite Element Method (FEM), Limit State Functions (LSFs), and Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS), we provide a comprehensive framework for assessing pipeline reliability. The study reveals significant impacts of defect dimensions on reliability and emphasizes the importance of robust maintenance strategies to ensure pipeline integrity.
conclusions:
The reliability of pipelines with corrosion defects is profoundly influenced by the dimensions of the defects, particularly their depths. This study highlights the paramount importance of minimizing the depths of defects to ensure high reliability and maintain the structural integrity of pipeline systems. Defect depth has emerged as the most critical factor, with deeper defects significantly undermining pipeline reliability. This adjustment helps to mitigate the adverse effects of defect dimensions, resulting in a more robust and resilient pipeline structure. The Monte Carlo simulation results underscore the significant variability in pipeline reliability due to differing defect dimensions material properties. A key takeaway from this research is the need to integrate advanced monitoring and predictive techniques into pipeline management practices. Real-time data analytics, combined with rigorous inspection routines, can significantly enhance the detection and management of corrosion defects. This study provides the relationship between defect dimensions and pipeline reliability. More accurate predictive models and maintenance strategies can be developed for how different defect geometries impact structural integrity. Integrating real-time sensor data, advanced predictive modeling, and machine learning techniques can revolutionize pipeline maintenance and reliability. Overall, this analysis highlights the critical influence of defect dimensions on pipe reliability under varying operating pressures. Defects with smaller depths and widths demonstrate higher reliability across pressure ranges, while defects with larger depths, widths, are more prone to failure. This research shows the need for better pipeline management to address corrosion for safer and reliable pipelines.
Future research should focus on developing advanced predictive models that incorporate real-time data from sensors to monitor defect growth and estimate its impact on pipeline reliability. Additionally, the effects of various environmental factors on corrosion progression and pipeline integrity will be explored to acquire more comprehensive understandings of pipeline reliability behavior.

title: A Simplified Testing Approach for Performance Analysis of Integrated Circuits through Reliability Testing
authors: Cher Ming Tan, Chang Gung University; Steve Wang, Moxa Inc.; Vimal Kant Pandey, Moxa Inc.; Henry YH Luo, Moxa Inc.; Key Words: accelerated life testing, temperature-humidity test, temperature cycling test, I-V characterization.
summary:
During the COVID (coronavirus disease) period, the semiconductor market was hit by the shortage of electronic chips affecting many industries. To cope with the issue in Moxa, two major steps were suggested, first is to use C-grade ICs (Integrated Circuit) instead of A-grade ICs and second, is to use the ICs of alternate vendor instead of the regular vendor. ICs are commonly classified into different grades based on their operating temperature specifications. For example, A-grade ICs are rated for temperatures between -40°C and 85°C, while C-grade ICs are rated for 0°C to 70°C. Although both grades of ICs share the same design and are manufactured using identical processes, the vendor employs a sorting method to categorize these ICs according to their respective operating temperature ranges. To verify that such steps will not impact the reliability of the system, accelerated reliability tests namely temperature-humidity and temperature cycle are conducted for the A-grade and C-grade ICs. Same tests are conducted for the alternate vendor and regular vendor ICs to compare their performance. However, testing complex ICs having multiple pins is not a straightforward way as it requires complex test circuits. This work proposed a simple method of testing such ICs by using just the I-V characterization pins of the ICs. I-V characterization is the process of measuring the current-voltage relationship of electronic devices. It involves sweeping the voltage from a specified minimum to a maximum value and recording the corresponding current. The proposed method is based on the fact that the failure in bond wires and bond pads are the common causes of ICs failures in the operational environment.
This article discusses temperature-humidity and temperature cycling testing, detailing their results, and computing reliability under normal environmental conditions. It starts by using I-V data to identify the resistance change associated with the pins of IC and define failure criteria. Through a series of failure analysis, we have identified corrosion as the root cause of IC failure. Consequently, leveraging this understanding of failure physics, we ascertain that its reliability model conforms to the PoF (Physics of Failure) models. Furthermore, analysis of test data reveals a statistical model consistent with log-normal distribution. By integrating information on product usage environment, we derive an acceleration model and subsequently estimate the 5-year reliability of the IC under normal operating conditions. The 5-year reliability results show that both A-grade and C-grade ICs as well as the alternate and regular vendors ICs are resilient to temperature-humidity but vulnerable to temperature variations. Interestingly, the performance of A-grade and C-grade remains consistent over 5 years. However, the 5-year performance of DUTs (device under test) from alternate vendors surpasses that of those from the regular vendors.
