title: Reliability Analysis of Dynamic Fiber Bundle Models with Local Load Sharing
authors: Tushar C. Tummala, VNRVJ Institute of Technology; Venkata R.C. Tummala, PhD, Consultant; Suprasad V. Amari, PhD, BAE Systems; Key Words: fiber bundle models, load sharing systems, local load sharing, system reliability,
summary: Dynamic fiber bundle models are useful tools in explaining dynamic failure behavior in heterogeneous materials. Such models shed light on diverse phenomena such as fatigue in structural materials and earthquakes in geophysical settings. This paper presents a new method for reliability analysis of dynamic fiber bundle models with local load sharing rule. According to this rule, a failed fiber redistributes its load onto its two nearest flanking survivors. As a consequence of the load transfer, the lifetime of the receptors is reduced, which in turn introduces the dynamic failure behavior. Unlike in the previous works, the proposed model is not restricted to any specific form of load-life relationship. Similarly, unlike the exponential distribution used in the previous works, the paper considers that the remaining lifetimes of the surviving fibers under the current load follow a general failure time distribution. The paper presents both exact reliability formulas and easy to compute bounds.  Further, the paper presents a fast simulation algorithm that greatly increases the bundle sizes that can be analyzed. As a special case, simplified formulas are presented for a commonly used case where the underlying failure time distribution is Weibull and the load-life relationship is described by power law.
conclusions: In this paper, we presented a new method for analyzing the reliability of dynamic fiber bundles models considering the local load sharing (LLS) rule. We provided easy to compute closed-form approximations for PHM-TFR model with power law breakdown rule and general failure time distributions. In addition, we also proposed an efficient hybrid simulation method by integrating analytical and simulation method. These results are applicable for a wide range of applications in the fields of materials science and statistical mechanics. As a future research work, we plan to extend the proposed method for other 2D fiber bundle models.

title: Semiconductor Parametric Yield Prediction: A Combination of Machine Learning and Physics-Informed Approach
authors: Karthik Sankaran, UCLA;; Ali Mosleh, Ph. D., UCLA; Kamran Hakim, Teradyne Inc.; Key Words: Machine Learning, ASICs, Semiconductor Yield, Process Nodes
summary: In summary, this research aims to provide a methodology to use process-based factors to improve the robustness of existing yield models. A Process Adjustment factor has been previously proposed by the authors to improve on the existing Defect-based yield by including physical factors to distinguish between various technology nodes. A data analysis methodology is proposed to reduce the dimensionality of the Sort data and perform Machine Learning on it to determine pass or fail based on the test results. This is further used to correlate with the corresponding E-test data to assign a “Pass” or “Fail” to each set of measurements based on the respective die locations. A parametric shift component is now added to the yield model and a data-based approach using the E-test data is made. Physical factors are being used in this case to help with estimation based on engineering features, rather than requiring a separate adjustment factor.

title: Four Problematic Methods In Reliability Analysis
authors: Harry W. Jones, Ph.D., NASA Ames Research Center; Key Words: Reliability analysis, reliability prediction, reliability growth, redundancy, fault tolerance
summary: Some basic methods used in reliability analysis are problematic because they produce incorrect and overoptimistic predictions.  Initially gratifying forecasts are often invalidated by testing and operational experience.  The problematic methods in reliability analysis include estimating the system failure rate as the sum of component failure rates, assuming that reliability growth continues indefinitely during testing, overestimating the benefits of redundancy, and using the fault tolerance count instead of a detailed reliability analysis.  Reliability analysis can produce more optimism than accuracy.  This bug may now be a welcome feature.  The optimistic bias inevitable in project planning should be corrected by realistic reliability analysis that reflects relevant experience.  That the inevitable overoptimism of reliability analysis is surprising suggests willful blindness.  Rigorous methods and impartial critical reviews are necessary to improve reliability analysis.
conclusions: The problematic methods used in reliability analysis involve estimating the failure rate, modelling reliability growth, implementing redundancy, and using fault tolerance.  While these methods are traditional, widely accepted, and often required, they are well known to be unsatisfactory and seem to reflect overoptimism and favorable bias.  Using actual data on the reliability results of similar projects can provide more realistic reliability analysis.

title: Towards Risk-based Rationality in Autonomous Systems and Operations
authors: Ingrid B. Utne, PhD, Norwegian University of Science and Technology; Tor A. Johansen, PhD, Norwegian University of Science and Technology; Asgeir J. Sørensen, PhD, Norwegian University of Science and Technology; Key Words: Autonomous systems, Supervisory risk control, Marine safety, Control system design
summary: This paper presents the novel concept called supervisory risk control (SRC) which provides risk-based rationality improving the safety and intelligence of autonomous systems. Autonomous cyber-physical systems enable new and challenging types of transport, efficient mapping and monitoring of oceans and land, and inspections and interventions of structures, with less dependence on human operators. More autonomous functionality may improve operational efficiency, but society and authorities are reluctant to approve highly autonomous systems due to uncertainties related to safe performances. The SRC concept therefore implements online risk assessment and modeling into control system algorithms. This enables the systems to assess the risk level and make decisions based on perception, comprehension, and projection of future operational risk scenarios (i.e., “risk- based rationality”), which today primarily is done by a human operator. In addition to presenting the concept, the paper gives results from development, simulation, and field experiments related to SRC. The research results show the feasibility of including risk aspects more extensively in the control systems than existing solutions, e.g., for machinery systems and navigation of autonomous ships. The paper also pinpoints the future research and development needs. The main application area so far is autonomous marine and maritime systems and operations, although the results are relevant across domains for improved system safety, integrity, and reduced accident risk.

title: Risk Assessments Integrating V2X into Cooperative Driving Automation
authors: Camila Correa-Jullian, University of California Los Angeles; Ali Mosleh, PhD, University of California Los Angeles; Jiaqi Ma, PhD, University of California Los Angeles; Key Words: Automated Driving Systems, Vehicle-to-Everything, Hybrid-Causal Logic, Driver Behavior
summary:
Cooperative Driving Automation (CDA) and Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) paradigms have been developed to address the limitations single-vehicle perception and decision-making capabilities across different Levels of Driving Automation [1], [2]. V2X encompasses a combination of technologies embedded into vehicles, infrastructure, and even pedestrians, relying on a combination of sensor data, wireless connectivity networks, and real-time calculations to enhance the driver’s and the vehicle’s perception, localization, and planning tasks [3]. While significant research efforts have been made towards designing and implementing V2X-enabled functions and cooperative driving technologies, many challenges must still be addressed. In particular, there is a need for systematic approaches to determine the safety impact and risk reduction benefits, including key aspects of hardware, software, and human reliability, connectivity, and improved methods to assess traffic and safety impacts.
This work presents an initial approach to perform risk assessments of V2X technologies based on the Hybrid Causal Logic (HCL) framework. This approach draws from novel hazard identification methodologies to define agents, critical events, and key tasks, failures, and errors. The methodology incorporates the effect driver-system team models [4], [5] on the overall system’s safety, as well as enhancing context representation to consider effects of road types, weather conditions, traffic levels, and technology effectiveness under limited data availability. An example application for cooperative collision avoidance is presented together with a discussion on data sources and potential data collection efforts to strengthen PRA-based analysis of V2X technologies.

title: Use of Inherited Items in Projects at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center
authors: Jeffrey W. Dawson, PhD, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; Key Words: risk assessment, spaceflight, COTS, inherited item, component
summary: The Inherited Item Risk Assessment (IIRA) process has been developed and refined at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) to ensure that Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA) requirements are chosen based on a risk assessment. Risk-based SMA is a holistic approach that allocates scarce project resources used for SMA to where they are most effective and eliminates unnecessary requirements. GSFC’s traditional SMA requirements for quality, parts selection, reliability, and inspection require significant oversight of contractor work and rigorous analysis of part selection and component designs. As commercial component quality has improved over time, and some contractors have shown their capability to produce space-proven, reliable components, not all traditionally-imposed SMA requirements are needed for proven hardware. Avoiding unneeded requirements can reduce risk in space missions and decrease cost. The IIRA process helps projects and contractors select appropriate SMA requirements based on the risk profile of the mission and the proven capabilities of component and spacecraft bus suppliers. The use of IIRAs allows projects to require only those SMA deliverables from contractors that actually reduce risk, while eliminating unneeded requirements that drive up cost, prolong schedules, and sometimes may actually increase risk.

title: Precursors: An Analysis System in Reliability Parallel with FAA Certification
authors: Jan B. Smith, PE; Key Words:  Event Interval Probability, P-values, Reductionism, Chaos Theory, Monte Carlo, Probabilistic Significance
summary:
The fatal crash rate for the worldwide jet scheduled carrier fleet has improved by a factor of 12 over the past 50 years.  This improvement is primarily due to the FAA, NTSB, and Boeing, as most planes are Boeing. This has been achieved through the design, manufacturing, and certification process, along with thorough investigation and correction of any problems that arise.  However, it is essential to note that since 1958, at least 28% of new fleet designs were certified, although later discovered to be unsafe, often after crashes, and the trend is not improving.  The recent incidents involving the Boeing 737 MAX, including two crashes and a door plug blowout, highlight this longstanding but unacknowledged issue with new fleet certification.  These events on the 737 MAX, avoidable with the specific data analysis methodology presented, emphasize the urgent need for this additional, independent layer of safety to supplement current certification technology and methods.
This paper underscores the necessity of augmenting current conventional methods for the safety and reliability assurance of new fleet designs with this new, unrecognized data analysis methodology.  Any event, instance, or happening in the arrow of time that is countable has a time interval since the last happening of the same type. The analysis technology, event interval probability (EIP), reveals a series of probability mass functions (PMF) for the event time intervals immediately upon every event.  These probability distributions reside in the history of any happening and extend to future happenings.  Because any change in anything can be a happening, an event, the method applies to precursors, even low-level signals of no importance, when the signal is taken in isolation.
These probabilities are determined using the 737 MAX crash and crash precursor and the door plug blowout precursor. With probability analysis of the precursors, all three primary events were avoidable.  The FAA conducted a 737 MAX risk assessment after the first crash, finding an uncorrected fleet life risk of 2,920.9 fatalities.  The true risk was 95 times greater. This difference is 275,258 fatalities.  The FAA should investigate the EIP technology and either use the method or explain why not.
The reliability of any system is described as an emergent property found with EIP.  The system is the set of causes producing an event.  The system does not need to be known, understood, or even describable, as causal information is not used in EIP.  This is difficult for anyone to understand, especially experts in the system producing the events, as the human reaction is to revert to reductionism – breaking the complex into smaller, more understandable pieces.  Social and human system examples are used to understand how system reliability can be known in maximum detail as a probability distribution with no system knowledge.  A single event is often all that is needed to recognize a reliability shift to a new level.   Again, this is difficult for professionals to accept because they immediately think of statistics, but EIP is fundamentally a probabilistic process, not a statistical process.
Child Protective Services (CPS) investigation dates are used as precursors to a child’s death, and police use of force citizen complaint dates are precursors to the death of George Floyd in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in 2020.  Dates for these social system precursors, as with 737 MAX precursors, identify actionable “reliability” that, if acted upon, could have easily avoided all primary events.  The term “reliability” is used in this unorthodox manner and applications as no better term to describe this universal emergent system property is known.
1    INTRODUCTION
Identifying and correcting the causes leading to the Boeing 737 MAX reliability issues is appropriate and is a current focus. This is the traditional way to achieve system reliability—working within the system and changing the system to solve potential and actual failures. This conventional viewpoint is that system reliability performance is determined and understood by working inside the system with the details (components, subsystems, and their interactions). Systems theory would call this reductionism— breaking down the complex into more fundamental and understandable pieces.  Thus far, all human progress is based upon reductionism, and an airplane would not exist without it.  As calculated from published data [1], reductionism has led to a 12-fold increase in worldwide fleet flights between fatal crashes over the last 50 years.  Without replacing reductionism, EIP is based on an additional but opposite viewpoint of system reliability as an emergent property determined by system performance – what comes out of the system instead of what goes in.  Reductionism is a bottom-up view, and emergence is a top-down view. Both views are needed, but reductionism is the only recognized viewpoint.
EIP recognizes the existence of a series of probability mass functions (PMFs) formed from past event time intervals. It identifies reliability deviation from an expectation and calculates PMFs for the future, doing so with unprecedentedly small datasets necessary for high-reliability systems.
The method, applied to the 737 MAX, using data available before the events happened, would have prevented both crashes and the door plug blowout.  Social and human systems are included as examples to demonstrate universal applicability and help better understand the why and how of using the method on precursors.
2	EIP concept with examples
Events (occurrences of any kind) occur over time, whether primary events or precursors.  They are countable, and each event has an associated time interval from the previous event of the same type.  When the event is a failure, this time between events (TBE) is synonymous with the time between failure (TBF), with which reliability engineers are familiar.  The event or happening can be a minor incident that may be a precursor to a primary event, such as a crash or death.
EIP is implemented in two parts. The first is to identify event intervals inconsistent with those from a comparison system. This is done with a null hypothesis that reliability equals that of the comparison system, such as a peer group, and the comparison system intervals are generated by a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) with events being independent and identically exponential distributed (IIED).  While complex systems often produce events in time as an HPP, there is no assumption that it does.  The null is evaluated with probability values (p-values); however, p-values are found not with statistics but with probability theory.
This analysis often identifies intervals that are a step change from the comparison with only a single interval. To take advantage of this sensitivity, the analysis should be contemporaneous, immediately upon an event being experienced. The driving purpose of EIP is to immediately identify probabilistic significance in event intervals, allowing quick intervention to prevent primary events.  This intervention ends the first part of EIP and uses the conventional, reductionist, bottom-up view working within the causal system.
The second EIP step is taken when needed. If the unreliable system remains in service due to the time required to investigate and correct it, the risk of continued uncorrected operation in service may need to be calculated. A numerical method and Monte Carlo simulation manage the math, and the results are a calculated cumulative failure (event) distribution showing time to the next event(s).  This distribution is a PMF.
While complex system reliability can only be determined at the system level as an emergent property and can never be determined through reductionism, this concept is not currently accepted.  Subject matter experts (SMEs) mistakenly believe the opposite is true.  It is difficult for anyone, and even more so for SMEs, to understand that system reliability can only be determined from a top-down view using system performance data.  The more knowledge one has of a system, the greater the tendency to immediately jump into causes and effects when a system reliability issue is suspected.  Applying EIP to social and human systems, where engineers do not know how the system works, may aid in understanding reliability as an emergent property.  In these social systems, the top-down view measures an unrecognized system property we call “reliability.” Once “reliability” is deemed problematic, fixing the system that generates that reliability requires reductionism – the bottom-up view.
2.1 Child Abuse Precursor
In 2022, a mother and another adult were charged with the 2020 murder of an eight-year-old child by starvation and abuse in Houston, Texas. Typically, child-specific data are unavailable to the public; however, because a death was involved, the Texas Family and Protective Services (that we will call the more general Child Protective Services or CPS) released CPS abuse investigation dates and findings [2].  These investigation dates can be used in the following precursor example.  This will demonstrate the analysis concept, application to precursors, and specifically how the little girl's years of living with abuse and starvation with eventual death were avoidable using the method proposed for the FAA.
Figure 1 provides a general description of the system that generates CPS investigation dates. This system consists of two major subsystems.  One is a system of complex causes and effects that produces an environment of abuse.  The other is a system of causes and effects that generates a report of suspected abuse.  Neither of these complex subsystems can be adequately described, much less the interactions between them and the environment.  System boundaries cannot be drawn without leaving a possible cause-and-effect out, yet to design a system, system boundaries are necessary.  For example, pilots act according to design assumptions inside the design system boundary.  This is appropriate and necessary for design; however, pilots' actions are a reality – not an assumption or design constraint when the design is in service.  Reality is not limited to artificial boundaries.  With EIP, the system is whatever produced the events.  Because system knowledge is not used, it is independent of conventional reductionism.

Before the blowout, there were three instances when the auto pressurization fail light came on in the cockpit.  Pilots switched to ‘ALTN,’ a backup system, during these events. The blowout date is the fourth event because the auto pressurization fail light would have been activated upon the blowout.  The airline noted the issue and restricted the plane from flights to Hawaii so that it could quickly return to an airport should an emergency arise. In hindsight, low-level precursor signals such as the alert light are always easy to see, but to avoid the primary events, these signals must be sought out in advance when there may be no apparent reason to do so.  These nonobvious reasons for addressing low-level signals will become evident later when justification and data analysis automation are presented.
Of course, it is too late to prevent the realized 737 MAX crashes and door plug blowout. However, by showing how the application of this new science could have prevented these primary events, we argue that this data analysis can prevent similar future occurrences.
3 Zero-point attractor
The TBE data of Figure 7, taken at face value, are not from a stable attractor.  The universal rule that produces stable attractors is e-λt [7].  This is the same equation for the reliability of steady-state repairable complex systems.  This engineering application has limits beyond which the equation does not apply, and the stable attractor has the same limits for the same reasons.  The event rate must be a constant average.  When λ, the event rate, increases, the TBE continually decreases; it is a point attractor approaching zero.  Chaos theory identifies point attractors, so calling this a zero-point attractor seems appropriate.  (The event rate can also decrease, which is not considered here).  It can be understood that an increasing event rate, with decreasing event TBE, given sufficient time with unchanging causes and effects, mathematically must approach but not reach a zero-length time interval.  A complex causality system with multiple contributing causes will generate a stable attractor.  In contrast, when a single failure mode dominates, the causal system can produce the zero-point attractor.  As reliability engineers know, complex system reliability allows using the equation R= e-λt.  However, they know this may not be useable for single failure modes because the failure rate λ is typically not a constant average.  We can deduce that a single failure mode generated the blowout precursor intervals.

Recognition of the increasing strength of evidence could have grounded the plane for investigating the cause.  Early recognition requires analyzing data before an obvious need becomes apparent, often requiring automated analysis.
4 Future event probability distributions
The driving purpose behind EIP is to identify any change in event intervals that should trigger an investigation into cause-and-effect – the causal system.  The first part of EIP does that. This second step calculates a probability distribution or PMF for the next TBE to be expected with the same cause-and-effect system.  Precursor analysis usually stops with the first part of EIP.  Precursor events trigger recognition that something is unusual, and investigation and correction eliminate the precursor events and prevent a possible primary event.  The second part of extending these probability calculations into the future is done if there is a delay in the investigation and implementation of correction and typically applies only to primary events.  Any delay in responding to unacceptable primary event attractors has a risk unknown to the engineering profession and all others.  The primary events of the 737 MAX crashes will demonstrate the mathematics supporting this EIP step and show the unrecognized risk of delayed response.  The first EIP step for the 737 MAX crash events is summarized in the probability map for these crash events in Figure 8, where time is replaced with departures, so intervals are DBE.  The p-values are such that a probabilistically significant deviation from the worldwide fleet MDBE is seen in the first crash, and a new and unacceptable attractor is evidenced.  The second crash provides stronger evidence.  The p-values are the false positive.
Figure 8- 737 MAX departures between crashes in green with worldwide MDBE in a Poisson probability map.  Equations for p-v1 and p-v2 calculate appropriate p-values in the rightmost columns of the spreadsheet.  The 1st event identifies an attractor that is unlike the expectation.  All future events will reside in that attractor until the causal system changes; however, there is a 1 in 50 chance this statement is wrong.
4.1 Second step concept
TBE probability distributions are obtained with Monte Carlo simulation.  Monte Carlo is used to solve the math problem of adding and multiplying random variables with a numerical method.  The distributions will provide the probability of the next event occurring as a function of time.  They are conditional on the causal system remaining unchanged.  When a future event interval does not lie on the calculated interval probability distribution within the confidence interval being used, it is evidence that the attractor has changed, i.e., the causal system has changed.
Figure 9 graphically demonstrates the process for Monte Carlo simulation to obtain samples of time to the next failure (TBF) where the events are failures, using terminology more familiar to reliability engineers.  Many random number draws, or iterations, form probability distributions – more accurately PMFs - for TBF.  The cumulative failure distribution, equation 1, is the complement of reliability, i.e., unreliability.    Equation 1 is well known and accepted by reliability engineers, so this will be used; however, we could start with the equation for reliability and get a mirror image of Figure 9 that contains identical information.  Figure 9 can be read as the probability of survival (reliability) by reversing the y-axis.  The math for the distributions applies to any system when the causes and effects generating the event are complex, i.e., events are IIED random variables.  This allows the use of a constant failure rate and cumulative failure distribution,
F(t) = 1-e-λt	                              (1)
Figure 9 – An event interval sample, called failure time sample, is determined with a random number drawn from the secondary y-axis that is transformed by equation 1 to a failure time.  The graph shows two samples of failure times derived by equation 1.
Failure rate λ in equation 1 is a constant average.  Before the null is rejected, the null hypothesis assures the constant failure rate by definition – it is inherent to the null hypothesis.  In all prior papers on the EIP concept, this second step's use of a constant failure rate has been identified as a justifiable assumption.  Integration of the principle of causality allows this second step to be viewed with even greater justification.  Probability distributions from equation 1 describing the time to the next future event are conditional upon a complex and unchanged causal system. They are akin to a Bayesian prior and are awaiting new evidence – the next event.
Equation 1 transforms a uniformly distributed zero-to-one random number into a time sample. It is the cumulative failure distribution function. All cumulative distributions have a linear 0 to 1 y-axis scale, which allows the function to be set equal to a 0 to 1 uniformly distributed random number (RN).
F(t) = 1-e-λt  = RN
where:
RN = uniformly distributed random number from 0 to 1
λ = failure rate or, more generally, event rate
t = time
Rearranging terms,
e-λt = 1- RN
The event rate is constant, so λ = 1/MTBE, and the complement of a 0 to 1 uniformly distributed random number is a 0 to 1 uniformly distributed random number, so
e-t/MTBE = RN 			        (2)
Taking the natural log of both sides and simplifying,
ln e-t/MTBE  = ln(RN)
-t/MTBE = ln(RN)
t = -MTBE*(ln(RN)) = TBE sample
The time to the first event sometimes must be distinguished from the subsequent time between events, but for constant λ, the term TBE can also be used for the first event.  So, equation 3 is for the length of any event interval, including the first:
TBE = -MTBE*(ln(RN)) 		       (3)
MTBE in equation 3 can be a population mean that is single-valued, as discussed thus far, and produces the blue distribution in Figure 10.  This is the TBE distribution for the worldwide fleet, using the worldwide mean.  When a comparative population is unavailable, the dataset running average is used and will be a sample statistic from a population of unknown mean.   After the null is rejected, the data are always a sample from a system of unknown mean.  MTBE as a random variable is explained in the context of calculating the next event distribution, i.e., MTBE is a random variable.
The number of events available is used in the calculation.  The number of TBE values available for the next event forecast is n, where n can be any positive integer, including only one.  Starting with a TBE dataset used to determine the next event interval distribution, equation 3 generates TBE samples using the dataset mean to get a sample of the population unknown mean as a random variable.
MTBERVs1 = (TBEs1 + TBEs2 +…… TBEsn)/n
where:
MTBERVs1 = 1st sample of the mean TBE as a random variable
TBEsn = Time between event random variable sample n
n = number of TBE values in the available dataset
Using equation 3 with the dataset mean:
MTBERVs1 = {[-MTBED*ln(RNs1)] + [-MTBED*ln(RNs2)] +  ……[-MTBED*ln(RNsn)}/n		(4)
where:
MTBED = dataset mean
RNsn = Random number draw, one for each n
The RN subscripts above ensure that each random number is independent of any other draw.  We can omit the RN subscript when the random numbers are assured to be independent during the Monte Carlo simulation – such as when a computer spreadsheet is appropriately designed.
Equation 3 is used a second time with the dataset mean replaced with the sample of the population unknown mean from equation 4.  But this is all within the same calculation – the same Monte Carlo iteration.  Equation 5 is a sample TBE for the next future event.
TBEPs= -MTBERVs1*ln(RNsn+1) 	         (5)
where:
TBEPs = Projected sample, sample of TBE
RNsn+1 = an additional unique RN.
Figure 10 is 100,000 iterations or samples of TBEPs from equation 5 sorted from smallest to largest to form a TBE PMF for the 737 MAX second crash using the number of departures to the first crash as input data.  This distribution is the projection or forecast for a second crash.  According to a calculated estimate, the actual experienced departures between the first and second crashes are 117,856 [10].  This number of intervals projected from the x-axis departures (the vertical black arrow) to the cumulative probability y-axis (the horizontal black arrow) shows the second crash actual interval to be expected with a probability of 0.69.  In other words, two-thirds of the time, the second crash would occur even sooner than it did.  The actual interval is near the center of the forecast.  Of course, this could happen only by chance. Still, reference 7 matches 29 forecasts, with the 29 actual results.  They are scattered along the cumulative distribution y-axis, approaching the ideal uniform scatter.  The distributions in Figure 10 should be viewed as math calculations and not as computer simulations in the usual sense of running a computer model.  Monte Carlo-generated random numbers are an efficient way to perform the convolution of multiple probability distributions with numerical methods.  The resulting distributions accurately reflect the uncertainty of the outcome, but because the addition and multiplication of probability distributions are by Monte Carlo, the accurate results have imprecision.  To illustrate the imprecision of the accurate forecast, the process for generating the second crash forecast distribution of Figure 10 was executed five times.  The actual interval of 117,856 projected to cumulative probability with five simulations of 100,000 iterations produced probability results ranging from 0.68737 to 0.68927.

5 JUSTIFICATIONS for parallel EIP use
This is the seventh paper since 2020 recommending the FAA incorporate EIP in decision-making.  Thus far, the concept has received no visible traction.  How can we expect CPS to use EIP to triage child abuse victims, and how can the next George Floyd event be avoided if the FAA, a highly respected and technology-based organization, does not use it for something as important as public safety with such an obvious need exposed by the 737 MAX incidents?  But would it be irresponsible for the FAA to use analysis methods beyond those endorsed by the engineering profession?  The engineering profession is likewise unaware.  Unfortunately, this log jam of reasons—all of them good reasons when taken individually—for why there is no traction necessitates leveraging the FAA and the 737 MAX issues by obligating the FAA to investigate the method and respond publicly.
5.1 TARAM Erroneous Results
Following the first crash, the FAA conducted a risk assessment [8] based on a total fleet of 4,800 planes with 190 occupants and 8.9 flight hours per day and predicted 2,920.9 fatalities over the fleet's life.  An airworthiness directive (AD) was recommended.  However, from Figure 8, the first crash interval of 135,980 departures rejects the null, and the alternative hypothesis is accepted – the fleet is unreliable relative to the worldwide average with a false positive of 0.02202.  Furthermore, we should make decisions as though the true fleet reliability is in a chaos theory attractor from which the scientific principle of causality dictates it can only escape with a causal system change.  But again, there is a 0.02202 probability we are wrong.  Our professional instinct to reject the idea that one data point can be sufficient stems from statistics and reductionism, neither of which affects EIP.
Using the TARAM risk analysis worksheet and changing EIP data from departures to flight hours for a direct comparison, EIP reveals a risk of 278,178 fatalities versus 2,920.9 – 95 times greater. The actualized second crash interval is inconsistent with TARAM but confirms EIP. The second crash is near the center of the forecast, as seen in Figure 10.
Improvements in TARAM cannot overcome reductionism's limitations in determining in-service system reliability, which we argue can only be determined via actual system-level performance.  The FAA should investigate and report on this claim.
5.2 Unrecognized Next Crash Probability Distribution
An airworthiness directive (AD) was issued nine days after the first crash, with a 90-day compliance time.  Even if the AD is 100% effective, the probability of another crash within 99 days is 0.676, based on the green distribution data in Figure 10, considering 250 planes and 4.5 departures per day used in the TARAM risk assessment.  The fatality risk through the compliance time is calculated as the probability multiplied by the consequence (190 persons per crash):
Fatality risk = 0.676 * 190 = 128.4 fatalities
Following the second crash, the probability distribution for the third crash, considering 384 planes and 2.85 departures per day, shows that the 3-day delay in grounding the fleet had a risk of 23.0 fatalities [10].  The FAA’s unawareness of actual fatality risk will be unacceptable in the future.

Throughout this history, 12 identified issues out of 43 new designs provide a priori reliability (safety) of only 0.72.
5.3 Unrecognized New Design Reliability History
Over the history of commercial aviation, at least 12 unacceptable safety issues have been discovered out of 43 new designs after they were certified (see Figure 11).  While overall reliability has grown remarkedly, the ability to keep unsafe planes from being introduced into service has stayed relatively constant throughout the history of commercial aviation.  Design and reliability assurance technology and methods have improved over time, but so has the difficulty of reliability and safety assurance because of greater complexity, automation, and software.  However, the most significant problem in this regard is success itself.  Expectations have grown along with the industry's reliability growth.  The initial 737 MAX reliability would be acceptable 60 years ago, as it would be as reliable as the average plane of the day.
Figure 11 identifies the safety issues found after certification, many early in fleet life and most with precursors.  Considering this history of unsafe fleets being placed into service, does it seem reasonable to double down on design, manufacturing, and certification alone?  Or is it reasonable to also regard the a priori probability of a new fleet being unsafe as about 0.28 probability and actively search for precursor events to find the unsafe fleets before the first primary event?
6 AUTOMATed eip analysis
Aircraft primary events are so infrequent and obvious that manual analysis is all that is appropriate.  Some precursors are also prominent and could be analyzed upon need, but they must be recognized.  The loss of flight control on the flight before the first crash is easily recognized as a precursor after the crash, but before the crash, it must actively be sought out.  The cockpit alert light precursor was identified by Alaska Airlines, but it was viewed as a technical issue to be resolved, not as a signal of a possible unreliable fleet.  Since the fleet is believed to be reliable because it has been certified, there is no perceived reason to look for unsafe fleets.
The DC 10 cargo door blowouts of 1972 and 1974 had numerous cargo door maintenance issues before each primary event [9].  The 1974 event resulted in 346 fatalities, the same as for the 737 MAX.  Recognizing events such as the DC 10 maintenance issues as alarming precursors may require automated data collection and analysis.  They are low-level signals spread over a long time, so they are not obvious.  This means if these signals are to be analyzed, they must be analyzed before a need is recognized.  Perhaps, for example, 100,000 signals may require analysis before a single signal helps identify a possible impending primary event.  In such a case, automation is needed.  Automation has been used in the process industry to monitor all maintenance events on 15,000 plant physical assets using structured data in the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.  All events are analyzed, but human eyes only see those with alarming p-values.  Most analyses have non-informative results without awareness that any specific analysis has been undertaken.  Big data tools and perhaps artificial intelligence (AI) could integrate unstructured data, such as in pilot logbooks, to complement structured input data.
Recommendations
The FAA should investigate the method demonstrated for application to both primary events and precursors as a second, independent layer of safety to conventional methods with a public report.  It may be many years before another situation like the 737 MAX arises again, and commercial aviation is not the greatest among the many needs for EIP.  For example, 1,840 children died from abuse in 2019 in the U.S. alone [12].  Still, sociologists and other professionals are not likely to use this science if it is not used by a technology-based authority such as the FAA, where the need is so apparent.  A public response from the FAA would help promote the application to these other needs.  For every day of delay, five children die from abuse in the U.S.  Avoiding some of these deaths and the torturous life leading to death may depend upon a public FAA response.
The engineering profession, especially academics, should likewise investigate EIP.  With the claimed difference in fatality risk associated with 737 MAX industry decisions versus EIP, there is a moral and professional obligation to do so.

conclusions:
The fatal crash rate for the worldwide jet scheduled carrier fleet has improved by a factor of 12 over the past 50 years.  This improvement is primarily due to the FAA, NTSB, and Boeing, as most planes are Boeing. This has been achieved through the design, manufacturing, and certification process, along with thorough investigation and correction of any problems that arise.  However, it is essential to note that since 1958, at least 28% of new fleet designs were certified, although later discovered to be unsafe, often after crashes, and the trend is not improving.  The recent incidents involving the Boeing 737 MAX, including two crashes and a door plug blowout, highlight this longstanding but unacknowledged issue with new fleet certification.  These events on the 737 MAX, avoidable with the specific data analysis methodology presented, emphasize the urgent need for this additional, independent layer of safety to supplement current certification technology and methods.
This paper underscores the necessity of augmenting current conventional methods for the safety and reliability assurance of new fleet designs with this new, unrecognized data analysis methodology.  Any event, instance, or happening in the arrow of time that is countable has a time interval since the last happening of the same type. The analysis technology, event interval probability (EIP), reveals a series of probability mass functions (PMF) for the event time intervals immediately upon every event.  These probability distributions reside in the history of any happening and extend to future happenings.  Because any change in anything can be a happening, an event, the method applies to precursors, even low-level signals of no importance, when the signal is taken in isolation.
These probabilities are determined using the 737 MAX crash and crash precursor and the door plug blowout precursor. With probability analysis of the precursors, all three primary events were avoidable.  The FAA conducted a 737 MAX risk assessment after the first crash, finding an uncorrected fleet life risk of 2,920.9 fatalities.  The true risk was 95 times greater. This difference is 275,258 fatalities.  The FAA should investigate the EIP technology and either use the method or explain why not.
The reliability of any system is described as an emergent property found with EIP.  The system is the set of causes producing an event.  The system does not need to be known, understood, or even describable, as causal information is not used in EIP.  This is difficult for anyone to understand, especially experts in the system producing the events, as the human reaction is to revert to reductionism – breaking the complex into smaller, more understandable pieces.  Social and human system examples are used to understand how system reliability can be known in maximum detail as a probability distribution with no system knowledge.  A single event is often all that is needed to recognize a reliability shift to a new level.   Again, this is difficult for professionals to accept because they immediately think of statistics, but EIP is fundamentally a probabilistic process, not a statistical process.
Child Protective Services (CPS) investigation dates are used as precursors to a child’s death, and police use of force citizen complaint dates are precursors to the death of George Floyd in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in 2020.  Dates for these social system precursors, as with 737 MAX precursors, identify actionable “reliability” that, if acted upon, could have easily avoided all primary events.  The term “reliability” is used in this unorthodox manner and applications as no better term to describe this universal emergent system property is known.
1    INTRODUCTION
Identifying and correcting the causes leading to the Boeing 737 MAX reliability issues is appropriate and is a current focus. This is the traditional way to achieve system reliability—working within the system and changing the system to solve potential and actual failures. This conventional viewpoint is that system reliability performance is determined and understood by working inside the system with the details (components, subsystems, and their interactions). Systems theory would call this reductionism— breaking down the complex into more fundamental and understandable pieces.  Thus far, all human progress is based upon reductionism, and an airplane would not exist without it.  As calculated from published data [1], reductionism has led to a 12-fold increase in worldwide fleet flights between fatal crashes over the last 50 years.  Without replacing reductionism, EIP is based on an additional but opposite viewpoint of system reliability as an emergent property determined by system performance – what comes out of the system instead of what goes in.  Reductionism is a bottom-up view, and emergence is a top-down view. Both views are needed, but reductionism is the only recognized viewpoint.
EIP recognizes the existence of a series of probability mass functions (PMFs) formed from past event time intervals. It identifies reliability deviation from an expectation and calculates PMFs for the future, doing so with unprecedentedly small datasets necessary for high-reliability systems.
The method, applied to the 737 MAX, using data available before the events happened, would have prevented both crashes and the door plug blowout.  Social and human systems are included as examples to demonstrate universal applicability and help better understand the why and how of using the method on precursors.
2	EIP concept with examples
Events (occurrences of any kind) occur over time, whether primary events or precursors.  They are countable, and each event has an associated time interval from the previous event of the same type.  When the event is a failure, this time between events (TBE) is synonymous with the time between failure (TBF), with which reliability engineers are familiar.  The event or happening can be a minor incident that may be a precursor to a primary event, such as a crash or death.
EIP is implemented in two parts. The first is to identify event intervals inconsistent with those from a comparison system. This is done with a null hypothesis that reliability equals that of the comparison system, such as a peer group, and the comparison system intervals are generated by a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) with events being independent and identically exponential distributed (IIED).  While complex systems often produce events in time as an HPP, there is no assumption that it does.  The null is evaluated with probability values (p-values); however, p-values are found not with statistics but with probability theory.
This analysis often identifies intervals that are a step change from the comparison with only a single interval. To take advantage of this sensitivity, the analysis should be contemporaneous, immediately upon an event being experienced. The driving purpose of EIP is to immediately identify probabilistic significance in event intervals, allowing quick intervention to prevent primary events.  This intervention ends the first part of EIP and uses the conventional, reductionist, bottom-up view working within the causal system.
The second EIP step is taken when needed. If the unreliable system remains in service due to the time required to investigate and correct it, the risk of continued uncorrected operation in service may need to be calculated. A numerical method and Monte Carlo simulation manage the math, and the results are a calculated cumulative failure (event) distribution showing time to the next event(s).  This distribution is a PMF.
While complex system reliability can only be determined at the system level as an emergent property and can never be determined through reductionism, this concept is not currently accepted.  Subject matter experts (SMEs) mistakenly believe the opposite is true.  It is difficult for anyone, and even more so for SMEs, to understand that system reliability can only be determined from a top-down view using system performance data.  The more knowledge one has of a system, the greater the tendency to immediately jump into causes and effects when a system reliability issue is suspected.  Applying EIP to social and human systems, where engineers do not know how the system works, may aid in understanding reliability as an emergent property.  In these social systems, the top-down view measures an unrecognized system property we call “reliability.” Once “reliability” is deemed problematic, fixing the system that generates that reliability requires reductionism – the bottom-up view.
2.1 Child Abuse Precursor
In 2022, a mother and another adult were charged with the 2020 murder of an eight-year-old child by starvation and abuse in Houston, Texas. Typically, child-specific data are unavailable to the public; however, because a death was involved, the Texas Family and Protective Services (that we will call the more general Child Protective Services or CPS) released CPS abuse investigation dates and findings [2].  These investigation dates can be used in the following precursor example.  This will demonstrate the analysis concept, application to precursors, and specifically how the little girl's years of living with abuse and starvation with eventual death were avoidable using the method proposed for the FAA.

One is a system of complex causes and effects that produces an environment of abuse.  The other is a system of causes and effects that generates a report of suspected abuse.  Neither of these complex subsystems can be adequately described, much less the interactions between them and the environment.  System boundaries cannot be drawn without leaving a possible cause-and-effect out, yet to design a system, system boundaries are necessary.  For example, pilots act according to design assumptions inside the design system boundary.  This is appropriate and necessary for design; however, pilots' actions are a reality – not an assumption or design constraint when the design is in service.  Reality is not limited to artificial boundaries.  With EIP, the system is whatever produced the events.  Because system knowledge is not used, it is independent of conventional reductionism.

The investigation dates are system-level performance data that reflect a property that emerges from the undefined total system.  The unknown complexity of causes and effects produces this emergent property, but the property cannot be known via cause and effect.  This system-level property is a systems theory emergent property universally applicable to any happening. This property is “reliability” for engineered physical systems.  The term “reliability” sounds strange for other systems, but this author knows no better term to describe this universal property.  The definition of reliability for the first EIP step is “the probability that the system event intervals are consistent with expectation.”
The expectation for this example is the mean time between events (MTBE) for an average Texas child that is 10,564 days, calculated from published data [3]. Once the causal system generating these event dates is in the attractor, the system cannot produce anything other than that in the attractor. 3 Zero-point attractor
The TBE data of Figure 7, taken at face value, are not from a stable attractor.  The universal rule that produces stable attractors is e-λt [7].  This is the same equation for the reliability of steady-state repairable complex systems.  This engineering application has limits beyond which the equation does not apply, and the stable attractor has the same limits for the same reasons.  The event rate must be a constant average.  When λ, the event rate, increases, the TBE continually decreases; it is a point attractor approaching zero.  Chaos theory identifies point attractors, so calling this a zero-point attractor seems appropriate.  (The event rate can also decrease, which is not considered here).  It can be understood that an increasing event rate, with decreasing event TBE, given sufficient time with unchanging causes and effects, mathematically must approach but not reach a zero-length time interval.  A complex causality system with multiple contributing causes will generate a stable attractor.  In contrast, when a single failure mode dominates, the causal system can produce the zero-point attractor.  As reliability engineers know, complex system reliability allows using the equation R= e-λt.  However, they know this may not be useable for single failure modes because the failure rate λ is typically not a constant average.  We can deduce that a single failure mode generated the blowout precursor intervals.

Recognition of the increasing strength of evidence could have grounded the plane for investigating the cause.  Early recognition requires analyzing data before an obvious need becomes apparent, often requiring automated analysis.
4 Future event probability distributions
The driving purpose behind EIP is to identify any change in event intervals that should trigger an investigation into cause-and-effect – the causal system.  The first part of EIP does that. This second step calculates a probability distribution or PMF for the next TBE to be expected with the same cause-and-effect system.  Precursor analysis usually stops with the first part of EIP.  Precursor events trigger recognition that something is unusual, and investigation and correction eliminate the precursor events and prevent a possible primary event.  The second part of extending these probability calculations into the future is done if there is a delay in the investigation and implementation of correction and typically applies only to primary events.  Any delay in responding to unacceptable primary event attractors has a risk unknown to the engineering profession and all others.  The primary events of the 737 MAX crashes will demonstrate the mathematics supporting this EIP step and show the unrecognized risk of delayed response.  The first EIP step for the 737 MAX crash events is summarized in the probability map for these crash events in Figure 8, where time is replaced with departures, so intervals are DBE.  The p-values are such that a probabilistically significant deviation from the worldwide fleet MDBE is seen in the first crash, and a new and unacceptable attractor is evidenced.  The second crash provides stronger evidence.  The p-values are the false positive.

All future events will reside in that attractor until the causal system changes; however, there is a 1 in 50 chance this statement is wrong.
4.1 Second step concept
TBE probability distributions are obtained with Monte Carlo simulation.  Monte Carlo is used to solve the math problem of adding and multiplying random variables with a numerical method.  The distributions will provide the probability of the next event occurring as a function of time.  They are conditional on the causal system remaining unchanged.  When a future event interval does not lie on the calculated interval probability distribution within the confidence interval being used, it is evidence that the attractor has changed, i.e., the causal system has changed.
Figure 9 graphically demonstrates the process for Monte Carlo simulation to obtain samples of time to the next failure (TBF) where the events are failures, using terminology more familiar to reliability engineers.  Many random number draws, or iterations, form probability distributions – more accurately PMFs - for TBF.  The cumulative failure distribution, equation 1, is the complement of reliability, i.e., unreliability.    Equation 1 is well known and accepted by reliability engineers, so this will be used; however, we could start with the equation for reliability and get a mirror image of Figure 9 that contains identical information.  Figure 9 can be read as the probability of survival (reliability) by reversing the y-axis.  The math for the distributions applies to any system when the causes and effects generating the event are complex, i.e., events are IIED random variables.  This allows the use of a constant failure rate and cumulative failure distribution,
F(t) = 1-e-λt	                              (1)
Figure 9 – An event interval sample, called failure time sample, is determined with a random number drawn from the secondary y-axis that is transformed by equation 1 to a failure time.  The graph shows two samples of failure times derived by equation 1.
Failure rate λ in equation 1 is a constant average.  Before the null is rejected, the null hypothesis assures the constant failure rate by definition – it is inherent to the null hypothesis.  In all prior papers on the EIP concept, this second step's use of a constant failure rate has been identified as a justifiable assumption.  Integration of the principle of causality allows this second step to be viewed with even greater justification.  Probability distributions from equation 1 describing the time to the next future event are conditional upon a complex and unchanged causal system. They are akin to a Bayesian prior and are awaiting new evidence – the next event.
Equation 1 transforms a uniformly distributed zero-to-one random number into a time sample. It is the cumulative failure distribution function. All cumulative distributions have a linear 0 to 1 y-axis scale, which allows the function to be set equal to a 0 to 1 uniformly distributed random number (RN).

λ = failure rate or, more generally, event rate
t = time
Rearranging terms,
e-λt = 1- RN
The event rate is constant, so λ = 1/MTBE, and the complement of a 0 to 1 uniformly distributed random number is a 0 to 1 uniformly distributed random number, so
e-t/MTBE = RN 			        (2)
Taking the natural log of both sides and simplifying,
ln e-t/MTBE  = ln(RN)
-t/MTBE = ln(RN)
t = -MTBE*(ln(RN)) = TBE sample
The time to the first event sometimes must be distinguished from the subsequent time between events, but for constant λ, the term TBE can also be used for the first event.  So, equation 3 is for the length of any event interval, including the first:
TBE = -MTBE*(ln(RN)) 		       (3)
MTBE in equation 3 can be a population mean that is single-valued, as discussed thus far, and produces the blue distribution in Figure 10.  This is the TBE distribution for the worldwide fleet, using the worldwide mean.  When a comparative population is unavailable, the dataset running average is used and will be a sample statistic from a population of unknown mean.   After the null is rejected, the data are always a sample from a system of unknown mean.  MTBE as a random variable is explained in the context of calculating the next event distribution, i.e., MTBE is a random variable.
The number of events available is used in the calculation.  The number of TBE values available for the next event forecast is n, where n can be any positive integer, including only one.  Starting with a TBE dataset used to determine the next event interval distribution, equation 3 generates TBE samples using the dataset mean to get a sample of the population unknown mean as a random variable.
MTBERVs1 = (TBEs1 + TBEs2 +…… TBEsn)/n
where:
MTBERVs1 = 1st sample of the mean TBE as a random variable
TBEsn = Time between event random variable sample n
n = number of TBE values in the available dataset
Using equation 3 with the dataset mean:
MTBERVs1 = {[-MTBED*ln(RNs1)] + [-MTBED*ln(RNs2)] +  ……[-MTBED*ln(RNsn)}/n		(4)
where:
MTBED = dataset mean
RNsn = Random number draw, one for each n
The RN subscripts above ensure that each random number is independent of any other draw.  We can omit the RN subscript when the random numbers are assured to be independent during the Monte Carlo simulation – such as when a computer spreadsheet is appropriately designed.
Equation 3 is used a second time with the dataset mean replaced with the sample of the population unknown mean from equation 4.  But this is all within the same calculation – the same Monte Carlo iteration.  Equation 5 is a sample TBE for the next future event.
TBEPs= -MTBERVs1*ln(RNsn+1) 	         (5)
where:
TBEPs = Projected sample, sample of TBE
RNsn+1 = an additional unique RN.
Figure 10 is 100,000 iterations or samples of TBEPs from equation 5 sorted from smallest to largest to form a TBE PMF for the 737 MAX second crash using the number of departures to the first crash as input data.  This distribution is the projection or forecast for a second crash.  According to a calculated estimate, the actual experienced departures between the first and second crashes are 117,856 [10].  This number of intervals projected from the x-axis departures (the vertical black arrow) to the cumulative probability y-axis (the horizontal black arrow) shows the second crash actual interval to be expected with a probability of 0.69.  In other words, two-thirds of the time, the second crash would occur even sooner than it did.  The actual interval is near the center of the forecast.  Of course, this could happen only by chance. Still, reference 7 matches 29 forecasts, with the 29 actual results.  They are scattered along the cumulative distribution y-axis, approaching the ideal uniform scatter.  The distributions in Figure 10 should be viewed as math calculations and not as computer simulations in the usual sense of running a computer model.  Monte Carlo-generated random numbers are an efficient way to perform the convolution of multiple probability distributions with numerical methods.  The resulting distributions accurately reflect the uncertainty of the outcome, but because the addition and multiplication of probability distributions are by Monte Carlo, the accurate results have imprecision.  To illustrate the imprecision of the accurate forecast, the process for generating the second crash forecast distribution of Figure 10 was executed five times.  The actual interval of 117,856 projected to cumulative probability with five simulations of 100,000 iterations produced probability results ranging from 0.68737 to 0.68927.
Figure 10 – Forecast for a second crash, in green, using the first crash interval as in equations 4 and 5.  This figure is like Figure 9, but with log scaling on the x-axis.  The blue distribution is the worldwide fleet null hypothesis.  The green distribution describes the 2nd crash probability if the causal system is unchanged, but it has a false positive of 0.02202 from Figure 8. The realized 2nd crash confirmed a stable attractor that will continue to produce new crashes until the causal system is changed.
5 JUSTIFICATIONS for parallel EIP use
This is the seventh paper since 2020 recommending the FAA incorporate EIP in decision-making.  Thus far, the concept has received no visible traction.  How can we expect CPS to use EIP to triage child abuse victims, and how can the next George Floyd event be avoided if the FAA, a highly respected and technology-based organization, does not use it for something as important as public safety with such an obvious need exposed by the 737 MAX incidents?  But would it be irresponsible for the FAA to use analysis methods beyond those endorsed by the engineering profession?  The engineering profession is likewise unaware.  Unfortunately, this log jam of reasons—all of them good reasons when taken individually—for why there is no traction necessitates leveraging the FAA and the 737 MAX issues by obligating the FAA to investigate the method and respond publicly.
5.1 TARAM Erroneous Results
Following the first crash, the FAA conducted a risk assessment [8] based on a total fleet of 4,800 planes with 190 occupants and 8.9 flight hours per day and predicted 2,920.9 fatalities over the fleet's life.  An airworthiness directive (AD) was recommended.  However, from Figure 8, the first crash interval of 135,980 departures rejects the null, and the alternative hypothesis is accepted – the fleet is unreliable relative to the worldwide average with a false positive of 0.02202.  Furthermore, we should make decisions as though the true fleet reliability is in a chaos theory attractor from which the scientific principle of causality dictates it can only escape with a causal system change.  But again, there is a 0.02202 probability we are wrong.  Our professional instinct to reject the idea that one data point can be sufficient stems from statistics and reductionism, neither of which affects EIP.
Using the TARAM risk analysis worksheet and changing EIP data from departures to flight hours for a direct comparison, EIP reveals a risk of 278,178 fatalities versus 2,920.9 – 95 times greater. The actualized second crash interval is inconsistent with TARAM but confirms EIP. The second crash is near the center of the forecast, as seen in Figure 10.
Improvements in TARAM cannot overcome reductionism's limitations in determining in-service system reliability, which we argue can only be determined via actual system-level performance.  The FAA should investigate and report on this claim.
5.2 Unrecognized Next Crash Probability Distribution
An airworthiness directive (AD) was issued nine days after the first crash, with a 90-day compliance time.  Even if the AD is 100% effective, the probability of another crash within 99 days is 0.676, based on the green distribution data in Figure 10, considering 250 planes and 4.5 departures per day used in the TARAM risk assessment.  The fatality risk through the compliance time is calculated as the probability multiplied by the consequence (190 persons per crash):
Fatality risk = 0.676 * 190 = 128.4 fatalities
Following the second crash, the probability distribution for the third crash, considering 384 planes and 2.85 departures per day, shows that the 3-day delay in grounding the fleet had a risk of 23.0 fatalities [10].  The FAA’s unawareness of actual fatality risk will be unacceptable in the future.
Figure 11- Fleets placed into service over 65 years.  Types are from Boeing’s annual statistical summary [11]. Missed issues are broadly defined but within certification scope, including in-service inspection and testing (777 P&W engines) and manufacturing QA (737 MAX 9 door plug). Throughout this history, 12 identified issues out of 43 new designs provide a priori reliability (safety) of only 0.72.
5.3 Unrecognized New Design Reliability History
Over the history of commercial aviation, at least 12 unacceptable safety issues have been discovered out of 43 new designs after they were certified (see Figure 11).  While overall reliability has grown remarkedly, the ability to keep unsafe planes from being introduced into service has stayed relatively constant throughout the history of commercial aviation.  Design and reliability assurance technology and methods have improved over time, but so has the difficulty of reliability and safety assurance because of greater complexity, automation, and software.  However, the most significant problem in this regard is success itself.  Expectations have grown along with the industry's reliability growth.  The initial 737 MAX reliability would be acceptable 60 years ago, as it would be as reliable as the average plane of the day.
Figure 11 identifies the safety issues found after certification, many early in fleet life and most with precursors.  Considering this history of unsafe fleets being placed into service, does it seem reasonable to double down on design, manufacturing, and certification alone?  Or is it reasonable to also regard the a priori probability of a new fleet being unsafe as about 0.28 probability and actively search for precursor events to find the unsafe fleets before the first primary event?
6 AUTOMATed eip analysis
Aircraft primary events are so infrequent and obvious that manual analysis is all that is appropriate.  Some precursors are also prominent and could be analyzed upon need, but they must be recognized.  The loss of flight control on the flight before the first crash is easily recognized as a precursor after the crash, but before the crash, it must actively be sought out.  The cockpit alert light precursor was identified by Alaska Airlines, but it was viewed as a technical issue to be resolved, not as a signal of a possible unreliable fleet.  Since the fleet is believed to be reliable because it has been certified, there is no perceived reason to look for unsafe fleets.
The DC 10 cargo door blowouts of 1972 and 1974 had numerous cargo door maintenance issues before each primary event [9].  The 1974 event resulted in 346 fatalities, the same as for the 737 MAX.  Recognizing events such as the DC 10 maintenance issues as alarming precursors may require automated data collection and analysis.  They are low-level signals spread over a long time, so they are not obvious.  This means if these signals are to be analyzed, they must be analyzed before a need is recognized.  Perhaps, for example, 100,000 signals may require analysis before a single signal helps identify a possible impending primary event.  In such a case, automation is needed.  Automation has been used in the process industry to monitor all maintenance events on 15,000 plant physical assets using structured data in the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.  All events are analyzed, but human eyes only see those with alarming p-values.  Most analyses have non-informative results without awareness that any specific analysis has been undertaken.  Big data tools and perhaps artificial intelligence (AI) could integrate unstructured data, such as in pilot logbooks, to complement structured input data.
Recommendations
The FAA should investigate the method demonstrated for application to both primary events and precursors as a second, independent layer of safety to conventional methods with a public report.  It may be many years before another situation like the 737 MAX arises again, and commercial aviation is not the greatest among the many needs for EIP.  For example, 1,840 children died from abuse in 2019 in the U.S. alone [12].  Still, sociologists and other professionals are not likely to use this science if it is not used by a technology-based authority such as the FAA, where the need is so apparent.  A public response from the FAA would help promote the application to these other needs.  For every day of delay, five children die from abuse in the U.S.  Avoiding some of these deaths and the torturous life leading to death may depend upon a public FAA response.
The engineering profession, especially academics, should likewise investigate EIP.  With the claimed difference in fatality risk associated with 737 MAX industry decisions versus EIP, there is a moral and professional obligation to do so.

title: Lessons Learned in an Aerospace Design for Reliability Program
authors: Donald L Hatfield, Raytheon Technologies Company; Dr. Sharon L Honecker, RaytheonTechnologies Company; Key Words: Reliability, Design for Reliability, DfR
summary:
This paper is intended to share lessons learned from an approach used to execute an Aerospace Design for Reliability (DfR) program in a Department of Defense (DoD) environment to achieve high reliability while maintaining a strict development schedule. Successful execution of a DfR program not only requires a solid understanding and application of the core principles of DfR, but also an ability to understand when the learning from a particular activity is sufficient to proceed with other follow on activities. The typical DoD program operates at an accelerated pace. This pace often puts pressure on a program to truncate certain activities as a trade for schedule. There are satisfactory compromises that can be reached. It is the role of the Reliability/Maintainability (R/M) engineer to balance between keeping to the schedule and maintaining good technical rigor. This does not mean providing an inferior analysis, but to ensure the following:
Deep integration of the R/M engineer into the design activities where design decisions are collaborative
Solid understanding the design’s maturity
R/M analyses and activities are updated incrementally as the design evolves as opposed to looking for “done”
Clear communication of R/M goals and objectives
There is ample information available on what to do in a DfR program, however, there is far less information available on when it is acceptable to move forward and the associated pitfalls with doing so.
conclusions: This paper described our approach to implementation of DfR on an Aerospace program in a Department of Defense (DoD) environment. Much of the existing guidance on DfR assumes there is adequate time in the schedule to perform reliability analysis and test activities sequentially so that learning from one analysis or test feeds the follow-on activity. We shared eleven lessons we learned along the way to try to address the trades we considered to allow us to adhere to a strict schedule while being true to the spirit of DfR. Although we had many learning opportunities, this program has remained on schedule and the product continues to meet, and in many cases has exceeded our reliability objectives. Compared to other programs without a DfR focus, this is an unusual outcome.

title: Reliability Engineering Reference Architecture for DoD Acquisition
authors: Justin Brown, Bell Textron Inc.; Galen Valentine, Bell Textron Inc.; Key Words: Reliability, System Architecture
summary: Ensuring that military equipment and technology operate effectively and sustainably throughout their lifecycle is a critical aspect of Department of Defense (DoD) systems development.  During early phases of acquisition (prior to Milestone B), the system’s physical architecture is undefined. For Line Replaceable Units (LRUs) or Weapons Replaceable Assemblies (WRAs), this means that methods for estimating Reliability and Maintainability (R&M) cannot include the physical hardware into which the LRUs/WRAs are integrated. A robust Reference Architecture (RA) serves as a foundational framework for integrating R&M considerations into the development process when functional and logical architecture are in development. A key component of this architecture is the R&M Reference Architecture (RMRA). The RMRA encompasses principles, methodologies, and tools to optimize system performance through the system life cycle. This is achieved by informing the system architecture model of R&M parameters to improving decision-making. By leveraging analytics in a model-based format, the RMRA supports the development of resilient and serviceable systems capable of meeting the stringent operational demands of the DoD. The integration of R&M considerations up-front into the architecture enhances system survivability, reduces life-cycle costs, and ensures future operational effectiveness in complex military environments. RMRA is a strategic enabler that enhances the reliability and maintainability of DoD systems and reinforces mission success and operational readiness.

title:
Assessing the Extrapolation Variance of Non-Orthogonal 
Response Surface Designs
authors: Marco Arndt, University of Stuttgart; Erich Rittmaier, University of Stuttgart; Dr.-Ing. Martin Dazer; University of Stuttgart; Key Words: extrapolation variance, EVG, RSM, orthogonality, reliability modeling, ALT
summary: In order to generate an empirical data set that is dependent on several loads for reliability or lifetime modeling in the most efficient way, one usually has to implement Accelerated Life Testing (ALT) through Design of Experiments (DOE). The Central Composite Design (CCD) is particularly suitable as one derivative of the Response Surface Methodology (RSM), which is generically performant but can also be efficiently adapted for extrapolation purposes. These become particularly relevant when the Response Surface Design (RSD) response is to be used for prediction at field level based on those End-of-Life (EoL) tests. Various methods for evaluating the prediction quality in terms of its variance and modified designs have been established so far, including the Variance Dispersion Graph (VDG) and the Fraction of Design Space (FDS) plot. However, for reliability engineering in particular, they did not allow direction-dependent assessments of the designs as in the case of extrapolation. Thus, a new variant of assessment tool for prediction, the Extrapolation Variance Graph (EVG), is presented here and its properties and strengths are demonstrated using exemplary configurations.

title: Equivalent Field Stress Level and Usage with Multiple Distributional Stress Types
authors: Jiliang Zhang, Rivian Automotive; Key Words: single-valued equivalent stress condition, multiple stress types, distributional stress condition and usage, acceleration model
summary: With one multi-variable acceleration model family, which is commonly used in real world practice, the distributional stress condition and distributional usage are converted to single-valued equivalent stress condition and single-valued equivalent usage, respectively. The derived single-valued equivalent stress condition is exact solution without approximation. The algorithm with approximation for single-valued equivalent stress condition in more general situations is also discussed. The equivalent usage is derived independently from the stress. These results significantly simplify the reliability analysis of the products subject to the random loading conditions with multiple stress types. The applications in reliability validation test and reliability prediction are discussed.
