title: Simulative Analysis of Statistical Power of Optimal Test Designs
authors: Erich Rittmaier, University of Stuttgart; Marco Arndt, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, University of Stuttgart; Key Words: design of experiments, response surface methodology, reliability modeling, optimality criteria, statistical power
summary: In conventional experimental designs, such as the central composite design (CCD), the behavior in terms of statistical test power has been studied. However, these standard experimental designs do not apply to all situations. In the case of restrictions of the experimental effort or available design space, optimal test designs offer an alternative, but their statistical test power properties are not documented. The statistical power is used as an indication of how effectively underlying effects are detected. This study quantifies the statistical test power of A-, D-, and V-optimal designs using Monte Carlo methods using simulations. The findings of this study demonstrate that optimal designs provide a viable alternative to standard test designs, showing superior power of effects compared to a CCD. However, reducing the number of runs indicates a clear negative impact on test power, which needs to be carefully considered in testing applications. Regarding effect detection, differences between optimal designs can be identified. Different optimal designs identify main, interaction, and quadratic effects with varying effectiveness and, thus, a different power. A qualitative relationship between optimality criteria and test power was observed, as improved optimality criteria indicate higher power. However, there is insufficient evidence that improved optimality will yield acceptable test power.

title: Point Unavailability and its Density Processes with Periodic Inspections in ISO 26262
authors: Sakurai, Atsushi, FS Micro Corporation; Key Words: Periodic inspection and repair (PIR), Probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF), Point unavailability (PUA), Point unavailability density (PUD), Unreliability
summary:
ISO 26262 is an international functional safety standard for electrical and electronic systems in automotive vehicles.  Part 5 of the standard covers the hardware design and verification phase of the safety lifecycle, which requires the probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF) as a quantitative safety benchmark.  However, this standard provides only the resultant formula for calculating the PMHF and does not offer a clear definition or process for the derivation of the PMHF.
In our prior studies, we clarified the mathematical definition and derivation of the PMHF formula.  We introduced the concept of the stochastic process of the point unavailability density (PUD) and proposed a definition of the PMHF as the average PUD over the lifetime of a vehicle.  This led to the development of our original PMHF formula.  We also developed the deterministic point unavailability (PUA) formula and applied to derive our PMHF formula.  Our approach not only identified potential inaccuracies within the standard’s PMHF formula but also demonstrated improved efficiency in the design time required for fault-tolerant subsystems.
In this paper, we derive the probabilistic formulas for the PUA and PUD in periodic inspection and repair (PIR) maintenance strategies.  These formulas have recursive properties and are revealed to be implicit functions.
The deterministic PUA and PUD formulas for the derivation of the PMHF were employed in our previous papers.   In contrast, this paper evaluates the errors between those formulas and the probabilistic ones.  It demonstrates that the deterministic formulas in the earlier paper are accurate, with no practical issues in the calculation of the PMHF.
To understand the PMHF, it is crucial to have clear insight into the PUA and PUD, from which the PMHF is derived, under the PIR strategy.  Therefore, this study details the behaviors of these four stochastic processes —the probabilistic and deterministic formulas of the PUA and PUD— aiming to improve automobile safety design through the proposed PMHF formula.

title: Modeling Imperfect Repair for Realistic RAM Analysis of Operating Facilities
authors: Supriyo Kar, ADNOC Offshore; Subhadip Sengupta, Consultant; Key Words: RAM analysis, Imperfect repair
summary:
Reliability, Availability and Maintainability analysis (in short RAM analysis), a significant decision-making activity of an operating facility, needs to deliver an accurate and realistic performance prediction of the facility over its complete design life i.e. typically, thirty years plus. Only then the short and long-term strategies, formulated based on the analysis outcome, can become effective and value-adding. Realistic performance prediction necessitates that the operating environment considered during analysis is representative of a real operating facility.
This paper investigates the main impediments to achieving this goal and finds out that failure to incorporate wear and tear and imperfect repair for rotating machinery to be the major reason. This inability causes the analysis outcome to drift far away from reality and portrays a much rosier version of the performance.
As a next step, the paper illustrates how wear and tear and imperfect repair of rotating machinery can be translated into modeling parameters to overcome this obstacle so that the predicted performance becomes far more accurate and realistic leading to more efficacious decision making and positive contribution to the company bottom line.
conclusions:
In a typical Oil and Gas operating facility, the aging of rotating machinery (due to wear and tear and imperfect repair) is a real phenomenon. As demonstrated, the prevalent practice eliminates the effect of age during RAM analysis. Consequently, the RAM model becomes non-representative and analysis outcomes become inaccurate and unrealistic.
This paper has successfully put forward a pragmatic approach to build RAM models where the operating environment is truly representative of a real operating facility. The paper has also illustrated by means of facts and figures how the same enabled the RAM analysis to deliver a far more accurate and realistic performance prediction.
Naturally, this accurate and realistic prediction paves the way for informed decision making – strategic decisions that are typically made after interpreting RAM analysis outcome e.g. optimum operating layout, redundancy allocation, selection of most opportune moments for maintenance intervention, spares stocking philosophy, optimum deployment of maintenance resources etc. become more efficacious. All these contribute positively to realize the highly coveted “low long-term cost of ownership”.

title:
Degradation Analysis and Optimum Inspection Intervals for High-
Pressure Mud Lines
authors: Gustavo Diniz Corgosinho, Foresea Drilling Company; Emanuel Santos, Foresea Drilling Company; Eloi Orlandini, Foresea Drilling Company; Key Words: Degradation Analysis, Life Data Analysis, Optimal Inspection Interval
summary: This study presents a reliability analysis of the high-pressure mud system pipelines present in the company's fleet of offshore drilling rigs, to identify the optimal time and interval for line replacement and inspection, using the methodologies of Degradation Analysis (DA) and Life Data Analysis (LDA). The study was carried out using the measurement data from the current line inspection procedure that is carried out biennially by the structural integrity inspection team. By applying reliability techniques and tools, it was possible to reduce the frequency of inspection from two to five years, without compromising the integrity of the lines or increasing process risk. This change will result in direct savings of 180,000 USD for the company over the next ten-years, in addition it will bring intangible gains to the process such as optimizing resources, reducing risk exposure, and alignment with company best practices.
conclusions:
The data obtained from this study supported the implementation of a new inspection interval, extending from two to five years for the mud system pipelines. This strategic choice, validated through detailed analysis and precise calculations, demonstrated a significant cost reduction, achieving a 60% savings over ten years compared to the current two-year interval strategy. The change also involved a thorough risk evaluation using the calculated reliability curves.
Beyond the financial benefits, the operational advantages were considerable. The current inspection routine, which can take up to 45 days due to bureaucratic processes in report preparation, accumulates to 225 days over ten years. By adopting a five-year inspection interval, this duration is reduced to 90 days over the same period, thereby enabling better utilization of manpower.
This study focused on the primary damage mechanism expected for the high-pressure mud piping system, namely erosion-corrosion. This damage is caused by the high-pressure fluid flow, which can erode material from the pipe sections, particularly at the curves. The monitoring of this erosion-corrosion is conducted through ultrasonic thickness measurements.
By leveraging detailed degradation and life data analysis, this study provided a tailored approach to determine the optimal inspection intervals based on the actual condition and performance data of the mud system pipelines. This method proved more effective in balancing safety and cost-efficiency, as it focused on the specific degradation patterns and failure probabilities of the system.

title: Wind Turbine Fault Detection through Autoencoder-Based Neural Networks
authors: Welker F. Nogueira, University of São Paulo; Arthur H. A. Melani, University of São Paulo; Luiz D. R. S. Custodio, University of São Paulo; Gilberto F. M. de Souza, University of São Paulo; Key Words: Wind turbine, Fault detection, Autoencoder, Neural network
summary: In the pursuit of sustainable and efficient energy solutions, wind turbines play a pivotal role. However, the operational efficiency of wind turbines can be significantly compromised by mechanical and structural faults. Early detection of such faults is crucial to prevent costly downtimes and extensive repairs. Traditional fault detection methods often fall short in accurately identifying complex fault patterns, particularly in the noisy environment characteristic of wind turbines. This research introduces a novel approach utilizing autoencoder-based neural networks to enhance the fault detection process in wind turbines. Autoencoders, a type of neural network, are well-suited for anomaly detection due to their ability to reconstruct input data and detect deviations from normal operational patterns. This paper details the development and implementation of a specialized autoencoder architecture designed to process and analyze monitoring data from wind turbines. The implications of this research are significant, offering a more reliable and efficient method for fault detection in wind turbines. This not only helps in reducing maintenance costs but also in extending the lifespan and operational efficiency of wind turbines. Future work will focus on refining the model's predictive capabilities, expanding the types of detectable faults, and integrating adaptive learning mechanisms to continually improve the model’s accuracy based on new data. This study serves as a proof of concept for the broader application of autoencoder-based neural networks in industrial anomaly detection and sets the stage for future research in this promising area.
conclusions:
The application of autoencoders for anomaly detection in wind turbine operational data offers a promising, unsupervised approach to enhancing predictive maintenance. This method does not require labeled fault data, making it particularly valuable for early fault detection.
However, some limitations need to be addressed to improve its robustness and reliability. Firstly, the effectiveness of the autoencoder model relies heavily on the quality and representativeness of the normal operating data used for training. If this data does not adequately capture all operating conditions, the model may fail to detect anomalies accurately.
Furthermore, the effectiveness of the autoencoder model is highly dependent on the initial feature selection process. However, integrating autoencoders with additional diagnostic techniques, such as Failure Mode and Symptoms Analysis (FMSA), could provide more precise fault localization. Future work should focus on combining autoencoders with other diagnostic methods and continually improving the model’s accuracy with adaptive learning mechanisms.
It is also important to note that the proposed method uses a fixed threshold based on the mean RMSE plus three standard deviations to detect anomalies. This approach assumes a normal distribution of errors, which may not always be the case in real-world data. Other threshold definition strategies will be explored in future work.

title: On-Board SOH Estimation Using Quantized Adaptive Dual Extended Kalman Filter in Resource Constraint Battery Management Systems
authors: Lakshmi Manoj, University of Illinois; Pingfeng Wang, PhD, University of Illinois; Key Words:  State-of-health, Battery Management Systems, Adaptive Dual Extended Kalman Filter, Quantization
summary:
State-of-Health (SOH) is a critical metric used to assess the remaining capacity and overall health of a battery. Accurate SOH estimation is essential for optimizing the performance and extending the lifespan of battery packs. While neural network-based algorithms offer precise predictions, their deployment on resource-constrained hardware and embedded systems poses significant challenges due to the high computational complexity and storage demands of such algorithms.
In response, this study integrates quantization—a method that reduces 32-bit floating-point values to lower-bit representations—into a self-cognizant Kalman filter for SOH estimation. A quantized feed-forward neural network (FFNN) models the battery dynamics, which is then incorporated into a dual extended Kalman filter algorithm. Model parameter updates, performed every cycle, are also executed in a quantized manner, thereby reducing the number of floating-point operations. This approach employs quantization to balance computational speed and accuracy, while lowering storage and processing requirements. Various quantization levels were tested, with 6-bit quantization proving particularly effective, enhancing the practicality of this method for on-board SOH estimations in battery management systems. Experimental findings indicate the reduction of computational time by 20.576% and memory requirements by 41.25%, while maintaining satisfactory accuracy in SOH estimation.
conclusions:
The quantization of neural network elements within the DEKF framework was successfully implemented. Experiments were performed to validate the framework, demonstrating significant efficiency and performance enhancements. By analyzing different quantization levels, 6-bit quantization was found to offer an optimal balance between accuracy and reduced computational time. Conversely, 8-bit quantization provided higher accuracy with slightly less time savings, making it a viable option depending on accuracy and computational requirements.
Implementing these quantization techniques led to a notable average reduction in running time of 20.576% and a 41.25% decrease in memory requirements. This reduction in memory footprint is particularly beneficial for deployment in resource-constrained environments and for on-board SOH estimation.
Overall, the successful application of quantization in DEKF enhances system efficiency and performance, making advanced neural network models more accessible and practical for a wider range of applications. The balance between accuracy and computational savings provided by 6-bit and 8-bit quantization levels underscores the flexibility and adaptability of quantization techniques in improving neural network deployments for on-board battery management systems.

title: Induction Motor Failure Detection Using Explainable Features from Motor Currents
authors: Wei Li, Northeastern University; Hariram Arni, FM Global Research; Bin Jou, PhD, FM Global Research; Sagar Kamarthi, PhD, Northeastern University; Key Words: Induction Motor, Failure Detection, Explainable AI (XAI), Feature Extraction
summary: Induction motors are critical to the reliable operation of various mechanical systems. Motor Current Signature Analysis (MCSA) provides a non-invasive way to monitor motor health and prevent costly diagnostics and repairs resulting from mechanical and electrical faults. The conventional MCSA techniques use the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to analyze three-phase voltage and current signals. To improve failure detection accuracy and provide actionable insights, this work proposes a framework for explainable feature extraction and modeling. The framework is designed to extract explainable features from current signal data and train an XGBoost classifier using failure modes as the model response. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis is then used to visualize the impact of the features on each failure mode. We collected training data using a Machinery Fault Simulator (MFS-Magnum) with a three-phase, 0.5 HP induction motor. Various defects were intentionally introduced into the experimental setup, including inter-turn short circuits, rotor unbalance, and broken rotor bars. By analyzing the relationship between extracted features and each failure mode, this approach facilitates the detection and identification of various impending motor failures.
conclusions:
This study presents an explainable machine learning framework for detecting induction motor failures using motor current features from time, frequency, and time-frequency domains. The XGBoost classifier, combined with SHAP analysis, has provided both high prediction accuracy and interpretation of feature importance for motor fault conditions, including inter-turn short circuits, rotor unbalance, and broken rotor bars.
Our findings show that key features such as acf_first_min, FFT_mean, and whiten_timescale are effective in accurately identifying motor health conditions. The SHAP summary plots reveal specific feature-fault affinity, which can help to explain the response from the machine learning model.
Future work will focus on improving the quality of features and the generalizability of the machine learning framework. To improve feature quality, we plan to work closely with domain experts to incorporate specialized yet user-friendly features derived from advanced Motor Current Signature Analysis (MCSA) techniques. It is important to strike a balance between the features' predictive power and interpretability to make sure that they are effective for fault detection while also being understandable for engineers and maintenance personnel.
To address the model’s dependence on high-quality labeled data and improve the model's generalizability in real-world industrial environments, we will explore transfer learning and domain adaptation methods. Additionally, using data from fleets of similar motors, which is common in production settings, can help alleviate data scarcity and enhance the model's performance. With adequate data, the problem definition can be expanded to include Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation beyond classification and anomaly detection.

title: Prognostics of Hall Thruster Erosion Using Multiphysics-Based Modeling and Machine Learning
authors: Yuan Jiang, University of Illinois; Alexandra N. Leeming, University of Illinois; Joshua L. Rovey, Ph.D., University of Illinois; Pingfeng Wang, Ph.D., University of Illinois; Key Words: Hall thruster, channel wall erosion, low-fidelity simulation, surrogate modeling
summary: Hall thrusters, a type of propulsion device with high specific impulses, have gathered substantial interest within the aerospace community. However, the challenge of thruster wall erosion induced by sputtering impedes their stable and reliable function. This paper proposes a novel prognostic framework for estimating Hall thruster channel wall erosion based on multiphysics simulation and machine learning. First, a one-dimensional (1D) plasma discharge code is introduced to simulate plasma dynamics within discharge channel. Then, the erosion rate is quantified based on a semi-empirical sputter yield model. In addition, an erosion profile estimation loop is proposed to accommodate the 1D simulation while leveraging 2D erosion profiles. Finally, a machine-learning polynomial regression model serves as a surrogate model, facilitating efficient erosion rate estimations without extensive computations. Results and comparisons demonstrate that the proposed low-fidelity prognostic framework reliably reflects the erosion trends observed in high-fidelity models and experimental data, while reducing both simulation and testing requirements.
conclusions:
This paper proposes a novel prognostic framework for Hall thruster erosion prediction based on low-fidelity multiphysics modeling and machine learning surrogate modeling. The multiphysics modeling combines a 1D low-fidelity plasma discharge model with a semi-empirical sputter model to estimate erosion rate and update channel wall profile based on an iterative update scheme. Then, a surrogate model based on machine-learning polynomial regression is introduced to estimate erosion rate with lower computation cost. Compared with traditional high-fidelity modeling and experimental testing, the proposed multiphysics simulation and surrogate modeling can not only provide the trend of channel wall erosion, but also reduce simulation and testing efforts.
Although the low-fidelity model provides the trends of erosion rates and wall profile changes promptly, the reduction of dimensionality can lead to inaccuracies in plasma behaviors, particularly at plasma sheath near the wall region. Therefore, future research will focus on multi-fidelity-based plasma simulation and Hall thruster erosion prognostics.

title: Transformer-Based Prognostic Modeling for Smart Grid Health Monitoring
authors: Phat K. Huynh, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Phi Huynh, International University - VNU-HCM, Vietnam; Om P. Yadav, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Chau Le, PhD, University of North Carolina at Charlotte; Harun Pirim, PhD, North Dakota State University
summary: Smart power grids, pivotal to modern infrastructure, face increased vulnerability due to their complex and interconnected nature, often leading to disruptions that can result in widespread power outages and significant economic losses. Traditional grid monitoring systems frequently fall short in both predicting and mitigating these disruptions, creating a critical need for more advanced predictive methods that can foresee and interpret the progression of these anomalies into distinct failure modes. This paper introduces a transformer-based prognostic model based on Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) data to enhance the predictive monitoring of smart grids. The method capitalizes on the advanced capabilities of transformer models to manage high-dimensional time-series data with complex dependencies. The methodology, validated rigorously against historical data, progresses through three main phases: (1) PMU data acquisition and preprocessing, (2) PMU-based feature engineering, and (3) prognostic modeling. In the data acquisition and preprocessing phase, high-resolution PMU data were collected, encompassing parameters such as voltage and current magnitudes, frequency, and phase angles. Next, we extracted 43 distinct features across four temporal windows, which were essential in characterizing the dynamic behavior of the grid. The prognostic modeling phase employed a transformer architecture with a sophisticated self-attention mechanism that efficiently handles the sequential PMU data, identifying subtle patterns indicative of potential grid failures. The prognostic model had a superior performance in predicting different types of grid failures—severe weather, lightning, and failed AC circuit equipment, which achieved an accuracy of up to 84.07% with low variability using five-fold cross-validation. This prognostic model enhances the predictive capabilities of smart grid monitoring systems and offers a robust framework for proactive management of grid health, potentially reducing the incidence and impact of power outages.
conclusions: In conclusion, our study presents the transformative impact of integrating the transformer-based prognostic framework with PMU data for smart grid health monitoring. By leveraging high-dimensional time-series data, advanced feature engineering, and tailored transformer architectures, our transformer-based model enhances predictive accuracy and responsiveness to grid disturbances. The self-attention mechanisms allow for the early detection of subtle anomalies, patterns and transitions, thus significantly improving upon traditional models and enhancing smart grid resilience. Model validation has demonstrated its robustness and superior predictive capabilities, particularly effective in grid management and reducing the risk of power outages. This work advances smart grid management and sets the stage for future innovations in grid reliability enhancement.

title: Data Assurance Plan for Safety and Reliability of Artificial Intelligence Enabled Systems
authors: Benjamin D. Werner, US Army DEVCOM Armaments Center; Benjamin J. Schumeg, US Army DEVCOM Armaments Center; Key Words: artificial intelligence, machine learning, reliability, safety, data, models, assurance
summary: With the continued integration and proliferation of artificial intelligence and machine learning AI/ML models into systems there is a gap in deliverables and artifacts to inform the assurance, safety, and reliability of these models and systems.  To that extent, a Data Assurance Plan is proposed as an artifact from a vendor or developer documenting and defining the properties, attributes, measures, and metrics of the data used to train, validate, and test an AI/ML model.  Information from the Data Assurance Plan can be leveraged in subsystem and system assessments to better understand the expected constraints, limitations, and performance of the models inherent from the data.  This document, through identification of data sourcing, control, and applicability, can provide insight into the future reliability and robustness of the developed model.  In its execution, the Data Assurance Plan not only is a conduit from developer to assessor but also from AI/ML scientists and engineers to assurance, reliability, and safety engineers.  It presents a means to measure and report on how the decisions made early in the design and development can impact risks, hazards, and failures not just of the model, but of the system and its functions.  This paper will explore the information that should be expected in such a deliverable as well as the expected impact and use of it by the appropriate assessors to begin to establish justified confidence.

title: OntoKGen: A Genuine Ontology and Knowledge Graph Generator using Large Language Model
authors: Mohammad Sadeq Abolhasani, Arizona State University; Rong Pan, PhD, Arizona State University; Key Words: Large Language Model, Ontology and Knowledge Graph Generator, Prompt Engineering, Neo4J,
summary: Extracting relevant and structured knowledge from large, complex technical documents within the Reliability and Maintainability (RAM) domain is labor-intensive and prone to errors. Our work addresses this challenge by presenting OntoKGen, a Genuine pipeline for Ontology extraction and Knowledge Graph (KG) generation. OntoKGen leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) through an interactive user interface guided by our adaptive iterative Chain of Thought (CoT) algorithm to ensure that the ontology extraction process and, thus, KG generation align with user-specific requirements. Although KG generation follows a clear, structured path based on the confirmed ontology, there is no universally correct ontology as it is inherently based on the user’s preferences. OntoKGen recommends an ontology grounded in best practices, minimizing user effort and providing valuable insights that may have been overlooked, all while giving the user complete control over the final ontology. Having generated the KG based on the confirmed ontology, OntoKGen enables seamless integration into schemeless, non-relational databases like Neo4j. This integration allows for flexible storage and retrieval of knowledge from diverse, unstructured sources, facilitating advanced querying, analysis, and decision-making. Moreover, the generated KG serves as a robust foundation for future integration into Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, offering enhanced capabilities for developing domain-specific intelligent applications.

title: Optimizing Software Defect Classification with Locally Linear Embedding Techniques
authors: Fatemeh Salboukh, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Hesam Saki, University of Tehran; Lance Fiondella, PhD, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Key Words: software reliability, software quality, defect classification, Locally Linear Embedding
summary: Software defect classification is crucial for enhancing the quality and reliability of software. This research explores the integration of Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) into the preprocessing stages of classification models to improve accuracy. LLE is particularly effective as it transforms complex, nonlinear data into a simpler, linear format. This transformation is instrumental in reducing the complexity of the data, facilitating a more straightforward analysis and potentially improving the predictive accuracy of classifiers. For this study, we used the KC2 dataset from the PROMISE repository and applied several feature selection techniques, including Correlation-Based Feature Selection, Gain Ratio, Sequential Forward Selection, and K-nearest neighbors. After selecting the most informative features, LLE was employed to linearize this data, aiming to enhance the classifiers’ performance by presenting them with data that is easier to interpret and analyze. The impact of LLE was evaluated by comparing the outcomes of five different classifiers, such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Machines, Non-Linear Support Vector Machines, and Naive Bayes, on both the original and the LLE-processed datasets. Our results demonstrated an average improvement of 4.5% in accuracy and 4% in F1-Score across the classifiers with the LLE-processed data, confirming the effectiveness of transforming nonlinear data into a linear space for enhancing software defect classification.

title: Estimating Software Reliability Without Test Hours
authors: Ann M. Neufelder, Mission Ready Software; Key Words: software reliability and testing, reliability growth analysis
summary:
Software reliability growth models [1] are used during testing to forecast reliability measures such as remaining defects, discovery rate, etc.  The models require the user to collect the number of test hours since software failures are a function of usage hours, not calendar hours. The problem is that collecting the test hours between failures or failures over some number of test hours sounds easier than it is.
This paper aims to present an alternative method that does not require the collection of usage time data. During software testing, the discovered defects will have varying levels of detectability, ranging from obvious to obscure.  By tracking the detectability of the software defects, one can estimate the percentage of total defects found so far compared to the theoretical estimate of all inherent defects. The percentage of defects discovered (also known as Defect Removal Efficiency or DRE) is a measure of the overall stability of the software, which can be used to make a release decision and estimate other reliability figures of merit.

title: Test Case Design for the System Level Reliability Testing of a Complex Electro-Mechanical Product+
authors: Robinson Lawrance, HCL America Inc; Nishith Kumar Reddy Gorla, PhD, HCL America Inc; Key Words: Reliability testing, reliability test case design, integration testing, reliability growth testing, , test to field correlation,
summary:
This paper demonstrates a systematic approach to define the range of parameters to consider and outline the process to be followed when designing a test case. This approach aids to uncover the failure mode and achieve desired output to improve product quality, performance, customer experience, and reliability of a complex electro-mechanical product.
Achieving field reliability that mirrors laboratory results is a complex and ongoing challenge in product development. Despite rigorous component and sub-assembly testing, discrepancies between lab performance and real-world use often lead to a significant proportion of unexpected failures. Specifically, while reliability analyses typically align with field performance 50% to 60% of the time, the remaining 40% to 50% of unforeseen issues contribute to substantially higher unreliability than anticipated in the field which is higher unreliability (~2X times) compared to the demonstrated reliability in lab environment, the question around is what get missed in the lab environment, and how this gap can address.
To bridge this gap, a more integrated approach is needed in reliability testing. So, this proactive approach effectively addresses the issue by consistently integrating the various analysis output into the lab test environment to increase the test to field correlation to over 95% from 60%. This extensive evaluation encompasses diverse situations, making the testing robust and aiming to minimize surprises in real-world deployments.
conclusions:

title: Modeling Recurrent Failure Processes using Padé Approximants
authors: Alex Yevkin, PhD, Software for Structures; Vasiliy Krivtsov, PhD, Ford Motor Company; Key Words: recurrent events, stochastic process, Padé functions, expected number of failures.
summary:
The practical goal of modeling the recurrent failure process of a system is to predict the expected number of failure events over time and to estimate various reliability indices (e.g., availability) of the system. Usually, the respective stochastic process is modeled by a sequence of random failure times from lifetime distributions as a function on the ordinal number of a consecutive event. Parameters of these failure time distribution functions are usually evaluated using the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). This approach becomes more and more challenging as the number of estimated process parameters increases.
The proposed approach is based on regression analysis of data obtained from a nonparametric evaluation of recurrent events. In the first step, the asymptotic formula for small failure numbers is obtained using traditional MLE considering only first failures. Then the obtained function is multiplied by the Padé (rational) function, and the regression procedure is applied to the product for the estimation of coefficients of the approximation function. The previously developed (for the case of Padé approximants) advanced method for minimizing the residual sum of squares is used.  In contrast to the traditional method, it leads to a system of linear equations and therefore is not limited by the number of estimated parameters. The efficiency of the model is illustrated by several examples. Limitations of the method (which are mostly based on the accuracy of nonparametric analysis) are discussed too.

title: Likelihood Ratio Bounds as Constrained Nonlinear Optimization Problems
authors: Michael Z. Spivey, ReliaSoft; Key Words: likelihood ratio, confidence bounds, nonlinear optimization
summary:
The standard method for finding likelihood ratio confidence bounds for a parameter of a lifetime model is the profile likelihood method.  This method entails eliminating all but the parameter of interest by effectively projecting the graph of the likelihood function onto a plane and solving the resulting single-variable optimization problem.  Confidence bounds on functions of parameters (such as reliability at a particular time or mean life) can be found by inverting the function of interest to create a reparameterization of the lifetime model and then proceeding as before.
Another, less well-known method, instead finds the likelihood ratio bounds on a parameter or function of parameters as the maximum and minimum of a constrained, multivariable nonlinear optimization problem.  The likelihood ratio is used to form the constraint set for this problem.
In this paper we discuss these two methods and indicate some practical advantages that the constrained nonlinear optimization method has over the profile likelihood method.  We also extend the theory on the constrained nonlinear optimization method.  Finally, we present numerical results indicating the asymptotic accuracy of the constrained nonlinear optimization method, as well as its improved speed versus the profile likelihood method.

title: Analysis of Censored Aggregate Failure-time Data Using Phase-type Distributions
authors: Haitao Liao, PhD, University of Arkansas; Samira Karimi, PhD, AICrete Corporation; Ke Yang, PhD, University of Arkansas; Neng Fan, PhD, University of Arizona; Key Words:  Phase-type distributions, censored aggregate failure-time data, maximum likelihood estimation
summary: Field failure time data provide ample sources of valuable information for product reliability estimation. However, actual failure times of individual units are usually not reported in many engineering applications. Instead, aggregate failure time data that give cumulative failure times of multiple units are collected and sometimes implemented with censoring. This raises big challenges in reliability estimation using those popular failure-time models and statistical methods. So far, only a few probability distributions have been utilized to handle aggregate failure time data while many widely used probability distributions (e.g., Weibull, Lognormal) are intractable. In this work, a statistical method using Phase-type (PH) distributions is proposed for analyzing censored aggregate failure-time data for the first time. Specially, a censored aggregate failure-time model based on the Coxian distribution is proposed, and an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for maximum likelihood (ML) estimation is developed for model parameter estimation. A simulation study and a real-world example illustrate the superior capability of the proposed method. Indeed, by mimicking the true underlying distributions that are incapable of handling such data, the proposed method provides practitioners with a flexible tool to overcome this challenge.
conclusions: This work uses PH distribution models to analyze censored aggregate failure-time data for the first time. To estimate the model parameters, an EM algorithm is developed for the ML estimation method. The simulation study shows the flexibility of PH distributions in approximating other probability distributions widely used in reliability engineering. Moreover, a real-world example demonstrates the capability of the PH-based method in the analysis of censored aggregate failure-time data. It is worth pointing out that the proposed method provides a new direction for analyzing such data generated from a variety of nonnegative random variables. From a technical point of view, this method can be used as a powerful substitute for those underlying probability distributions that are mathematically intractable in analyzing such data. For a practitioner, it alleviates the burden of model selection and provides great flexibility in determining the model complexity and interpretability based on computational challenges and other needs. It is also worth pointing out that our proposed PH-based models and statistical estimation method can be implemented in other applications, such as modeling the length-of-stay of patients in a hospital, stochastic operating room scheduling, and warranty data analysis.

title: A Two-Phase Arrhenius Model for Film Capacitors for Large Temperature Ranges
authors: Achim Benz, University of Stuttgart; Clemens Uhl, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, University of Stuttgart; Jan Knoch, Electronicon Kondensatoren GmbH; Key Words: reliability test, Arrhenius life model, two-phase Arrhenius life model, glass transition temperature, film capacitors, polypropylene
summary: This paper introduces a refined Arrhenius life model, termed the "Two-Phase Arrhenius Model", designed to enhance the reliability predictions of film capacitors across extensive temperature ranges.  This model integrates the glass transition temperature of polypropylene (PP), a common capacitor material, to forecast capacitor longevity under diverse environmental conditions more accurately.  The necessity for this research is driven by the current limitations of traditional life models that often fail to account for real operational stresses, leading to suboptimal component design and economic inefficiencies.
conclusions:
From the evaluations presented in the previous sections, it can be deduced that for certain components the standard Arrhenius service life model cannot correctly represent the temperature dependence of the damage over the full width of temperature range which was studied.  The Two-Phase Arrhenius can model the behavior much better and can cover the material-dependent glass transition temperature.  It can be included as a parameter in the service life model.  However, the problem of wide confidence intervals due to limited specimens must be regarded as even more critical due to more parameters to be estimated.
The Two-Phase Arrhenius Model provides a robust framework for accurately assessing the longevity of film capacitors under a wide range of environmental temperatures.  This research not only contributes to the theoretical understanding of capacitor aging but also has significant practical implications for designing more reliable and economically efficient electronic components, especially in applications facing extreme temperatures.

title: All-Terminal Network Reliability Estimation Using a Link Degradation Prediction Model
authors: Risat Rimi Chowdhury, North Carolina A&T State University; Om Prakash Yadav, PhD., North Carolina A&T State University; Shah M Limon, PhD., Slippery Rock University; Maneesh Singh, PhD., Western Norway University of Applied Sciences; Ajay Pal Singh Rathore, PhD., Malaviya National Institute of Technology
summary:
Many real-world networks exhibit degradation behaviors that lead to a gradual decline in performance, potentially resulting in network failures if not addressed. Maintaining optimal performance and reliability in critical infrastructures presents significant challenges, especially as traditional network monitoring techniques often fail to predict complex degradation patterns before they impact system performance. This paper introduces a comprehensive machine learning (ML) based approach to predict the degradation rate of network components. Our model integrates several ML algorithms, including K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Trees (DT), and Random Forests (RF), to develop a predictive model for link degradation. The results demonstrate that the KNN model performs particularly well on this degradation dataset. The prediction results can be used to generate degradation data, serving as the baseline for building degradation models for network components.
In this study, we considered an all-terminal network representing a power system with perfect nodes and links that degrade over time. Due to the complexity of the degradation process, this study incorporates Bayesian methods (BM) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations to evaluate reliability. The resulting network reliability shows dynamic behavior and reveals how the system approaches failure once the degradation threshold is reached. The method can also be applied to telecommunications and computer networks. For example, in telecommunication networks, predicting degradation in cables due to physical wear allows for proactive maintenance, reducing outages and improving network resilience. This framework advances the field of network reliability and serves as a foundational model for future research in network health prediction using advanced data analytics.

title: State of Quantum RNNs for Time-Series Forecasting
authors: Auguste Hirth, University of California, Los Angeles; Enrique Lopez Droguett, PhD, University of California, Los Angeles; Key Words: forecasting, quantum machine learning, recurrent neural network, variational quantum algorithms
summary: This paper is a survey on the use of fully-quantum digital recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) for time-series forecasting with real-world data. It discusses precedent QRNN papers, their methodology and evaluation strategies, and highlights that, despite their intuitive applicability to the problem, QRNNs haven't been rigorously evaluated with forecasting tasks. Finally, it presents some real-data forecasting experiment results and a couple examples of how experiment setup can affect the outcomes. These results serve to inform and motivate future work, with the goal of useful QRNN prediction.
conclusions: Despite the success of classical RNNs with time-series forecasting tasks, most existing implementations of quantum RNNs evaluate either function approximation tasks or non-time-series sequence classification tasks instead. Only one QRNN paper [8] evaluates QRNNs for forecasting, but its results seem to indicate a model returning its most recent input instead of a future value. The experiments and results presented here replicate this issue with a new dataset, indicating a QRNN that is optimizing itself into the naive benchmark model. To facilitate evaluation, the Additive Absolute Error metric is used to compare the QRNN’s error against that of the naive benchmark. Presented experiment results begin to demonstrate that larger, deeper QRNN models may be necessary to outperform the naive model for useful forecasting.

title: Forecast Accuracy: Weibayes Versus Generic Weibull Using Monte Carlo Simulation
authors: Dylan Chase, NextEra Energy; Van Culver, NextEra Energy; Dina Zreik, NextEra Energy; Key Words: reliability forecasting, Weibayes, Monte Carlo simulation
summary:
This study examines the forecast accuracy of a common Weibull applied to multiple subpopulations (henceforth referred to as a “Generic Weibull”), as compared to unique Weibayes models applied to each subpopulation, by means of Monte Carlo simulations. Accurate forecasting of component failures is vital for business operations, but there are numerous factors that can negatively affect forecast accuracy. This study focuses on one of those factors that is commonly encountered: limited failure counts across non-homogenous subpopulations of a given component, which may be installed in different operational environments or include variations in manufacturing or maintenance practices, potentially affecting shape and/or scale parameters.
Weibull models are widely used in forecasting component reliability. Ideally, a unique Weibull model, or Weibayes model with a known shape parameter, would be developed for a homogeneous population for a single failure mode with many failures. However, in practice, we often have non-homogeneous populations encountering multiple failure modes with unknown shape parameters and limited failures within each subpopulation. One approach to this practical challenge is to combine similar non-homogeneous subpopulations to increase the number of failures, with the expectation that the benefit of the additional failures will outweigh the negative impacts of population variability (validation of this expectation is outside the scope of this study). For example, the analyst may combine subpopulations that have similar characteristics that might affect component lifetimes, such as ambient temperature and other environmental factors. Once the non-homogeneous population has been formed, the analyst is left with two options: apply the Generic Weibull model for this population to all components in the non-homogeneous population or apply a Weibayes model, using the Generic Weibull shape parameter, to each homogeneous subpopulation separately. We hypothesize that using the Weibayes models will consistently yield more accurate failure forecasts, due to improved model flexibility to fit different operating environments that can impact component aging. However, we do expect that relative accuracy improvements will be affected by variables such as subpopulation sizes and failure quantities, as well as the magnitude of variation in true shape and scale parameters amongst the subpopulations that are combined.
We tested our hypotheses by means of Monte Carlo simulations. First, we generated sets of failure and censor ages at specified intervals of time using different “true” Weibull distributions for three subpopulations. We then fit a single Generic Weibull distribution to the combined simulated lifetime data at a chosen point in time. Next, we created a Weibayes fit for each subpopulation using the Generic Weibull shape parameter and the subpopulation’s failure and censor data at that same point in time. Using these models, we forecasted future failures from the chosen point in time for each approach and calculated the error of each forecast compared to the actual simulated “truth” to determine the relative accuracy of the two approaches. Finally, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by running multiple Monte Carlo simulations while varying a single factor, such as population size, component age, as well as shape and scale variation across the three subpopulations. Understanding these variables' impact on forecast accuracy allows the analyst to choose the method expected to consistently yield the most accurate forecast for a given circumstance, thereby creating greater business value.
conclusions: Our study indicates that it is preferable to use a Weibayes model when the change in scale between sites is larger than 10%. When scale variation is less than 10%, Weibayes is more accurate than the Generic Weibull at the population level, but less accurate at the subpopulation level. Weibayes models are also preferred over Generic Weibulls for non-homogenous populations that are older and thus have higher failure quantities. Variation in site ages is not as significant of a factor as the ages themselves and can be safely excluded from model selection criteria, as can subpopulation size variation. Finally, Generic Weibulls are advised instead of Weibayes, if the true shapes or failure modes are thought to be significantly different between the subpopulations.

title: Tackling Difficult Data: A Multi-Faceted Approach Using Accessible Techniques
authors: Carol Parendo, Collins Aerospace; Dan Bickelhaupt, Collins Aerospace; Key Words: Data Analysis, Difficult Data, CRISP-DM, Statistics, Machine Learning, Problem-Solving Framework
summary: In most data analysis projects, the overwhelming majority of attention is paid to the data analysis techniques that produce its results. Much less attention is paid to the myriad steps that produce the dataset to execute this data analysis upon. In almost all situations, the dataset received is not one suitable to perform data analysis upon and requires much effort to wrangle it into a usable condition. This is what we call difficult data: data that is distributed across multiple locations, aggregated at different levels, etc. that make it ill-suited to operate upon in its current form. In this paper, this important “grunt” work of wrangling difficult data takes centerstage. We present a systematic framework to deal with difficult data, offer powerful suggestions to avoid pitfalls, and provide two examples to illustrate the process in action.

title: Enhancing FMEA with ChatGPT: Structured Outputs, Qualitative Evaluations, and AI-Human Hybrid FMEA
authors: Meng Xu, PhD; Key Words: ChatGPT, FMEA, JSON, Failure modes, effect analysis, quantitative evaluation
summary:
The integration of ChatGPT into Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) marks a significant advancement in risk assessment methodologies within reliability engineering. By leveraging ChatGPT's extensive knowledge base and sophisticated natural language processing capabilities, the conventional FMEA process can be significantly automated and accelerated. This study demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of incorporating ChatGPT into FMEA through a structured approach that includes creating a system hierarchy and detailing the FMEA in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. The proposed method streamlines the identification and evaluation of failure modes and enhances the thoroughness and accuracy of the analysis. Our case study on an electric scooter patent illustrates how ChatGPT can generate relevant failure modes with detailed causes and mitigation actions, showcasing its potential to uncover failure modes that human analysts might overlook. Another case study on car seats shows that ChatGPT can reveal 81% of failure modes mentioned by customers.
Despite these advancements, several challenges remain. ChatGPT's performance in predicting Severity, Occurrence, and Detection (SOD) values was found to be inconsistent, highlighting the need for improved training data and methodologies. Future research should focus on developing public datasets for FMEA, enhancing domain-specific knowledge integration, and improving the accuracy of SOD value predictions. By addressing these challenges, the reliability engineering community can fully harness the potential of AI-human hybrid FMEA to enhance product safety and reliability in complex manufacturing environments.
conclusions: This paper integrated ChatGPT into the traditional Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) process, demonstrating its potential to enhance risk assessment and mitigation strategies. By employing a structured approach that involves creating a system hierarchy and detailing the FMEA in JSON format, ChatGPT can efficiently and accurately identify and evaluate failure modes. The case study on an electric scooter patent illustrates ChatGPT's ability to generate detailed and relevant FMEA results, uncovering potential failure modes that human analysts might miss. However, challenges such as inconsistencies in predicting Severity, Occurrence, and Detection (SOD) values and managing response length limitations highlight the need for improved training data and methodologies. Future research should focus on developing public datasets for FMEA and AI-human hybrid FMEA that enhance AI-driven analysis accuracy to fully realize the benefits of this innovative approach in reliability engineering.
keywords: reliability, safety, FMEA, risk assessment, AI

title: Risk Mitigation using Design Optimization, Tolerancing Analysis and Test Coverage Analysis
authors: Yavuz Goktas, Ph.D., Schneider Electric; David D Yellamati, Schneider Electric; James Ezhaya, Ph.D., Schneider Electric; Key Words: Risk Mitigation, Fault Tree, FMEA, Tolerancing
summary: Design Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (DFMEA) is a commonly used tool for managing design risks. RPN (Risk Priority Number) which is a Product of Severity, Occurrence and Detection is used to prioritize the risks and to plan appropriate actions to mitigate the risks. Severity is assessed based on the End Effect associated with a Failure Mode; Occurrence is assessed based on Capability of Design Controls and Detection is assessed based on capability of Design Verification & Validation Tests to detect the Failure Mode and the Cause. To mitigate the risks, we need to improve both Occurrence Rating and Detection Rating (the lower the better). To provide justification and to improve the Occurrence Rating, we performed Design Optimization and Tolerancing Analyses. Likewise, to provide justification and to improve the Detection Rating, we performed Test Coverage Analysis. In this paper, we will provide an illustration of the aforestated analyses using a case study of Variable Frequency Drive (VFD)’s Capacitor Bank sub-system. We used p-diagram and DFMEA to identify the opportunities for Tolerancing Analysis and Design Optimization to determine design mitigations and to improve the Occurrence Rating. We also developed a new process to detect gaps in test coverage to detect failure mode as well as the associated causes and close the gaps by adding new tests and/or by improving the existing tests to improve the Detection Rating. This approach provides an effective framework for conducting Risk Assessment and Mitigation during the Design process.
conclusions:
In this paper, we have proposed an effective process for managing design risks using DFMEA. We applied this process on VFD Capacitor Bank and were able to successfully mitigate the risk.
Although DFMEA is commonly used in many industries, there is a lot of ambiguity around how to justify and improve the occurrence and detection ratings. In this paper, we have illustrated application of Design Optimization, Tolerancing Analysis for reducing Occurrence Ratings and Test Coverage Analysis for reducing Detection Ratings and in turn for reducing RPNs for Critical Failure Modes leading to safety consequences using Capacitor Bank as a Case Study. We can apply this process for any safety critical or mission critical product or system.
Our future work in this domain is to incorporate Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence technologies in the Risk Management process [5].

title: A Comprehensive System Level Reliability Assessment: Modeling Guided by FMEA
authors: Wei Huang, PhD, Maxar Space Systems; Dale Borja, Maxar Space Systems; Key Words: FMEA, cross-strapped redundancy, single point failure, failure propagation, acceleration factor; of units or configurations than standard reliability modeling.  An example is presented to illustrate the benefits of considering the FMEA results in system level reliability assessments.  A proposed path-forward is outlined at the end of the paper.
conclusions:
For the first time, this paper proposes a novel approach in system level reliability assessment by linking unit or configuration level FMEA to system level reliability modeling.  Starting from categorizing failure modes in terms of failure effects at the system level, a comprehensive set of system level reliability models are developed, with each model to be applicable to a specific failure scenario.  This set of models provide more accurate numerical assessments of system level reliability than standard models since they can be used for different types of failure modes and effects.  The example illustrates the consequence of ignoring potential failure modes that could result in a loss of an entire redundant set of units or failure propagation to external units that degrade the reliability performance of the external units significantly.
Assessing system level reliability quantitively is often time consuming and sometimes challenging, even for reliability experts.  Linking the unit or configuration level FMEA to the system level reliability assessment could further burden reliability practitioners who have desires to get more accurate assessments from actual unit or configuration designs.  To make the proposed approach more appealing to most reliability practitioners, a tool that can extract analysis results from unit level FMEA and generate proper system level reliability models automatically would be desired.  Developing such a tool may be achievable by taking advantage of extended applications of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for reliability engineering.  This may be a future task to be pursued.

title: Three Aspects of Making Successful FMECA’s with MBSE: People, Process and Tools
authors: Nilgun Kutay, Turkish Aerospace; Özlem Erdener Sönmez, Turkish Aerospace; Cem Talip Öndeş, Turkish Aerospace; Key Words: FMECA, MBSE, FTA, seamless integration
summary:
This document provides detailed information regarding how one of the central reliability engineering analyses, Failure Modes, Effects and Criticality Analysis (FMECA), is managed with Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Methodology and how this helps overcome various interface problems. As a central analysis, FMECA serves many disciplines such as system safety, reliability, testability, maintainability, and integrated product support.
Especially in complex projects, seamless integration between these disciplines can be very challenging. MBSE methodology helps to overcome this challenge by connecting these disciplines in one integrated digital environment.
This paper places FMECA at the center and presents an example of how MBSE effectively integrates various disciplines from the design phase to the in-service phase of the lifecycle. During design, functions identified from customer requirements will feed into Functional FMECA, which will then support the development of Hardware/Piece Part FMECA, along with Systems Design Description information.  Subsequently, Hardware/Piece Part FMECA serves the system safety, reliability, testability, and IPS disciplines by providing detailed data and necessary information for their analyses. Any change in any part of the data will be reflected in all analyses through the MBSE methodology. This helps in developing today’s complex products by using valuable time and resources efficiently.
conclusions:

title: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems Reliability Modeling
authors: Jiliang Zhang, Rivian Automotive; Key Words: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems, feature-driven system reliability, system structure function
summary:
While Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) technology has being rapidly adopted across the automotive industry globally, the reliability of the ADAS system is of great concern and interest. System reliability modeling is the key for many other reliability tasks. Hence, it is very important. Meanwhile, there has not been enough significant studies specifically for ADAS system reliability modeling in publications. ADAS systems  presents some unique challenges that are encountered while applying the traditional system reliability modeling techniques to the ADAS systems. ADAS systems are more feature-driven instead of the hardware component-driven. Software is an integral part of the system reliability, along with hardware components, to support each individual ADAS features and then entire ADAS system. The traditional hardware-centric methods are ineffective in this situation. On the other hand, this is a new opportunity of study for the new system reliability modeling technique that can be more suited for ADAS systems.
In the approach presented in this paper, one focuses on the ADAS feature or features that the system provides and then look for the lower-level features along with other hardware and software components to support the upper-level features. This feature-driven approach connects the lower-level features and components to the more complicated or advanced upper-level feature or features. It applies to individual ADAS features, more advanced ADAS features, feature sets, and entire vehicle ADAS systems. This fits ADAS and autonomous vehicles very well.
Active Cruise Control (ACC) as an individual ADAS feature and Highway Assist (HWA) as a more advanced ADAS feature are taken as examples to illustrate the feature-driven system reliability modeling methodology. The proposed new method can potentially find more applications beyond ADAS and autonomous vehicles, while the product features and supporting software become more significant elements in products.

title: Applying Innovative AI Techniques to Complex U.S. Army Datasets
authors: Jordan Mills, Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation; Megan Shumate, DEVCOM Aviation & Missile Center; Kris Walker, DEVCOM Aviation & Missile Center; Russ Alexander, SpecTrum A&T Solutions, LLC; Key Words: Big Data Analytics, RAM Analysis, Dimensionality Reduction, Clustering Techniques, Shapley Analysis
summary: As the amount of data that engineers and analysts needed to evaluate increases, the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques become more critical. Big data analytics tools can be used to find patterns and relationships within large data sets and the domain of Reliability, Availability, and Maintainability (RAM) for aircraft and missiles provides an ideal application for these big data methods.  For aviation data, looking at relationships and patterns within and between maintenance events and on-board flight sensor data can provide added value for maintenance and logistics managers.  For missile system data, looking at relationships and patterns within different collections of test data for the weapon system helps support important RAM decisions related to root cause analysis, the identification of reliability degradation trends, and the extension of missile shelf life. In this paper, the authors detail the integration of big data analytics tools and techniques to provide value to RAM stakeholders through the innovative analysis of aviation and missile datasets.
conclusions: As the amount of data that engineers and analysts need to evaluate increases, the use of AI methods and big data analytics become more critical. RAM data for aircraft platforms and weapon systems provides an ideal application for these big data methods.  The authors have researched, tailored, implemented, and performed big data analysis on multiple datasets for the U.S. Army RAM customer base.  The authors have developed dual workflows for aviation and missile data, specifically tailoring the analytics based on data content and objective results.  SME review of our processes and results indicates that our methods are successfully validating known and anecdotal relationships within the data.  Future work will include further refinement of our methods and algorithms to provide prioritized, user-friendly dashboards and reports to enable rapid application of our results to benefit the RAM community.
keywords: reliability, maintainability, availability, degradation, logistics, AI

title: The Future of Availability: Integration of AI in RAM Operations
authors: Charles Etheredge, Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation; Haven Brown, Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation; Tony Donatelli, Reliant Technologies Inc.; Seth Farrington, U.S. Army Aviation & Missile Center; Key Words: Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, Big Data, Repairable Systems
summary: This paper explores the recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and the application of these technologies within the Reliability, Availability, and Maintainability (RAM) domain. It includes a review of recent developments in AI research and literature, an overview of the current industry focus, and an outline of problems faced in RAM today. Our goal is to provide relevant explanations for RAM professionals on the significant improvements in reliability, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness that AI technologies provide and encourage the integration of these technologies to increase operational availability.
conclusions: In summary, AI is reshaping the landscape of RAM operations by improving maintenance efficiency, reducing logistical costs, and enabling longer service periods for maintained systems. As the technology continues to evolve, its integration into the RAM industry is expected to deepen, further revolutionizing maintenance practices and contributing to the future advancements in availability. The potential of AI in this field is vast, and its continued development will likely bring about even more innovative solutions to the complex challenges faced by RAM today.

title: Using Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Techniques for Industrial Robot Selection
authors: Behin Elahi, PhD, San José State University; Rakshitha Gokuldas, San José State University; Sourabh Hegde, San José State University; Shikha Uppala, San José State University; Sonali Kini, San José State University

title: Web Application for Failure Analysis Applying Text Mining Methods
authors: Carlos Recalde, PRONACA; Key Words: failure analysis, text mining, web application, term document matrix, clustering, topic modeling
summary:
This paper outlines the development of a web application for failure analysis applying text mining methods using R, to efficiently process and analyze textual data from maintenance records.  The goal is to automate the extraction of failure mode information, traditionally a labor-intensive and time-consuming task, thereby enhancing maintenance operations' efficiency and effectiveness.
Key features of the web application include preprocessing, which allows data upload in Excel or CSV format, cleaning text data by removing noise and converting it into a Term Document Matrix (TDM); association analysis, which identifies correlations between terms to uncover hidden patterns within the text data; clustering, which groups similar words based on term frequencies, revealing natural groupings and underlying failure patterns; and topic modeling, which uses Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to discover abstract topics within the text data, offering a high-level understanding of main themes and issues.
The web application represents a significant advancement in maintenance analytics by automating the extraction and analysis of failure mode information, addressing key challenges faced by maintenance organizations.  Enhanced efficiency is achieved as automation reduces the time and effort required for manual analysis.  Its scalability and flexibility make the web-based application easily deployable and accessible, suitable for various organizational settings and data sizes, and available at this link.  The web application's code is shared on this GitHub repository to encourage further development and foster collaboration within the maintenance community.  Actionable insights from association analysis, clustering, and topic modeling can improve maintenance strategies and equipment reliability, reducing downtime.
The development of this web application and its use in the case study demonstrate the transformative potential of text mining methods in maintenance practices.  By automating the extraction and analysis of failure mode information, maintenance teams can perform detailed failure analysis on 795 maintenance records of one machine in approximately 3 minutes.  The web application enhances maintenance operations by enabling human experts to analyze maintenance records, identify recurring failure patterns, and pinpoint frequently implicated components.  It also validates existing assumptions and uncovers new insights, contributing to continuous improvement in decision-making processes.

title: Mitigating Risk of Overload Cascading Failures in Storage Area Networks
authors: Guixiang Lyu, University of Massachusetts, Dartmouth; Liudong Xing, University of Massachusetts, Dartmouth; Guilin Zhao, Southwest Jiaotong University; Key Words: cascading failure, dynamic threshold, load reallocation, mitigation, reliability
summary:
Despite being a dependable storage solution, storage area networks (SANs) may suffer from cascading failures caused by overloading, hindering the required quality of service delivered to users or even incurring significant financial losses.  This work proposes mitigation strategies based on inverse-proportional load reallocation to alleviate the risk of cascading failures.  Upon reaching the workload threshold of a SAN switch, reallocation is triggered among a set of switches selected based on their load or reliability levels.  The reliability of SAN switches is assessed in accordance with the accelerated failure-time model.  The overall SAN reliability is assessed using the analytical model of binary decision diagrams.  Using a detailed case study of a mesh SAN, mitigation strategies using static and dynamic workload thresholds are considered and compared.  Effects of the step size used in dynamic schemes are examined.  Inverse proportional and proportional reallocation strategies are also compared.
Based on the observations from the case study, it is recommended that for mesh SANs, using the dynamic threshold-based scheme with a lower step value and the load-sensitive node selection rule is more effective for mitigating the risk of cascading failures due to overload conditions and improving the overall SAN reliability.  Moreover, the load data of switches is more readily available than the reliability data, making the load-sensitive node selection rule more feasible for the mitigation implementation than the reliability-sensitive selection rule.
conclusions:
Despite being a dependable storage solution, storage area networks (SANs) may suffer from cascading failures caused by overloading, hindering the required quality of service delivered to users or even incurring significant financial losses.  This work proposes mitigation strategies based on inverse-proportional load reallocation to alleviate the risk of cascading failures.  Upon reaching the workload threshold of a SAN switch, reallocation is triggered among a set of switches selected based on their load or reliability levels.  The reliability of SAN switches is assessed in accordance with the accelerated failure-time model.  The overall SAN reliability is assessed using the analytical model of binary decision diagrams.  Using a detailed case study of a mesh SAN, mitigation strategies using static and dynamic workload thresholds are considered and compared.  Effects of the step size used in dynamic schemes are examined.  Inverse proportional and proportional reallocation strategies are also compared.
Based on the observations from the case study, it is recommended that for mesh SANs, using the dynamic threshold-based scheme with a lower step value and the load-sensitive node selection rule is more effective for mitigating the risk of cascading failures due to overload conditions and improving the overall SAN reliability.  Moreover, the load data of switches is more readily available than the reliability data, making the load-sensitive node selection rule more feasible for the mitigation implementation than the reliability-sensitive selection rule.

title: Dual Machine Learning Models for IoT Quality and Supply Chain Management
authors: Mourad Larbi, PhD, Hewlett Packard Enterprise; Yongjin Choi, PhD, Hewlett Packard Enterprise; Chris Cheng, Hewlett Packard Enterprise; Key Words: machine learning, predictive maintenance, supply chain management, dual prediction models
summary:
We have developed dual machine learning models that can be used for predicting an imminent component failure and a longer term fail parts quantity demand for supply chain management.
Machine learning techniques were used to select the relevant sensor data that can be used to build the imminent failure model and the long-term failure quantity model.
In deployed examples, we observed close to 80% prediction accuracy on failures resulting in close to 2/3 reduction of system outages due to multiple component failures. Different strategies can be used to deploy our predictive maintenance model: from conservative but costly replacing every predicted unit to only removing multiple failure cases to prevent system outages. Our model is flexible and suitable for deployment in production. We observed 90-95% accuracy in predicting quantity of fail parts needed for one quarter ahead of time.
We believe sensor-based machine learning predictive models can be extended to many critical electronic components in the field if there is sensor data and sufficient failure history available.

title: Artificial Intelligence Is Not Going to Replace Your Fault Tree Analysis
authors: John E. Weglian, EPRI; Key Words: artificial intelligence, fault tree analysis, probabilistic risk assessment
summary:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are expected to revolutionize many industries in the near future. There are multiple examples of AI that can generate lifelike images, make predictions, compose essays, and classify objects on images. However, while opportunities exist to leverage AI to support more robust and efficient fault tree analysis (FTA), there are a number of hurdles that make the use of AI ill-suited to replace a human performing FTA.
AI programs require a large amount of training data to generate the internal relationships that they use to make predictions on new data. Getting a sufficient amount of data to train an AI algorithm on PRA results will be extremely challenging. PRA results can be highly non-linear, so the training data would need to include many examples of this non-linear behavior for an AI algorithm to adequately predict risk results. AI programs are generally meant to maximize agreement with the “average” case, but in risk assessment, it is often the outlier cases that are most important.
PRA models are often updated over time to reflect changes in the systems represented by the PRA. These changes can be due to things such as changes in the concept of operations or changes in failure rate data. Changes in the PRA could invalidate previous data used to train the AI algorithm, which could require frequent re-training of the model.
In some industries, the risk results from PRA models are used to meet regulatory requirements. There is currently no way to efficiently verify that the results from an AI algorithm would meet the accuracy results that would be needed to rely on the results to ensure that regulatory requirements based on the PRA are actually met.
Although AI is not going to replace FTA, there are a number of areas where AI may be of benefit to PRA analysts. One could be training an AI algorithm to be able to interpret a cutset and provide a narrative that explains the context represented by the cutset. Extraction of a fault tree from a technical drawing, especially when this information is contained in a digital model of the system, may be a good use of AI. AI may be able to support risk-informed decision making by providing relevant information (both risk information and other pertinent information) to decision makers in an efficient way to decision makers. AI may also help with a review of fault trees and the associated PRA documentation to make these reviews more efficient.
As AI matures, additional uses for AI within PRA are likely to be identified.
