title: Exploring Grover-Enhanced QAOA for Minimal Cut Set Identification
authors: Gabriel San Martín Silva, University of California, Los Angeles; Enrique López Droguett, PhD., University of California, Los Angeles; Key Words: Fault Tree Analysis, Minimal Cut Set Identification, Quantum Computation, QAOA, Grover
summary:
Fault Tree Analysis is a powerful technique used in a wide variety of fields to perform both quantitative and qualitative analysis of complex systems. Among the capabilities of Fault Tree Analysis, one of the most critical and computationally expensive is the identification of Minimal Cut Sets. With the ever-growing demand for more efficient, sustainable, and safe systems, we can expect the computational complexity of finding minimal cut set configurations to increase even further. To prepare for this challenge, this paper explores the feasibility of finding minimal cut set configurations in standard, coherent fault trees using a novel quantum-based optimization approach. The approach, previously proposed to find satisfying clauses for 3-SAT problems in general settings, is modified to accommodate the context of Fault Tree Analysis. To validate the proposed approach, we perform numerical tests on a quantum computing simulation environment. The results show that while the identification of minimal cut sets is feasible, challenges arise when the size of the fault tree increases.
Overall, the experimental results verify the feasibility of identifying minimal cut sets in standard, coherent fault trees using the G-QAOA methodology. However, due to hardware limitations, this verification was only conducted in relatively small fault tree models. Regarding the use of a modified mixer operation, as proposed by Mandl et al., the results demonstrate significant performance advantages over the mixer operator used in traditional QAOA. Therefore, our main recommendation for future studies in this area is to focus on incorporating this modified operator into newly developed models.

title: Reliability Analysis of PEM Electrolyser Balance of Plant
authors: Salim Ubale, University of Nottingham; Rasa Remenyte-Prescott, University of Nottingham; Alastair Stuart, University of Nottingham; Adam Hague, ITM Power; David M. Grant, University of Nottingham
summary:
Polymer Electrolyte Membrane (PEM) electrolysers are devices that use electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. They have garnered significant attention in industry due to their improved efficiency and potential for contributing to emission reduction in the industrial and transport sectors. Hydrogen is one of several solutions to accelerating the energy transition and can be utilised in transport, such as cars, and trains, manufacturing processes, such as steel, and power to gas applications .
The balance of plant (BoP) of the PEM electrolyser consists of the stack and all the subsystems required to ensure the proper functioning of the stack and the generation of high-purity hydrogen. The presence of impurities in PEM electrolyser feed water significantly impacts the lifetime, operation, and performance of a PEM electrolyser plant . Inadequate water management can lead to water impurities and interruption of water supply to the stack. These factors can contribute to downtime, reduced reliability of the water subsystem components, and degradation or failure of the stack.
In order to ensure reliable and efficient operation of PEM electrolyser plants, understanding failure events, including repair and replacement procedures, are essential. Although some studies have been conducted on reliability modelling of electrolyser cells/stacks, to our best knowledge, there are currently no published studies on the reliability analysis of PEM electrolyser BoP. This paper, therefore, presents a model for failure analysis of PEM electrolyser plant using Fault Tree Analysis (FTA). It demonstrates how this approach is suitable for reliability and availability analysis of the PEM electrolyser BoP, understanding failure modes, determining time to system failure and identifying system critical components. The deficiencies of the traditional analysis methods are also discussed.
conclusions:
Reliability analysis methods such as FTA have been shown
to gain further understanding of failure modes of PEM electrolyser systems.
Figure 6. Petri net example
This work has provided one of the first studies in analysing top level events of a PEM electrolyser BoP using available information of a commercial PEM electrolyser plant. It has shown the importance of the WPU and how improper water management, in addition to other factors, can lead to uncontrolled H2/O2 mixtures. The lack of complete quantitative data has limited the analysis. In addition, although, component failure modes including critical ones, have been highlighted, the interdependencies between the failure modes have not been taken into account of.
For these reasons, a more advanced modelling approach,  such as Petri nets, is currently developed, and the dynamic behaviour of the system can be studied in detail. For example, Figure 6 shows an example of a Petri net for membrane degradation. Places p1 and p2 represent no membrane degradation, and membrane degradation respectively, whilst the non-standard tokens, <X>, <Y>, and <Z>, depend on the operating parameter of the stack, such as temperature, humidity, and conductivity. In addition, partial failure modes of the membrane, such as membrane thinning and perforation, can be represented using Petri nets. Petri nets can effectively capture the interactions and dependencies between various failure modes, and therefore can be used for a more detailed analysis in the future study.

title: Reliability Modeling Using Weibull Analysis and AI Based on Field Returns
authors: Awni Qasaimeh, Ph.D., Zebra Technologies Corporation; Eva Kosiba, P. E., Zebra Technologies Corporation; Key Words: Field and warranty data, Weibull Analysis, Artificial Neural Networks (ANN)
summary:
Traditional Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) Prediction estimates the overall failure rate by adding up failure rates of every component making up the product. These failure rates are usually derived from historical data collected from industry and military maintained databases such as MIL-HDBK-217, Telcordia and others where failure rate is assumed to be constant, i.e. the reliability of each component is exponentially distributed. This may provide an approximation for random failures but provides predictions of limited value for overall system reliability. Also, it does not provide any practical information for repair technicians at service depots. This approach also ignores wear out and material degradation. Furthermore, MTBF predictions do not account for different use cases but rather assume normal use conditions, an “ideal” mechanical design and 50% electrical stress.
The proposed work focuses on developing a framework for modeling part reliability based on products’ family and end user environment. The intent of this work is to close the gap between the prediction and the actual failure rate. Historical field data for previous generations of the same/similar product, and testing data for products currently in development are considered. A “reliability functions” database will be developed for main modules and technologies such as display, housing, and main board based on field and service data, for specific user environments (postal, retail, etc). This can be used to forecast spare parts availability and cost associated with them for each group of customers and products’ family. Unlike the constant failure rate model, this would account for time-dependent failure rate and different use case environments to better predict overall system reliability.
First, warranty data is cleaned and classified based on different attributes. This data includes several fields such as end-user (customer), location, manufacturing date, failure date, part replaced and time to failure. An additional field, called “Sale Vertical” was added to categorize end-user environments such as Outdoor Postal, Indoor Retail, Healthcare, and others. Every end user is grouped into one of these categories. Generative AI was used to classify the end user into one of these environments based on the Customers Name. The second step is to calculate the reliability function of high-return parts based on the given end-user data set. This will then be used as an input to Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model. Finally, ANN is trained to predict the reliability of the overall product at certain field time. The inputs for the model account for historic time-to-failure, customer environment, manufacturing date, and product family. Preliminary results showed that typical MTBF using traditional parts counts method for hand-held devices can vary from 10-20 years, while actual MTBF are 3-5 years. The accuracy of the ANN model was around 99%. Predicted MTBF was approximately 3 years. Only three modules were considered in this study for illustration which led to high accuracy. This method can be expanded to include other failure modes and modules/subsystems.
conclusions: There is always a need to be able to predict the reliability of a product during development stages. Traditional MTBF prediction method has several limitations especially when it comes to handheld devices and other products where mechanical wear, material degradation and fatigue are present. Several factors related to user environments and the ruggedness of products are also of utmost importance. This paper has two primary objectives. The first objective is to forecast the failure/return quantity of various parts for different user environments or sales verticals. This is particularly important for helping service depots plan more effectively with respect to resources and parts inventory. The second objective is to build a database of the reliability of different parts across various environments and product classes. This database can then be used to predict the overall reliability of a given product under development, using its Reliability Block Diagram (RBD) and intended use case. Unlike the constant failure rate model used by MTBF predictions, this would account for time-dependent failure rate and different user environments to better predict overall product’s reliability. It was also shown that ANN can be used to provide better accuracy prediction than just simply using mathematical model. ANN accounts for the dependency between different parts which normally is ignored to simplify the mathematical calculations. Accuracy was found to be around 99% for the product considered in this work. This model can be expanded to include other products and factors, as well as other failure modules and modes. Only three subsystems were considered (main board, Display and housing) in this case study which led to very high accuracy. In reality, a system (product) would have more than three modules.
keywords: reliability, availability, Weibull, RBD, degradation, spare parts, AI

title: Efficient Reliability Analysis: Debiasing Machine Learning with Partial Data
authors: Yanwen Xu, University of Texas at Dallas; Key Words: Debiasing machine learning, gaussian process model, partial data, uncertainty propagation
summary:
In safety-critical applications, ensuring high reliability is essential for operational success and regulatory compliance. Reliability analysis is crucial for evaluating system performance, yet precise event analysis remains a challenge due to multiple parameters and significant computational demands. To reduce these costs, researchers have increasingly utilized machine learning models as substitutes for expensive physical experiments. The accuracy of these models depends heavily on the quality of training samples. This paper focuses on the Gaussian process-based model, which has gained attention in reliability analysis and real-world applications. Gaussian process (GP) model has gained increasing attention in both reliability analysis and real-world applications. Constructing GP-based models usually requires fully observed data, but many engineering scenarios suffer from missing values due to unobserved inputs, unreliable sensors, and data collection errors. While integrating partially observed datasets could expand the dataset size, naive imputation may introduce bias. Though data augmentation techniques can help, bias is unavoidable, causing trade-offs in prediction accuracy.
To address these challenges, this paper introduces a hierarchical Bayesian Gaussian process model for partial data (HBGP-PD) framework designed to minimize bias. This framework leverages partially observed data for model training and quantifies the uncertainties arising from the heterogeneous partial data. This technique is particularly valuable for complex real-world problems where data comes from multiple sources and exhibits diverse formats and structures. We provide theoretical guarantees for our approach, enabling inference and construction of confidence intervals. This is crucial for efficient reliability estimation, offering insights into the precision and uncertainty of the estimate. Supported by solid theoretical proof, we evaluate HBGP-PD through numerical experiments, demonstrating its superior performance. In conclusion, the HBGP-PD model provides an effective solution for developing high-fidelity predictive models from partially observed datasets, while also enabling uncertainty propagation and quantification. It is particularly well-suited for high-dimensional, complex systems where fully observed data is limited, but low-fidelity or noisy data is more accessible. However, as the sparsity of partial data increases, the model's performance may decline due to the introduction of greater uncertainty. Therefore, the model’s accuracy is best maintained when there is a balanced mix of fully observed and partial data.
conclusions: This paper introduces the Hierarchical Bayesian Gaussian Process model for partial data (HBGP-PD) to address challenges posed by data heterogeneity and scarcity in real-world applications. Through theoretical analysis and numerical studies, we demonstrate the model's ability to achieve accurate and robust predictions even with limited or incomplete data. Future research should focus on scaling HBGP-PD for larger datasets and exploring its performance across diverse domains and data types to enhance its applicability. Integrating HBGP-PD with other machine learning approaches or ensemble methods could further improve prediction accuracy and robustness in complex scenarios.

title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Battery Pack Thermal Management
authors: Zheng Liu, University of Illinois; Yuan Jiang, University of Illinois; Yumeng Li, PhD, University of Illinois; Pingfeng Wang, PhD, University of Illinois; Key Words: Physics-informed machine learning, battery thermal management, heat transfer
summary:
With the popularity of electric vehicles, the demand for lithium-ion batteries is increasing. Temperature significantly influences batteries’ performance and safety. Battery thermal management systems can effectively control the temperature of batteries; therefore, batteries’ performance and safety can be ensured. However, the development process of battery thermal management systems is time-consuming and costly due to the extensive training dataset needed by data-driven models requiring enormous computational costs for finite element analysis. Therefore, a new approach to constructing surrogate models is needed in the era of AI. Physics-informed machine learning enforces the physical laws in surrogate models, making it the perfect candidate for estimating battery pack temperature distribution. In this study, we first developed a 21700 battery pack indirect liquid cooling system with cold plates on the top and bottom with thermal paste surrounding the battery cells. Then, the simplified finite element model was built based on experiment results. Due to the high coolant flow rate, the cold plates can be considered as constant temperature boundaries, while battery cells are the heat sources. The physics-informed convolutional neural network served as a surrogate model to estimate the temperature distribution of the battery pack. The loss function was constructed considering the heat conduction equation based on the finite difference method. The physics-informed loss function helped the convergence of the training process with less data. As a result, the physics-informed convolutional neural network showed more than 15% improvement in accuracy compared to the data-driven method with the same training data.
Figure 1. Battery pack indirect liquid cooling with cold plates simplification.
conclusions: This paper proposes a multi-fidelity physics-informed CNN for battery temperature distribution prediction. First, a 3D battery cooling problem is simplified to a 2D heat transfer scenario, which is simulated using finite element tools. Then, domain-specific knowledge is incorporated into deep learning models through a physics-informed loss function that follows the low-fidelity heat transfer PDEs. The UNet CNN with a multi-fidelity projection head is introduced as surrogate model, predicting the battery temperature distribution with a small amount of labeled dataset. Results indicate that the proposed method enhances temperature distribution estimation accuracy by 15% over traditional data-driven approaches with comparable limited training datasets. Future research will concentrate on battery optimal design and control leveraging physics-informed machine learning techniques.

title: Which Chapters and Topics Should Be Included in a Safety Case?
authors: Thor Myklebust, SINTEF Digital; Dorthea Mathilde Kristin Vatn, SINTEF Digital; Tor Stålhane, NTNU; Key Words: Safety case, artificial intelligence, safety standards, compliance, human aspects
summary: The research presented in this paper highlights the need for updating and expanding the chapters and content of safety cases to accommodate the evolving technological and regulatory landscape, particularly with the integration of AI in safety-critical systems. We have evaluated the relevant topics and chapters for a safety case based on studying relevant safety standards, safety regulations, the EU AI Act, current literature, and interviews with safety experts. As a basis, we have used EN 50129 for railway, which divides safety cases into six parts. We suggest four new parts being included. We included an introduction part (0) to establish scope and context since our solution includes several domains. Due to recent developments in AI, AI regulations and AI standards (RQ1) we have established two new parts: Part 7 “The AI safety report” and Part 8 “Human aspects and oversight”. To ensure that our safety case solution can be used in different domains (RQ2), we have also established two new parts: Part 2, “Operational design domain,” and Part 3, “Concept of operation.” In addition, our AI and cross-domain evaluations resulted in several new and improved subchapters, as shown in the table below. We elaborate on the content of the suggested new parts and which subchapters require improvements.

title: Reliability and Safety Assessment Model for LOCA Event in BWRX-300
authors: Saikat Basak, Ontario Tech University; Lixuan Lu, PhD, Ontario Tech University; Key Words: Dynamic PRA, EMRALD, Reliability, LOCA, BWRX-300
summary:
The BWRX-300, an advanced Small Modular Reactor (SMR), represents the latest evolution in boiling water reactor technology, drawing on over six decades of experience. This reactor emphasizes the use of Passive Safety Systems (PSSs) that leverage natural forces, such as gravity and natural circulation, to enhance safety and reliability while minimizing the need for active components and manual interventions. Building on the design of the Economic Simplified Boiling Water Reactor (ESBWR), the BWRX-300 aims to improve safety features while reducing capital costs. However, the innovative nature and complexity of these passive systems present significant challenges in accurately assessing their reliability. In the event of a Loss-of-Coolant Accident (LOCA), critical safety functions are performed by systems including the Control Rod Drive (CRD) system and Boron Injection System (BIS) for reactivity control, the Isolation Condenser System (ICS) for core cooling and long-term heat removal, and the Reactor Pressure Vessel Isolation Valves (RPVIVs) for reactor isolation. Each of these systems plays a vital role in preventing core damage by ensuring over-pressure protection and maintaining sufficient coolant levels. This paper conducts a comprehensive reliability and safety assessment for a LOCA scenario in the BWRX-300 using dynamic Probabilistic Risk Assessment (PRA) modeling through the EMRALD tool.
The study evaluates the effectiveness of these safety systems and identifies potential vulnerabilities in their interdependent functions. The findings advance the understanding of the BWRX-300's operational safety under critical conditions and provide insights that could guide future improvements in SMR design and regulatory standards, underscoring the importance of robust safety systems in nuclear reactor engineering.
The findings of this paper underscore the importance of robust maintenance protocols and the potential need for further simulations to explore low-probability failure modes. The results contribute valuable insights into the operational safety of the BWRX-300, offering recommendations that could inform future improvements in SMR design and regulatory frameworks, ultimately enhancing the safety and reliability of nuclear reactor operations.
conclusions:
The dynamic PRA conducted using the EMRALD tool for the BWRX-300 has provided valuable insights into the reactor's safety performance during a LOCA. The results indicate that core damage is primarily associated with the failure of the ICS, particularly during loop tests or maintenance activities. The analysis highlights that by effectively mitigating failures related to ICS loop tests and maintenance, the CDF due to ICS failure can be significantly reduced. No core damage was observed due to RI or RS failures, suggesting that the CDF for these systems is extremely low.
The findings of this paper highlight the critical importance of implementing robust maintenance protocols and the need for additional simulations to investigate low-probability failure modes. These results provide valuable insights into the operational safety and offer recommendations that could guide future enhancements in SMR design and regulatory standards, ultimately contributing to the improved safety and reliability of nuclear reactor operations.

title:
Sensitivity of a Video Detection System and the Impact on 
Availability vs Safety
authors: Sven W Scholz, PhD, TUD Dresden University of Technology; Key Words: availability, safety, video analytics, object detection, sensitivity, false alarm rate
summary:
Automated and unattended transit systems form integral parts of many airports (Airport People Movers Systems, APM) but also urban transit systems (subways). Most of such systems have onboard CCTV technology that can be used to determine the status onboard the vehicle, i.e. whether it is empty or not.
Passengers, luggage or any other kinds of objects shall not remain onboard when the vehicles are removed from service, e.g. send to the depot or to the workshop or parked alongside the track. A video-based detection system has been developed to automatically detect passengers or objects left behind.
Such as with all detection systems, thorough calibration of the sensors, i.e. cameras in our case, is essential to minimize false alarms but also achieve a very high detection rate.
This paper presents an empiric and heuristic approach to analyze the detection performance and choose suitable parameter settings to achieve both a low number of false alarms and a low number of wrong side failures to detect every object which is present. because they impact the systems’ availability and to provide no wrong side failures to detect every present object). The interdependency between operational availability which is impacted by the number of false alarms and the detection accuracy not to fail to the wrong side is presented based on numerous (hundreds) of real-life tests of an APM system. The results provide insights into the challenging calibration of a detection system and can help understand the contradictory requirement to satisfy availability and safety.
The detection performance of this system was analyzed with collected video footage of different test cases (people, groups of people, small and large objects). A specific system configuration was identified which can provide both an accurate detection (higher 99%) and very few false alarms (less than 0.5%). The interdependency between system availability and safety is revealed, i.e. the higher the detection accuracy, the more false alarms appear and vice versa. A “phenomenon” that some practitioners may not be well aware of, even due to the fact, that real-world systems cannot be used as lab-installations to modify parameter settings and reveal this interrelation.
In the future, more systematic search strategies for optimum parameters could be implemented and can use the heuristically found parameters as initial solution. Numerical search algorithms can then help solve this trade-off problem in an optimal way.

A “phenomenon” that some practitioners may not be well aware of, even due to the fact, that real-world systems cannot be used as lab-installations to modify parameter settings and reveal this interrelation.
In the future, more systematic search strategies for optimum parameters could be implemented and can use the heuristically found parameters as initial solution. Numerical search algorithms can then help solve this trade-off problem in an optimal way.

title: A Standard for Reliability Block Diagrams in SysML
authors: Myron Hecht, Aerospace Corporation; Tomas Juknevicius, Dassault Systèmes; Kyle Post, Ford Motor Company; Andrius Armonas, Dassault Systèmes; Key Words: SysML, Reliability Block Diagrams, RAAML, Standard, Object Management Group
summary:
This paper describes the Reliability Block Diagram capability in the Object Management Group (OMG) Risk Assessment and Analysis Modeling Language (RAAML) specification. The OMG is the standards organization that governs SysML. The RAAML 1.1 RBD method is an important step to achieving the goal of standardized interoperable integration of reliability engineering and Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) as well as with other analysis methods such as Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Failure Modes and Effects Analysis.  The benefits of this integration are identifying and addressing reliability requirements and engineering constraints from the early stages of system definition thereby producing better designs and more reliable systems. The use of standard cross-model and cross-vendor methods enables wider adoption and interoperability of models from multiple organizations involved in large scale projects.
Future enhancements to the method include more distributions, more system reliability/availability situations (e.g., Heterogeneous K-out-of-N and Markov models), and more sophisticated maintenance models.  Because reliability and life cycle costs are closely related, additional standard and methods to allow for interoperable evaluation and optimization of total ownership costs (i.e., both acquisition and sustainment costs) are possible.  If realized, such profiles would offer the decision makers in large scale projects to make better decisions earlier by means of MBSE.

title: A New View to Mission Profiles
authors: Horst Lewitschnig, PhD, Infineon Technologies Austria AG; Marcus Mayrhofer, TU Vienna; Peter Filzmoser, Prof., PhD, TU Vienna; Key Words: Functional Data Analysis, Mission Profile, Usage Profile
summary:
Mission profiles cover the conditions that a component, e.g., an electronic component of a vehicle, is exposed to during its lifecycle. Currently, these profiles typically provide descriptive summaries, such as histograms, of single stress parameters like temperature, humidity, or voltage.
This is highly aggregated information. New requirements for electric and autonomous driving cars require much more information how applications are used. In this work, we present a new approach for mission profiles which contains detailed usage information. We suggest a functional description over time, which allows joint modeling of various characteristics such as temperature, humidity, and voltage. The entire lifecycle history is covered, and the method can control the temporal resolution, i.e., the level of details of a mission profile. As a result, more accurate mission profiles can be generated, user quantiles can be derived, and usage outliers can be identified. This model establishes a framework to exchange usage data between suppliers, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), and end customers while data integrity and protection are assured.

title: Optimizing Operational Readiness of Complex Systems Previously Thought to Be Non-Optimizable
authors: Justin Woulfe, CTO, Systecon North America; Key Words: Operational Readiness, Onboard Spares Optimization, Multi-Variate Optimization, Dynamic Simulation, Non-Steady State Scenarios
summary:
Opus Evo is a cutting-edge tool designed to optimize the operational readiness of complex systems operating under non-steady-state conditions, which traditional steady-state models struggle to address. Opus Evo provides a robust solution for optimizing spares and maintenance resources in complex and variable operational scenarios by integrating advanced heuristic optimization techniques, dynamic simulation, and detailed reliability modeling. It overcomes the limitations of traditional models by capturing time-dependent variations and intricate component dependencies and adapting to changing operational conditions.
This paper explores the shortcomings of steady-state spares optimization models and demonstrates how Opus Evo addresses these challenges through its innovative features. It highlights the tool’s ability to balance operational effectiveness and cost, ensuring that spares strategies align with both mission requirements and budget constraints. A case study is presented to showcase the significant improvements in system performance and cost efficiency achievable with Opus Evo, underscoring its value in enhancing the readiness and resilience of complex systems in real-world environments.
conclusions:
Opus Evo represents a significant advancement in the field of spares optimization for complex systems operating under non-steady-state conditions. By integrating dynamic simulation with heuristic optimization techniques, Opus Evo overcomes the inherent limitations of traditional steady-state models. It provides a robust framework for accurately modeling and optimizing spares strategies in environments characterized by complex reliability structures, time-dependent failure rates, and fluctuating operational demands.
The tool's ability to simulate detailed interactions within complex reliability block diagrams, account for interdependent failures, and dynamically adjust spares provisioning based on real-time operational data ensures that system availability is maximized while adhering to budgetary constraints. Opus Evo’s advanced reliability modeling and high temporal resolution offer unparalleled insights into the long-term spares needs of systems, enabling proactive and adaptive planning that aligns closely with mission requirements.
Furthermore, Opus Evo's comprehensive cost and availability analysis empowers decision-makers to balance operational effectiveness with financial sustainability, identifying spares strategies that deliver optimal performance at the lowest possible cost. This approach not only enhances system reliability and reduces overall costs but also ensures sustained operational readiness across diverse and unpredictable scenarios.
The case study presented in this paper underscores the practical value of Opus Evo in real-world applications, demonstrating its capacity to deliver superior results compared to traditional methods. By embracing the capabilities of Opus Evo, organizations can achieve a new level of efficiency and resilience in their spares optimization processes, ultimately enhancing the readiness and performance of their complex systems in challenging operational environments.

title: Functional Requirement and User’s Needs for Food Serving Robots

title: Evaluating Success Conditions for Predictive Maintenance
authors: Paula Fischer, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, University of Stuttgart; Key Words: Predictive Maintenance, Parameters for PHM, Decision making, Maintenance strategies, RUL, Reliability
summary: The simulation study effectively demonstrates the feasibility of different maintenance strategies. The derivation of regression equations for all three maintenance strategies — reactive maintenance (RM), predictive maintenance (PM), and preventive maintenance (IM) — [1] provides valuable insights into the cost implications of each strategy across a wide range of parameter combinations. These regression equations enable calculating costs for each operational strategy based on various input parameters. It is, therefore, possible to calculate which operational strategy is likely to be the most cost-effective under the given conditions, providing clarity on whether the implementation of a predictive maintenance strategy can be successful. A case study shows that when using predictive maintenance with RUL (Remaining Useful Life) prediction, the prediction quantile that determines the maintenance timing should be chosen at a low level. It was also shown that, for certain cost ratios between predictive costs and reactive costs, the range within which predictive maintenance can work under given circumstances can be very narrow (or even nonexistent).
conclusions:
The parameter study indicates that the prediction quantile is an efficacious parameter for successfully implementing a predictive maintenance strategy. Predictive maintenance will not represent the most cost-effective operational strategy if the cost ratio to the prediction quantile ratio within a given application is unfavorable. For the specified parameter combination, it can be demonstrated that the lower the selected prediction quantile, the broader the cost ratio range within which predictive maintenance can be successful. In contrast, the median of the predicted failure times does not appear to be an effective quantile for determining the optimal maintenance time at the prediction point. It is, therefore, evident that considering the uncertainty of the predicted failure times is crucial in successfully establishing a predictive maintenance strategy within an enterprise. As the accuracy of failure time prediction increases, the loss of remaining useful life (RUL) at lower prediction quantiles is observed to decrease.
The regression models provide a framework for decision-making, enabling the selection of the most cost-effective maintenance strategy based on specific operational conditions and parameter values.

title: Feature Engineering Toolkit for Predictive Analytics in Engineering and Healthcare Informatics
authors: Haozhou Zhou, Northeastern University; Wei Li, Northeastern University; Srinivasan Radhakrishnan, PhD, Northeastern University; Sagar Kamarthi, PhD, Northeastern University; Key Words: Feature Extraction, Feature Learning, Condition-based Maintenance, Predictive Maintenance, Prognostics and Health Management
summary: This paper presents a feature engineering toolkit that includes complexity-based and recurrence-based feature extraction methods, along with dependency-focused and importance-focused feature selection methods. The toolkit is designed to extract information with predictive power from sensor data, thereby enhancing the capability of diagnostics, prognostics, and health management (PHM). Complexity-based features measure randomness and dynamic variations within the sensor data, while recurrence-based features identify recurring patterns. Dependency-focused and importance-focused feature selection methods improve model performance by identifying the most relevant features for given tasks. This paper demonstrates the toolkit on four applications: wind turbine bearing condition classification, hydraulic systems condition monitoring, CNC tool wear estimation, and respiratory health monitoring. The analytical results exhibit robust prediction accuracy and improved result explainability.
conclusions:
This paper presents a feature engineering toolkit, combining two feature extraction methods and two feature selection methods, and demonstrates their application on relevant real-world problems.
The results show that complexity-based feature extraction is effective for understanding structural complexity, in signals such as vibration signals from bearing structures, while recurrence plot-based extraction is better for analyzing chaotic, non-linear data in pattern recognition tasks, in applications like estimating tool wear in CNC machines. Dependency-focused feature selection is suited for datasets with relational structures, useful for mining conditional dependencies in high-dimensional spaces. In contrast, importance-focused selection works well for tabular data with many features, especially in predictive modeling, such as medical diagnosis. Future work will analyze the suitability of these feature extraction and selection methods for a variety of problems and investigate hybrid approaches that leverage the strengths of different techniques, such as combining recurrence plot-based feature extraction with dependency-focused feature selection to better handle time series data with complex relational structures.

title:
Comparative Study On Remaining Useful Life Prediction
Using Testing Data
authors: Alicia Auer, University of Wuppertal; Stefan Bracke, PhD, University of Wuppertal; Key Words: Remaining Useful Life (RUL), statistical data-based approaches, shape memory alloys, Prognostics
summary:
In this paper, a comparative study of Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction approaches is conducted using real data from life testing of cyclically stressed linear actuators made of shape memory alloys as an application example contributing to the understanding of forecasting methods in the testing phase.  Multivariate cycle data from long-term tests carried out experimentally in a test rig are given.  A failure threshold is determined as the base of operations for the RUL estimation based on the prognosis.
The focus is on statistical data-driven RUL prediction approaches, which, in contrast to modern machine learning (ML) methods, deliver 100% reproducible results.  The approaches linear and non-linear regression, methods of the ARIMA family (AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA), exponential smoothing, and Bagged model are applied.
These are the key findings of the study:
With linear, non-linear regression and ARIMA a reasonable RUL prediction was conducted.
Exponential smoothing and Bagged model were unsuitable for the RUL prediction in the given application example (overestimated RUL and failed forecasts).
The best result was achieved using linear regression (mean absolute error of 1,747 cycles in an average time series length of 9,900 cycles).
With regard to the results, it should be considered that some assumptions were made for the RUL prediction.  E.g., the determination of the failure threshold based on a correlation analysis or the boundary conditions set for the forecasts are to be respected as uncertainty factors.  In future work, an extension of the analyses using forecasting approaches for multivariate data sets (e.g. multiple regression, VARMA family or vector exponential smoothing) is planned.

title: Generative Twins: A Deep Learning Approach to Next-Gen Digital Twins
authors: Giuseppe Mannone, University of Stuttgart; Kim D. Hintz, University of Stuttgart; Martin Dazer, Dr.-Ing., University of Stuttgart; Key Words: Digital Twins, Deep Learning, Generative Adversarial Networks, Data Generation, Generative Twins.
summary: The generative twin model offers a significant enhancement to traditional digital twins, addressing key challenges such as scalability, real-time data processing and data generation in complex industrial systems. By integrating advanced generative algorithms like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), generative twins improve the generation of synthetic data, simulation accuracy, and data quality. GANs adversarial training, which involves a generator and a discriminator, refines data generation and enhances decision-making processes. This paper has explored the theoretical foundations and practical applications of these generative algorithms, highlighting advanced techniques such as Wasserstein GANs (WGANs) and Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) that enhance training stability and data quality. Additionally, we have demonstrated these concepts on real gear sensor data, showing the generative twin's ability to generate high-quality synthetic data and its potential for future steps in anomaly detection. The findings demonstrate that generative twins can provide robust solutions for industrial optimization and maintenance, making them a valuable tool for future technological advancements.

title: A Systemic Approach of Reliability Allocation in the Development of Multizone Well Completion
authors: Pankaj Shrivastava, Halliburton; Key Words: Reliability Allocation, Reliability Block Diagram, Well Completion, Feasibility of Objectives
summary:
Reliability allocation allows to assign failure rate or reliability target to different system units in the well solution. The simplest method of allocating reliability is ‘equal’ allocation which distributes reliability equally across all components. But that’s not an effective way to allocate reliability for a complex well solution. For developing an effective and systemic approach, reliability allocation methods were classified into two major categories – (a) weight factors-based approach, and (b) cost optimized methods. Weight factor-based approach involves subjective (or objective) assessments to estimate the allocation weight factors and failure rate of systems and subsystems. Whereas cost optimization method involves the use of mathematical programming techniques to estimate reliability allocation which minimizes system and/or development cost under constraints.
For well solution reliability modelling, a weight factor-based approach such as Feasibility of Objectives Reliability Allocation (FORA) method was determined to be effective. It’s based on the numerical ratings for the criteria related to subsystem design and operations such as system complexity, mission operating time, environment, mission criticality, etc. Ratings are typically based on engineering group’s experience and judgement. For every well system, these ratings are multiplied to get an overall rating and are normalized so that the sum is 1.
In the new product development for complex well solution, FORA method has certain benefits – (a) its criteria are related to subsystem design and operations, and (b) it can be applied at any level of system hierarchy i.e., systems, subsystems, failure mechanisms, etc. FORA technique was found to provide a structured and unbiased approach of reliability allocation for modelling well solution reliability requirements.
This paper highlights a successful application of FORA technique to model well solution reliability and determine reliability targets of well systems and subsystems. Key process steps involved in reliability allocation was (a) use of FORA technique to evaluate weight factors of all well systems, (b) develop well solution architecture for multi-zone completion, (c) develop reliability block diagram for well solution architecture and (d) use system weights to determine reliability targets.
The case study of multizone well development presented in this paper describes the effective use, challenges as well as lessons learned of applying FORA technique in achieving multizone well solution reliability targets.

title: Recommended Best Practices for Allocating Reliability/Availability Requirements
authors: Matthew W. Daniels, General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems; Key Words: Reliability Requirements, R&M Management, Allocations, Design Optimization
summary: This paper addresses how reliability allocations are performed for any design and includes best practices for most appropriately incorporating margin at various levels by accounting for the maturity of the design. Also discussed are more complex decomposition situations such as designs that include redundancy, duty cycles, and block redundancy across subsystem boundaries. Many potential pitfalls when allocating reliability and availability requirements are examined as well as their consequences, and techniques for avoiding them. Finally, the value of allocating requirements early in the project lifecycle is discussed and how this effort, when performed well, can help shape and optimize the design.

title: RelOps – Introduction to Reliable Operations
authors: Nemat Bidokhti, Bloom Energy; Key Words: Reliability, Operations, DevOps, Risk Management, Fault Management, AI
summary:
This paper discusses and introduces the concept of RelOps. It is the process of combining the Reliability New Product Introduction, design, development, deployment, and sustaining functions. Reliability does impact product development, here we are utilizing the DevOps model to establish a new approach to manage product reliability function. It must be noted that there are challenges in implementing RelOps since traditional reliability engineers and functions have not been organized and trained as such. What are some of the challenges of today’s product reliability functions that we want to address?
Lack of end-to-end product reliability visibility.
Siloed experiences.
Connection between key functions such as hardware, software, test, fault management, analytics among others.
Too much focus on failure prediction based on old data.
Difficult to scale due to various headcounts needed to cover the main activities.
Lack of domain knowledge by the data scientist.
RelOps is about multidisciplinary reliability team and enabling the culture of addressing multiple needs of reliability practices. What we mean by this, is the ability of the reliability engineer to cover multiple disciplines within the reliability team for a product. The challenge is to expand the reliability engineer’s capabilities and streamline the reliability activities associated with any product. We will discuss this in more detail later in this paper. Let’s breakdown this concept in such a way where we can define the functions, roles, and responsibilities. In a similar way as DevOps, we have the pipeline of building, testing, and releasing the products with planning and monitoring feedback loop. The key is how we break it down to make it feasible to implement. We are going to divide this subject into two main parts, reliability functional activities and skill development and requirements.
In this paper we discussed the concept of RelOps and what are the expectations of a RelOps engineer. Clearly, we need to rethink the role of reliability function and its engineers in the new paradigm where AI plays a big role in how products are designed and operated. As new technologies are developing the impact of RelOps engineers is becoming more pronounced. The data driven strategy is the way to ensure products are performing their intended functions for the length of time they are designed for.

title: A Decision-Theoretic Perspective of Maintenance Optimization of a Complex System
authors: Fahad Izhar Khan, University of Arizona; Allan T. Mense, University of Arizona; Key Words: Maintenance Optimization, Decision Theory, Risk Analysis
summary:
The purpose of this paper is to provide better formulation for maintenance optimization by considering all applicable non-monetary variables along with costs, uncertainty management of failure modes, logical redundancy and protections in the system and most importantly decision-maker preferences and risk attitudes as huge costs are involved in the maintenance of the whole system together. These considerations are important to manage the safety of operating plants under the given budgetary constraints. Though there are some assumptions as well as complications with the use of this method like failure of aggregation of multiple decision makers as per Arrow’s impossibility theorem, but elegant justification of risk-averse decision makers cannot be explained in such a simple manner by any other approach. As decision theory distinguish between the decision-making process and outcomes of the decision, decision-making should be judged by its conformity to principles of rationality, the validity of reasoning, and the clarity of the process, which are also the hallmark of the process mentioned.
However, there are still some serious challenges for decision theoretic framework which include consideration of expected value, valuation of life and dummy bet which no decision maker experiences in real life. The most important issue associated with decision-making process in practice is biases [15]. The decision-making process to manage the risks can become faulty when the decision-maker does not consider readily available options, fails to consider relevant constraints, or does not project consequences of the various courses of action. The decision makers are sometimes also overwhelmed by multiple objectives as company owners want maximization of profit and minimization of organizational liabilities while regulatory agencies demand that public safety should be the topmost priority. Market competition, company image, and sales requirements build another contextual dimension for decision-makers to complicate things. The communication language among stakeholders and decision-makers is money such that losses and profits are projected in monetary value. In this way, the system context is reduced to the profit maximization only. This is the point where the decision maker underestimates the risk, fails to simulate outcomes associated with various courses of action, and leads to the objectives related to the profits, dominating in the decision space. The perspective vision of the decision maker also plays an important role in achieving balanced targets. If a decision maker judges a long-term duration decision using short hindsight goals, then an unrealistic picture would appear in front of the decision maker which results in the removal of highly attractive alternatives. The issues like sustainability, environment, and safety require long-term goals and cannot be compared against other short-term objectives. Motivational biases are also implanted in people’s minds by the kind of treatment given to them. In the maintenance world, organizations reward people for heroic acts that are related to either an increase in production/revenue or reducing the interval of shutdown after a failure. This results in a general motivation among all to show monetary results by cost-cutting and adopting other shortcuts. Similarly, immediate reinforcement is more powerful than delayed reinforcement. Though doing timely planned investment is good, its results appear after a long time and the reward for decision-making is delayed. This biases the approach of the decision maker to use wrong assumptions during decision making process. What was explained for motivation to get reward can be related to fear of negative criticism i.e., being held responsible for the over-budget or bad financial health of the company. A major change that appears at this stage is that a decision maker who might be risk-averse may turn out to be a risk-taker due to his motivation and vision dilemma.  Any wrong assumption in preferences also aggravates the final ranking process as explained in an Allais Paradox, whereby individuals tend to place too much weight on a certain outcome as compared to uncertain outcomes. Impact of the safety and environment targets are uncertain in long term, and the postponement of investment benefits is obvious, the decision maker prefers the delay option as its expected utility is more than other options on the selected preference curve.
Though proper awareness and calibration techniques have been developed to guard against the biases in uncertainty elicitation and other motivational biases, there is still a need to model and quantify such behavioral errors in maintenance decision making. This would make the optimization process true representative of natural decision-making scenario and bring further realistic predictions of preventive maintenance interval.

Impact of the safety and environment targets are uncertain in long term, and the postponement of investment benefits is obvious, the decision maker prefers the delay option as its expected utility is more than other options on the selected preference curve.
Though proper awareness and calibration techniques have been developed to guard against the biases in uncertainty elicitation and other motivational biases, there is still a need to model and quantify such behavioral errors in maintenance decision making. This would make the optimization process true representative of natural decision-making scenario and bring further realistic predictions of preventive maintenance interval.

title: Human Reliability Analysis For Maintenance Operations: Phoenix Methodology And An Example Application
authors: Tingting Cheng, PhD, UCLA; Marilia A. Ramos, PhD, UCLA; Camila Correa-Jullian, UCLA; Ali Mosleh, PhD, UCLA; Key Words: Maintenance operation, Human reliability analysis, Human error assessment
summary:
In complex engineering systems, maintenance operations are vital for safety and system life cycle management, increasing the availability and reliability of equipment, instruments, and other elements. Human activities are a core ingredient of maintenance operations, which involve developing and following procedures and action plans to support installation, inspection, and repair tasks, among others. Human errors occurring during maintenance activities, such as installing or replacing a wrong part or assembling the part in the wrong sequence, can lead to severe accidents despite all technological enhancements and advanced organizational controls [1].
The majority of Human Reliability Analysis (HRA) methodologies to identify human error and estimate their probabilities have been developed for control-room operations in Nuclear Power Plants (NPPs). However, the nature of human activities in maintenance operations differs from control room operations and may even impact these considerably; hence, the modes and probabilities of potential errors by maintenance personnel require further investigation. The key steps are developing a general event sequence and tailoring a set of Performance Influencing Factors (PIFs) to adequately represent maintenance operators’ activities and their context. The Phoenix HRA methodology was developed to support NPPs risk studies and has been adapted across different industries, including oil & gas, aviation, power generation, and others [2-3]. This paper aims to extend the Phoenix methodology to identify and assess human errors focusing on maintenance operations and presents an example application.

title: Air Defense System-of-Systems: Reliability Concerns, Practices and Challenges
authors: Hava Avshalom, Israel Aerospace Industries; Grauer Emanuel, Israel Aerospace Industries; Tahar Effi, Israel Aerospace Industries; Key Words: Air Defense, Mission Critical Failures, MTBCF, System of Systems
summary: Military defense products are mission critical means to eliminate threats to citizens and strategic assets.  They are expected to operate for decades, under harsh environmental conditions, in different mission profiles.  Inevitably, the above characteristics are imperative for these products to be significantly reliable.  An Air Defense System (ADS) is a highly sophisticated System-of-Systems (SoS) built of fundamental elements, where each element may be considered an SoS in itself.  Achieving high reliability in ADS is a challenging task.  It starts in the early design stages, continues through production screening, testing and demonstration and ends with field monitoring.  This paper presents the major concerns regarding ADS reliability late activities, considers the limitations of qualification as against reliability demonstration, focusing on the interface between the seller and the customer. The use of MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) calculations is compared to that of MTBCF (Mean Time Between Critical Failures) calculations, and the effect of the repair policy on the MTBCF is discussed.  Besides specifying contractual reliability goals, both sides must establish a mutual effort to properly capture effective field data, demonstrate the reliability of the ADS, analyze field failures and initiate reliability growth processes if required.  These efforts are long term and require continuous cooperation, understanding the customer needs and the seller limitations.  Following each of these concerns, the paper presents best practice based on lessons learned, such as minimization of expected conflicts, by defining in advance, preferably in a Reliability Demonstration Plan (RDP), clear guidelines for failures classifications. Also, the best practice for data collection via FRACAS and field data analysis is indicated. Alternative methods to cope with these issues are also suggested.

title: Establishing Common Values in Design for Sustainability
authors: Joseph B. Kroculick, Winifred Connects; Key Words: Human-Centric, Industry 5.0, Human-Machine, Engineering Leadership, Education, Sustainability, Unified Architecture Framework, UAF, Architecture Development Method, Engineering Ethics, Human Sustainability Viewpoint
summary:
Sustainability is central to the engineering and manufacturing development (EMD) process and systems of systems such as complex electronics, software systems, and physical platforms. The DoD definition of sustainability typically signifies maintaining an operational capability as part of the sustainment function, which includes systems readiness [1] and supportability concepts [2] to enable a mission [3]. A sustainment concept accompanies each system to maintain its operations.
Sustainability can be approached from different perspectives, such as economic, environmental, and social. One popular perspective is the environmental dimension of doing business [4]. The U.S. DoD Sustainability Plan, which views sustainability as essential to ensuring the nation’s security, has adopted an environmental perspective in addition to managing the supply chain and resources for missions  [5] ￼.
Technical analysis is needed to support a system and implement sustainability requirements throughout its operational lifecycle. These requirements will be aligned with the system's intended usage and mission requirements, as well as an understanding of its behavior. The functionality and physics of systems must be understood to apply models that adjust performance and behavior adequately. Sustainability requirements may include readiness, supportability, and operations and should be interrelated and decomposed to achieve desired outcomes.
If environmental sustainability is an objective, associated technical analyses may need to be performed to understand physical processes’ impact on the environment. For example, manufacturing complex electronics is resource-intensive and can deplete resources such as land and air. Software systems control these systems and indirectly affect heat dissipation and power use. Software-intensive systems that involve data processing technologies offer opportunities to consider how sustainability requirements can be incorporated [6].
Establishing a shared vision is considered a core sustainability leadership practice [7]. Central to establishing a shared vision is achieving common values that can guide the engineering process in a multi-functional team. Establishing shared values also makes teams more effective [8]. This paper presents a conceptual architecture schema that can inform sustainability leadership practices. The desired outcome is to inform engineering leadership practices better to achieve the sustainable development goals (SDGs) that address planetary challenges for the benefit of society [9].
conclusions:
This paper motivated the use of values in defining sustainability processes. The values instilled by a leader and held by engineering practitioners will influence the I5.0 implementation and human-machine interactions. A key area of study is determining how engineering practitioners form sustainability values. A Human Sustainability Viewpoint that reflects the values and attitudes of Engineers toward an Organization's sustainability goals could be integrated and serve as a Systems Thinking model to establish a shared vision. Technical leaders can use this information to encourage consistent action in corporate sustainability strategies [61].
A human-sustainability viewpoint can represent sustainability values in designs. The view diagram includes a process to consult all stakeholders and discover unknown stakeholders who would supply requirements. It also proposed a model of individual learning and personnel change. This data should be added to the architecture of the manufacturing process. The individual’s understanding of a phenomenon affects how that person will consult other people. A mapping between values that can be established in a formative framework like Value System Design and mapped to an Enterprise Architecture represented in a modeling language such as UML [55].

title: Risk-Based Optimization of Periodic Maintenance for Power Grid Equipment
authors: Miguel Diago, PhD, Hydro-Québec; Xavier Lebeuf, Polytechnique Montréal; Toualith Jean-Marc Meango, PhD, Hydro-Québec; Alain Côté, PhD, Hydro-Québec; Claude Rajotte, PE, Hydro-Québec
summary:
Maintenance of electrical transmission equipment is key to ensure reliable power supply. Maintenance tasks are triggered by equipment failures (corrective maintenance), observed anomalies expected to lead to failures (condition-based maintenance), time (periodic preventive maintenance), or other factors. Periodic maintenance tasks are typically scheduled at fixed time intervals so degradation mechanisms can be detected and corrective measures applied as needed. Engineers generally choose these intervals based on their knowledge of failure mechanisms. In the context of electric power transmission systems, this should be a compromise considering at least equipment reliability, maintenance costs (for inspections, repairs, replacements and so forth), value of lost load (VoLL) and other risks inherent in power transmission (environmental, health, safety and so forth).
Herein, an asset behaviour model, an event stochastic simulator, a power-flow simulator, and a risk model with a VoLL estimator are combined to quantify the total cost of periodic maintenance strategies. A blackbox optimization solver is then used to search for periodic maintenance strategies that minimize costs within specified constraints. As the event simulator uses a Monte Carlo method to output grid states where equipment fails according to preset statistical distributions, the problem is non-deterministic. However, timely and meaningful results can be obtained by adjusting the number of Monte Carlo cycles as well as the length of the timespan simulated and other parameters. This opens the way for multi-fidelity optimization, where these parameters are automatically adjusted during optimization. Ultimately, engineers may use this approach to select optimal periodic maintenance schedules that minimize the global risk for the system operator. The procedure is implemented with NOMAD (Nonlinear Optimization by Mesh Adaptive Direct Search), an open-source blackbox optimizer.
conclusions:
The method described in this study can help decision makers determine and update periodic maintenance schedules. Modules for estimating the impacts of prospective maintenance schedules on asset reliability and on energy not supplied and its cost are described as well as a blackbox optimization method for an efficient search for optimal schedules.
Our next step will be to use the method to update the maintenance schedules of a large set of asset types. Blackbox optimization will be conducted on a large number of variables, and evaluation times will increase significantly. To minimize the number of unique cases fed to the power-flow simulator, strategies are under development to dynamically adjust the number of Monte Carlo cycles on each call to the stochastic simulator or interrupt the blackbox evaluation altogether before calling the power-flow simulator [19]. Parallel computing enhancements to the NOMAD algorithm, such as the parallel space decomposition variant of MADS (PSD-MADS) [20] or early evaluation of points likely to appear in future iterations [21], are under consideration to manage high-dimensional blackbox problems that will be encountered.

title: Predictive Maintenance for Smart Buildings: Balancing QoS and Cost Efficiency
authors: Anas Hossini, Paris Saclay University; Leïla Kloul, Paris Saclay University; Maël Guiraud, Paris Saclay University; Benjamin Cohen Boulakia, Paris Saclay University; Key Words: Smart Building, System of Systems, Predictive Maintenance, Reinforcement Learning
summary: The rapid advancement of sensing technologies and connectivity has revolutionized predictive maintenance (PdM), particularly for smart buildings (SB). Despite these advancements, implementing data-driven approaches faces challenges, mainly due to scarce failure data and the SB systems complexity. In this paper, we propose a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) based approach to address these challenges in which each agent is responsible for maintaining one subsystem. As a case study, we consider three subsystems within the SB: lighting, network, and IT. The network subsystem ensures power supply, while the IT subsystem controls and shares data. The proposed approach enables the design of comprehensive maintenance decision processes that minimize maintenance costs for these subsystems while satisfying their quality of service (QoS) standards. Our approach's advantage lies in its ability to ensure the effective operation of each SB subsystem and the SB itself, even with limited data. Moreover, the proposed approach is adaptative according to the operating conditions of each SB subsystem.

title: Queueing Theory-Based Spare Parts Prediction Through Machine Learning
authors: Hongzhou Wang, PhD, RTX; Brian Hart, RTX; Key Words: Spare Parts; Machine Learning; Queueing theory; Maintenance Models; Repairable Systems; Life Data Analysis; Digital Engineering
summary:
Wang and Hart [1] introduced a new spare parts prediction model based on the Erlang C queueing model under general conditions including intermittent uses, that overcomes the drawback in the existing models in which if spares demand cannot be fulfilled it may be lost. The Erlang C model permits infinite spare parts requests and no spares demand is lost. So the Erlang C model is the best in theory. This paper first studies spares prediction via the Erlang B queueing model where only limited spares requests are allowed at any time. Then it compares the spares estimation results of the Erlang C, Erlang B, and Poisson process models. The numerical comparison verifies that the Erlang B and Poisson process models may underestimate spares as compared with the Erlang C model. A software tool has been developed to facilitate computing and comparison of these spares prediction models.
Machine learning is then used in the Erlang C queueing model-based spares prediction model in this paper. Unlike other machine learning-based spares prediction methods, which deal with time series data in nature and forecast spares directly, this paper uses machine learning to estimate parameters of the queueing theory-based spares prediction models. This is advantageous in situations where the installed bases are different or historical spare parts data are not available, thereby constraining the utility of time series forecasting models. Data preprocessing, feature engineering, training and test data, variable importance, performance of different machine learning algorithms including gradient boosting, random forest, deep learning, and stacked ensemble modeling are discussed. Our ultimate goal is to build an accurate artificial intelligence/machine learning spares prediction system.

title: Large Language Models Maintenance Approach for Commercial/Fleets
authors: Lukmon Rasaq, North Carolina A&T State University; Om Prakash Yadav, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Madhuri Siddula, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Rhonda Walthall, Collins Aerospace Systems; Key Words: Airworthiness Directives, Large Language Model, Finetuning, PEFT, AviationQA, Retrieval Augmented Generation, Boeing 767, LoRA
summary:
This paper presents a Large Language Model (LLM) framework to assess and map each failure mechanism and failure mode of individual Airworthiness Directives (ADs) available in the historical dataset. In addition, this framework can provide insights into related maintenance procedures and practices to help maintenance crews react faster and more effectively.
Commercial and military regulators ensure the performance and protection of the aircraft by investigating and mitigating aircraft system failures through Airworthiness Directives (ADs). ADs, which delineate the total cost impact on operators, are imparted by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and United States Airforce (USAF). For example, the Boeing 767 (B767) and its military derivative, USAF’s KC-46A dataset provide an understanding of failure mechanisms and related maintenance practices that may mitigate these costs.
Additionally, AviationQA dataset was also used in this research work to finetune the LLMs. As compared to the B767 ADs historical dataset, this dataset is large as it contained about 1 million records in the training set.
To facilitate faster extraction of maintenance-related information and ensure the reliability/accuracy of the information extracted, we proposed the use of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approach. As a result, this framework will help the maintenance crews promptly resolve any symptoms of failure.
Essentially, two LLMs which include Mistral 7b instruct model and Facebook Llama-2-7b-chat-hf, were finetuned individually. However, the result obtained shows that Mistral 7b outperformed the Llama-2-7b-chat-hf model on the ADs historical dataset and AviationQA dataset. Consequently, the Mistral 7b instruct model is used in the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework.
conclusions:
This paper proposed a Large Language Model (LLM) maintenance method for commercial aircraft that maps the failure mechanism of each ADs to their corresponding failure mode in the historical dataset. Furthermore, from the experiment, it was observed that the mistral 7b instruct model outperformed Llama-2-7b-chat-hf in both datasets and as a result, the mistral 7b instruct model is then used in the RAG framework. Additionally, given any failure mode, this framework provides the root causes of the failure, and the location where the failure occurs and extracts the most suitable maintenance action and procedure from the AD documents to the maintenance crews. Furthermore, it shows that the higher the training set the better the accuracy of the LLMs. However, finetuning LLM on a larger dataset is computationally intensive. As a result, one would need higher system resources which could serve as a roadblock for some organizations that do not have higher GPU machines. However, the RAG framework is less computationally intensive, and it is also good for when you have new information to retrieve from a big document. Therefore, human lives are very important; we need prompt ways of identifying failure, causes of failure, location where the failure occurs, and maintenance procedure to mitigate the failure.
Future research work is planned to get more ADs historical datasets, more computational resources, further tuning the hyperparameters, use other finetuning approaches to get good accuracy, use RAG to add more functionality to the finetuned model, and connect the RAG framework to the ADs database.

title: Optimizing RAMS with DES using Operational Data for Enhanced Maintenance
authors: Rahul Gottumukkala, PHM Technology; Deepak Tripathy, PHM Technology; Jono Jarvis, PHM Technology; Chris Stecki, PHM Technology; Key Words: Digital Risk Twin, Model-based RAMS, Discrete Event Simulation, DES, Maintenance Optimization
summary:
This paper presents a comprehensive approach to Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Safety (RAMS) analysis through the development of a Digital Risk Twin (DRT) and the application of Discrete Event Simulation (DES) for optimizing maintenance strategies. The research focuses on modeling the DRT of a generic aircraft, emphasizing subsystems such as the Airframe, Control System, and Powerplant. By defining functional dependencies and interactions within these subsystems, the DRT provides a detailed representation of system behavior, facilitating accurate RAMS analysis.
The implementation of Reliability-Centered Maintenance (RCM) during the early stages ensures the establishment of effective maintenance strategies. These strategies are dynamically updated based on real-time operational data and environmental conditions. The integration of DES within this framework allows for the evaluation of various scenarios, providing insights into the impact of maintenance strategies on key performance indicators (KPIs) such as reliability, availability, and cost.
The case study demonstrates the application of the DRT and DES to an aircraft system, highlighting the significance of breakdown and scheduled maintenance strategies. The DES model simulates the impact of different maintenance intervals on system performance, offering a robust tool for optimizing maintenance activities. The results are presented as a Pareto front, enabling users to identify the optimal balance between cost and downtime for different maintenance strategies.
Future work will focus on incorporating sensitivity analysis into the DES model, allowing users to understand the interactions between input parameters and their impact on KPIs. Additionally, redefining reliability metrics, such as introducing the "Number of Unexpected Failures," will provide more meaningful insights over extended operational periods. These enhancements will offer deeper insights into system performance, aiding in the continuous improvement of maintenance strategies.
In conclusion, the model-based RAMS approach utilizing DRT and DES provides a powerful framework for enhancing system design and maintenance strategies. By continuously integrating real-time data and simulating various scenarios, this approach ensures a responsive and effective maintenance strategy, ultimately improving system reliability, availability, and cost-effectiveness throughout the lifecycle.
