title: Contingency Assessment Based on Cost and Schedule Planning
authors: Paul Franklin, McKissack and McKissack; Key Words: final paper preparation, format instructions, RAMS Proceedings
summary:
Contingency represents an estimate of the management reserves for cost, schedule, and other resources needed to complete a project.
Schedule and cost estimates have three common components that contribute to differences between planned requirements and actual performance.  They include:
Variation inherent in the estimating procedures used
Changes in scope
External events that impact performance
Cost estimates also vary due to changes in prices over time.  This is commonly called escalation or inflation.  Commonly, escalation varies based on the particular commodity being used and indices like the PPI are generally only rough guides.
It is possible to estimate the magnitude of these differences, and to include allowances for them even while a project is being planned.  It is also possible to update these estimates over the life of a project to project estimated resource needs to completion.
This paper will describe a three component model for schedule contingency estimation and a four component model for cost.
Examples are included to illustrate each component as well as the updating process to illustrate how this model can be used to support a learning approach to managing contingency.
conclusions:
This paper has proposed a simple model to estimate the necessary cost and schedule contingency at various stages of a project’s life cycle. This model is straightforward, and it uses data that the organizational governance process can produce.
This allows leadership to use a data-driven approach to estimating contingencies and updating them as the project advances.

title: Reliability Test Monitoring: Detection of Time-to-Failure With Specific Instrumentation
authors: Marco Bonato, PhD, Valeo Power; Arnaud Maire, MSc, Valeo Power; Key Words: Failure detection, automotive, Heat Exchangers, Reliability, Physical Measurements.
summary:
The experimental design validation of automotive components is carried out on testing facilities that verify the mechanical resistance under various types of stresses such as vibration, thermal shock, cyclic pressure, etc…  The components must endure for a period of time specified by customers, expressed in hours or number of cycles, which represents an equivalent lifetime of the vehicle. If the product exhibits functional failure before completing the test duration, its design requires modification.  It is therefore essential to identify the failure zone and to provide an accurate estimation of the time-to-failure.  Some of these tests can be lengthy, and potential failures might occur during off-hours, such as night or weekends, when no lab technician is present to detect them.  As a consequence, in these cases, the exact time of the precise failure time is not known.  Moreover, when several failures are observed afterwards, it is difficult to conclude which failure occurred first, and due to the weakening of the assembly, it may lead to further failures.  The authors (reliability practitioners working for an automotive Tier 1 supplier) have developed several customized instrumentation techniques that enable the test to be stopped at the first indication of failure.   The methods primarily rely on continuously measuring a “physical indicator”, which could be a variable such as a displacement, a pressure, or current, closely associated with the loss of function in the component.  Once this value exceeds a predefined threshold, the test can be automatically stopped and submitted to the control of an operator when available.   Alternatively, even if the validation test continues, the recording of the failure time can be extrapolated from the measurements.  The exact knowledge of the failure mechanism and time-to-failure is essential for an accurate estimation of the durability of the component undergoing validation.  Given the diverse nature of tests, various detection techniques have been devised, tailored to address the failure mechanisms (fatigue, wear out) and the nature of the failure component (mechanical, electrical, mechatronic).
This paper will present several real-world instances of instrumentation employed in the validation process of the products from the authors’ company, specifically heat exchangers, throughout accelerated validation tests. The objective is to precisely measure the time when the initial failure occurs, therefore enabling more realistic reliability predictions.
conclusions:
This project was very useful to point out:
1)	The importance of testing the part in its real environment during the design validation phase
2)	The importance of measuring the dynamic response of the component under investigation
Figure 1. Water cooled intercooled rigidly fixed (without brackets) on vibration shaker.
The same method was found to be useful during a research project dealing with fatigue of short fiber polymer specimens [7].  The failure time was recorded thanks to real time measurements. The shift in the first natural frequency could be used as an indicator of the incoming failure (crack propagation until rupture of the specimen), together with an increase of the damping ratio (decrease of the stiffness), and used to predict the failure time for specimens with different fibers orientations.

title: PrivateAIDELPHI: Adopting and Adapting Private AI for Risk Assessment of Safety Critical Systems
authors: Nikolaos Papakonstantinou, Fortum Power and Heat Oy; Douglas Van Bossuyt, Naval Postgraduate School; Ryan Bell, Naval Postgraduate School; Ryan Longshore Naval Postgraduate School; Mika Heikkilä, Fortum Power and Heat Oy
summary:
Recent advancements in generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) have produced tools able to convincingly answer questions and instruct humans through complex tasks. This is achieved after a computationally intensive training based on a large set of documents. Although the results can be impressive, there are cases of problematic responses. Even though there is significant motivation and interest to introduce these kind of AI tools in safety engineering processes, it is recognized that this needs to be done carefully and with human experts in control. Additionally, it is common that system design information is sensitive and cannot be shared with cloud-based AI platforms.
The PrivateAIDELPHI method presented in this paper introduces “AI experts” in early risk identification and scoring for complex safety critical systems. It extends the established Delphi iterative method for reducing subjectivity and reaching consensus among experts. These AI experts are enabled by tools that can be hosted locally and without a connection to the Internet.
The benefit of introducing AI experts, with the current technology is the potential to get different perspectives and trigger/inspire human experts to expand their view.
The basic steps of the PrivateAIDELPHI are the definition of the questions to be answered, the preparation of the background information material and then the collaboration of human and AI experts on the identification and scoring of risks. The method includes sanity checks by humans on the AI-generated answers as well as the fact that the final risk prioritization step involves only humans. Practically the AI with its answers is used to expand the thought horizon of the human experts and not to just provide an answer.
Although the PrivateAIDELPHI is designed to operate using confidential data (system design and background information), for practical reasons it was demonstrated in this paper using public information on the NuScale Small Modular Reactor (SMR) design and a small set of relevant public documents giving background on nuclear system risks. Four AI models (three that can be considered private/local and ChatGPT) were used, this case study did not experiment on the optimization of the LLMs and the results are not to be seen as a comparison/benchmark of the different AI models (between them or against humans).
The integration of human and AI experts in the limited NuScale case study showed that the AI can bring valuable input to the group of experts tasked with risk identification and prioritization, thus it was successful. While not being able to express risks in a systematic manner (the AI results can be seen more like talking points - food for thought) the integration of AI experts together with humans does enhance the risk assessment process. It is very important to highlight that humans are in control and finally responsible for the final results.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Failure Mode Identification from Warranty Data
authors: Prerna Awasthi, PhD, CNH; Mathew Thomas, PhD, CNH; Dinesh Junghare, CNH; Massimo Bianco, CNH; Key Words: Machine Learning , Natural Language Processing, Knowledge Management, Failure Effects, Failure Modes
summary:
Warranty reporting system is a goldmine of data on issues reported by customers regarding product problems. Having a customer and dealer feedback allows the OEMs to gather valuable insights from regarding product performance and issues. By systematically storing and analyzing the dealer comments, an OEM can identify recurring problems, understand failure modes, and enhance product reliability. This data-driven approach not only helps in improving product design and quality but also strengthens the commitment to customer satisfaction and continuous improvement.
This paper presents a machine learning-based approach to identify Failure Modes from warranty data. Warranty data, a rich source of information, is often underutilized due to its unstructured nature. Our approach leverages natural language processing (NLP) and supervised learning techniques to analyze warranty claims, identifying common failure modes and their associated effects and causes specifically for systems, sub systems and components. By preprocessing text data and employing Machine Learning algorithms, we extract meaningful patterns and insights. Our results demonstrate that ML can significantly reduce the time and effort required for warranty data analysis, leading to improved insights on product reliability and customer satisfaction.
By leveraging natural language processing (NLP) and supervised learning techniques, the approach outlined in the paper enhances the identification of failure modes, particularly for systems, subsystems, and components. As noted, the superior performance of the Support Vector Classifier (SVC) model, especially in System 4, highlights its accuracy and reliability in classifying dealer comments. This indicates that the choice of ML algorithm plays a crucial role in achieving precise and effective results.
The “RESULTS” section provides concrete evidence of the accuracy improvements achieved by SVC, which outperformed other algorithms like Random Forest, Naive Bayes, and Logistic Regression as depicted in Figure 3, showcasing comparative analysis of the accuracy achieved by different machine learning models across six systems. For instance, System 4 achieved the highest accuracy of 83.2%, which underscores SVC’s strength in handling structured datasets derived from unstructured warranty data. This data transformation is essential, as it allows the ML models to process and categorize the complex information within dealer comments more efficiently.
In conclusion, the application of ML significantly reduces the time and effort required for warranty data analysis, delivering critical insights into product reliability and customer satisfaction. The findings support the importance of proper data structuring and algorithm selection, with SVC emerging as a key tool in achieving optimal results in warranty claim analysis.

title: Graph Neural Networks and Fault Tree Analysis for Runtime Dynamic Risk Assessment of Autonomous Systems
authors: Joachim Grimstad, University of Stuttgart; Andrey Morozov, University of Stuttgart; Key Words: Quantitative Risk Assessment, Fault Tree Analysis, Graph Neural Networks, Autonomous Systems
summary:
To our knowledge, this paper offers two novel contributions in this field. First, it addresses the need for runtime dynamic risk assessment in autonomous systems by proposing a framework that enables continuous risk evaluation in complex and dynamic environments at runtime. This framework uses dynamic and inductive graph neural network methods that update and predict during runtime to reflect changes in the environment and can process large amounts of data efficiently. Secondly, it integrates traditional quantitative risk models, to introduce some degree of explainability of the graph neural network by converting the graph into traditional models such as fault trees. The second contribution is the partial proof-of-concept of the proposed concept by training a graph attention network to predict top event probabilities of simple fault trees represented as graphs. The implementation tries simple off-the-shelf algorithms but conducts some initial experimentation with loss functions, dropout layers, and distribution shifted datasets to evaluate the generalization capability of the models.
Initial results show promise, demonstrating the potential of using GATs to predict top event probabilities in fault tree analysis. Future research should focus on optimizing dropout probabilities, expanding datasets, and exploring hyperparameter optimization. Additionally, investigating the necessary node features and subdividing graphs for better model handling are key areas for further exploration. Additionally, other methods such as GraphSAGE might be more suitable, and a comparison should be made. This work paves the way for integrating advanced machine learning techniques with traditional risk assessment methodologies, contributing to the development of safer, more reliable, and partially explainable autonomous systems.
conclusions:
As autonomous systems spread across various domains, there is a need for methods that can handle all operational contexts, adapt to rapidly changing situations, and provide some degree of explainability. This paper introduces the novel concept of maintaining graphs for quantifying risks and GNN techniques to solve or update them for RDRA of autonomous systems.
The concept is partially demonstrated by using a GNN model (GAT) to predict the outcome of a QRA model (FT). This is as far as we know, a novelty unto itself.
Initial results show promise for using GATs to solve top event probabilities in FTA. The findings suggest that training GATs with Huber loss generally yields better performance, while the MSE-trained model with dropout performed best on OOD data. Further research should explore different dropout probabilities, more diverse datasets, and extensive hyperparameter optimization to achieve better results. Additionally, determining which node features are required or most impactful in relation to computational resources remains an open question, as all node features must be calculated for the graph before predicting the top event probability. This presents a trade-off between prediction time and accuracy that could be optimized. Poor generalization can be mitigated by models with good prediction times and accuracy by subdividing the graph into smaller graphs or structures that the model handles exceptionally well. This subdivision could be achieved using other GNN methods, representing another interesting direction for future research.
There are numerous additional directions for future research, extending to more complex FT paradigms such as Dynamic Fault Trees (DFT), incorporating statistical and structural dependencies, addressing uncertainties, or potentially Training models using GraphSAGE framework. Exploring methods with different target features, such as identifying MCSs or node importance, can also provide valuable insights.
While there remains considerable skepticism about AI within the safety community, this caution is not necessarily shared by everyone developing these systems. It is crucial to make a concerted effort to develop methods that can evaluate risk and maintain safety, while also providing some degree of explainability. Although a certain level of skepticism is warranted, it is important to note that partially demonstrated concept demonstrated in this paper is conceptually similar to existing techniques for calculating top events, where MCSs are ranked and unimportant ones are discarded for computational expediency.
keywords: safety, FTA, risk assessment, machine learning, AI

title: Use Cases for AI in Reliability and Maintainability
authors: David A. Nelson, Andromeda Systems Incorporated; Key Words: Asset Reliability, Maintainability, R&M, Use Cases, AI.
summary:
This paper explores writing a use case for applying AI to support asset reliability and maintainability. The primary concentration is on establishing a system description, defining actors, and outlining objectives. Use cases when applied in systems engineering or other contexts are a valuable tool for describing with clarity the different ways actors (i.e., users) will interact with a system and what constitutes success resulting from those interactions. AI is a complex technology requiring subject matter experts in the field. Most organizations will not have sufficient capability to apply AI without some outside assistance. It is unrealistic to assume that outside assistance, though skilled in AI, will have a working knowledge of your industry. A use case brings together the skill and knowledge of AI experts with the skill and knowledge of your organization and its operations into a common framework.
Writing a use case is a multistep process. System function and system interaction are logically connected. Use cases applied to complex systems will be hierarchical to mirror those connections. This results in a compilation of use cases at multiple levels and with connections to multiple actors. Each actor typically has multiple objectives, some common with other actors and some unique to individual actors. Objectives are often intertwined with multiple linkages across different actors. In most organizations that use assets to provide a product, service, or perform a mission there are groups and departments with specific focus areas that relate to each other but do not have a detailed understanding of what each other do and what it take to be successful. Exploring all the steps of writing a use case for applying AI in R&M will require more writing space and time than the constraints of this paper and conference will allow. The exploration will be confined to the first three steps: 1) system description; 2) identifying actors; and 3) defining the goals and objectives for each actor. These three steps are foundational in uncovering the information needed to outline all the ways in which AI can provide valuable capability to enhance use of R&M data to elevate an organization’s performance.
Reliability and Maintainability (R&M) touches all aspects of management, operations, and maintenance in organizations that use physical assets to produce products, provide services, or perform missions. Asset reliability is needed for operations to perform their function. It is also the purpose of maintenance to sustain and restore reliability efficiently so downtime is minimized. Finally, management needs asset reliability to meet the organization’s commitments and realize success. R&M is a data driven undertaking. AI is a major turning point in all technical fields going beyond what is considered evolutionary progress into what most will agree is a true revolution in how data can be used in detecting, defining, and clarify problems then ultimately deriving and evaluating solutions. Making the effort to compile use cases for all the actors (any group within the organization who will interact with the AI technology or its outcome) prior to stepping into an arrangement with AI professionals to implement AI in your organization will increase probability of success. It is the simplest and oldest intention when communicating between individuals or groups to clearly state in easy-to-understand terms what is expected and what is the end goal. The use case is purposefully designed as a means for the provider to understand what the customer expects.

title: Bayesian Model of Risk Informed Scheduling
authors: Geoffrey Berlin, PhD, McKissack and McKissack; Paul Franklin, McKissack and McKissack; Key Words: Bayesian Statistics, Predictive Analytics, Statistical Inference
summary:
The Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority (MARTA) is presently engaged in an aggressive program to upgrade the appearance and functionality of its heavy rail stations. Often this work is done on the weekends and during the night to minimize the inconvenience to passengers. To shut down a particular section of track requires a six-week advance request to permit the necessary arrangements for flaggers, staging of materials and equipment, and coordination with adjacent stations. Not receiving the requested track allocation can delay projects by many months and thereby increasing project costs.
The goal of this effort is to assist the Track Allocation group in assessing of the likelihood that contractors will be prepared to take advantage of their assigned “track time” by using as much information about expected contractor performance as possible. Firstly, this risk assessment reflects the natural variability of construction projects in addition to other circumstances. These circumstances may reflect last minute cancellations of track requests for any number of reasons including unavailability of flaggers in addition to emergency maintenance. Secondly, anticipated contractor performance is included employing the Bayes Rule to improve the risk assessment.
The proposed Bayesian analysis combines statistical estimates of anticipated contractor performance for completing preparatory tasks. As these tasks are completed the likelihood of success is updated, and thus, improving the accuracy of the risk assessment and confidence in using allocated track time.
conclusions: This paper has demonstrated a practical application of Bayesian methods to scheduling.  This result can be applied to any situation where there is a gating action, that is, an action or event must complete before another action can start.  This has significant value for risk management when the successor event easily changed. It must be recognized that the probabilities could be used to downgrade the expectations. It is also important to recognize the application of the Bayesian interpretation is just as application to analysis of the portion of the schedule as to the entire schedule.

title: Common Mistakes in Analyzing Reliability Data
authors: John Healy, Consultant; Key Words: Life Data Analysis, Stress-Strength Models, Poisson Regression
summary:
This paper will describe a number of common mistakes in analyzing reliability data. These mistakes occur quite often. Some of the mistakes could result in improper conclusions from the data while others provide an erroneous interpretation of the problem at hand.
The first mistake arises when zeroes are not included:
The second mistake arises when graphs of strength/stress models shade areas under the curve.
The third mistake arises when simple metrics are used and censoring of data is ignored.
The fourth mistake arises when trends are eyeballed and linear regression is improperly applied.
conclusions: This paper has provided a description of several common mistakes in the analysis and interpretation of reliability data. These mistakes are not the only mistakes that are commonly found. Several others include improper extrapolating of various reliability models, over parameterizing data models, not using covariates in models, improper consideration of outliers, ignoring past information, simulating models that are easy to analyze directly, graphing data with reduced scales that magnify tiny trends – lying with statistics, etc. We do believe these four mistakes can easily be corrected with the proper analysis of reliability data.

title: Defining Minimum Fleet Flight Hour Reliability Limit for a DOD Aircraft Program
authors: James F. Wasko, Bell Textron Inc.; Gerardo E. Burciaga, Bell Textron Inc.; Key Words: Reliability, RCM, Binomial Distribution, Acquisition Program
summary:
All Department of Defense (DOD) aircraft acquisition programs assess well-defined Reliability and Maintainability (R&M) Technical Performance Measures (TPMs) during the design phase. Mean Time Between System Abort, Mean Time Between Failure, or Mean Time To Repair are examples of R&M TPMs. While R&M TPMs can be calculated in the early design phase, only time will tell whether early R&M TPM predictions are valid. The timeframe for validating the R&M TPM predictions is not well defined. However, over the aircraft program lifecycle, R&M TPM assessments will mature.  A certain number of fleet flight hours is needed to confirm previously calculated R&M TPM predictions.
A method to calculate the Minimum number of Fleet Flight Hours (MFFH) for R&M TPM maturity is proposed with the goal of documenting the method and validating the calculated value. Although MFFH is not a currently utilized R&M metric, the proposed method aims to define a point in time when the R&M engineer can substantiate R&M TPM values based on total flight hours flown by the aircraft fleet. Utilizing the proposed method can also determine an aircraft program MFFH early in program development before an aircraft is built or flown. Determining the MFFH for R&M TPM maturity early in the planning and design stages helps to manage expectations once initial field data begins to be collected.
A documented method for calculating R&M TPM maturity adds value to aircraft program R&M metrics by clarifying a topic that is prone to high levels of scrutiny.  Initial flight hours may incur significantly misleading R&M TPM values while the crew and maintainers go through learning curves or experience malfunctions for the first time and mitigations have not been developed. Socializing the MFFH R&M TPM maturity point can drive wider aircraft program understanding of R&M TPMs and provide guidance to the program regarding timelines needed to properly assess early R&M TPM predictions.

title: Reliability and Mission Engineering: Improving Mission Success
authors: Justin Brown, Bell Textron Inc.; Key Words: Reliability, Digital Engineering
summary: Mission engineering and reliability engineering are systems engineering disciplines used throughout product development and sustainment of a system. This paper highlights the commonalities and differences between the two disciplines of mission and reliability engineering. Mission engineering generally lacks standardization and precision of analysis due to less guidance documentation, uncertainty, and data limitations. Reliability analysis can improve the results of mission engineering analysis and thus, should be embedded within mission engineering. A recommendation is to include reliability as a component of the system Measures of Success (MOSs), Measures of Effectiveness (MOEs), and Measures of Performance (MOPs).  Additional recommendations are centered around how reliability is represented in a mission engineering architecture and determining a logical approach to improve mission engineering decision capability and outcomes. Conclusions focus on an integrated approach to measuring system and mission effectiveness throughout system design and sustainment.
conclusions:
In conclusion, mission engineering and reliability engineering, while distinct disciplines, share a common goal of ensuring system success and directly impacting MOSs, MOEs, and MOPs. Their complementary strengths, when used together, offer significant improvements in system design, evaluation, and management. By fostering collaboration, incorporating diverse metrics, and leveraging each other's insights, these disciplines can collectively enhance mission effectiveness, system reliability, and overall SoS success. As technology and operational environments evolve, the continued synergy between mission engineering and reliability engineering will remain crucial for tackling the complex challenges of modern systems and SoS in an ever-changing landscape.

title: Reliability Growth Modeling and Testing
authors: Harry W. Jones, Ph.D., NASA Ames Research Center; Key Words: reliability growth, reliability growth modeling
summary:
Reliability growth has been modelled as an exponential decline in the cumulative failure rate that continues indefinitely as long as testing continues.  Contrary to this, most reliability growth data show a brief high initial failure rate due to infant mortality followed by a long period of constant low failure rate.  A two part failure rate model with an initial exponential decline followed by a constant failure rate usually fits the data and provides a more realistic description of reliability growth.  The reliability growth process consists of testing, experiencing failures, finding the failure causes, and redesigning the system to remove them.  The cost of reliability growth increases with the number of inherent failure modes and the time needed for them to occur and be removed.  The failure modes with the lower failure rates will tend to occur later, because their Mean Time Before Failure (MTBF) is the inverse of the failure rate.  Reliability growth testing has diminishing returns, since it takes longer to find and remove the less probable failures.
This paper first discusses the reliability bathtub curve and then explains that reliability growth is produced by testing, identifying failure causes, and designing to remove them.  A simple model of reliability growth is introduced, with a brief group of early failures followed by a constant failure rate.  The cumulative failure rate n(t)/t can decline as rapidly as 1/t or t-1 but declines more slowly if additional failures occur.  The 56-failure Crow data set is used to demonstrate the two-phase model of reliability growth followed by a constant failure rate.  13 additional data sets are modeled, with 9 of the 14 data sets showing reliability growth approximately as n(t)/t = 1/t or t-1 and substantial final failure rates.  The model fits most of the data sets, but 4 of the 14 show no reliability growth.  The reliability growth period typically includes six failures and extends to one-quarter or half the total test time.  As reliability growth testing continues, the cumulative failure rate should be tracked to estimate the reliability growth exponent and the final failure rate.

The 56-failure Crow data set is used to demonstrate the two-phase model of reliability growth followed by a constant failure rate.  13 additional data sets are modeled, with 9 of the 14 data sets showing reliability growth approximately as n(t)/t = 1/t or t-1 and substantial final failure rates.  The model fits most of the data sets, but 4 of the 14 show no reliability growth.  The reliability growth period typically includes six failures and extends to one-quarter or half the total test time.  As reliability growth testing continues, the cumulative failure rate should be tracked to estimate the reliability growth exponent and the final failure rate.

title: Supporting R&M in MBSE Development: Lessons Learned in Vertical Lift Platforms
authors: Heather Shar, PE, Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation; Dainys Carrasquillo, U.S. Army; Joshua Hasty, Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation; Mike Petersen, Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation; Key Words: aerospace, model-based systems engineering, reliability & maintainability, rotorcraft, vertical lift
summary: Digital Transformation across Department of Defense (DoD) agencies will enhance the systems engineering process by enabling the integration of various discipline’s digital artifacts/models during system life cycle development, including Reliability and Maintainability (R&M). This paper discusses lessons learned in developing Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) models for both Enduring Fleet and Future Vertical Lift (FVL) platforms, with focus on the unique considerations of R&M based on the authors’ experience working on MBSE models across multiple Program Executive Office – Aviation (PEO AVN) program offices.
conclusions:
PEO Aviation is focused on deploying digital capabilities as part of the digital transformation strategy.  Three of the initial five key initiatives are focused on implementing new or improving existing R&M impacts.  This aligns with the overall community interest in exploiting the power of digital modeling and artificial intelligence to improve our ability to analyze and to predict reliability and maintainability outcomes.  In this way, we think that the combination of MBSE with “live” reliability modeling and analysis, along with the recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), and the large data sets available from previous data warehousing projects have made R&M modeling an exciting topic for experimentation with algorithm development and potential cost savings for the U.S. Army.
We postulate that pending the successful application of a quasi-real time reliability database update, a more theoretical application could include the incorporation of an AI program trained to model the reliability calculations feeding the data into the MBSE model. Current Large Language Models (LLM) evaluate and score Army maintenance data. These models could be further trained using the FMECA within the MBSE models to identify likely failure modes and improve the evaluation of corrective action implementation.
The second area that this team views as a growth area for the combination of MBSE and R&M is specifically within software development.  The Reliability and Maintainability Engineering Guidebook published by the Secretary of the Navy, July 2022, contains an entire section on Reliable Software.  Software development, for standalone projects within a larger system or for subsystem development, can be modeled with MBSE and the software reliability metrics will impact the overall system R&M metrics.
keywords: reliability, maintainability, FMECA, software reliability, AI

title: Multi-Scale Temporal Analysis for Failure Prediction in Energy Systems
authors: Anh Le, North Dakota State University; Phat K. Huynh, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Om P. Yadav, PhD, North Carolina A&T State University; Chau Le, PhD, University of North Carolina at Charlotte; Harun Pirim, PhD, North Dakota State University
summary:
Many previous studies on power networks focus on identifying disturbances but they often miss how the system behaves across different time scales. Many existing models struggle to predict these systems’ complex, nonlinear behavior of these systems during extreme weather conditions. This study proposes a multi-scale system temporal analysis for failure prediction in energy systems, focusing on predicting failures in electric power networks using Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) data. The model integrates multi-scale analysis with advanced machine learning techniques to capture both short-term and long-term behavior. By analyzing disturbances across multiple temporal scales, we aim to improve failure prediction accuracy in complex energy systems. One of the main challenges with PMU data is the lack of labeled states, despite the availability of disturbance times logged as failure records. This limitation makes distinguishing between normal, pre-disturbance, and post-disturbance conditions difficult. We apply multi-scale system dynamics modeling to address this issue and extract key predictive features from PMU data for failure prediction. First, multiple domain features were extracted from the PMU data from time series data.  Second, a multi-scale windowing approach was applied, using window sizes of 30s, 60s, and 180s to capture both short-term and long-term system dynamics. This multi-scale analysis allowed the model to detect patterns across different time scales. Third, feature selection was performed using Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset and identify the most important features. We selected RFE as the best feature selection for its ability to systematically eliminate less important features, thus improving model interpretability and reducing complexity. This step was crucial for identifying the most relevant features for predicting disturbances. Fourth, these features were used to train multiple machine-learning models. Our main contributions include:
Identifying significant features across multi-scale windows.
Demonstrating LightGBM as the best-performing model, achieving 0.896 for precision with multi-scale windows.
Showing that multi-scale window sizes (30s, 60s, 180s) significantly improved model performance by capturing both short-term and long-term trends, outperforming single-window models (0.841 score).
Our current work focuses on weather-related failure modes, with future research extending this approach to other failure modes, equipment failure, and lightning events.
conclusions: The study indicates the most significant features with different window sizes. It also demonstrates the robust approach in feature engineering using t-SNE visualization. It effectively detects normal classes. However, there is still overlap between the pre- and post-classes across all window sizes. This implies that the feature engineering does not fully differentiate pre-disturbance from post-disturbance states. Multiscale window size shows the best separation, but more improvement is needed to better distinguish the classes. This aligned with the performance in the machine-learning model. LightGBM- the best model faces challenges when classifying pre- and post-disturbances. LightGBM with built-in feature importance achieves the highest accuracy (0.896 ± 0.028 with 20 features), outperforming Random Forest, XGBoost, and other models. LightGBM builds deeper trees faster than XGBoost and RF, helping it capture complex feature relationships, even in smaller datasets. Future studies could apply this system approach to different failure modes, such as circuit failures or lightning strikes, and improve feature engineering to enhance the performance of the model.

title: Enhancing Maintenance Data Analytics: A Novel Failure Mode and Effect Analysis-Natural Language Processing Integration
authors: Mathieu Payette, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières; Georges Abdul-Nour, PhD, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières; Toualith Jean-Marc Meango, PhD, Centre de recherche d’Hydro-Québec; Miguel Diago, Centre de recherche d’Hydro-Québec; Alain Côté, Centre de recherche d’Hydro-Québec
summary: Machine learning models require considerable amounts of data, which is often a significant limitation in many real-world applications due to the scarcity of quality data. Information recorded in management systems, such as enterprise resource planning software (ERP), can nevertheless be supplemented by text fields, which can be used to enhance its quality. Natural language processing (NLP) techniques seem theoretically capable of meeting this challenge. However, the technical nature and structure of industrial text fields require further analysis to fully exploit state-of-the-art NLP models. This article presents a new methodology to leverage already available information to facilitate the implementation of NLP applications. The approach is then tested specifically in the context of reliability and maintenance, by exploiting failure modes and effects analyses (FMEA) to improve the quality of maintenance descriptions, within the framework of an NLP approach. This case study demonstrates the usefulness of the methodology, by applying it to the maintenance data of a power transmission utility.
conclusions:
This work has presented a novel approach to text preparation for technical language processing. The use of an existing documentation in a failure mode and effects analysis enabled text pre-processing to be focused on the most important terms, while minimizing the need to involve specialists for text annotation. The method developed considerably improved the quality of the textual data and, what’s more, certain tasks in the process could be handed over to data clerks. For example, 48 different spellings were listed for transformer, a key asset in a power system. By focusing on the important words from the FMEA, the size of the vocabulary was reduced by more than 87%, considerably decreasing the variation in the texts analyzed. This is a crucial step in the application of sophisticated models, which perform poorly when there is too much variability. Another advantage of this process is that it makes it feasible to reuse knowledge already gathered in structured processes. The methodology could be extended to other areas, where relevant terms are listed in an organized way in existing documentation. In the future, it would be interesting to measure the improvement of text classifiers, before and after data preparation with the new procedure.
In conclusion, this work has allowed the testing of a new approach for preprocessing data, so that industrial datasets can be used with state-of-the-art natural language processing techniques.

title: Reliability Assessment of Select Natural Gas Infrastructure Under Hydrogen Blending
authors: Theresa M. Stewart, PhD, University of California, Los Angeles; Ali Mosleh, PhD, NAE, University of California Los Angeles; Narasi Sridhar, PhD., MC Consult LLC; François Ayello, PhD, PE, Energy Systems DNV USA, Inc.; Abhishek N. Salilkumar, University of California, Los Angeles
summary: This paper presents a part of an ongoing research effort to analyze the potential change in system reliability caused by blending hydrogen gas into the existing natural gas pipeline infrastructure. The model scope covers target industrial-use distribution and transmission systems in the state of California. These systems include both geographically extended components (pipelines), and discrete components, such as valves and compressors. The probability of failure can vary significantly for each component and across locations along a pipeline due to differences in local stresses, metallurgy, history, operations, and natural forces. This project utilizes existing data on material and component performance in hydrogen as well as data from current laboratory testing by the project team on materials that will be exposed to hydrogen. In this paper, the modeling approach for discrete components is presented for the example of valves. The modeling approach uses fault trees to model component failure modes, combined with a Bayesian Net (BN) modeling approach to predict the effects of hydrogen on component materials given the operating and environmental conditions present. Historical laboratory data and modeling efforts from publicly available literature are combined with the BN model to provide an estimated unavailability for an individual component. Where data is unavailable for these models, data from similar systems or expert opinion is used, but as more laboratory testing is completed, the conditional probabilities of the BN’s can be updated to reflect the new information. The calculations show that increasing hydrogen blending increases the valve unavailability factor.

title: Fault Tree Analysis and Risk Importance Measures Applied to Electric Grids
authors: Martin Royer, Hydro-Québec; Vincent Poiré, Hydro-Québec; Jérémie Turcotte, McGill University; Dragan Komljenovic, Hydro-Québec/IREQ; Key Words: Fault tree analysis, R&M applications in manufacturing, service or infrastructure management, reliability modeling, availability, repairable systems and maintenance models
summary:
This paper describes the application of fault tree analysis (FTA) and risk importance measures to medium- and low-voltage electric distribution systems. Today, with the aging of assets, climate change and a scarcity of resources, targeted interventions are required to improve service quality. With the methodology suggested in this paper, intervention priorities can be set, critical zones identified, and the impact of corrective measures assessed.
To address the scope and complexity of electrical systems and the need for periodic review of analyses given the frequent changes in system topology, models were generated automatically. The processing of outage and unavailability data was also automated.
Application of this method offers a multitude of analytical and representation possibilities allowing optimal management of electric distribution systems.
conclusions:
Application of the method described in this paper to two distribution lines identified the same PZs as priorities for corrective action as did a panel of experts. The main benefit of our decision-making aid is that it is a systematic method that standardizes analyses and allows quantification of corrective measures, unlike the qualitative findings of experts.
In addition, the method proved to be very versatile, a key factor given the aging of utility assets, climate change and a scarcity of resources. A multitude of analyses are possible using importance measures alone or with fault tree analysis, providing an opportunity to deepen our understanding of the system. Quantified results may also offer better guidance for making decisions about corrective measures to be taken. As we develop the methodology further, one of the next steps is to introduce planned outages. Furthermore, we aim to develop a common-cause failures (CCFs) prototype that would take widespread and extreme failures into account, which would be better adapted to assets spread over a larger territory. Lastly, we also plan to adapt the model to perform essential forecasting analyses given the current context where service quality and the energy transition are key concerns. A minimal cut providing the consumption profile in PZs could be integrated during the simulation.

title: Bridging Static and Dynamic Design for Enhanced Safety Analysis
authors: Tim Gonschorek, Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg; Hannes Stützer, Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg; Frank Ortmeier, Prof. Dr., Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg; Michael Oppermann, Dr.-Ing., Airbus Operations GmbH; Key Words: Model Continuity, SysML, Simulink
summary:
In conclusion, this paper aims to provide a solution for bridging the gap between static and dynamic system design representations while highlighting the importance of model reuse for cross-functional collaboration, particularly in the domain of functional safety. By ensuring model continuity and enabling the reuse of model artifacts for automated safety assessment, our approach contributes to a more rigorous and efficient system design and analysis process, ultimately improving the overall safety and reliability of complex systems.
This paper presents a model continuity approach and supporting model transformations to bridge the gap between static and dynamic system design representations. Our approach employs a semantics-aware transformation of a system's static architecture into the structural foundation of a dynamic system model. This transformation encompasses:
Hierarchical Decompositions: Translating functional, logical, and technical decompositions with their relationships.
Failure Injection Points: Mapping defined failure injection points to the dynamic model.
Design Retransformation: Enabling updates to the static architecture based on adjustments made during dynamic modeling.
When enriched with behavioral details, we demonstrate that the transformed model is a robust starting point for automated formal safety analysis. In a case study from the aerospace domain, we employ model-checking techniques to generate minimal failure mode cut sets initially defined within the static structural architecture. The minimal failure mode cut sets should replace the often-used fault trees.

title: Resilience Assessment and Optimization of Image Classifiers
authors: Berit Schuerrle, University of Stuttgart; Andrey Morozov, University of Stuttgart; Key Words: Neural Network Robustness, Image Corruption, Sensitivity Analysis, Fault Injection, Bayesian Optimization
summary:
In this paper, we aimed to address the limitations of neural network models when dealing with corrupted images by implementing a two-fold approach: sensitivity analysis and Bayesian optimization. Sensitivity analysis was conducted to understand how different types of faults affected model performance, and Bayesian optimization was used to improve the models' resilience to these faults. Our approach was tested on a subset of1000 images from the ImageNet validation data.
The sensitivity analysis involved injecting 14 different types of faults into images and evaluating the performance of five neural network architectures on these corrupted images. Through this sensitivity analysis we were able to gain insights into the models’ resilience and identify the strengths and weaknesses. For example, EfficientNetB4 showed strong performance against brightness, pixelate, and JPEG compression faults but struggled with contrast and zoom blur.
Building on these insights, we used Bayesian optimization to identify the most effective combinations of preprocessing steps and neural network architectures. The optimization process involved iteratively testing different parameter combinations to maximize accuracy on corrupted images. This approach led to an average improvement of 10.11% in accuracy across all fault types, demonstrating the efficacy of targeted preprocessing in enhancing model performance.
Our methodology effectively identified and mitigated the weaknesses of neural network models when faced with various image corruptions. The sensitivity analysis provided detailed insights into model vulnerabilities, and the Bayesian optimization approach systematically improved model performance. These findings underscore the importance of tailoring preprocessing steps to specific fault types to enhance the robustness and accuracy of neural networks. This targeted approach can be widely applied to improve the reliability of image recognition systems in real-world scenarios where data corruption is common.
conclusions:
In conclusion, we highlight the key findings of this paper:
Sensitivity Analysis Insights: Different architectures exhibited varying levels of robustness to specific faults. The proposed analysis enable users to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the models, effectively illustrating their limitations.
Bayesian Optimization Effectiveness: The optimization process led to an average accuracy improvement of 10.11% across all fault types. Preprocessing functions such as denoising and contrast adjustment played crucial roles in enhancing performance. The approach proved effective, with improving 12 out of the 14 fault types.
Limitations: Results are highly dependent on the specific images and neural networks used. The study was limited to a subset of 1,000 images and four preprocessing techniques. Implementing a broader variety of selected preprocessing functions and further optimization rounds could refine results.
Our paper demonstrates the potential of Bayesian optimization in enhancing the resilience and performance of neural networks under various image corruptions. The insights gained from the sensitivity analysis and the effectiveness of the optimization approach underscore the importance of targeted preprocessing and model selection in developing resilient perception systems for real-world applications.

title: Extending Coverage Modeling to Voter Behavior for Spacecraft Reliability Modeling
authors: Leila Meshkat, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology; Key Words: Coverage Modeling, Voters, Reliability, Fault Tolerance
summary: Embedded computer-based systems, or digital systems, are used in applications, such as spacecraft, which require high reliability.  Meeting the reliability requirements at the lowest possible cost, typically involves trade studies that aim to quantify the value of different mechanisms for obtaining high reliability.  One of these mechanisms is fault tolerance, which involves the detection, location, isolation, and recovery of the system upon occurrence of a fault.  The coverage parameter has been defined as the likelihood of successfully recovering from a fault that has occurred.  If the fault and error handling mechanisms cannot successfully cover all the faults in the system, then the coverage factor is less than one and the system has imperfect coverage.  An accurate reliability analysis of the system thus must take into consideration the coverage parameter, for systems with imperfect coverage.  Methods for incorporation of the coverage parameter in system reliability analysis have been developed.  These methods consider the uncovered failure of components both at the subsystem and system level.  At the subsystem level, and in the context of hierarchical systems, the uncovered failure of a component can cause the failure of a given subsystem.  At the systems level, the uncovered failure of a component can cause systems level failures.  One of the mechanisms for including fault tolerance in the system is masking faults using voters.  We propose to extend the existing methods for coverage modeling to consider the behavior of voters and their contribution to the prevention of uncovered failures.  We consider that the system can have three states: successful, fail covered and fail uncovered and find the likelihood of each of these states as a function of the likelihood of the coverage parameter for each component as well as the likelihood of successful fault masking by the voter.

title: Application of FTA for Design of Safety Critical Systems
authors: David D Yellamati, Schneider Electric; Pascal Gabeur, Schneider Electric; Yunwei Hu, Ph.D., Schneider Electric; Yavuz Goktas, Ph.D., Schneider Electric; Key Words: Circuit Breaker, Minimum Cut Sets, Fail Safe Systems, P-Diagram, DFMEA, FTA, FTD
summary: This paper provides a case study on application of the Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) methodology for design of Safety Critical Systems such as Power Control and Energy Management Systems. These systems are widely used in many industrial and commercial applications and failure of these devices can potentially lead to Safety or Regulatory issues. In many industries, FTA is used reactively to quantify the probability of the Top Unwanted Event once there is a safety incident in the field or to meet a compliance standard such as ISO26262, it is seldom used as a proactive tool to drive design improvements. In this paper, we have delineated a process that includes identification of safety risks and development on an FTA from a P-diagram (Parameter-Diagram) driven Design, Failure Modes & Effects Analysis (DFMEA). Next FTA is analyzed Qualitatively to derive Minimum Cut Sets (MCS) and appropriate Failure Tolerance/Fail Safe features are designed in to mitigate the risks due to Single Points of Failure (SPOF) and combination of events that are of concern. Lastly, the impact of the designed in fail safe features was quantified to show improved safety level as compared to original design. We have applied the aforementioned  methodology on the design of Industrial Circuit Breaker, where risk of Arc Flash Hazard, which can potentially lead to human injury, was mitigated by systematically analyzing the design by diving deep into MCS generated by Qualitative FTA and incorporating Firmware fail-safe features (Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) control) that trips the circuit breaker in the event of a short-circuit condition, thereby preventing the Arc Flash. This risk mitigation was quantified using Quantitative FTA, where the probability of occurrence of Arc Flash hazard was reduced to a negligible level.

This risk mitigation was quantified using Quantitative FTA, where the probability of occurrence of Arc Flash hazard was reduced to a negligible level.

title: Common Cause Failures Dominate and Defeat Redundancy
authors: Harry W. Jones, Ph.D., NASA Ames Research Center; Key Words: common cause failures, redundancy, beta factor
summary:
Common cause failures occur when several malfunctions are produced by a single event or process.  They are especially damaging when they eliminate an entire set of redundant systems and disable their intended function.  Redundancy is used when the individual system failure probability is unacceptably high.  Redundancy can improve the overall system failure probability if the failures are independent, but the reliability gain is limited if there are dependent failures having a common cause.  No amount of redundancy can reduce the total failure probability below the common cause failure probability.  Common cause failures defeat redundancy.
Systems with high reliability requirements often use extensive redundancy.  These highly redundant systems rarely fail unless all the redundant components providing a particular function fail.  Complete failures of such highly redundant systems are then usually common cause failures.  Common cause failures are prevalent in highly redundant, high reliability systems.  Common cause failures dominate redundancy.
Redundant systems may fail due to specification, design, manufacturing, operations, or maintenance problems that disable all the identical redundant systems.  Common cause failures typically account for one tenth of all failures.  If the failure probability is relatively low and common cause failures are significant, adding more than two or three redundant identical units usually gives little added reliability improvement.  Common cause failures can be reduced by using diverse components with different technologies and manufacturers, by separating and shielding subsystems, and by avoiding shared control, power, or location.  External events and shared vulnerabilities may still cause common cause failures.

title: Availability Risk Management for Systems with Multiple Configurations
authors: Joseph Molvar, RTX; Alastair Moubray, RTX; Nobel Mathew, RTX; Joshua Danker, RTX; Key Words: Risk Analysis and Management, Availability
summary:
This paper discusses four primary topics. First, it describes the creation of a predictive model, used to determine the quantity of spares to sustain a geographically distributed set of systems with varying configurations. Second, it explains an approach to availability risk management, which analyses and identifies the parts which drive fleet availability risk.  As elimination of all spares-related sustainment risk is frequently hindered by budgetary limitations, accurate identification of key drivers of system availability is important for effective risk management, so mitigations can be created and high system availability maintained.  Third, the paper demonstrates how availability risks change with adjustments to spares stock levels and repair strategies.  Lastly, it illustrates how to assess the effects of product modernization and upgrade activities, predicting and comparing sparing-related availability risks of new hardware configurations against the historical baseline.
The availability risk analysis and management strategies described in this paper produce meaningful results, allowing easy comparison of current predicted availability risk vs predicted availability risk after implemented mitigations. This availability risk comparison has the additional benefit of facilitating comparison of multiple mitigation strategies, aiding decision making.  The strategies described here represent an improvement over previous approaches, which (1) did not analyze multiple configurations in-depth, (2) did not accurately accommodate system redundancies, and (3) often made it difficult to identify high-risk spare drivers in more detailed system configurations.

title: Analysis of the Repairability of Ship Machinery Failures
authors: Spencer A. Dugan, Norwegian University of Science and Technology; Ingrid B. Utne, Norwegian University of Science and Technology; Key Words: repairability, maritime risk, navigational risk assessment
summary:
Repairing ship capabilities following a machinery failure is essential for the prevention of maritime accidents, yet limited research exists on repair times. This study reviews the assumptions in navigational risk models and summarizes the literature in the maritime domain. These assumptions are compared to class standards, design guidelines, and repair information taken from accident databases. The objective is to determine real-world repair distributions for more accurate risk assessment and mitigation strategies.
Two data sources are consulted for repair information: the first is a database of drifting ships collected by the Vessel Traffic Services of the Norwegian Coastal Administration. The second is accident reports from 2013-2022 published by several major flag states.
The results indicate that repair times differ by ship type. Passenger ships have the quickest repair times, and the distribution corresponds well with a distribution used in navigational risk assessments. Cargo ships and other ships have a much greater mean time to repair (MTTR) and skew in the data. Reasons for these differences are discussed in addition to their implications. The research in the bulk power industry is used to make suggestions for the further research.
conclusions:
This study is motivated by the lack of research onto the repair time for ships in the maritime industry. Following a failure, quick restoration of ship capabilities is essential to prevent maritime accidents. To analyze repair times, two data sources were utilized. The first is a database compiled by the VTS of the NCA. The second is accident reports from several major maritime flag states for a ten-year period. This study shows significant differences in repair times between ship types and highlights the need for more research into autonomous and self-healing systems.
Understanding current repairability trends is critical for future autonomous ships and comparisons with manned systems. Furthermore, the maritime industry should look to advancements into resilience and self-healing systems prevalent in the power distribution and transmission industries.

title: Framework for Identifying Failure Mechanisms in Consumer Electronics Using Large Language Models
authors: Eunseo So, University of Maryland; Mohammad Modarres, PhD, University of Maryland,; Key Words: Consumer electronics, Large language models, Durability, Use case, Failure mechanism
summary: As electronic waste becomes a growing concern, extending the lifetime of devices by increasing their durability has become a key lever for promoting sustainability. Although a durability index was proposed in a previous study, determining tests to cover the entire lifespan of target devices remains a challenge. To identify the necessary tests, it is essential to first identify potential failure mechanisms. This study proposes a framework for identifying failure mechanisms from brief information, such as the product description of the target device. The proposed framework leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate use cases and identify potential stresses and failure mechanisms. A modularized design is adopted for better flexibility in accommodating additional information between the modules.
conclusions:
To promote the sustainability of consumer electronics, a durability index was developed in a previous study. One of its attributes, the promise of life, requires life testing, but determining which tests to perform remains a challenge. To address this, the paper proposes an approach to identify failure mechanisms from the product description using LLMs, helping to determine the appropriate tests for the target device. The proposed framework consists of three modules: use case generation, stress identification, and failure mechanism identification. For more accurate results, several iterations of LLMs have been done, and structured prompts have been developed. The modularized design also increases its flexibility to engage additional information. The remaining challenges for each module are discussed in each section. Module 4 of test planning will also remain a work in the future.

title: Strategic Artificial Intelligence Learning (SAIL) And Applications – Mastering Risk in Space Explorations
authors: Prince Kalia, NASA; Humberto Calvani, NASA; Jonathan Patterson, NASA; Tim Crumbly, NASA; Key words: Artificial Intelligence, Modeling and Simulation Validation, Automation Uncertainties, Gray Rhinos risks
summary:
The focus of this paper is to provide a framework for an interdisciplinary approach on Artificial Intelligence (AI) system applications with space exploration in line with National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) perspective on AI.
Aerospace and other industries are investing heavily in this field to increase performance and improve operational reliability of complex systems, minimizing the risks associated with cross-cutting common cause failure (CCF) modes/causes and human errors. AI applications were developed and used for NASA’s Space Shuttle program in the Mission Control Center (MCC) to make flight decisions for a real space mission [1, 2]. There is a great opportunity to capitalize and further strengthen our excellent systems engineering and safety-reliability practices at NASA with the additional lessons learned from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), other robotic missions and Human Space Flight Program involved in the suite of Artemis missions, in partnership with leading players in the AI field. Also addressed in this paper are AI implementation barriers related to automation/software uncertainties, cognitive biases, complex mission architectures, modeling validation and sanity check of simulation results, failure to assess aggregate and cross-cutting risks associated with hardware, software, firmware, and human interactions. The proposed AI framework has great potential to improve safety, reliability, improve resilience and performance of these flagship space exploration missions despite multiple challenges and organizational barriers overcoming Grey Rhino risks and Black Swan events.
1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background
Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are getting rapid attention in aerospace, supply-chain management, medical, financial, human resources, Wall-Street, customer service, travel, and many other fields. Aspects of this technology are used in a wide variety of applications from medical devices to autonomous vehicles, with tools like ChatGPT capable of mimicking human thought processes. Some of the key AI applications across NASA include a storm prediction tool that uses image recognition technology to identify atmospheric conditions to provide early warnings for destructive weather events and space vehicles such as the Mars Perseverance rover, which uses an autonomous navigation system. It has great potential for space exploration too, based on its progressively value-driven contribution during the life cycle of complex programs/ missions at NASA, Department of Defense (DoD), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and others. The expected key benefits are: (a) Improved operational reliability, mission safety and resilience, (b) Improved performance, (c) Minimization of high impact mission risks due to cross-cutting common case failure categories, and (d) Facilitation of driving mission risk optimization based on program/project risk tolerance (i.e.  mission profile), architecture, and other strategic goals.
1.2 What is Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Artificial intelligence (Figure 1) refers to computer systems that can perform complex tasks normally done by human-reasoning, decision making etc. [3]
Traditional AI systems often require human guidance, with pre-programmed rules limiting their scope of operation. In contrast, autonomous AI possesses the ability to analyze and interpret data, learn from experiences, and execute actions without constant human supervision.
AI tools used at NASA sometimes use machine learning, which uses data and algorithms to train computers to make classifications, generate predictions, or uncover similarities or trends across large datasets.
Deep Learning is a subset of machine learning that involves neural networks with many layers. It distinguished from other forms of neural networks primarily through its capability to learn features automatically from unstructured data set.
Figure 1 – How AI, Machine and Deep Learning fit together: What is Artificial Intelligence? - NASA
1.3 NASA’s perspective on AI
While there is no single accepted simple definition of artificial intelligence because AI tools are capable of a wide range of tasks and outputs.  NASA follows the definition of AI found within Executive Order (EO 13960), which references Section 238(g) of the National Defense Authorization Act of 2019:
Any artificial system that performs tasks under varying and unpredictable circumstances without significant human oversight, or that can learn from experience and improve performance when exposed to data sets.
An artificial system developed in computer software, physical hardware, or other context that solves tasks requiring human-like perception, cognition, planning, learning, communication, or physical action.
An artificial system designed to think or act like a human, including cognitive architectures and neural networks.
A set of techniques, including machine learning that is designed to approximate a cognitive task.
When used safely, transparently, and responsibly, AI can help support our missions, drive our research, analyze our data, and develop systems that benefit our missions, aeronautics, and space and earth science, among many other things. Artificial intelligence accelerates the pace of discovery.

NASA has been safely using artificial intelligence for decades for aeronautics, select mission activities of the human space flight program, science data from robotics missions, mission planning and scheduling for planetary rovers, analysis of satellite datasets, detection, diagnosis of anomalies, and more. Key examples of integrated modeling and simulations along with integrated safety and reliability include:
JWST - Morpheus is an artificial intelligence system developed by NASA that is used to analyze JWST images. Data from weather satellites that warns of inclement weather and provides weather predictions (Figure 3).

AI algorithms can analyze the movement patterns of debris objects and identify deviations from expected behavior. This early anomaly detection allows for proactive measures to be taken, such as adjusting satellite orbits or planning debris removal missions [8].
(h) Pre-planned contingencies for robotics missions - autonomously and with ground interventions.
AI helps support missions and research projects across the agency, analyze data to reveal trends and patterns, and develop systems capable of supporting spacecraft and aircraft autonomously. AI is helping to achieve advances in the areas of astronomical sciences, resource efficiency, technological innovation, telecommunications, Earth observation, planetary defense, mission strategy, human life support systems, and artificial astronauts.

There are a host of functional areas in Artemis (NASA missions to Moon, Mars, and beyond) and robotic missions, where AI can continue to support mission execution as a valued addition.

Guidance and navigation

Analysis of alternatives approach per risk management practices
Safe AI progressive development and deployment depends on seamless, simultaneous integration of detailed, value-driven design architecture modeling and simulation (hardware, software, firmware and associated human factors), effective process control for the whole supply-chain, and robust integration and test processes. This entails integrating engineering analysis/assessments with Flight Hazard reports, Failure Modes, and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Critical Items Control Plans (CICP), Fault Tree, detailed prognostics for generation of algorithms, modeling, and simulations on real-life possible situations. This would also include Non-Conformance Reports (NCRs) and Failure Review Board (FRB) data analysis followed by performing effective, risk-mitigating corrective actions. When human interfaces are involved, whether from the astronauts in space or ground, it is always prudent to address any unforeseen situations. This was a lesson learned from the recent June 6, 2024, Boeing Starliner autonomous and last minutes docking maneuvers by the astronauts to the International Space Station, as well as other successful NASA missions.

4 AI TRANSFORMATION WITH SAFETY AND OPERATIONAL RELIABILITY
The lessons learned from (a) the NASA benchmarking study across the best of the aerospace industries, entitled, “Exploring the Design Excellence leading to enhanced Safety and Reliability”, for NASA flagship missions [9], (b) NASA Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV) Smart Buyers  Launch Abort System (LAS) team that finalized the architecture (now part of Artemis system architecture), and (c) the results of  Ultra-reliability, an integrated systems analysis approach, for NASA space exploration missions figure 6 [11], provided path-forward to the next steps of cross-discipline integration.
This background acted as a catalyst to the proposed AI framework (Figure 7). This framework provides an opportunity to pursue AI applications by learning and prudently selecting higher-value applications to meet challenging mission needs. This requires the coordinated, seamless efforts of NASA team members with the prime contractor and their experts using the role models of JWST and Artemis 1, which achieved 100% mission success [6, 10, 11, 12].
For the human space flight program, besides human interaction during contingencies, there are other safety and reliability-focused areas where AI processes have provided valuable contributions during critical phases of the mission, such as autonomous guidance and navigation systems, and fault detection, isolation, and recovery (FDIR).
Figure: 7: Framework of AI-driven Reliability and System Safety for Space Exploration
Figure: 8 AI Management Framework at NASA:   https://oig.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ig-23-012.pdf
Detail of NASA AI management framework (Figure 8) was released by the Office of Inspector General (OIG) report, May 2023 [12] to pursue AI for organizational pursuits.
AI – Implementation Barrier
NASA has been safely using artificial intelligence for decades to plan and schedule missions for planetary rovers, analyze satellite datasets, diagnose, and detect anomalies. However, there are limitations of AI for some space exploration missions involving complex architecture or unproven/ sufficiently matured technology and data:
Complex mission architecture and technology readiness state/timeline.
Inadequate or no verifiable trustworthy data regarding mission profile and environment
Organization culture (cognitive biases) with no compelling reason to change. (RAMS-2024 paper -Integrated Systems Engineering, Safety, Reliability and Risk Management – Minimizing Black Swan Events [11].
Gaps in the current system engineering practices are addressed by strategically integrating safety, quality, and reliability where AI can be a true value-driven opportunity. The merit/trade of these opportunities can be assessed using concepts such as (a) return-on-investment (ROI), (b) qualitative/quantitative assessment of improvements to drive robust design (LOC, LOV, LOM) and down the line processes, (LOC – Loss of Crew, LOV: Loss of Vehicle and LOM: Loss of Mission) [12, 13, 14,16]
Lack of effective rigor to make a proactive assessment for identification of Gray Rhino’s risk and an effective action plan to mitigate them. Gray Rhino risks are high-impact (even catastrophic and cascading events) but seemingly unexpected high-to-low probability risks that can be shuttled to the sidelines due to multiple organizational reasons such as cognitive biases, engineering assumptions, human errors, and failure to assess aggregate and cross-cutting risks related to hardware (especially mechanisms and/or mechanical items), software, firmware, and human interactions [10, 11, 13].
6  SOFTWARE AUTOMATION RISKS
Software creates automation and reliance on that automation is increasing the amount of software in NASA programs. Recently the NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) software team examined historical software incidents in aerospace to characterize how, why, and where software or automation is most likely to fail. The goal is to better engineer software to minimize the risk of errors, improve software processes, and better architect software for resilience to errors (or improve fault-tolerance should errors occur). [15]
Figure 9: Software Automation risk
Some key findings shown in the above charts: Software more often does the wrong thing rather than just crash. Rebooting was found to be ineffective when software behaves erroneously. Unexpected behavior was mostly attributed to the code or logic itself, and about half of those instances were the result of missing software—software not present due to unanticipated situations or missing requirements. This may indicate that even fully tested software is exposed to this significant class of error. Data misconfiguration was a sizeable factor that continues to grow with the advent of more modern data-driven systems. A final subjective category assessed was “unknown unknowns”—things that could not have been reasonably anticipated. These accounted for 19% of software incidents studied [14].
Conclusion
Since most mission work is being performed by prime contractors and their sub-tier contractors, a seamless public-private partnership and integration would help unify AI capability development and deployment under NASA’s leadership. It is vital to verify and validate the AI algorithms and Integrated Systems Engineering models based on documented ground-rules, assumptions, and NASA’s safety practices. Proactive risk informed decision making (RIDM) would play a key role in the details of acquisition management with operational reliability- and safety-focused supply chain auditing (Continuous Risk Management - CRM). This approach will help minimize the Gray Rhinos risks that could significantly affecting flight safety, operational reliability, and mission success goals. [7, 8, 9, 14, 15, 16, 17]
For risks identified post mission launch/deployment, we also need to consider unintended and malicious risks arising from AI in space, which could have catastrophic consequences for life on Earth, space stations, and space settlements. As a response to mitigate these risks, we call for urgent expansion of existing “responsible use of AI in space” frameworks to address “ethical limits” in both civilian and non-civilian space economy ventures, alongside national, bilateral, and international cooperation to enforce mechanisms for robust, explainable, secure, accountable, fair, and societally beneficial AI in space.
