title: Leveraging Generative AI Tools for Proactive Risk Mitigation in Design
authors: Yunwei, Hu, Ph.D., Schneider Electric; Amith Nag N A, Schneider Electric; David D Yellamati, Schneider Electric; Yavuz Goktas, Ph.D., Schneider Electric; Key Words: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI), Machine Learning, Large Language Models (LLM), Risk mitigation
summary:
This paper explores how Generative AI can transform Design for Safety & Reliability (DfSR) by proactively identifying and mitigating risks throughout the product development lifecycle. It examines three key approaches to leveraging generative AI in DfSR:
Assistive AI: This approach employs Large Language Models (LLMs) or Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to interact dynamically with users. While highly flexible and agile, interpretability and control of AI-generated outputs remain areas of concern. Potential applications include providing diverse perspectives during brainstorming sessions.
Scripted AI: This approach uses predefined rules and scripts to automate repetitive tasks to improve the efficiency and consistency. However, its inflexibility limits its effectiveness in complex scenarios. We suggest using Scripted AI to automate routine tasks.
Agentic AI: This approach involves AI systems autonomously executing tasks, demonstrating a higher degree of “agency”. While offering real-time analysis and continuous learning capabilities, ethical considerations and system complexity present challenges.
The paper highlights how these approaches can be applied across various stages of the DfSR workflow, from defining requirements and planning to risk assessment, design optimization, and sustainment. Each stage benefits from the unique strengths of each AI approach.
We also emphasize the limitations of Generative AI tools. We recommend maintaining human oversight in critical decisions, treating AI as collaborators, and continuously monitoring AI systems for reliability and performance.
As AI technology advances, its integration into engineering workflows promises safer, more reliable, and innovative products. Continued research and development in AI will be crucial for realizing the full potential of AI in shaping the future of DfSR.

authors: Jordan Long, Raytheon; Kimberly Malone, Raytheon; Key Words: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, FRACA, failure trending, automation
summary:
This paper introduces a novel concept aimed at using Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI / ML) to enhance operational efficiency using a Failure Reporting, Analysis, and Corrective Action system (FRACA).  Over a few decades, failure data, with root cause, and the associated corrective actions have been collected in several databases and spreadsheets. This paper will explore the critical role of a FRACA system in enhancing operational reliability and efficiency across various industries. Our theory is that by systematically capturing failure data, analyzing root causes, and implementing corrective actions, a FRACA system combined with AI / ML can not only mitigate the risk of future failures but also fosters a culture of continuous improvement and efficiency.
The proposed idea is currently in the exploration phase, with the potential to evolve into a practical tool designed to streamline the process of utilizing the associated data collected when managing failures.  In the current process, there are repetitive steps that require human interaction as part of the process.  Those steps have been identified as candidates that AI / ML would be beneficial.  A proof-of-concept project has been established to implement an AI /ML solution that will address the identified inefficiencies of these repetitive tasks.  Plans have been established to continue fully enhancing capability.  It is important to note that, as of now, no empirical testing or validation has been conducted to assess its effectiveness.
Developing AI / ML solutions for unique products and systems takes significant effort to plan out.   Future research and experimentation is necessary to determine its viability, practical application, and solve challenging implementation.  Developing automated capabilities, predictive models, and best practices will aide in realizing efficiency, accuracy, and early detection with product failures.  Iterations of this paper will include results and updates from that experimentation to assess the effectiveness of the tool.

title: Q-Weibull Distribution: A Versatile Model in Accelerated Life Testing with Accelerated Failure Time and Proportional Hazards
authors: Meng Xu, PhD; Key Words: accelerated life testing, q-Weibull distribution, proportional hazard, accelerated failure time
summary: Accelerated Life Testing (ALT) is a methodology used to estimate the reliability and lifespan of products under normal usage conditions by testing them at elevated stress levels. This paper introduces the Q-Weibull distribution as a versatile and robust lifetime distribution for modeling ALT test data. The Q-Weibull distribution was proven to maintain its form under both Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) and Proportional Hazards (PH) assumptions, offering unparalleled flexibility in modeling ALT data. We demonstrated the Q-Weibull distribution's applicability through extensive case studies, showcasing its performance under both AFT and PH assumptions. In the AFT case study, we evaluated the failures of insulation in electric motors at high temperatures. The Q-Weibull distribution under the AFT assumption provided a robust fit across various stress levels, enabling accurate lifespan predictions. However, we found the AFT assumption fails in many applications. Instead, the Q-Weibull distribution under the PH assumption effectively captured the failure distributions of components subjected to different stress levels, which validated the proportional hazards assumption. We also designed novel plots to (1) graphically test if the Q-Weibull distribution fits the data at different stresses, (2) graphically evaluate if all data fits into the same q-Weibull distribution when normalized, and (3) graphically test if the PH assumption holds. By showcasing the Q-Weibull distribution as a promising candidate for ALT, this paper aims to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of product reliability assessment and failure time estimation for the baseline stress.
conclusions: This paper has demonstrated the effectiveness of the Q-Weibull distribution in Accelerated Life Testing (ALT), showcasing its flexibility and robustness. The Q-Weibull distribution maintains its form under both Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) and Proportional Hazards (PH) assumptions, making it a versatile model for predicting product lifespan and reliability under varied stress conditions. Our case studies highlighted the Q-Weibull distribution's superior performance in fitting ALT data compared to traditional models. The Q-Weibull with AFT model accurately predicted the lifespan of electric motor insulation under high temperatures, while the Q-Weibull with PH model effectively captured failure patterns under different stress levels.

title: Beyond Computer Aided Design: Holographic Collaboration in Enhancing Product Life Management
authors: James Pesculis, Raytheon; Robert J. Pavlovich, Jr., Raytheon; Eisen Montalvo-Ruiz, Raytheon; Christopher P. Sullivan, Raytheon; Key Words: Extended Reality, Holography, Product Design, Human Factors, Maintainability, Digital Thread, Digital Transformation, Product Lifecycle Management
summary:
For aerospace and defense companies, the US government’s initiative to implement comprehensive digital thread frameworks becomes imperative to improving reliability and maintainability (R&M) performance across complex product lifecycle management (PLM) processes and global supply chains. Targeted digital transformation efforts, that challenge standard processes through research and development of innovative technologies and novel approaches, can provide incremental contributions to business process improvement that unlock customer value by enabling personnel to work differently through new digital capabilities.
Developing manufacturing capabilities that incorporate R&M principles, particularly in the aerospace and defense industry, is key to lowering production costs and speeding time to market by gaining manufacturing efficiencies and reducing risks on multi-million or billion-dollar programs prior to entering production.
To realize these efficiencies and reduce risk, advanced visualization capabilities offer new approaches to system design and development to create significant improvement opportunities targeted at select PLM use cases. Through immersive interactive experiences created with the assistance of digital design tools, techniques, and ideation spaces, engineers can generate novel approaches to improve the product design process through the insertion of digital technology. These opportunities reach beyond the decades old 2D and 3D computer aided design (CAD) technology to include the realm of extended reality (XR).
One such approach includes the use of XR hardware and software to allow one or more persons to collaborate on full-scale holographic models in real-world space, whether in the same physical space or joined remotely. With the release of enterprise-level head mounted spatial computers (HMSCs) in the commercial market, holographic collaboration use cases now have practical industrial applications in areas including digital prototyping, design reviews, human factors analysis, work instruction validation, factory layouts, mission operations analysis, and customer product reviews. This realization has led our team to add a holographic collaboration project to our roadmap with research objectives to assess the practical application of collaborative holographic technology and its potential return on investment (ROI). This paper highlights the approach, methodology, and results of that endeavor.

title: Physics of Failure Modeling for Improved Automotive Warranty Cost Predictions
authors: Marco Bonato, PhD, Valeo Power; Aziz Moudoub, Valeo Power; Key Words: Corrosion, Physics-of-Failure, Weibull, Predictions, Warranty
summary:
In the automotive industry, it is well known for reliability practitioners experienced in warranty studies that forecast and warranty estimation are primarily performed using the Weibull distribution.  Moreover, it is widely accepted to interpret the Weibull parameters as indicative of the underlying failure mechanism, but also as confirmation that different samples might have the same failure mode by looking at the shape parameter. In this regard, the physical phenomena provoking the failures need to be fully understood by adopting a Physics of Failure (PoF) approach, which is the most appropriate to properly perform an accurate risk assessment.
In this paper, the authors will present a case study from the automotive industry where one product experiences early failure within the warranty period, provoked by material corrosion.  Despite having the same failure mode and failure location, the field claims can be split in two populations having distinct Weibull distributions.  The papers will analyze how the appearance of potential failures in a third market location drove the authors to undergo a deep analysis of the physics explaining the failure root cause, the failure mechanism and the kinetics of the failure.  The investigation illustrates in detail how the physical model describing the corrosion event and its kinetics were integrated to the field data (warranty claims) thereby enhancing the accuracy of reliability predictions and proposing a risk mitigation plan.
In particular, the focus will go on the extrapolation the degradation physical model and corrosion kinetics from input data such as:
Climatic data (temperature and humidity)
Different mission profiles according to the geographical regions
Types of AC loop usage (heat pump or cooling-only)
The variable percentage of the products affected by the potential corrosion issue
As a result, this approach has allowed to transfer, with excellent accuracy, the predictions from one geographical region to another, helped to mitigate the occurrence of the risk, and allowed the final risk assessment for the whole fleet of vehicles carrying the component.
In conclusion, while performing Weibull analysis from field claims data, PoF should always be considered as the leading criteria to better “understand” the field data.  The benefits of such an approach are applicable both in the phase of data processing as well as the analysis of the results: interpretation of the shape parameter; splitting of the dataset in sub-populations (mixed Weibull); detection of possible outliers; presence of a failure free period; selection of the factors that affects the failure rate (time in service or mileage).
conclusions:
This paper investigates a comprehensive case study within the automotive industry, focusing on warranty cost predictions.  By integrating an in-depth analysis of field data (warranty claims) with a physics-of-failure approach, it allows improved accuracy in reliability predictions and establishes a more robust risk mitigation plan.  The approach presented here is based on fundamentals that are per se not known, since warranty costs analysis based on field claims and reliability predictions based on the PoF have been applied in the automotive industry for many years.  However, it is the combination of these elements within a unique framework that allows for the integration of all available information—from field data, bench tests, and quality metrics.

This approach enables more accurate warranty cost predictions by factoring in additional variables such as geographical locations, climate conditions, and usage profiles.  It also represents a shift towards a more collaborative multidisciplinary attitude, where experts from warranty, reliability, material science and quality work together for a more efficiently proactive risk assessment and more accurate warranty accrual forecast.  Indeed, the involvement of experts from multiple disciplines permits to achieve a more comprehensive analysis.  The adoption of this combined approach is recommended in future reliability assessments to enhance accuracy and reduce warranty costs.

title: Machine Learning with Weibull Analysis and Mixed Failure Mechanisms
authors: Vinayak Hegde, Procept Bio-Robotics; Key Words: Weibull Analysis, Mixed Failure Mechanism, Machine Learning, Beta, Scale Parameter
summary:
Meaningful data analysis to understand the mixed failure modes using survival probability plots will help the product behavior and analyze the failure mechanisms of the populations. The Weibull plot with mixed failure mechanism would help to segregate failure modes effectively when the system starts adapting machine learning techniques. If the data points approximately lie on a straight line, the Weibull model is appropriate.
The analysis is based on the Weibull distribution, which can model various types of failure rates (increasing, decreasing, or constant). It is characterized by two parameters: shape (β) and scale (η). In the Machine Learning model the set value of shape parameter falls below the set threshold, ML model should segregate that data and categorized separately and inform the owner of the database for designers notifications and for potential design improvements.
In this Machine Learning (ML) model, Shape parameter and Scale Parameter are the major contributors to success of the design intents. Shape Parameter (β): Indicates the failure rate behavior.
β < 1: Decreasing failure rate (infant mortality or early failures).
β = 1: Constant failure rate (random or chance like failures).
β > 1: Increasing failure rate (fatigue, wear-out failures and age-related failures).
Scale Parameter (η): Indicates the characteristic life, or the time by which 63.2% of the population will have failed.
Weibull analysis requires life data, which can be times to failure or times to success for a group of units.

title: Cluster Analysis to Define Operational Conditions for Systems Fault Detection
authors: Renan Favarão da Silva, PhD, University of São Paulo; Miguel Angelo de Carvalho Michalski, PhD, University of São Paulo; Gilberto Francisco Martha de Souza, PhD, University of São Paulo; Key Words: cluster analysis, fault detection and diagnosis, hydroelectric power plant, operational conditions
summary: The reliable operation of engineering systems is essential for the proper functioning of asset-intensive industries.  For this, it has been increasingly common to establish Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) processes to enable the Condition-Based Maintenance (CBM) strategy.  However, accurately detecting and diagnosing faults is not trivial, particularly when considering the different operational conditions of the equipment and systems being monitored.  In this context, this paper proposes a method for defining operational conditions for fault detection in engineering systems based on the application of Cluster Analysis.  It comprises three main stages: Collection and transformation of monitoring data, Application of Cluster Analysis, and Analysis of operational conditions for fault detection.  To demonstrate the proposed method, a case study was conducted considering a hydroelectric power plant in Brazil.  The results showed that Cluster Analysis was able to support the definition of operational conditions by identifying well-defined clusters based on the physical assets monitoring database.  Thus, the proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy of the FDD processes in organizations which contributes to the reliability of engineering systems and the reduction of the unavailability of physical assets and maintenance costs.
conclusions:
In asset-intensive organizations, maintenance management performance has gained increasing relevance.  It is through maintenance processes that the organization ensures operational availability and controls the risks associated with the failure of physical assets.  Given the increasing complexity of equipment and engineering systems, the CBM strategy has been widely applied, requiring condition monitoring, and fault detection and diagnosis processes implemented.
Nevertheless, the definition of operational conditions for monitored physical assets remains a challenge, often carried out without the support of decision-making tools.  For example, hydroelectric power generating companies commonly rely on a manual method that involves defining bounded rectangular regions using values derived from the two principal system variables, such as active power and net head.  This approach is based solely on personnel's knowledge of the system without further analysis. In this context, this paper proposes a method for defining operational conditions for FDD processes of engineering systems based on the application of Cluster Analysis. This approach enables a more precise distinction between operating conditions, thereby facilitating a more accurate FDD process.
The proposed method was presented and demonstrated through a case study considering the context of a hydroelectric power plant. It began with the collection and transformation of monitoring data for Cluster Analysis.  The elbow analysis determined that four clusters were the optimal choice for this specific case study.  Subsequently, the clusters underwent further examination through descriptive analysis and graphical representation, enhancing their comprehension.
In future works, it is recommended to apply this method to other industrial systems and conduct a comprehensive analysis of its outcomes.  To evaluate cluster quality could be considered utilizing metrics like the silhouette score, which can supplement the existing WSS method.
Moreover, a potential advancement could involve developing multinomial logistic regression models to define operational conditions based on the labeled dataset derived from the presented method.  This supervised model could be evaluated using a separate dataset of monitored data, enabling a comparison with the results of the Cluster Analysis.
Finally, the research results are expected to benefit maintenance professionals and researchers and promote the use of machine learning to address challenges in the area.
